Word order is flexible but usually verb-initial, with common patterns like VS, VO, and V; when both subject and object are expressed, VOS and SVO are most common, and a pre-verbal position can mark focus or contrast. The passage also outlines clause types: negation uses the particle *kuina*, imperatives and prohibitives have several special constructions, hortatives use *jaje*, and questions rely on intonation for polar questions and on specific question words for content questions.

text: complex sentence|( A sentence may be complex because it contains several clauses or several predicates, i.e. Paunaka exhibits biclausal and monoclausal constructions that contain more than one predicate. There are different semantic types of complex sentences, which include coordination on the one hand and subordination, or more precisely adverbial,adverbial relation complement,complement relation and relative relationsrelative relation on the other hand. Construction types comprise asyndetic and syndeticsyndesis/asyndesis|( juxtaposition including finite verbs,finite verb dependency marking on a verb or deranking of a verb,deranked verb with the latter type signifying the loss of verbal and gain of nominal characteristics. Deranked verbs contain the marker -i ‘subord’ directly following the last consonant of the verb stem.verbal stem As for subordinate relations, the reality status reality status|( of the subordinate verb can be predetermined by the semantic type or by the construction type of some complex sentence. There is no neat correspondence between semantic type, construction type, predetermination of RS,reality status|) and bi- or monoclausality. Coordination presupposes biclausality.coordination|( There are asyndetically and syndetically coordinated clauses,syndesis/asyndesis the latter type includes a connective, e.g. the adversative connective pero in ( -COORD-syn), while the former does without one, see ( -COORD-as). Connectivesconnective are free forms which occur between the coordinated clauses. nÿti kuina nÿnika pero punachÿ tiniku\\ nÿti kuina nÿ-nika pero punachÿ ti-niku\\ 1sg.prn neg 1sg-eat.irr but other 3i-eat\\ ‘I don’t eat them, but another one eats them’\\ biyunu bibÿsÿupunutu naka\\ bi-yunu bi-bÿsÿupunu-tu naka\\ 1pl-go 1pl-come-iam here\\ ‘we went and then came here’\\ coordination|) In order to express adverbialadverbial relation|( relations, all of the construction types are found. Nonetheless, dependency marking is only found on purpose verbs in the specific motion-cum-purpose construction, see ( -MCPC) above. Adverbial relations are expressed in mono- and biclausal constructions. An example of a biclausal construction with a syndetically juxtaposed adverbial clause is ( -ADV-syn), which includes the connective kue ‘if, when’, while ( -ADV-der) is an example of a purpose clause including the deranked verb chinikianube. kue kaku arusu banau pan de arroz\\ kue kaku arusu bi-anau pan de arroz \\ if exist rice 1pl-make rice bread \\ ‘when there is rice, we make rice bread’\\ chibÿtupaiku echÿukena chinikianube ipitiumu\\ chi-bÿtupaiku echÿu-kena chi-nik-i-a-nube ipiti-umu\\ 3-make.fall demb-uncert 3-eat-subord-irr-pl bee- \\ ‘it seems that it makes it fall so that they can eat honey’ adverbial relation|) Complement relationscomplement relation|( are usually expressed in a monoclausal construction, in which the complement verb is asyndetically juxtaposedjuxtaposition to the complement-taking verb, as in ( -COMPL). In addition, there are minor types. One builds on a deranked complement verb,deranked verb the other one is a syndetic construction with the demonstrativenominal demonstrative eka being used as a complementiser. The latter type might be biclausal, but there are actually not enough examples in the corpus to test this hypothesis. tisachu tumapi\\ ti-sachu ti-uma-pi\\ 3i-want 3i-take.irr-2sg\\ ‘she wants to take you’\\ complement relation|) Relative relationsrelative relation|( are expressed by asyndetic or syndetic juxtaposition with the latter building on the nominal demonstratives,nominal demonstrative mainly echÿu but also eka as a relativiser. Asyndetic juxtaposition is predominantly found with headedhead and syndetic juxtaposition with headless relative clauses, see ( -headed-RC) and ( -headless-RC) respectively. Relative relations can also be expressed with the help of a deranked verb, this is typically done if the relativised entity has the role of an oblique inside the relative clause, but may also occur if its role is that of an object. The relative relation is always expressed in a separate clause, i.e. we are dealing with a biclausal construction. i kaku echÿu pisemÿnÿ nimumuku uchuine\\ i kaku echÿu pise-mÿnÿ ni-imumuku uchuine\\ and exist demb bird-dim 1sg-look just.now\\ ‘and there is this bird that I have just watched’ \\ echÿu timÿuji aparte chetukunube\\ echÿu ti-mÿu-ji aparte chÿ-etuku-nube\\ demb 3i-be.wet- .mass aside 3-put-pl\\ ‘the wet things (i.e. clothes), they put aside’\\ relative relation|) syndesis/asyndesis|) deals with complex sentences. Finally, deranked verbs,deranked verb which are typically associated with subordinate clauses, can also occur in constructions that more closely resemble main clauses. This is described in detail in § .complex sentence|)
summary: Paunaka complex sentences can be biclausal or monoclausal and may contain coordination or several kinds of subordination, including adverbial, complement, and relative relations. These constructions may be asyndetic or syndetic, and subordinate verbs can be deranked with the suffix -i ‘subord’; however, there is no simple one-to-one correspondence between semantic type, construction type, reality status marking, and clause structure. Coordination always presupposes biclausality, while adverbial, complement, and relative relations can be expressed in different clause patterns, with relative relations always involving a separate clause.

text: This chapter provides a description of the segmental and suprasegmental phonology of Paunaka. The phonemic inventory is presented in . In , I describe rhinoglottophilia and vowel nasalisation. deals with the orthography chosen to transcribe Paunaka throughout this work. The morphophonological processes of vowel elision and vowel assimilation at morpheme boundaries, as well as the very restricted process of haplology is the topic of . deals with possible syllable types and the minimality requirements of a Paunaka word. is about stress and describes the two rhythmic patterns found in the language. Finally, in , I share some preliminary observations about intonational patterns.
summary: This chapter describes the segmental and suprasegmental phonology of Paunaka. It covers the phonemic inventory, rhinoglottophilia and vowel nasalisation, the orthography used in the work, morphophonological processes such as vowel elision, vowel assimilation, and restricted haplology, as well as syllable structure, word minimality, stress, and preliminary intonational patterns.

text: segmental phonology|( The phonemic inventory of Paunaka is relatively simple with twelve consonants, which are described in , and five vowels presented in . Each vowel can follow any other one, e.g. when two morphemes are adjoined; vowel sequences are described in . Section deals with the realisation of sounds in loan words.
summary: Paunaka has a relatively simple phonemic inventory consisting of twelve consonants and five vowels. Any vowel can follow any other vowel when morphemes are joined, and the text also notes that vowel sequences are discussed separately. It further indicates that the realisation of sounds in loanwords is treated in a later section.

text: consonant|( Paunaka has twelve contrasting consonants plus another two that only occur in loans.borrowing|( The consonants are presented in Table . All of them occur word- and stem-initially and -internally, with two exceptions. The palatal nasal /ɲ/ is only found in a very small number of words of assumed Paunaka origin and in a number of Spanish loans.borrowing|) The flap /ɾ/ occurs very infrequently, too. All consonants can precede all vowels, except for the glide /j/, which does not precede /i/. As for /ɲ/, it cannot be said with certainty whether there are any distributional constraints, because there are not enough words containing the nasal to make any firm statement. There is hardly any allophonic variation regarding the realisation of consonants, except for the realisation of the bilabial fricative /β/, which can be , , , or depending on the following vowel. The glottal stop can only appear on the emphatic/affirmative marker,emphatic which is realised as or . It is thus not considered phonemic here. The consonant inventory is typical for a Southern Arawakan language. It also fits the pattern of the greater Arawakan phonemic profile presented by . Most noticeable in comparison with other Arawakan languages is the absence of the postalveolar fricative /ʃ/ in native words. This sound does occur, but only in loans from Bésiro (see ). As already mentioned above, the palatal nasal /ɲ/ occurs very infrequently (see ), which is atypical for Arawakan languages in general, but not for the ones spoken in Bolivia. There are no voiced, aspirated, or palatalised plosives.
summary: Paunaka has twelve contrastive consonants, plus two additional sounds that occur only in loans. Most consonants can appear word- and stem-initially and internally, though /ɲ/ is very rare, /ɾ/ is infrequent, and /j/ cannot precede /i/; there is little allophonic variation except for /β/, and the glottal stop is not treated as phonemic. The inventory is typical of Southern Arawakan languages, but it lacks native /ʃ/ and has no voiced, aspirated, or palatalized plosives.

text: There are three nasals: bilabial /m/, alveolar /n/, and palatal /ɲ/. While /m/ and /n/ are fully productive, /ɲ/ only occurs in two words of presumable Paunaka origin. The bilabial nasal /m/ is presented in ( .1) in word-initial position and in ( .2) in word-internal position. The bilabial nasal contrasts with the bilabial plosive. This is shown in ( -p). The alveolar nasal /n/ occurs in word-initial position, as in ( .1), and in word-internal position, as in ( .2). The alveolar nasal contrasts with the alveolar plosive. Some minimal pairs are presented in ( -t). The alveolar nasal contrasts with the bilabial nasal. There are no exact minimal pairs in my corpus to demonstrate this contrast, but some near minimal pairs do occur. They are presented in ( -m) below. The palatal nasal /ɲ/ is not fully productive. It only occurs in a few words, some of which are from Spanish and Bésiro.borrowing|( Examples are shown in ( ). An infrequent occurrence such as the one of /ɲ/ may suggest that the sound has been borrowed into the language together with some words, as is the case for the Spanish loans containing the palatal nasal like anyo ‘year’ (/aɲo/, Span. año). However, the closely related Mojeño languages have similar forms for the ‘gray brocket’ – ona in Trinitario and ana in Ignaciano . Baure has nor. The words may well be cognates, which speaks against the hypothesis that the phoneme was borrowed together with the word.borrowing|) In both Mojeño languages, Trinitario and Ignaciano, the palatal nasal is rather infrequent, too, but there are more words containing the sound than in Paunaka ( ), and it has been claimed that the nasal formed part of the consonant inventory of Proto-Mojeño . Baure does not have phonemic /ɲ/. The nasals are spelled as <m>, <n>, and <ny>, respectively, throughout this work.
summary: The language has three nasals: bilabial /m/, alveolar /n/, and palatal /ɲ/. /m/ and /n/ are fully productive and contrast with the corresponding plosives and with each other, while /ɲ/ is very limited, appearing only in a few words that may be borrowings or cognates. The nasals are written as <m>, <n>, and <ny> throughout the work.

text: Paunaka has one flap, the alveolar /ɾ/. Word-initially, it is found very rarely with most of the words being well-integrated loansborrowing|( from Spanish that originally had initial /d/. The restriction on word-initial /ɾ/ is widespread among the Arawakan languages and interestingly, it also holds for BésiroBésiro|( where /ɾ/ is restricted to a few Spanish loans word-initially . In my corpus, the only word of non-Spanish origin starting with the flap is the noun rupinu ‘banana sp.’, which is presented in ( .1). The same noun (though with a final retroflex : rupinux) is used in the local variety of Bésiro spoken in Concepción, but probably not native to this language either considering its own restriction on the sound /ɾ/.Bésiro|) Strikingly, found out that Paunaka lost /ɾ/ in inherited words and thus concludes that all words containing this consonant must have been borrowed. However, there are two words containing the flap in Paunaka that have cognates in the other Bolivian Arawakan languages: urupunu ‘red brocket’ (Mazama americana) and ajumerku ‘paper’. As for urupunu, the cognate forms are arapana in IgnacianoMojeño Ignaciano and ropo in Trinitario,Mojeño Trinitario while ajumerku seems to be related to Baure -ajmer/jamerok, Ignaciano ajumerucu and Trinitario ‘jiumeruko. borrowing|) ( .1) presents some words that begin with /ɾ/, including Spanish loans. There are some verb stemsverbal stem that begin with /ɾ/ like the onomatopoeiconomatopoeia verb \=/ramuku ‘thunder’, and /ɾ/ is also found stem-internally. Some examples are presented in ( .2). /ɾ/ contrasts with all other consonants. ( -t) lists some minimal pairs with the alveolar /t/. ( -n) presents the contrast between /ɾ/ and /n/. The orthographic representation of the flap is <r> throughout this work.
summary: Paunaka has a single flap consonant, the alveolar /ɾ/, which is very rare word-initially and in most such cases appears in Spanish loans; this restriction is common in Arawakan languages and also found in Bésiro. Although the author suggests /ɾ/ was lost in inherited words, two Paunaka words with /ɾ/—urupunu ‘red brocket’ and ajumerku ‘paper’—have cognates in other Bolivian Arawakan languages, so they may not be loans. The flap can also occur stem-internally and in a few verb stems, and it contrasts with other consonants such as /t/ and /n/; orthographically it is written <r>.

text: There are three contrasting fricatives: the bilabial /β/, the alveolar /s/, and the glottal /h/. All of them can occur word- and stem-initially and -internally. The bilabial fricative /β/ has four allophones , , , and . Paunaka shares this kind of allophony with the other Bolivian ArawakanSouthern Arawakan languages: the Baure phoneme is analysed as /v/ with the allophones , , , and , the Mojeño Ignaciano phoneme as /β/ with the allophones and , and the TrinitarioMojeño Trinitario phoneme as /w/ with the allophones , , , and . In Paunaka, the vowel that follows the phoneme detemines the choice of the allophone. is found before the front vowels /i/ and /ɛ/, and before the mid vowel /ɨ/ as well as in the word -ubiu ‘house’. The sequences /βu/ and /βa/ are pronounces with either or, more rarely, . The choice of or is dependent on the individual speaker. Occasionally, may also be heard before /u/ and /a/ and the sequence /βu/ may be reduced to in rapid speech. ( -1) to ( -3) show all allophones in word-initial and word-internal position. ( -1) presents examples with the allophone . ( -2) presents examples with the allophone . ( -3) shows the distribution of the allophones and . The phoneme /β/ contrasts with the bilabial stop /p/, as can be seen in ( -p). ( -m) shows the contrast between /β/ and /m/. The alveolar fricative /s/ occurs word-initially and word-internally; see ( .1) and ( .2), respectively. The alveolar fricative contrasts with all the other consonants, e.g. with the alveolar /ɾ/ in ( -r). ( -t) presents the contrast between /s/ and /t/. The contrast between /s/ and /n/ is shown in ( -n). ( -b) shows some minimal pairs including the fricative /β/. borrowing|( The postalveolar fricative /ʃ/ and the retroflex fricative /ʂ/ were not originally phonemes of Paunaka, but have entered the language via Bésiro.Bésiro|( However, they seem not be considered as “foreign” by the speakers, since the words containing these sounds are not considered foreign. The retroflex sound has two allophones, voiceless and voiced in Paunaka. The sounds /s/ and /ɾ/ of Spanish words are sometimes replaced by /ʂ/ when integrated into Paunaka speech. As for /ɾ/, this sound is also often pronounced as a postalveolar ( ) or retroflex ( ) sound in the speakers’ Spanish, but a syllable-final /s/ tends to be in Eastern Bolivian Spanish. In any case, all of the words that contain one of the fricatives are loans from other languages, either Bésiro or Spanish or Spanish via Bésiro (see ), but not necessarily identified as such by the speakers.Bésiro|) Examples for the postalveolar fricative can be found in ( ) and for the retroflex fricative in ( ). The glottal fricative contrasts with all other consonants, including the fricative /s/, see ( -s). Some minimal pairs with /β/ are shown in ( -b). The contrast between /h/ and the velar plosive /k/ is presented in ( -k). Throughout this work, the spelling of the fricatives is <b> for /β/ and <s> for /s/. Analogous to Bésiro, <xh> is the spelling for /ʃ/ and <x> for /ʂ/. Due to the orthographic conventions of Spanish, <j> represents /h/.
summary: Paunaka has three native fricatives: bilabial /β/, alveolar /s/, and glottal /h/, all of which can occur word- and stem-initially and internally. The bilabial /β/ shows vowel-conditioned allophony with four surface variants, while /s/ and /h/ contrast with other consonants in minimal pairs. Two additional fricatives, /ʃ/ and /ʂ/, entered the language through borrowing from Bésiro and Spanish, and the passage also notes the orthographic conventions used to represent these sounds.

text: There is one affricate, the voiceless postalveolar /ʧ/. It appears word-initially as well as word-internally, as shown in ( ). /ʧ/ contrasts with the alveolar plosive as well as with the alveolar fricative. ( -t) presents some minimal pairs with /t/. ( -s) shows the contrast between /ʧ/ and /s/. The affricate is represented as <ch> throughout this work.
summary: The language has a single affricate, the voiceless postalveolar /ʧ/, which occurs both word-initially and word-medially. It contrasts with the alveolar plosive /t/ and the alveolar fricative /s/, and is written as <ch> throughout the work.

text: Paunaka has one approximant /j/. It can occur word-initially and -internally, as shown by the following examples. /j/ does not usually precede /i/ in Paunaka. /j/ could therefore be argued to be an allophone of /i/ in rising diphthongs.vowel sequence However, onset-less diphthongs are only found word-initially (see ). Additional support for the assumption that /j/ is a separate phoneme comes from comparison with the Mojeño languages and Baure, where the phonemic status of /j/ is clearer ( ; ). Some cognates are listed in : /j/ contrasts with all the other consonants. Two minimal pairs with the glottal fricative /h/ are presented in ( -h). The approximant is spelled <y> throughout this work. consonant|)
summary: Paunaka has a single approximant /j/, spelled <y>, which occurs word-initially and word-internally and contrasts with the other consonants, including /h/ in minimal pairs. Although /j/ might be analyzed as an allophone of /i/ in rising diphthongs, its distribution and comparison with related Mojeño languages and Baure support treating it as a separate phoneme.

text: vowel|( There are five phonemic vowels, which are presented in . This set of vowels is typical for an Arawakan languageArawakan languages, but unlike a number of other Arawakan languages, Paunaka has no contrastive long vowels. The same is true for closely related Baure and Mojeño Ignaciano . All vowels can be nasalised,nasalisation when they are surrounded by nasal consonants.consonant In addition there is rhinoglottophilia, which makes vowels sound as if they were nasalised after /h/ (see ). However, nasality is not a contrastive feature for vowels. Most surprising is the existence of a phonemic high central /ɨ/, which does occur in some Arawakan languages , but is not phonemic in the other Southern Arawakan languages. However, it has been shown that /ɨ/ results from fronting of the back vowel *u of a presumed proto-language, while /u/ derives from *o ( ; ).
summary: Paunaka has five phonemic vowels, a typical Arawakan inventory, but unlike some related languages it has no contrastive long vowels. All vowels may be nasalized in nasal environments, and there is rhinoglottophilia after /h/, but nasality is not contrastive. The language also has a phonemic high central /ɨ/, which is unusual for Southern Arawakan but is explained as a historical development from proto-language *u, while /u/ comes from *o.

text: The high vowel /i/ can occur word-initially, -internally, and -finally. When unstressed, it is sometimes pronounced as , but there is certain variation among speakers. Especially María C. tends to pronounce the high vowels /i/ and /u/ lower than other speakers do. Some examples with the high vowel /i/ are given in ( ). The high vowel /u/ can occur word-initially, -internally, and -finally. When it appears in unstressed syllables, and especially in word-final syllables, it is frequently pronounced lower, i.e. or , although it may well be , too. The pronunciation depends on speech rate, the place of the word inside an utterance, and also on the speaker. ( ) shows the occurrence of /u/ in different positions in the word. The minimal pairs in ( -i) show that the high vowels /u/ and /i/ fully contrast. The high vowel /ɨ/ is presented below in word-initial, -medial and -final position. /ɨ/ is less stable than the other high vowels. It is often hard to distinguish it from /u/ and /ɛ/, because it is often pronounced more like or . Thus, a speaker may pronounce the word /kusiɨ/ (kusiÿ ‘ant’) like in rapid speech, and only when she utters the word very carefully and slowly, it is . This may be a hint that the fronting from *u to /ɨ/ has not been totally completed. The confusion with /ɛ/ is due to the fact that both vowels may be reduced to in unstressed syllables. /ɨ/ has a tendency towards nasalisation, so a nasalised schwa is more likely to be an instance of /ɨ/ than of /ɛ/. Some near minimal pairs with /i/ are presented in ( -i). ( -u) shows the contrast between /ɨ/ and /u/. The orthographic representation of the high vowel /i/ is <i>, /ɨ/ is spelled <ÿ>, and /u/ is given as <u> and in loansborrowing also as <o> throughout this work.
summary: The passage describes the distribution and pronunciation of the three high vowels /i/, /u/, and /ɨ/. It notes that /i/ and /u/ can occur word-initially, medially, and finally, but are often lowered in unstressed syllables depending on speech rate, position in the utterance, and speaker; /i/ and /u/ contrast fully, while /ɨ/ is less stable and often hard to distinguish from /u/ and /ɛ/ because it may be realized as a reduced or nasalized vowel. The orthographic spellings used are <i> for /i/, <ÿ> for /ɨ/, and <u> or, in loanwords, <o> for /u/.

text: There is one mid vowel in Paunaka, which is /ɛ/. It can occur in all positions in a word. When unstressed, it may centralise and be realised as . ( ) presents some words containing the mid vowel in different positions in the word. Since /ɨ/ has an identical allophone (see above), it is often hard to tell whether a sound corresponds to /ɛ/ or /ɨ/. Nevertheless, in stressed syllables there is a clear audible difference between /ɨ/ and /ɛ/, as can be seen from the following examples. The mid vowel also contrasts with the other high vowels. ( -i) presents some examples for the contrast with /i/. ( -u) shows that /ɛ/ and /u/ are fully contrastive. The mid vowel is written <e> throughout this work.
summary: Paunaka has a single mid vowel, /ɛ/, which can appear in any word position and may centralise when unstressed. Although its centralised allophone is identical to that of /ɨ/, stressed syllables show a clear difference between the two, and /ɛ/ also contrasts with the high vowels /i/ and /u/. It is written as <e> in this work.

text: There is one low vowel, the central /a/, which can occur at the beginning, in the middle or at the end of words. This is shown in ( .1) to ( .3). /a/ contrasts with all other vowels. For some minimal pairs with the high vowel /i/, see ( -i) below. In ( -ÿ), some examples for the contrast between /a/ and /ɨ/ are given. ( -u) shows that /a/ contrasts with /u/. There is also a contrast with the mid vowel /ɛ/, as shown in ( -e). However, there are a few words that have variants with either /a/ or /ɛ/ without any difference in meaning according to the speakers, e.g. apuke ‘ground, down’ has an alternative form as , the verb stem -semaiku can also be realised as . The low vowel is represented as <a> throughout this work.
summary: The passage states that the language has one low vowel, the central /a/, which can appear word-initially, medially, or finally. It contrasts with all other vowels, including /i/, /ɨ/, /u/, and /ɛ/, though a few words show free variation between /a/ and /ɛ/ without a change in meaning. In this work, the vowel is written as <a>.

text: vowel sequence|( There are a lot of vowel sequences in Paunaka, and it is not always clear whether such a sequence is better analysed as a diphthong or hiatus. If we compare the other Bolivian ArawakanSouthern Arawakan languages and also take the reconstructed proto-lan\-guage into account ( ; ), it becomes clear that many vowel sequences result from the deletion of consonants in unstressed syllables. Mojeño Trinitario, for instance, often has either /ɾ/ or /ʔ/ and sometimes other consonants between two vowels, where Paunaka has a sequence of two vowels (Rose 2014, p.c.); see for a few examples. The fact that some of these sequences have fused into a diphthong and others rather belong to two syllables may then reflect different time depths or degrees of conventionalisation of consonant deletion. I consider a sequence of two vowels a diphthong, if it sounds short and the whole sequence is either stressed (most of the times) or unstressed. Two vowels in hiatus sound longer, and stress is assigned to only one vowel, but not to the other (if stress falls on one of the syllables at all). However, at a higher speech rate, a hiatus may also sound like a diphthong. It would therefore be worth doing a phonetic analysis of vowel sequences in the future, and the analysis given here can only be considered as tentative and preliminary. The clearest example of a hiatus is the word ue, a word that is exceptionally composed of only two V syllables. /uɛ/‘rainbow, water spirit’\\% There are more words with a final /ɛ/ preceded by another vowel, and the two vowels usually belong to two different syllables. The nounsnoun ending in an /ɛ/ syllable mostly refer to animals or plants (or their fruits), so the final /ɛ/ may go back to an old nominal suffix or classifier, which is not transparent anymore. There are even two cases in which the final /ɛ/ is preceded by a syllable with a nucleus /ɛ/, and in this case the last syllable has a long vowel. The Mojeño languages often have -re in plant names, where Paunaka has -e (Sell 2021, p.c.). /itiɛ/ ‘eel’\\ /mukɨɛ/ ‘squash’\\ /kɛʧuɛ/ ‘snake’\\ /saβaɛ/ ‘tobacco’\\ /inɛɛ/ ‘fish sp.’ (Hoplias malabaricus) \\ /mukɛɛ/ ‘rodent sp.’ (Span. cujuchi) \\% An exception is the word chapie ‘thank you’, a loanborrowing from Bésiro, which is disyllabic with a diphthong /iɛ̯/ in the second syllable. Another vowel sequences that is often found in hiatus is /ia/. /βia/ ‘God’ (lit.: our father) \\ /kuɛpia/ ‘kidney’\\ /nikuβiakuβu/ ‘I am tired’\\% The exception is again a Bésiro loan;borrowing the word mukianka ‘animal’ which has a palatalised . Most likely to be fused into diphthongs are the sequences /ai/, /ɛi/, /ui/, /ɨi/, /au/, /ɛu/, and some instances of /iu/, /ua/, and /uɛ/. Here are some words with the diphthong /ai̯/. /mai/ ‘stone’\\ /tihai/ ‘day’\\ /tɨnai/ ‘long’\\% The following words all have a diphthong /ɛi̯/. /kupɛi/ ‘afternoon’\\ /ʧumɛiku/ ‘he/she/it steals it’\\ /tɛihuku/ ‘he/she/it stinks’\\% The diphthong /ui̯/ is articulated with a semi-vowel after /k/. Here are some examples of the diphthong. /kuina/ ‘neg’\\ /βɛmusuika/ ‘we wash (irr)’\\ /ʧuβui/ ‘old man’\\% Some words containing /ɨi̯/ are given below. /nipɨi/ ‘my body’\\ /kɨikɛ/ ‘peanut’\\ /nɨkɨiki/ ‘pot’\\% Here are some examples for the diphthong /au̯/: /aumuɛ/ ‘chicha’\\ /isipau/ ‘strong (fermented) chicha’\\ /nanau/ ‘I make’\\% The words below all have a diphthong /ɛu̯/. /sɛunuβɛ/ ‘woman’\\ /nipɛu/ ‘my animal’\\ /muβɛu/ ‘bird sp.’ (Columbina picui) \\% There are only a few words containing the diphthong /aɨ/, two of which are given below. /kupisaɨɾɨ/ ‘fox’\\ /ʧumutaɨ/ ‘stool’\\% The sequence /iu/ often occurs in hiatus, especially in subordinate verbs,deranked verb where -i is the subordinating suffix, but in rapid speech the suffix may also only palatalisepalatalisation the preceding consonant, which is mostly /k/. Nevertheless, there are some instances where the sequence /iu̯/ is a diphthong, most often after /s/. /tisiu/ ‘puma’\\ /musisiupa/ ‘sand’\\ /tiβɛɾiuku/ ‘he/she/it returns’\\% There are not many words with the diphthong /ua̯/ in the corpus, but some can be found. As with /ui̯/, it is articulated with a semi-vowel after /k/. Some examples are given below. /kuahi/ ‘fishing net’\\ /nɛmua/ ‘my belly’\\ /puakɛnɛ/ ‘other side’\\ As with /ui̯/ and /ua̯/, the diphthong /uɛ̯/ is articulated with a semi-vowel after /k/. The semi-vowel also occurs in the sequence /suɛ̯/ (which is thus pronounced ). Some words with the diphthong are given below. /kuɛpi/ ‘sweet potato’\\ /ɛpɛnuɛ/ ‘hole’\\ /kusuɛnu/ ‘rabbit’\\% In addition, there is also one triphthong, which only shows up in one word, to my knowledge: /tsɨɛ/ ‘it is cold’\\% vowel sequence|) vowel|) segmental phonology|)
summary: Paunaka has many vowel sequences, and their status as diphthongs or hiatus is often unclear because many arise from consonant deletion in unstressed syllables, as shown by comparison with related Arawakan languages. The author treats short, unified sequences as diphthongs and longer sequences with stress on only one vowel as hiatus, but notes that faster speech can make hiatus sound diphthongal, so the analysis is preliminary. Clear hiatuses include words like *ue* ‘rainbow, water spirit’ and many forms with final /ɛ/ or /ia/, while sequences such as /ai/, /ɛi/, /ui/, /ɨi/, /au/, and /ɛu/ are commonly analyzed as diphthongs; there is also one reported triphthong.

text: borrowing|( This section provides information about how the sounds of words with a foreign origin – as far as recognisable – are adapted.consonants in loans|( Spanish and Bésiro are the two major sources for loans. In addition, a few words are strikingly similar to the ones found in Guarayu, a Tupi-Guarani language, today spoken in an area north of the Chiquitania. Not every loan is recognised as such by the speakers of Paunaka. As for words with a Spanish origin, there are some regular correspondences between Spanish and Paunaka sounds. They comprise /x/ and /g/→ /k/, /d/ and /l/ → /ɾ/, and /f/ → /β/ or /p/. presents some examples of these correspondences, but there are also be words that retain the original sounds. This may partly have to do with how well words containing the sounds are integrated into the language and can be considered part of the Paunaka lexicon. Well-integrated loans tend to have a fixed phonological form. If speakers spontaneously resort to Spanish and Bésiro words in conversation, the degree of adaption to Paunaka phonology may be lesser or greater from occasion to occasion (i.e. it is not the case that some speakers are more likely to adapt words phonologically than others). This also applies some words they use regularly, i.e. where a certain integration into the lexicon can be assumed. To give but one example, the word kanela ‘cinnamon’ from Spanish canela always retains /l/ in Juana’s speech although she uses this word relatively frequently in the corpus. vowels in loans|( The vowel /u/ of Paunaka has an allophone (see ), so that borrowed words containing an /o/ (precisely in Spanish) may be pronounced either with an or and , e.g. the Spanish word año ‘year’ may be or in Paunaka. vowels in loans|) Since I do not speak Bésiro, it is much harder for me to detect possible loans as long as they have the same syllabic and phonemic structure as native Paunaka words. Clearly noticeable are all words containing the retroflex fricative or the postalveolar fricative , which are retained in Paunaka loans. The sounds are allophones in Bésiro Bésiro|( according to . Examples have been given in . The phonemic inventory of Bésiro further differs from the Paunaka because it contains a palatal plosive /c/ and a phonemic /o/. I did not encounter instances of in Paunaka, and as for Bésiro /o/, it may be retained in Paunaka or be pronounced as , similar to the loans from Spanish (e.g. we find both and ‘noon’, originally from Span. doce ‘twelve’ but probably borrowed via Bésiro). Some words with a Spanish origin must have entered the Paunaka lexicon via Bésiro. Such words have a postalveolar in Paunaka and in Bésiro, but not in Spanish.Bésiro|) Three examples are provided in . Note that while the sound is retained in Paunaka, syllable structure (see ) or stress assignment (see ) may change to match the Paunaka system. Paunaka speakers also frequently pronounce a word-initial /ɾ/ of a Spanish loan as or , but this is also done in the local variety of Spanish and thus no adaption takes place (see also above). Peculiar, however, is that a syllable-final /s/ of words with Spanish origin can be pronounced as or in Paunaka. It remains unclear whether Paunaka speakers replace /s/ in this case, because the word is borrowed from Bésiro, not from Spanish, or to make it sound less Spanish-like, in general. At least for the loan max ‘more’ from Spanish más , there is a similar loan in Bésiro, too, which is pronounced . consonants in loans|) Finally, there are some words of Guarayu origin that are worth mentioning. I already mentioned in (Footnote ) the Paunaka verb -yÿseiku ( ) ‘buy’ could well derive from Guarayu -yusei ‘want or wish sth. edible’. If this is correct, the word must have entered the language before the shift from /u/ to /ɨ/ took place in Paunaka (see ). The other two loans I could detect are merÿ ( ) from mberɨ ‘plantain’ and patabi ( ) from patavɨi ‘sugar cane’. The first of these, i.e. merÿ, actually already includes the high central vowel in the donor language. The prenasalised stop of the original language is replaced by the nasal in Paunaka. In the second loan patabi, the final diphthong is resolved. Both words are otherwise unsuspicious. -1.9ptWe know that the Paunaka language has also been in close contact with Napeka (of the Chapacuran family); however, since there are almost no data obtainable about this language, possible loans (and other kinds of influences) cannot be detected for the time being.borrowing|)
summary: The passage explains how Paunaka adapts loanwords, mainly from Spanish and Bésiro, with some possible loans from Guarayu and no identifiable loans yet from Napeka. In Spanish loans, regular sound correspondences include /x, g/ → /k/, /d, l/ → /ɾ/, and /f/ → /β/ or /p/, though well-integrated words may keep original sounds and adaptation can vary from token to token. Borrowed words may also undergo changes in vowel quality, syllable structure, stress, or final consonants, while some words appear to have entered Paunaka via Bésiro rather than directly from Spanish.

text: rhinoglottophilia|( Paunaka has rhinoglottophilia, defined originally by as an interaction between glottality and nasality which causes nasalisation on vowels following or in various languages over the world.consonant|( Phoneticians later found out that it is not precisely nasalisation that is caused by “high airflow segments like voiceless fricatives and aspirated stops”. Instead, the “coupling between the oral and the subglottal cavities” that appears on vowels in rhinoglottophilia has the effect that vowels are perceived as nasal, although they are not nasal . Rhinoglottophilia can be found in a number of Arawakan languages, like Paresi , Nanti , Iñapari , Warekena , Kurripako and Yucuna , among others, and also in some other Amazonian languagesAmazonian language that are not genetically related . It is not found in the other Bolivian Arawakan languages as far as I can tell. In Paunaka, rhinoglottophilia affects all vowelsvowel and diphthongs following /h/. Those vowels are marked with a tilde throughout this chapter. Some examples are presented in ( ) below. More examples can be found in . /hanɛ/ ‘wasp’\\ /himu/ ‘fish’\\ /ɛhui/ ‘cock’\\% rhinoglottophilia|) nasalisation|( Vowelsvowel can be nasalised if they are surrounded by nasal consonants.consonant|) However, this seems to be optional. I have not encountered any case in which nasalisation of a vowel distinctive. Some examples of nasalised vowels are given in ( ). /nuinɛkɨ/‘door’\\ /mɨuhi/‘clothes’\\ /mɨnɨ/‘dim’\\% nasalisation|)
summary: The passage says that Paunaka has rhinoglottophilia, a phenomenon in which vowels and diphthongs following /h/ are perceived as nasal because of the interaction between glottality and nasality, and these vowels are marked with a tilde. It also notes that this pattern is found in several other Arawakan and some non-Arawakan Amazonian languages, but not in the other Bolivian Arawakan languages mentioned. By contrast, ordinary nasalization in Paunaka can occur when vowels are surrounded by nasal consonants, but this seems optional and not distinctive.

text: consonant|( orthography|( Paunaka is not a written language. Indeed, most of the remaining speakers are illiterate. When the Paunaka Documentation Project started in 2011, there was no orthography that people had agreed upon. Nonetheless, there are some entries of Paunaka vocabulary by and some more by d’Orbigny scattered through his works, there are several unpublished word lists composed by Riester in the 1950s and 1960s, and there is even an unpublished grammar sketch compiled by Villafañe (in three different versions). None of the solutions how to write Paunaka was very consistent or practical. Therefore, during my first field trip in 2011, the members of the PDP conducted a workshop with the speakers and their families, in which an orthography was established for the production of an alphabet booklet . The result is an orthography which is based on the Spanish one, but differs from it in some important details, like having <ny> instead of <ñ> and <k> instead of <c, qu>. It is therefore easy to read, but still shows the difference with Spanish. The choice of the letter <ÿ> over <ɨ> manifests Paunaka’s difference from Bésiro. At the same time it is easy to type on Spanish keyboards, which have a key for diaeresis (¨). In comparison, the <ɨ> is prone to be typed as <i>, simply because people do not know how to get the barred i into their texts (Interview with Guarayu speakers, 05.05.2012). Decisions on orthography were made back in 2011, and ten years later, Paunaka people hope to get their language officially recognised (see ). It may thus well be the case that an official orthography will be created in the future that differs from the one used throughout this work. Time will tell. The graphemes and digraphs used in the Paunaka alphabet throughout this work are the following: a, b, ch, e, i, j, k, m, n, ny, (o), p, r, s, t, u, x, xh, y, ÿ, (’). shows how the phonemes of Paunaka are represented orthographically in this grammar, comparing it to previous attempts to transcribe the sounds of the language. As for punctuation, the Spanish system is used, including reversed question (¿) and exclamation (¡) marks to indicate the beginning of a question or exclamation.interrogative clause orthography|) consonant|)
summary: Paunaka is not a written language, and when the documentation project began in 2011 there was no agreed-upon orthography, only scattered earlier word lists and grammar sketches with inconsistent transcription systems. A workshop with speakers and their families established an orthography based largely on Spanish spelling but with important differences such as <ny> for <ñ>, <k> for <c, qu>, and <ÿ> instead of <ɨ>, making it easy to read and type while remaining distinct from Spanish and Bésiro. The grammar uses this orthography and Spanish punctuation, including inverted question and exclamation marks.

text: There are some morphophonological processes, i.e. phonological processes that occur at morpheme boundaries. First of all, Paunaka has vowel elision in person markers that attach to vowel-initial stems (see ), a process typical for Arawakan languages. In addition, it also often deletes the initial vowel of the non-verbal irrealis marker, when it follows a stem that ends in a diphthong.vowel sequence If the last vowel of the stem is /a/ and the irrealis marker -ina is attached, both vowels can fuse into a diphthong /ɛi/, see . There is also a small number of cases of haplology, which are presented in .
summary: Paunaka shows several morphophonological processes at morpheme boundaries. These include vowel elision in person markers attached to vowel-initial stems, deletion of the initial vowel of the non-verbal irrealis marker after stems ending in a diphthong-vowel sequence, and occasional fusion of final /a/ with the irrealis marker -ina into the diphthong /ɛi/. The language also has a small number of haplology cases.

summary:
Paunaka has several kinds of vowel elision, especially at morpheme boundaries. With person markers before vowel-initial stems, the vowel of the person marker is usually deleted, while the irrealis marker -ina loses its initial vowel after stems ending in diphthongs or adjacent vowel sequences.

The pattern is clearest with verbs, but nouns show more irregularity: some noun stems trigger elision and others do not, with /u/-initial bound nouns notably resisting it. A separate, more limited type of elision also affects a few words beginning with /a/ or /u/ before /p/ or /k/, without changing stress placement.

If a grammatical marker that ends in nu is followed by the plural marker -nube, the two syllables nu may fuse. Thus for instance the regressive markerregressive/repetitive -pupunu plus plural marker -nube can fuse into -pupunube, as in ( ). tibÿsÿupupunube\\ ti-bÿsÿu-pupunu-nube\\ 3i-come-reg-pl\\ ‘they came back’ As for the prior motion marker -punuassociated motion followed by -nube, it is hard to interpret whether there are cases of haplology, since there is also a dislocative marker -pu, and both can occur in similar contexts, see . haplology|)
summary: Haplology in Paunaka is the avoidance of adjacent identical or very similar syllables, but it occurs only rarely. The passage gives a few examples, such as first person plural marking on *-beu* ‘take away’ sometimes appearing as *beu* instead of *bibeu*, omission of *chÿ-* in *chukuyae*, and fusion of syllables in forms like *-pupunube* from *-pupunu-nube*. text: In Paunaka, all content words are at least bimoraic, and most of the bimoraic words are disyllabic. There are only a few monosyllabic words, and they all have a heavy syllable with an onset consonant and a diphthong.vowel sequence Some examples are given in ( ). There are some monomoraic verb roots,verbal root but they obligatorily combine with person and reality status markers, so that they never appear as monomoraic forms in actual speech. There are also a few monomoraic function words. /mai/ ‘stone’\\ /pɛi/ ‘agouti’ \\ /ʧɨi/ ‘fruit’ \\ /jui/ ‘bread’ \\% There is a large number of disyllabic and trisyllabic content words. Disyllabic words of the structure CV.V are very rare, and there is also only one word, to my knowledge, which is composed of just two V syllables (see also ). ( -V) lists two words with the structure (C)V.V. /uɛ/‘rainbow, spirit’\\ /nɨa/‘my father’\\ Tetrasyllabic nouns,noun especially names of animals, often, but not always, contain repeated syllables, have the same vowel in all four syllables or have a specific pattern (C)V$_ 1 $CV$_ 2 $CV$_ 2 $CV$_ 1 $. Examples are given in . Paunaka words can be very long. This is especially true for verbsverb that can undergo several derivational processes like reduplication of roots or stems, insertion of classifiers, noun incorporation, and several inflectional processes. ( ) gives a verb with twelve syllables. Usually, however, verbs are much shorter. tijatÿtÿkeikukukÿubunubeji\\ \\ ‘they went pulling themselves up with the help of sticks, it is said’
summary:
In Paunaka, content words are at least bimoraic, and most are disyllabic, while monosyllabic words are rare and have heavy syllables with an onset consonant plus a diphthong-vowel sequence. Some verb roots are monomoraic, but they always combine with person and reality status markers, and the language also has a few monomoraic function words.

The language has many disyllabic and trisyllabic content words, but CV.V disyllables are very rare and only one word of two V syllables is known. Longer words, especially tetrasyllabic nouns and complex verbs, may show reduplication or fixed vowel patterns, and verbs can become very long through derivation, noun incorporation, and inflection.

text: stress|( A stressed syllable in Paunaka is generally louder and longer than an unstressed one and has a higher pitch; thus it has features that are cross-linguistically wide\-spread to mark stress . There is remarkable variation between the speakers here; Juana pronounces stressed syllables with such a high pitch that her Paunaka sounds like a tonal language at first impression. She does not produce such a high pitch on accented syllables when speaking Spanish. However, there are only two words that are distinguished solely by stress (see ( ) in ). Thus, the definition by of a tonal language as “one in which an indication of pitch enters into the lexical realisation of at least some morphemes” does not hold for Paunaka. Stress assignment is best explained on the basis of metrical patterns . It is similar to the stress patterns found in the Mojeño languages and usually follows an iambiciambic|( pattern with left-to-right parsing, which is sensitive to morae ( ). The last syllable of a word is always extrametrical, i.e. it is “invisible” for stress parsing. Morae are organised into feet, and primary stress is usually found on the last foot of the word, sometimes on the last foot that belongs to the word stem, depending on how many markers are attached. Secondary stress is on every other foot. Bimoraic words have a trochaictrochaic|( pattern for stress assignment ( ). When grammatical markers are attached to the word stem, the metrical pattern of the stem is maintained, i.e. words with iambic stems follow an iambic pattern, words with trochaic stems have a trochaic pattern.ctrochaic|)
summary: In Paunaka, stressed syllables are typically louder, longer, and higher in pitch than unstressed syllables, though speakers vary considerably in how extreme the pitch difference is. Stress is not tonal in the lexical sense, since only two words are distinguished solely by stress, and stress assignment is best analyzed metrically: it generally follows left-to-right iambic parsing sensitive to morae, with the final syllable extrametrical and primary stress on the last foot of the word. Secondary stress falls on every other foot, bimoraic words show trochaic stress, and attached grammatical markers do not alter the stress pattern of the stem.

There is even one case in which two words containing the syllable are distinguished by stress placement, as shown in ( ). ‘I speak’\\ ‘I harvest’\\ It could be the case that all verb stemsverbal stem in ( ) to ( ) that do not follow the iambic pattern actually start with an /i/, which is then merged with the person marker, so that the iambic pattern holds for an underlying form, but not for the surface form. summary: The passage argues that most words with stems of three or more morae follow an iambic stress pattern, and this holds across uninflected and minimally inflected words of different syllable lengths, including cases with diphthongs where stress is determined by mora count rather than syllable count. It also notes a few apparent exceptions, some of which are explained by vowel deletion in person markers or by underlying forms, while others involve reduplication or verbs containing /hi/ or /hɨ/ that sometimes attract stress and disrupt the expected pattern.

text: trochaic|( The trochaic pattern (x .) is found on bimoraic words. This holds for disyllabic ones ( ) as well as well as monosyllabic ones ( ). Disyllabic words with trochaic pattern (x .)\\ ‘mouse’\\ ‘water’\\ ‘(my) mum’ \\ ‘my father’ \\ Monosyllabic words with trochaic pattern (x .)\\ ‘priest’ \\ ‘agouti’ \\ ‘stone’\\ ‘bread’\\ That we are dealing with a trochaic pattern and not with an iambic one with degenerate feet becomes apparent when we attach grammatical markers to these word stems: the parse remains trochaic, as shown in . However, there is some variation concerning primary stress placement: it sometimes remains on the word stem and sometimes shifts to the marker to keep with the rule that stress is on the last foot of the word. This latter option seems to be preferred if the locative marker -yae is involved. If more than one marker is added, stress is also more likely to fall on the last foot instead of the stem. In other cases, primary stress often remains on the stem, but with possible variations depending on the position of the word inside an utterance, a topic that deserves further investigation. A marker with an initial vowel fuses with the last vowel of the stem, but underlyingly, the parse is still trochaic: there are four morae, two belonging to the lexical stem and two to the grammatical marker. Primary stress is usually assigned to the first vowel of the grammatical marker in this case, unlike grammatical markers that start with a consonant and often receive secondary stress only, as was shown above. The first vowel of the vowel-initial marker is also its first mora. When this vowel fuses with the preceding one of the lexical stem, stress falls on the diphthong (or single vowel in case the final vowel of the lexical word and the first vowel of the marker are identical), thus on the second syllable of the word. Secondary stress should be on the first syllable of the word then, but it is deleted to prevent stress clash. See for examples. trochaic|) stress|)
summary: The passage argues that bimoraic words in this language are trochaic, including both disyllabic and monosyllabic forms, and that this remains true when grammatical markers are added. Stress placement can vary: it may stay on the stem or shift to the marker to satisfy the rule that stress falls on the last foot, with shifting especially likely with the locative marker -yae or when multiple markers are present. Vowel-initial markers fuse with the stem’s final vowel, but the underlying foot structure is still trochaic, and stress is assigned to the marker’s first vowel unless fusion creates a diphthong, in which case stress falls on the second syllable and secondary stress is deleted to avoid stress clash.

text: intonation|( For the time being, I cannot present an in-depth study of intonational patterns in Paunaka. Nevertheless, there are some observations that I consider worth mentioning here. Polar questionspolar question can be identified by a rising tone at the end of the utterance. Declarative sentencesdeclarative clause usually have a falling tone and a pitch accent on the stress-bearing syllable of the word in focus, which is often the last content word of the utterance. nÿti nichuna nijiku \\ \\ ‘I know how to spin’ Speakers may, however, emphasise the last syllable of an utterance with stress, a lengthening of the vowel and greater loudness. It is not clear to me what the intended effect is. I observed that María C., who uses this emphasis most often, employs it when complaining about her health, the lack of interest of the young generation in speaking Paunaka, etc. nemusuikamÿnÿ kuinabu naimubÿkemÿnÿ\\ \\ ‘I wash a little bit, I can't see anymore’ María C. is the oldest speaker. The other speakers do not frequently make use of this intonational pattern. But interestingly, in a personal narrative about two old Paunaka ladies, whom she met when she was a young woman (jxx-p120515l-1), Juana also often emphasises final syllables of utterances when she reproduces the old ladies’ speech. It may thus be a speech style that speakers used to adopt in old age, but which has gone out of usage among most of the remaining speakers. It may also signal the end of a turn and offer the conversational partner the possibility to take the turn. In the old recordings of Riester, the lengthening of final syllables is almost absent, but that may be due to the monologue character of the interviews, with a researcher unable to understand what the speaker was saying. Stressing of utterance-final syllables appears only in one file (nxx-a630101g-3), which is about the intended or imagined theft of a young woman and directed to an imaginary addressee, who is included into the discourse by usage of first plural. Another characteristic that is more prominent in the speech of Juan Ch. is a reduced speed towards the end of the utterance. The word with the intonational pitch is even more often the last one of an utterance. The monologic character of many of the recordings that make up my corpus may also have an influence on the rarer occurrence of emphasised utterance-final syllables. Most often there is only one speaker present together with one or two interviewers, who certainly got more acquainted with the language over time, but cannot replace a fully proficient Paunaka speaker as a conversational partner. A fine-grained study of Paunaka discourse style could certainly shed light on the function of this and other intonational patterns. intonation|)
summary: Paunaka polar questions are marked by a rising final tone, while declarative clauses usually have a falling tone and a pitch accent on the stressed syllable of the focused word, often the last content word. Some speakers also emphasize utterance-final syllables with stress, vowel lengthening, and greater loudness, a pattern observed especially in María C. and sometimes in reported speech or at turn boundaries, though its function remains uncertain.

text: This chapter starts with a description of what I mean when talking about a Paunaka “word” ( ). It goes on to a discussion of the structure of words in and grammatical markers that can attach to words belonging to various word classes in . The general word formation processes found in the language are summarised in to . At the end of this chapter, provides a short characterisation of the different parts of speech that can be identified in Paunaka.
summary: The chapter first defines what is meant by a Paunaka “word” and then examines word structure, including the grammatical markers that can attach to words from different word classes. It also summarizes the language’s main word formation processes and ends with a brief description of the different parts of speech in Paunaka.

text: In this grammar, I make use of the notion of “word”, since I believe a grammatical description without this concept would unnecessarily complicate the matter. The words I identified as such are separated from each other by spaces, just as in writing with Greek-derived alphabets . However, “word” is not an unproblematic concept. remind us that we have to be careful to distinguish phonological from grammatical words, and even showed that there are no criteria that can be implied in a cross-linguistically valid definition of “word”. How do I come to my decisions as to how strings of sounds are instantiations of different words? Actually, I did not “examine wordhood using test batteries” , i.e. I did not apply different kinds of available criteria that have been proposed in the definition of word and considered the results. My decisions were rather based on intuition. Intuition does not come out of the blue, of course. In doing fieldwork with a language previously unknown to me, the first attempts to transcribe the utterances produced by speakers and sort them into different words were heavily influenced by prosodic criteria, such as stress assignment and pauses. This was rather perceived unconsciously, because from the beginning, I had been busier trying to decipher the meaning of the utterances than phonological structure, due to my personal preference for certain kinds of linguistic topics over others. Nonetheless, in the very first step, I considered purely phonological words. With growing knowledge on how different parts of the identified words (i.e. the morphemes) realise different meanings and how these morphemes are ordered with respect to each other, these criteria became ever more important in the analysis. I am, of course, biased in my decisions by decisions made by others for all the languages I have acquired, tried to learn or studied in my life, as well as the scholarly literature on languages both related and not related to Paunaka. This may sound trivial, but I think it is necessary to be clear about it. Thus what constitutes a word in this grammar (as indicated by being put between spaces) is determined by a mixture of grammatical and phonological criteria as well as tradition in Arawakan or Amazonian linguistics. Other researchers with different backgrounds and/or applying other criteria may arrive at different results. Thus a “word” in this work is a convenient solution that is apt, I believe, to describe grammatical properties of Paunaka. The questionclitic|( whether the grammatical and phonological word coincides largely depends on how the status of certain markers is analysed, which are phonologically bound to words belonging to different word classes.word class Does this mean they are clitics? And if so, is it a logical consequence that they are grammatical words of their own? I pursue this issue further in the following section.
summary:
The author uses the concept of “word” in the grammar as a practical tool, even though wordhood is not a straightforward cross-linguistic notion. Word boundaries in this analysis are based on a mixture of intuition, phonological and grammatical criteria, and established tradition in Arawakan/Amazonian linguistics, rather than on a formal test battery.

The author also notes that the coincidence of grammatical and phonological words depends on how certain bound markers are analyzed, especially clitics, and says this issue is discussed further in the next section.

text: affix|( A word can be composed of different layers in Paunaka. This especially applies to verbs,verb where we can often distinguish roots,verbal root stems,verbal stem derivational affixes,derivation|( and inflectional markers.inflection I hardly make use of the concept of “clitic” in this work; the reasons will become apparent throughout this section.clitic|) Root and affix have been defined as two kinds of morphemes, one of which encodes lexical, the other grammatical meaning. Although this distinction is not always unproblematic, especially as to what is the semantic basis of lexical vs. grammatical meaning , it is a widely accepted one. Roots can encode very basic lexical meaning, which is enhanced by derivation. A root together with all derivational processes is a stem, which may still be different from a full word form . In particular, verb stemsverbal stem can be fairly complex. Derivational processes can be marked by derivational affixes, but there are also other means, e.g. reduplication (see ). In addition, compounding and incorporation as non-derivational processes can alter the meaning of a word, while attachment of classifiersclassifier lies on the edge between compounding and derivation. Some derivational processes are clear-cut. This is the case whenever we find a derivational affix together with various roots, where it exhibits the same meaning or has the same function. There are other cases of totally opaque derivational processes, i.e. we can identify a root and a stem, but not the affixes or processes that lead from the root to the stem. Most derivational affixes follow the root, i.e. Paunaka is mainly suffixingsuffix in this regard. Consider ( -1), which shows the composition of four related verb stems.verbal stem|( The rootverbal root is -pa ‘die’ in all cases. This root is minimally accompanied by the thematic suffixthematic suffix|( -ku (irrealis -ka). The meaning of this thematic suffix is very opaque, but it only appears on active verbsactive verb|( and it has cognates in the most closely related languages. From the verb stem -paku ‘die’, the verb -kupaku ‘kill’ can be derived by a causative prefix ku-. The stem -kupaku is the base for insertion of the extension applicative suffix -i, which yields -kupaiku ‘slaughter’. This again is the base for another derivation whose result is -kupaikechu with the pluractional meaning ‘kill all’ or ‘kill everybody’. However in this case, it is not clear which affixes are involved. It is possible that the last sequence -chu of -kechu is the other thematic suffix -chu ‘th2’, and it is also possible that the /k/ is a remnant from the more frequent thematic suffix -ku. Nonetheless, the function of ke (or e) remains unclear. There is only one other verb stem with a similar derivation, the related -paikechu ‘all die’, and it is not possible to derive new verbs with -kechu. -paku, -kupaku, -kupaiku, -kupaikechu\\ pa-ku ku-pa-ku ku-pa-i-ku ku-pa-i-ke-chu\\ die-th1 caus-die-th1 caus-die-ext-th1 caus-die-ext-?-th2?\\ ‘verb stems: die, kill, slaughter, kill all/everybody’ Another example is ( -2). In this case, -yunu ‘go’ has no thematic suffix, and it seems we are dealing with a root here.verbal root If we consider, however, that there is also -yuiku ‘walk’, which looks as if it is related to -yunu, we might conclude that the root must be only -yu. But unlike a thematic suffix like the one we have found in ( -1) above, the syllable nu does not detach from -yunu in any case of inflection, and we cannot assign any specific function to this syllable. There are two more possible derivations though that seem to build on -yu only, -yupu and -yupunu, both meaning ‘go out, come out, sprout’. -yunu, -yuiku, -yupu, -yupunu\\ yunu yu-i-ku yu-pu yu-punu\\ go go?-ext-th1 go?-dloc go?-am.prior\\ ‘verb stems: go, walk, come out, come out’ thematic suffix|) The exact derivational relation between rootverbal root and stem is thus not always clear, especially if there do not happen to be several related verb stems. active verb|) Furthermore, since most verb stems are totally lexicalised,lexicalisation it is not always possible to determine which part of the meaning is realised by which part exactly. As a citation form in text and interlinear glosses, I have therefore chosen the stem and not the root.verbal stem|) There are some exceptions to this, mainly if a classifier or incorporated nounincorporation is part of the verb stem, which is not generally lexicalised on it. This happens relatively rarely, and thus I believe it is worth highlighting these cases. More information on the composition of verb stems is given in Chapter .derivation|) The verb stems of ( -1) and ( -2) are not complete words, nor are they citation forms used by the speakers themselves, e.g. in offering a translation for a Spanish word. Verbsverb need to minimally inflectinflection|( for personperson marking and reality status (RS).Actually according to my own analysis, RS marking of active verbs fuses with the last suffix or vowel of the stemverbal stem or of the marker directly following the stem, so that the forms in (\getref -1 ) and (\getref -2 ) can be analysed to already contain RS inflection, which is realis in this case by absence of irrealis marking. The irrealis forms of (\getref -1 ) are -paka, -kupaka, -kupaika, -kupaikecha and of (\getref -2 ) -yuna, -yuika, -yupa, and -yupuna. This will be explained in more detail below, and especially in . Cross-linguistically, inflection is often carried out by inflectional affixes. However, the case is not totally clear in Paunaka, which may be claimed to use mainly cliticsclitic to encode inflection (see discussion below in this section). Regardless of whether inflectional markers are analysed as affixes or clitics, most of them follow the stem. The boundaries between derivation and inflection are not sharp, both processes can rather be defined as two points on a continuum . In Paunaka, this is especially clear for all kinds of markers that attach to the edge of an active verb stemverbal stem replacing or directly following the thematic suffixesthematic suffix (if applicable, as we have just seen in ( -2), not all
summary:
The passage explains that Paunaka verbs can have multiple layers, including roots, stems, derivational affixes, and inflectional markers, though the boundary between these categories is often unclear. It gives examples showing that derivation may be transparent or opaque, most derivational affixes are suffixes, and verb stems are often lexicalized enough that the author chooses to cite stems rather than roots.

It also notes that verbs must minimally inflect for person and reality status, with irrealis forms contrasting with the forms cited. Finally, the text argues that inflection in Paunaka may be expressed mainly by clitics or affix-like markers, and that derivation and inflection form a continuum rather than a sharp division.

text: active verb stems have a thematic suffix), thus those markers which fuse with RS marking.reality statusinflection|) transcategorial morphology|( Turning to the notion of “clitic”clitic|( now, this term has been applied to a wide range of phenomena , which is not surprising because “no rigorously defined cross-linguistically applicable concept of clitic seems to exist” . The most important feature to distinguish a clitic from an affix on which most authors agree is their non- (or low) selectivity or promiscuous attachment, i.e. clitics can attach to words belonging to more than one word class. However, this seems to be at most a necessary condition of clitichood, rather than a sufficient one, if we consider, for instance, the way formulate the matter: “An element is a clitic only if it can attach to hosts of diverse categories”. As for Paunaka, there are many markers with low selectivity, but if this criterion is only a necessary condition, it does not automatically follow that they are clitics. Considering other criteria of clitics that have been proposed in the literature does not help. propose seven properties, only two of them set clitics apart from affixes, one being their low selectivity and the other one a possible fixed position in the clause, most commonly the second position. None of Paunaka’s markers with promiscuous attachment are confined to a specific syntactic position inside the clause. states that “there is no single set of properties that always uniquely identifies clitics and distinguishes them from affixes”. This is also reflected in the way in which low selectivity has been treated in research on Arawakan languagesArawakan languages|(. In applying her proposed criteria to characterise clitics, analyses some markers of low selectivity as clitics and others as affixes in Tariana, an Arawakan language distantly related to Paunaka. She carefully explains her analysis as clitics for those markers she identifies as such, but does not offer an explanation why she dismisses the analysis as clitic for the other markers that can be attached to different parts of speech, such as the privative and attributive markers, as well as the person markers . Person markersperson marking|( are an interesting case in the Arawakan languages. They are cognate throughout the whole family, at least in parts of the paradigm, and they can be used to mark possessorspossessor on nouns and S/Asubject participants on verbs in general . Thus they can be claimed to show low selectivity. In descriptions of individual languages, some researchers have defined them as affixes and some as clitics. Person markers behave differently throughout the family, e.g. with regard to co-occurring or alternating with pronouns,pronoun and this may be a decisive factor in the choice of one or the other analysis. Yet there is some insecurity about their status. Concerning Alto Perené, a language of the Kampan branch, thus more closely related to Paunaka than aforementioned Tariana, states: “The syntactic status of person/possessor morphemes remains a difficult issue. In my doctoral thesis (Mihas 2010), I classified them as phrasal clitics. Additional evidence, collected during the last years, indicates they are more affix-like in their behavior”. Another solution to the matter has been proposed by for Apurinã of the Purus branch (also more closely related to Paunaka than Tariana). Disagreeing with the sharp distinction between clitics and affixes, mainly because he objects to the view that clitics are subject to the rules of syntax and not morphology, he proposes a language-specific class of “special bound formatives” which contains the person markers, but also others like the oblique marker and TAME markers. All of them show low selectivity and some may float in the clause . They partly encode concepts similar to the ones expressed by the Paunaka markers with low selectivity.person marking|) I think the previous short discussion has sufficiently shown that defining clitics is not straigthforward in general and also specifically as regards Arawakan languages.Arawakan languages|) Many have noted this before me. I thus decided not to make use of the notion of “clitic” in this grammar and consequently not to use equal signs (=) as opposed to dashes (-). There is only one exception: nominal demonstrativesnominal demonstrative can occasionally be realised as a phonetically reduced, unstressed form attached to a preceding word. If this happens, the process may be referred to as cliticisation. It is different from the other cases dealt with below (see ), because there is a corresponding free form that would occur in the very same position of the clause. With regards to terminology in explanatory texts, I make use of the neutral term “marker”. A markers is a grammatical morphemes that marks a feature of a grammatical category and is phonologically attached to a word. This includes affixes, clitics (if one wants to maintain the concept) and borderline cases.affix|) The following section is dedicated to those markers with promiscuous attachment in terms of their possible hosts and loci, as well as their possible different functions on words belonging to different word classes. More complete descriptions of their semantics are found in subsequent chapters. As for the organisation of these chapters, I decided to describe person and number marking separately for nouns and verbs. Diminutives are described in the chapter on nouns, because they primarily relate to nouns, even if they are attached to another part of speech. Correspondingly, TAME markers are described in the chapter about verbs, because they primarily relate to predicates, and most predicates are verbs. In addition, degree markers are also found in the chapter about verbs.
summary:
The passage argues that “clitic” is not a straightforward or cross-linguistically stable category, since low selectivity of attachment is only a necessary condition and other proposed criteria do not clearly separate clitics from affixes. In Paunaka and related Arawakan languages, many markers show promiscuous attachment but lack the fixed clause position often associated with clitics, and person markers in the family have been analyzed inconsistently as clitics, affixes, or special bound formatives.

For this reason, the author decides not to use the term “clitic” in the grammar, except for occasional reduced nominal demonstratives that attach to a preceding word when a corresponding free form exists. Instead, the author uses the neutral term “marker” for grammatical morphemes that are phonologically attached to a word, including affixes, clitics, and borderline cases.

text: verb|( This section gives an overview of the markers that can occur with different parts of speech. Since active verbsactive verb are usually among the classes of words that markers with low selectivity attach to, provides a schematic overview of the structure of such a verb. Markers that only occur on verbs are marked in grey, and they will not be considered in this section. Reduplication as a “nonlinear formative” will not be considered here either. sidewaysfigure Template of an active verb sidewaysfigure Everything marked with an asterisk * must be expressed on a verb: subject marking, verb stemverbal stem and reality status (RS) markingreality status are always obligatory, although RS marking fuses with either the last suffix of the stem or one of the markers directly following the stem. As for the object markers and the plural marker, they are only demanded under specific conditions: if the verb has an SAP object, an object marker occursperson marking obligatorily, and if it has a humananimacy third person plural subject or object, the plural marker has to be used. Not all of the markers can co-occur on a verb: only one aspect marker is possible (incmp, prsp, dsc, iam) and only one that encodes epistemic modality (uncert, ded). Intensive (ints)intensifier and limitative (lim1 and lim2) markers are not compatible either. There is often no morphology at all besides the obligatory categories of person/numberperson marking and RS.reality status If other markers are added, there are usually maximally two of them, though exceptions are found, which shows that the possible number of markers is not restricted to two. For some markers, namely lim1, lim2, and emph2, it was not possible to determine their exact position in the template with certainty due to lack of examples. This is why they are marked with ?. Some markers can appear in two different slots, which is indicated by a superscript number, the one closer to the stem taking the number 1 in these cases. Besides the ones overtly marked by these numbers, some other markers have occasionally also been found in other slots. Since most of them are disyllabic and encode only one feature, they are easily recognisable as meaningful units. This makes them manipulable. If, for instance, a speaker has forgotten to insert a marker in its usual slot, she can just add it later. In real speech, we thus find verbs with orders of markers that deviate from the template. Nonetheless, in elicitation such forms are not accepted. I believe that this general recognisability and 1:1 correspondence between form and meaning is a prerequisite for these markers being able to attach promiscuously to words of different classes. At the same time, the high number of low selectivity markers shows us that in Paunaka (and presumably also in other Arawakan languages that have similar systems) the distinction between different parts of speech playsword class a more minor role than it does in other languages. This also becomes apparent when looking at syntactic relations: nounsnoun (and also adjectives)adjective can be predicates (see Chapter ), and verbs (in headless relative clauses)relative relation can act as argumentsargument (see ). It is a reduction of linguistic effort if the same (or very similar) notions can be expressed by one marker instead of two or more. The following sections are dedicated to different morphemes with low selectivity.
summary:
The passage outlines the template of an active Paunaka verb, noting that subject marking, the verb stem, and reality-status marking are always obligatory, while object and plural markers are required only in specific contexts. It also describes restrictions on marker co-occurrence and notes that, although some markers have uncertain positions or can appear in more than one slot, they are generally recognizable and can be reordered in speech, even if such forms are not accepted in elicitation.  

The author argues that the many low-selectivity markers suggest that word-class distinctions are relatively less important in Paunaka than in many other languages, and this is supported by the fact that nouns and adjectives can serve as predicates and verbs can function as arguments.

text: classifier|( Classifiers combine with verbs, nounsnoun|( and adjectivesadjective|( in Paunaka. They derive nounsderivation from verb stemsverbal stem and nouns with new meanings from other nouns.nominal stem The combination of noun or verb stem with a specific classifier is often totally lexicalisedlexicalisation in these cases.noun|) When combined with adjectives and verbs, classifiers specify some properties of a referent, mostly shape and consistency.adjective|) ( -1) shows a noun and a verb stem lexicalised with the classifier -pa, which is used with dusty things, flour, small particles and the like. In the case of the noun in ( -1.1), the stem never occurs without a classifier (*mute), while in the case of the verb in ( -1.2), the root -yÿti ‘set on fire’ also occurs without a classifier in the stem -yÿtiku ‘set (a pot) on fire’. Classifiers occur inside the verb stem.verbal stem Their nature is not inflectional in Paunaka, they can be considered purely derivational devicesderivation on the edge of being lexical, such that if a classifier derives a new noun, the process resembles compounding. Thus due to their position close to the rootverbal root and their derivational function, I consider them a special type of lexical affix in spite of their promiscuous attachment. Classifiers are described in more detail in below. classifier|)
summary:
In Paunaka, classifiers combine with verbs, nouns, and adjectives, where they often derive new nouns or new meanings and are frequently lexicalized with particular stems. When used with adjectives and verbs, they specify properties of a referent, especially shape and consistency, and they occur inside the verb stem.  

The passage argues that these classifiers are not inflectional but derivational, functioning as a special type of lexical affix; because of their close position to the root and their role in creating new lexical items, their use can resemble compounding.

summary: Associated motion markers in the corpus mostly attach to verbs, though a few concurrent motion markers also occur on a numeral and a noun. The passage argues that these rare nonverbal uses do not undermine their status as suffixes, but instead show the flexibility of the inflectional system; the markers are semantically close to derivation but also form a small, mutually exclusive inflectional paradigm. It also notes that AM markers can replace or follow a thematic suffix, take over reality-status inflection, and that the regressive/repetitive marker is derived from an AM marker and can occur on verbs, nouns, and adverbs.
