As can be seen in ( -3), however, the iamitive follows the 1sg object marker. tekichunÿtu\\ ti-ekichu-nÿ-tu\\ 3i-invite-1sg-iam\\ ‘she invited me (food)’ There are two exceptions to this placement remote from the stem.verbal stem First, the discontinuous marker, meaning ‘(not) anymore’, can either precede or follow the plural marker. I do not know what lets the speaker choose one or the other option. Both combinations are rare in the corpus. The difference does not depend on the plural marker belonging to the subject or object participant. kuina nichupuikabunube\\ kuina ni-chupuika-bu-nube\\ neg 1sg-know.irr-dsc-pl\\ ‘I don’t know them anymore’ kuina tisamuikanubebu\\ kuina ti-samuika-nube-bu\\ neg 3i-listen.irr-pl-dsc\\ ‘they don’t listen anymore’ Second, the incompletive marker precedes not only the plural, but also the distributive marker in its second possible slot, and is thus even closer to the verb stemverbal stem than the discontinuous marker. tujikukuÿjaneyu\\ ti-ujiku-kuÿ-jane-yu\\ 3i-suckle-incmp-distr-ints\\ ‘they still suckle a lot’ In summary, most TAME markers follow the ones connected to personperson marking (i.e. person, plural, distributive, diminutive), but two of them always or sometimes precede them. summary:
The passage explains that TAME markers in the language show low selectivity, since they can attach not only to verbs but also to non-verbal predicates, particles, and even adverbs. It notes several special properties: some markers have corresponding free forms, the remote marker can refer to deceased human nouns, and markers may be used more than once in a clause.  

It also shows that most TAME markers occur relatively far from the verb stem, usually after person-related markers, which violates the expected affix-ordering hierarchy. However, the discontinuous and incompletive markers are exceptions, since they can precede some of these person-related markers, so the TAME class is not uniform in its position within the verb template.

text: person marking|( possessor|( There are two sets of related person markers, one preceding stems and the other one following stems. One of the two third-person markers, ti- ‘3i’, only appears on verbs and only precedes the stem,verbal stem thus this one certainly qualifies as a prefix. All other person markers occur on verbs, nouns and sometimes words of other parts of speech. I first consider person markers preceding stems. On verbs they mark subjects, as in ( .1), and on nouns they mark possessors, as in ( .2). possessor|) Regarding the person markers following the stem, they mark objectsobject|( on verbs,verbal stem ( .1) and subjectssubject|( on non-verbal predicatesnon-verbal predication of different types, e.g. nouns, as in ( .2). subject|) object|) As is apparent from ( ) and ( ), person markers do show low selectivity, but the functions encoded differ for nouns and verbs. This may be more apparent for the ones preceding the stem, because on verbs they mark arguments while on nouns they mark possessors, although as Danielsen (2021, p.c.) rightly remarks, in both cases “it is all about the primary argument”. The person markers following the stem both mark secondary arguments, but there is a very clear distinction as to the syntactic function of the argument. Person markers do not alternate with pronounspronoun in Paunaka. In applying the terminology by , they are also called “indexes” in this grammar. More information on argument indexing on verbs can be found in . Encoding of possession is discussed in , and argument indexing on non-verbal predicates is among the topics of . person marking|)
summary: The language has two related sets of person markers, one placed before stems and one after them. The pre-stem markers mark subjects on verbs and possessors on nouns, while the post-stem markers mark objects on verbs and subjects on non-verbal predicates; the third-person marker ti- is a prefix that appears only on verbs. These markers do not alternate with independent pronouns in Paunaka and are referred to as indexes in this grammar.

text: plural|( The plural marker -nube is found on nouns and verbs, as well as on numeralsnumeral and nominal demonstratives to express non-singularity of humananimacy referents, as in ( -1). The plural marker combines with the third person markersperson marking ti- and chÿ-/chi-. Both are underspecified for number; if plural number of a human participant indexed by a person marker is encoded, the plural marker is simply added after the stem.verbal stem The plural marker thus occurs in the same contexts in which (third) person markers occur (see above). As for possession marking, if both possessor and possessed are humananimacy third person, there is ambiguity between belonging to the possessor and belonging to the possessed. Consider the following examples: in ( -2.1) the plural marker belongs to the possessed, in ( -2.2) it belongs to the possessor, but in ( -2.3) it can belong to the possessed, to the possessor, or to both. It is only the context that can clarify what precisely is meant. The plural marker on verbs is also ambiguous as to whether it refers to a third person plural subject or object. If the verb is intransitive, it can only belong to the subject marker, as in ( -3.1). If the subject of a transitive verb is a speech act participant (SAP), it can only mark the object, see ( -3.2). However, if both subject and object of a transitive verb are humananimacy third persons, it is again only the context that can clarify who is the plural participant (see ( -3.3)). If a clause has both an index on the verb and a conominal NP,conomination the plural marker usually occurs on both the verb and the NP,noun phrase as in ( -aff). suntabunube chumunubetu labionyae\\ suntabu-nube chÿ-umu-nube-tu labion-yae\\ soldier-pl 3-take-pl-iam plane-loc\\ ‘the soldiers (i.e. policemen) took her to the plane’ In complementation,complement relation however, there is no such agreement marking: if the subject has a human third-person referent, the plural marker often occurs only once, namely on the complement verb as in ( -4). It sometimes also attaches to both verbs, but it can only occur on the complement-taking verb alone if the complement verb has a different subject, i.e. where there is no other subject to agree with, as in ( -FirstPlural). tisachu tinikanube\\ ti-sachu ti-nika-nube\\ 3i-want 3i-eat.irr-pl\\ ‘they want to eat’ tisachunube bitupupuna echÿu betea\\ ti-sachu-nube bi-itu-pupuna echÿu bi-etea\\ 3i-want-pl 1pl-master-reg.irr demb 1pl-language\\ ‘they want us to learn our language again’ The plural marker also occurs only once if a plural noun is modifiedmodification by a demonstrative as in ( -5). It can be attached to demonstratives as well, but in those cases there is usually no noun. echÿu jentenube\\ echÿu jente-nube\\ demb man-pl\\ ‘these men’ For Proto-Arawakan,Arawakan languages a separate third person plural index *na has been postulated, but there are a number of languages that encode plural separately from third person .person marking|( The plural marker was probably first used with nouns exclusively and was subsequently extended to number marking together with the underspecified third person markers. We can state that its function is to express plural number of human nouns (and demonstratives referring to humans) or plural number of the third person markers. Subject,subject object and possessor marking derive from the latter. On non-verbal predicatesnon-verbal predication with human third person referents, it can also specify the number of a subject without this being bound to person marking, as in ( -6), which builds on the non-verbal third person expression for ‘come’ (see for more information on this topic). person marking|) kapununube naka ...\\ kapunu-nube naka\\ come-pl here\\ ‘they came here...’ The marker has some properties of an agreement affix, such as being attached to both noun and verb as in ( -aff), but it fails to indicate agreement in other cases, like complementation ( -4) and modification of a noun by a demonstrative ( -5). More information about plural marking is given in for nouns and in for verbs as a part of person marking . plural|)
summary:
The plural marker -nube appears on nouns, verbs, numerals, and demonstratives to mark non-singular human referents, and it combines with underspecified third-person markers ti- and chÿ-/chi-. Its interpretation is often context-dependent: on possessive forms and transitive verbs with third-person human participants, it can refer to the possessor, the possessed, the subject, or the object, while in simpler cases it is unambiguous.

The text argues that plural marking likely originated on nouns and was later extended to number marking with third-person person markers. Although it sometimes behaves like an agreement affix, it does not consistently show agreement in constructions such as complementation or noun modification by demonstratives.

text: distributive|( The distributive marker -jane is used to mark plural number of non-humananimacy referents. Theoretically, the same kind of ambiguities described in above also apply to the distributive marker, but, being optional, it is generally employed less frequently than the plural marker. There are, for instance, no examples in the corpus in which -jane would mark a plural possessor, but this is possibly due to pragmatic reasons, because non-humananimacy entities are in general less likely to be construed as possessors. In addition, contrary to the plural marker, if an NP conominatesconomination an argument indexed on a verb, -jane often appears only on the NP argumentnoun phrase or only on the verb, the latter being shown in ( -janeV). It may, however, also be attached to both NP and verb. If the non-verbal copulanon-verbal predication kaku is the predicate of the clause, -jane usually attaches to the nounnoun only; this is the case in ( -2). More information about distributive marking on nouns can be found in and on verbs as part of person marking in . In addition, -jane is also occasionally found on demonstratives and it may be found on adjectives, too, although there is only one example that includes a borrowed adjective in the corpus, which is given here as ( -yellow). echÿu amariyujane\\ echÿu amariyu-jane\\ demb yellow-distr\\ ‘the yellow ones (speaking about piranha)’ distributive|)
summary: The distributive marker **-jane** marks plural number on non-human referents and is used less often than the plural marker because it is optional. It may appear on an NP, on the verb, or on both, and with the copula **kaku** it usually attaches only to the noun; it is also occasionally found on demonstratives and adjectives.

text: collective|( The collective marker -ji is highly selective, but for semantic reasons rather than for word class. It has been found on nouns,noun adjectivesadjective and stative verbsstative verb (which is why it does not show up in the verb template in , since this template shows an active verb).There seems to be one exception to this: the verb for ‘fight’ has a reciprocal suffix followed by the collective marker (see (\getref -2 ) below). I have not found any other active verb taking the collective marker, which is why I neglect this single case here. Regarding adjectivesadjective and stative verbs, it is used only with expressions of colour and size, often in combination with a classifier or incorporated noun.incorporation ( -1) is an example of an adjective and ( -2) of a stative verb bearing the collective marker. temetapuji\\ teme-tapu-ji\\ big- -col\\ ‘big ones (referring to piranhas here, but it can also refer to other fish species)’ tisururukiji\\ ti-sururu-ki-ji\\ 3i-be.clear- -col\\ ‘they are all light-coloured’ Some nounsnoun referring to small animals that occur in groups or swarms show up in the collective rather than in the singular form, especially some fish species. The same is true for -muki-ji ‘hair’. Strikingly, the collective marker also obligatorily occurs on the kinship terms for ‘mother’, ‘father’, ‘brother’, ‘sister’, ‘sibling (of same sex)’ and ‘son’ if the possessor, the possessed or both have plural referents,possession as well as on the plural-only noun sesejinube ‘children’. The collective marker then precedes the plural marker, as in ( -3). Other nouns do not usually take the collective marker. chipijijinube\\ chi-piji-ji-nube\\ 3-sibling-col-pl\\ ‘his/her siblings (of the same sex)’\: ‘their sibling’\: ‘their siblings’ More information about collective marking on nouns can be found in and on verbs in . Some more examples with adjectives taking the collective marker are scattered through . collective|)
summary:
The collective marker **-ji** is selective for semantic rather than grammatical reasons, appearing on nouns, some noun adjectives, and stative verbs, but not generally on active verbs. With adjectives and stative verbs, it is restricted mainly to color and size expressions, often alongside a classifier or incorporated noun.

On nouns, -ji commonly marks small animals that occur in groups, certain terms like hair, and obligatorily appears on several kinship terms when possessors or possessed items are plural, as well as on the plural-only noun for ‘children.’ In these cases, the collective marker comes before the plural marker.

text: diminutive|( The diminutive marker -mÿnÿ can attach to nouns, adjectives, verbs, and more rarely nominal demonstratives and numerals. It can express smallness, but also emotional affection (sympathy, pity, modesty), and the latter is often more important in the choice than mere size. The diminutive usually expresses that the speaker has some emotional affection towards one specific participant in the clause, that one participant is small or both. It does not matter to which word it attaches; in ( -1) it attaches to a noun, in ( -2) to a stative verb, but in both cases it refers to a participant of the clause. kaku kabemÿnÿ naka\\ kaku kabe-mÿnÿ naka\\ exist dog-dim here\\ ‘here’s a little dog’ kuina tatÿkemiumÿnÿ\\ kuina ti-a-tÿkemiu-mÿnÿ\\ neg 3i-irr-be.quiet-dim\\ ‘it (i.e. the little baby) doesn’t calm down’ The diminutive is also marginally used to attenuate a verb’s meaning, which is, of course, another extension from smallness and affection marking. However, it acquires an extra function on verbs, different from the ones encoded when it is attached to nouns. One example is given in ( -3), which could be produced to describe that somebody is eating a small quantity of food, but also that somebody is eating at least a bit of light food again after having been ill, although she might still not be eating properly. In the first scenario, the diminutive refers to the object participant, while the second scenario is a case of attenuation. tinikumÿnÿtu\\ ti-niku-mÿnÿ-tu\\ 3i-eat-dim-iam\\ ‘he is already eating a bit’ The diminutive marker is described in more detail in . diminutive|)
summary:
The diminutive marker **-mÿnÿ** can attach to nouns, adjectives, verbs, and more rarely demonstratives and numerals, and it can express both literal smallness and emotional attitudes such as affection, sympathy, pity, or modesty. In many cases the emotional meaning is more important than size, and the diminutive typically indicates that the speaker feels affection toward one participant in the clause, that the participant is small, or both.

On verbs, the diminutive can also marginally **attenuate** the meaning of the verb, adding a separate function beyond the nominal uses. Examples show that it may refer either to a small quantity of something being eaten or to a weaker, partial return to eating after illness.

text: degree marker|( The category of degree markers subsumes the intensive marker (or intensifier) -yu, the limitative markers -jiku and -yÿchi, additiveadditive -uku, and the emphatic markersemphatic -ja and -kene. They occur in different slots of the verb, some closer, some more remote from the stem.verbal stem The intensifierintensifier|( -yu can be translated with ‘very’ or ‘a lot’ most of the time. It mainly occurs on predicates, which may be verbs, adjectives,adjective quantifiersquantifier or nouns.nominal predicate Thus, while it is not selective to word class, it is selective to syntactic function. One example with a verbal predicate is given in ( -1) and one with an adjective in ( -2). The additive also occurs prior to inflectional suffixes like the middle voice marker -bu, as in ( -3). pikubiakukubu\\ pi-kubiaku-uku-bu\\ 2sg-be.tired-add-mid\\ ‘you are tired, too’ |) There are two emphatic markers.emphatic|( One of them, -kene ‘emph2’, occurs very sporadically and will thus not be considered further here. The other one has the form -ja with the gloss ‘emph1’. It can attach to words of different classes and exhibit wide or narrow scope in the clause. One example is given in ( -1), where the emphatic marker attaches to the free form of the uncertainty marker. The translation of the question as referring to the manner of an event is due to the context. ¿kenaja? kuina nimua\\ kena-ja kuina ni-imua\\ uncert-emph1 neg 1sg-see.irr\\ ‘how might it have happened? I have not seen it’ emphatic|) degree marker|) verb|) More information about the degree markers is given in .
summary: The category of degree markers includes the intensifier -yu, the limitative markers -jiku and -yÿchi, the additive -uku, and the emphatic markers -ja and -kene, which occupy different positions relative to the verbal stem. The intensifier -yu usually means ‘very’ or ‘a lot’ and occurs mainly on predicates, regardless of whether they are verbs, adjectives, or nouns, while the additive -uku can appear before inflectional suffixes such as the middle voice marker -bu. Of the two emphatics, -kene is rare, whereas -ja is more common, can attach to different word classes, and may have wide or narrow scope in the clause.

text: non-verbal irrealis marker|( The non-verbal irrealis marker -ina is selective in a negative way: it is never found on verbs. In non-verbal predication, it can attach to a range of words from different classes, e.g. the copula kaku as in ( -kaku), verbs borrowedborrowing from Spanish that are integrated as non-verbs as in ( -forget) (and see on the topic of verbs borrowed from Spanish), and adjectivesadjective as in ( -weather), the latter being rare. kuina kakuina Krara\\ kuina kaku-ina Krara\\ neg exist-irr.nv Clara\\ ‘Clara is not here’ eka nijinepÿi kuina arbidauna\\ eka ni-jinepÿi kuina arbidau-ina\\ dema 1sg-daughter neg forget-irr.nv\\ ‘my daughter doesn’t forget ’ michamuenatu\\ michamue-ina-tu\\ of.good.weather-irr.nv-iam\\ ‘the sky will be nice again now‘ (i.e. ‘it won’t rain anymore’) As for its occurrence on nouns,noun there is a predicative and a referential use of the non-verbal irrealis marker. It is used predicatively if the noun is the predicate of the clause. This is similar to the use of an adjective as predicate as in ( -weather). Nonetheless, if a verbal predicate is present, the non-verbal irrealis marker signals non-existence of an argument or adverbial of the clause independent of predication. This is explained in detail in . non-verbal irrealis marker|) inflection|) clitic|) transcategorial morphology|) The following sections are dedicated to some affixes and mechanisms found in word formation.
summary: The non-verbal irrealis marker **-ina** never occurs on verbs, but can attach to non-verbal predicates such as the copula, borrowed Spanish forms treated as non-verbs, and occasionally adjectives. With nouns, it has both a predicative use, where the noun functions as the clause predicate, and a referential use, where it marks the non-existence of an argument or adverbial even when a verbal predicate is present.

text: classifier|( Classifiers constitute a special class of lexical suffixsuffix in Paunaka. Most of them have CV shape. They combine with stems of nouns, adjectives, and verbs (see for combinations of classifiers with nouns, for adjectives and and for verbs). Classifiers do not occur with numerals in Paunaka, which may be important to mention explicitly, because this is the only word class with which classifiers obligatorily occur in the related Baure and the Mojeño languages, see more on this below. Since classifiers do not show up very often in Paunaka, except for nouns that are lexicalised with a classifier, it is not entirely clear how many classifiers there are. The ones I could identify are summarised in . Most of these classifiers have a semantic basis in shape, which is typical for classifiers in general ( ; ). All of these classifiers, except for -tapu ‘ ’, have cognate forms in at least one of the Mojeño languages, and most of them also in Baure. The classifier -tapu derives fromgrammaticalisation an identical noun -tapu ‘scales’; however, when used as a classifier, it refers to animals with scales (or a carapace), not to the scales themselves, as in ( -1). kaku mutemetapuji\\ kaku muteme-tapu-ji\\ exist big- -col\\ ‘there are big ones (piranhas)’ Many objects fall into the same classes in all Bolivian ArawakanSouthern Arawakan languages, but there are also some differences. To give just one example, the classifier for pointed objects is -be ‘ ’ in Paunaka. TrinitarioMojeño Trinitario has a cognate form -ve, but the classifier seems to be absent from Baure and Ignaciano. Instead of this, in both languages (and partly also in Trinitario), pointed objects are classified with -po/-pa, i.e. a form identical to the classifier for dusty things. In Paunaka, some objects that are possibly conceived as pointed are also formed with final -pa. As for -jimunepa ‘ribs’ and -musipa ‘eyelashes’, there is also a special parallel arrangement of single longish items. This does not seem to hold for tÿmuepa ‘knife’. Thus we find that most pointed objects are classified by -be in Paunaka and by -pa/-po in IgnacianoMojeño Ignaciano and Baure, but a few of them are also classified by -pa in Paunaka. There seem to be several (temporal) layers of how classifiers come into being and go out of use again, some shared by all languages, some only by a subset of them or restricted to a single language. This results in several possible classes an item can be assigned to and in differences between the related languages. It has already been mentioned that numeralsnumeral do not take classifiers in Paunaka, but suspiciously, the numeral chÿnachÿ ‘one’ has a syllable na, as does the related adjective punachÿ ‘other’. Baure and the Mojeño languages have a neutral or unspecified classifier, which has the form -no in Baure and -na in Trinitario and Ignaciano . This classifier is also used with human referents, and this is why it has been glossed as ‘ ’ by . This very same classifier can be used with numerals to replace any other more specific classifier, and indeed, this is very frequently the case in these languages. Thus speaks of a generic classifier. In Paunaka, there are also a few adjectivesadjective|( and stative verbsstative verb|( that have a sequence na in their most neutral form, and some of them change exactly this syllable for a specific classifier or a noun denoting a body or plant part. This is why I postulate that there is a default or general classifier -na in Paunaka, cognate to the forms found in the other Bolivian ArawakanSouthern Arawakan languages. The words containing the general classifier are summarised in . stative verb|)adjective|) Processes related to classifiers include compounding and incorporation (see ). classifier|)
summary:
Paunaka has a set of lexical suffix classifiers, usually of CV shape, that combine with nouns, adjectives, and verbs, but not with numerals. Most classifiers are semantically based on shape, and many have cognates in related Mojeño and Baure languages; one classifier, -tapu, appears to have developed from a noun meaning ‘scales’ and is used for animals with scales or a carapace.

The passage also shows that classifier systems differ across related languages and may have changed in different historical layers, so the same item can belong to different classes in different languages. Although numerals do not normally take classifiers in Paunaka, the author argues that Paunaka likely has a default or general classifier -na, parallel to the neutral classifiers found in Baure and the Mojeño languages, and classifier-related processes also include compounding and incorporation.

text: reduplication|( Repetition is found on stems of verbs, nouns, and adjectives, but true reduplication is only found on verbs, i.e. “the repetition of morphemes or parts of morphemes by which a new morpheme with a new, related meaning is created, or by which a grammatical function is systematically expressed” . Reduplication can express iterative, durative, and intensive aktionsart on active verbsactive verb (see ) and possibly inchoative aktionsart on stative verbsstative verb (see ). These categories, among others, have been identified by to be expressed by reduplication cross-linguistically. Consider ( -see), which includes the verb -imu ‘see’, and compare with ( -look), which has the related stem -imumuku ‘look, watch’, including a reduplicated syllable (+ thematic suffix -ku). pero eka nipiji chimu\\ pero eka ni-piji chÿ-imu\\ but dema 1sg-sibling 3-see\\ ‘but my sister saw it’ timumuku echÿu chipeu mase\\ ti-imumuku echÿu chi-peu mase\\ 3i-look demb 3-animal squirrel\\ ‘he is looking at his squirrel’ Most nouns with a repeated syllable are totally lexicalised.lexicalisation If we consider the few stemsnominal stem that have been found with and without repeated syllables, we must note that the ones including repetition also bear the collectivecollective|( marker (see ). The collective marker also triggers repetition of the general classifier on adjectives (see )). In any case, the meaning conveyed by repetition plus collectivecollective|) marking on nouns is distributivity. There is almost exclusively progressive partial reduplication (and repetition), and it is usually restricted to duplication. However, a few cases of triplication exist in verbs, e.g. -japipipiku ‘wag tail’ and -pÿsisisiku ‘smoke, smoulder’. A reduplicated syllable occurs in continuous and optionally also in concurrent associated motion marking, but is accompanied by additional material. The forms are -CViku for continuous marking, while the concurrent associated motion markers have the forms -(CV)kuÿ and -(CV)kÿupunu respectively, with CV standing for the reduplicated syllable. Reduplication is not obligatory in this case, thus we can assume that there are two affixes -kÿu and -kÿu(punu), which can be accompanied by reduplication of the last syllable of the preceding stem (see ). Reduplication does not add any semantic content to the markers. The cislocative concurrent motion marker -kÿupunu is only sometimes accompanied by a reduplicated syllable, but the translocative associated motion -kuÿ is accompanied by a reduplicated syllable most of the times. Thus at least for the latter, we can possibly speak of “automatic reduplication”, defined as “reduplication that is obligatory in combination with another affix” , although reduplication is not obligatory but only highly preferred in this case. The case of continuouscontinuous|( marking is harder to classify. The reduplicated syllable is accompanied by material which presumably consists of two separate markers, -i and -ku/-ka. Those markers occur also elsewhere in the stem, -i as an extension applicative and -ku/-ka as a thematic suffix. It is the combination of reduplication with these two markers that expresses the continuous reading as in ( -1). For more examples of continuous marking, see .continuous|) tikusabenunuiku chisabenu\\ ti-kusabenu-nuiku chi-sabenu\\ 3i-play.flute-cont 3-flute\\ ‘he was playing the flute’ reduplication|)
summary: The passage says that while repetition occurs on verbs, nouns, and adjectives, true reduplication is found only on verbs, where it can express iterative, durative, and intensive aktionsart, and possibly inchoative meaning on stative verbs. On nouns, repeated syllables are mostly lexicalized, but when combined with the collective marker they indicate distributivity, and some verbal reduplication also appears with continuous or associated motion marking, though in these cases the reduplication is optional or only highly preferred and does not itself add meaning.

text: compounding|( Compounding and incorporation are both minor processes in Paunaka, at least as far as productivity of these processes is concerned. A number of body part terms result from compounding, but productive compounding is largely restricted to inalienably possessedinalienability nouns denoting plant parts attaching to plant names. One example is given in ( -compound). rupinupune\\ rupinu-pune\\ banana.sp-leaf\\ ‘banana leaf’ compounding|) incorporation|( Incorporation is largely restricted to plant- and body-part terms. The latter also belong to the class of inalienably possessedinalienability nouns at large. These nouns can incorporate into active and stative verb stemsverbal stem and combine with adjectives.adjective Some stative verbs have lexicalisedlexicalisation with a body-part term, and some of them even do not have forms without the incorporated noun. Ohers do, but have developed idiosyncratic meanings . ( -incorporation) illustrates a verb combining with the same noun -pune ‘leaf’ as ( -compound) above. bipÿrupune\\ bi-pÿru-pune\\ 1pl-burn-leaf\\ ‘we roasted the leaves’ incorporation|) As regards derivation, some processes show a certain productivity and are thus an\-a\-lys\-able. Examples have already been given as ( -1) and ( -2) in above. As far as derivational processes are an\-a\-lys\-able, they are discussed in the individual chapters on nouns, verbs, and other parts of speech. Other processes are totally opaque, often to the degree that they are not recognisable anymore.
summary:
In Paunaka, both compounding and incorporation are minor and only weakly productive processes. Compounding is largely limited to inalienably possessed nouns denoting plant parts attached to plant names, while incorporation mainly involves plant- and body-part terms, some of which are lexicalized in verb stems or have developed special meanings. 

The passage also notes that some derivational processes remain productive enough to be analyzable and are discussed in the relevant chapters, whereas others are completely opaque and no longer recognizable as derivational.

text: word class|( This section provides a very short overview of the different parts of speech. More complete descriptions are given in the following chapters. The most important distinction is between verbs as typical predicates and nouns as typical arguments of a clause. All other classes can be considered minor. Pronounspronoun and demonstrativesdemonstrative are closed classes. All others are open, and they can gain new members by borrowing, grammaticalisation, derivation etc. However, some classes certainly acquire new members more easily than others.
summary: The passage gives a brief overview of parts of speech, emphasizing that the key distinction is between verbs as typical predicates and nouns as typical arguments of a clause. It also notes that pronouns and demonstratives are closed classes, while the other classes are open and can gain new members through processes such as borrowing, grammaticalization, and derivation, though some open classes expand more easily than others.

text: noun|( Nouns typically express “the most time-stable concepts” in a language, and this is also the case in Paunaka. Paunaka distinguishes three classes of |( inalienably possessed, alienably possessed and non-possessable. Inalienablyinalienability possessed nouns obligatorily take a person marker that expresses the possessor.person marking However, non-possessed nouns can be derivedderivation from some of them. Alienablyalienability possessed nouns do not need a possessor, they can stand on their own. Some alienably possessed nouns can take a possessor marker without any further change, while others need to derive a possessable form first. summary:
Paunaka nouns are divided into inalienably possessed, alienably possessed, and non-possessable classes. Inalienably possessed nouns must take a person marker for the possessor, alienably possessed nouns may stand alone or take possession marking, and non-possessable nouns cannot be marked for possession directly, though some can indicate possession by juxtaposition.  

Plural marking is obligatory for human nouns and optional for non-human nouns, and nouns may also take diminutive, irrealis, deceased, and possibly past marking. In clauses, nouns mainly serve as arguments, can be modified inside noun phrases, show no case marking, and may also be used predicatively; new nouns are formed by compounding, classifier attachment, nominalization, and borrowing from Spanish and Bésiro.

summary: Verbs in this language mainly function as predicates and obligatorily inflect for person and reality status, with stative verbs marking irrealis by a prefix and active verbs marking irrealis through suffix alternations. Stative verbs are generally intransitive, while active verbs may be intransitive, transitive, or rarely ditransitive, and only active verbs allow causative, benefactive, and middle-voice mechanisms; there is no passive voice. The passage also notes that some Spanish past participles are borrowed as non-verbal predicates, and that verbs can serve as arguments when combined with a nominal demonstrative, forming a headless relative clause.

Paunaka has personal pronouns for first and second person singular and plural, but not for third person; third-person reference is instead expressed by nominal demonstratives or topic pronouns, including a special topic pronoun for inanimate obliques. The language has only a few true adjectives, since most properties are expressed by stative verbs, and most numerals except ‘one’ are borrowed from Spanish, with some showing a third-person marker -chÿ.  

The passage also notes borrowed and native quantifiers, adverbs expressing spatial, temporal, aspectual, and modal meanings, and connectives of mixed origin. text: The major word classes in Paunaka can be considered nouns and verbs, just like in many other languages around the world. They are large and open and described in detail in Chapters and , respectively. There are, however, also minor word classes, minor in the sense that they are rather small, with considerably fewer members. Only one of them can be considered absolutely closed, this is the pronouns and nominal demonstratives (§ ). Adpositions can also be considered a fairly closed class (see ). Among adjectives, numerals, and quantifiers ( ), adverbs ( ), and connectives ( ), however, we find loansborrowing from Spanish and Bésiro, which shows that these classes are open for new members.
summary: Paunaka has two major open word classes, nouns and verbs, which are large and central to the language. It also has several minor word classes: pronouns and nominal demonstratives are fully closed, adpositions are fairly closed, and classes such as adjectives, numerals, quantifiers, adverbs, and connectives are open enough to admit borrowings from Spanish and Bésiro.

summary:
The passage describes Paunaka pronouns, including personal, topic, nominal demonstrative, and a few indefinite pronouns, noting that indefinite pronouns are rare in discourse. Paunaka has first- and second-person singular and plural personal pronouns but no third-person personal pronoun; instead, third reference is typically expressed with topic or demonstrative pronouns, while demonstratives before nouns mainly mark definiteness and can also stand alone.

It also explains several formal overlaps among these forms: personal pronouns contain a person marker plus -ti, topic pronouns use a third-person marker with -bu, and some demonstratives and adverbs share prefixes or suffixes such as ne-, chÿ-, -ka, and -uku. The passage further notes a negative third-person pronoun chÿina and indefinite forms like chija ‘something, someone’ and juchubu ‘somewhere,’ which derive from question words.

The passage explains that personal pronouns are built from person markers plus the syllable *ti*, probably related to the non-possessed marker, and that they closely resemble forms in other Bolivian Arawakan languages. There is no third-person pronoun; instead, a topic pronoun or nominal demonstrative is used, and personal pronouns are mainly used for emphasis in preverbal position while still co-occurring with person marking on the verb.  

The text also notes that pronouns can take additional markers such as diminutive, additive, limitative, and tense/aspect/modality/evidential markers, including a special locative copular morpheme *-uku* used for predicating location. text: topic pronoun|( There are two topic pronouns, chibu and nebu. Both exclusively have third person referents, chibu is used with subjectssubject and objects,object the latter being exemplified by ( -top1), and nebu with obliques,oblique mainly locations, as in ( -top2). ( -top1) comes from María S. talking about the past. kuina punaina chija binika chibu biniku\\ kuina puna-ina chija bi-nika chibu bi-niku\\ neg other-irr what 1pl-eat.irr 3top.prn 1pl-eat\\ ‘there was nothing else that we could eat, this we ate’ ( -top2) comes from one of Juana’s descriptions of making a clay pot. i banau barerekiche nebu betuka yÿtÿuku binika\\ i bi-anau barerekiche nebu bi-etuka yÿtÿuku bi-nika\\ and 1pl-make big.pot 3obl.top.prn 1pl-put.irr food 1pl-eat.irr\\ ‘and we made big clay pots, there we could put the food and eat’ The term “topic pronoun” topicalisation|(focus|( has been chosen as a short label for a more complex issue. Prototypical topicstopic are encoded by person markersperson marking alone. The pronouns rather have to do with topicalisation of accessible, but non-topical participants, and chibu is also often used to indicate contrastive topics or focus. Both pronouns thus contribute to discourse cohesion. They always occupy the first position of a clause, which is associated with topicalisation or focus (see ). Chibu is found in more contexts than nebu and can partly be used to fill the gap in the paradigm of personal pronouns (see above). Considering chibu first, we can distinguish an endophoric – or more precisely ana\-phoric – and an exophoric use of the pronoun. In its anaphoric use, it takes up a referent mentioned, but only if there is low referential distance to the previous occurrence of it . In other words, the referent has been mentioned very shortly before. This can be the preceding clause or a left dislocated NP. In ( -1), there are two left-dislocated NPs,left dislocation which introduce the contrastive topics of the two coordinated clauses. They are both resumed by chibu, which serves as the co-nominal subject of the verbs. The example comes from Juana telling me how she learned different languages. The commas indicate clause boundaries by intonation. yeye Maritina, chibu timesumeikunÿ eka tiseteiku, i nÿuse Kuana chibu\\ timesumeikunÿ paunaka\\ yeye Maritina chibu ti-mesumeiku-nÿ eka tiseteiku i nÿ-use Kuana chibu ti-mesumeiku-nÿ paunaka\\ granny Martina 3top.prn 3i-teach-1sg dema Bésiro and 1sg-grandmother Juana 3top.prn 3i-teach-1sg Paunaka\\ ‘Mrs. Martina, she taught me Bésiro, and my grandmother Juana, she taught me Paunaka’ A similar example with a contrastive topic preceded by a left-dislocated subjectleft dislocation is ( -6). The left-dislocated subject is expressed by an unmarked headless relative clause in this case (tikuyaechi ubiae ‘the one who owns the house’). It is common that verbs of possession (with the attributive prefix) are used as arguments in Paunaka. The sentence also comes from Juana who was afraid that their landlord was betraying them, since they had to pay for electricity. “kue arkilaubina tikuyaechi ubiae chibu tisipuiku”, tikechu\\ kue arkilau-bi-ina ti-kuyae-chi ubiae chibu ti-sipuiku ti-kechu\\ if rent-1pl-irr.nv 3i-own-3 house 3top.prn 3i-pay 3i-say\\ ‘“if we rent (a house), the owner of the house, he pays (for electricity)”, she said’ In ( -7), the referent of chibu is mentioned in the preceding clause. This example also includes contrast. The two clauses, i.e. the one including the antecedent and the one with chibu referring to this antecedent, are produced by one and the same speaker in this case, but this is not necessarily the case. It is also possible to connect to an antecedent mentioned by another speaker with the pronoun. Chibu is the object of the clause in this case, but this only became apparent because María S. translated her sentence for me later on, it could also well be the subject (i.e. ‘he accompanied her to town’). The statement is about her sister Juana, who was the one who did the shopping in town for the family in the old days, buying soap and salt and other things that the family could not grow on their field. Later on, she founded her own family and then did the shopping for herself together with her husband. kakutu chima chibu chebaneupu uneku\\ kaku-tu chi-ima chibu chi-eibaneu-pu uneku\\ exist-iam 3-husband 3top.prn 3-pursue-dloc town\\ ‘when she had a husband, it was him whom she accompanied (going) to town’ One peculiarity is that in clauses that include chibu,person marking|( verbs with a third person subject and third person object are most often indexed by the person marker ti- for the subject and the person marker -chÿ for the object (insofar, ( -7) is exceptional). It is very unusual in general that this combination of indexes is used (see ), 3>3 relationships are normally encoded by the index chÿ-, see . One example of subject and object indexing by a combination of ti- and -chÿ is given in ( -15).person marking|) It comes from María C. who had just described how sorcerers killed her father. This sentence thus provides a kind of summary. chibu tikupakuchÿ\\ chibu ti-kupaku-chÿ\\ 3top.prn 3i-kill-3\\ ‘this killed him’ If the referent of chibu is the object, speakers generally prefer a cleftcleft|( construction. In this case, chibu is followed by a relative clause (see also ). This does neither mean that a cleft construction is demanded if chibu is the object, nor that a cleft construction is excluded if chibu is the subject, but a tendency is noticeable. ( -8) is an example of chibu used in a cleft construction. It comes from Juana who told me how some of her siblings died. tikutiukumÿnÿ Akustin, chibu echÿu nÿmijÿkubane Akustin\\ ti-kutiu-uku-mÿnÿ Akustin chibu echÿu nÿ-mijÿku-bane Akustin\\ 3i-be.ill-add-dim Agustín 3top.prn demb 1sg-raise-rem Agustín\\ ‘Agustín also got ill, he is the one I raised, Agustín’ cleft|) Chibu can also be used as the argument of a non-verbal predicate.non-verbal predication This is the case in ( -9), a sentence Miguel produced when telling me about the history of Santa Rita. chanaunubetu echÿu albanilnube echÿu ubiae chibu echÿu xhikuera\\ chÿ-anau-nube-tu echÿu albanil-nube echÿu ubiae chibu echÿu xhikuera\\ 3-make-pl-iam demb bricklayer-pl demb house 3top.prn demb
summary:
The passage describes two topic pronouns, **chibu** and **nebu**, both restricted to third person referents: **chibu** is used with subjects and objects, while **nebu** is used with oblique expressions, especially locations. Although labeled “topic pronouns,” they mainly mark topicalization of accessible but non-topical participants, contribute to discourse cohesion, and always occur clause-initially; **chibu** is more frequent and can also signal contrastive topics or focus.

For **chibu**, the text distinguishes an anaphoric use, where it resumes a recently mentioned referent, and an exophoric use. When **chibu** refers to an object, speakers often prefer a cleft construction, and in clauses with **chibu** there is a tendency for third-person subject and object indexing to appear as **ti-** and **-chÿ** rather than the more usual **chÿ-**.

text: school\\ ‘the bricklayers made the house, which is the school’ The pronoun can not only refer to a single aforementioned item, but also to whole situations. This is the case in ( -10). Juan C. had just explained that he would like to have a book which shows pictures of animals together with their names in Paunaka. Miguel uses chibu to refer to all the things he mentioned; the book, the drawings and the names. chakuyekena chibu echÿu tisumachunube eka donya Lena, donya Sintia\\ chÿ-a-kuye-kena chibu echÿu ti-sumachu-nube eka donya Lena donya Sintia\\ 3-irr-be.like.this-uncert 3top.prn demb 3i-want-pl dema hon Lena hon Swintha\\ ‘it will be like this, this is what Lena and Swintha want’ Chibu often occurs in sentences that sum up what has been said before. If used in such a way, chibu signals that a discourse topic is coming to an end. It anticipates the switch to a new discourse topic, as in ( -2) and ( -3), and is thus an important means of discourse organisation. In ( -2), María S. speaks about the scarcity of meat, when she was a child. She listed some crops her parents grew and explained that they made patasca, a thick stew. Chibu refers back to the stew, the clause finishes the food topic by expressing that this was an exhaustive listing. María S. reinforces this reading by closing the section with the stem kuye (abbreviated from the manner demonstrative verb chi-kuye) ‘it was like that’ or ‘that’s it’. Actually, in this specific case, María S. went on telling me that they ground peanuts, but this can be considered an addition, something that she had just remembered was missing in her account about nutrition in her childhood. tebuku esekeÿ banau pujukeke chibu biniku. kuye\\ ti-ebuku esekeÿ bi-anau pujukeke chibu bi-niku kuye\\ 3i-sow bean 1pl-make patasca 3top.prn 1pl-eat be.like.this\\ ‘they sowed beans, we made patasca, this we ate. text: nominal demonstrative|( Paunaka has three nominal demonstratives, eka ‘dema’, echÿu ‘demb’ and nechÿu ‘demc’. All of them can have exophoric and endophoric referents, and all can be used pronominally and adnominally without change of form. According to , “most languages use the same demonstrative forms in the position of independent pronouns and adjacent to a cooccuring noun”; this type of demonstrative has been called “nominal demonstrative” by . When used adnominally, the nominal demonstratives always precede the noun in Paunaka. There are no articles, neither definite nor indefinite ones, with which the nominal demonstratives could contrast. ( -intro) to ( -intro) show the pronominal use of the three demonstratives. In ( -intro), María S. uses eka (with plural marking) to refer to her aforementioned sisters who moved to town, thus the Supepí family does no longer live together in Santa Rita. depue tiyununube ekanube uneku\\ depue ti-yunu-nube eka-nube uneku\\ afterwards 3i-go-pl dema-pl town\\ ‘then they went to town (to live there)’ In ( -intro), Juana uses echÿu to refer to her aforementioned grandson for whom she cared. i trabakuyÿchina repente echÿu tanÿma tenikane\\ i trabaku-yÿchi-ina repente echÿu tanÿma ti-nika-ne\\ and work-lim2-irr.nv maybe demb now 3i-feed.irr-1sg\\ ‘and once he works, maybe he will support me’ ( -intro) comes from Clara repeating some information she just obtained from María C. aa kaku ubiae nechÿu\\ aa kaku ubiae nechÿu\\ intj exist house demc\\ ‘ah, there is a house there’ As can be seen in ( -intro), nechÿu is used in spatial contexts. This is explained in more detail in the end of this section. I first provide more information about eka and echÿu. In short, both of these demonstratives seem to have partly developed into definite articles,definiteness but speakers differ in which of the two is generalised. Because of this confusion, it has been impossible to find out in which feature(s) eka and echÿu contrast. They are both generally translated with a definite article throughout this work. The following examples show the adnominal use of the two nominal demonstratives. ( -intro-2) was produced by Juana when she collected loam in the vicinity of Santa Rita to make an earthen pot for her daughter. netuka eka muteji naka nichÿtiyae\\ nÿ-etuka eka muteji naka ni-chÿti-yae\\ 1sg-put.irr dema loam here 1sg-head-loc\\ ‘I will put the loam here on my head’ ( -intro-2) was produced by Miguel, when he told the story about the two hunters who meet the devil in the woods. The devil eats up all the animals they hunted. tibukubutuji echÿu chÿeche\\ ti-buku-bu-tu-ji echÿu chÿeche\\ 3i-finish-mid-iam-rprt demb meat\\ ‘the meat was finished, it is said’ (i.e. there was no meat left) As has been stated above, the semantic or functional distinction between eka and echÿu is not straightforward. Demonstratives usually “indicate the relative distance of an object, location or person vis-à-vis the deictic center” . Nonetheless, I never got the impression that distance plays a role in the speakers’ choice of one or the other nominal demonstrative. I had actually planned to spend some time on demonstrative elicitation on a fieldtrip that was originally scheduled for 2020, but could not take place due to the COVID pandemic. Thus I can only rely on the use of demonstrative as found in the corpus.corpus|( Unfortunately, I found that there is little concordance between the speakers in their usage of the two demonstratives. illustrates how different speakers use the nominal demonstratives eka and echÿu. The number of a speaker’s annotations, in which a demonstrative occurs is hereby correlated with the total number of annotations by that speaker. The whole transcribed part of the corpus is included, i.e. the count contains elicitation as well as more spontaneous speech. I counted only non-inflected uses of eka and echÿu. I only included the speakers for whom I have more than 500 annotations. Annotations are relatively short and comprise intonation units. One annotation unit may be a complete sentence, a clause or less than this, in some cases also more. However, average length of annotations is relatively consistent throughout the corpus. There are still shortcomings, e.g. especially in the beginning of the project, Spanish comments by the speakers were sometimes transcribed on the same tier as Paunaka speech. The corpus was never created to do statistical analyses, so I explicitly do not want to make any absolute claims here. Nonetheless, I think that this count is apt to show certain tendencies in the usage of the nominal demonstratives. What becomes apparent is that my three main consultants, Juana, Miguel and María S., use nominal demonstratives very differently: Juana prefers eka to echÿu, while Miguel uses echÿu more often than eka. Both seem to have (partly) grammaticalisedgrammaticalisation one demonstrative as a determiner, but not the same one. María S. on the other hand, does not use many demonstratives in general – the number of annotations with demonstratives is significantly lower for her than for any other of the speakers compared here. Given these differences, it is extremely hard to make any generalisations about the use of nominal demonstratives in general and about the distinction between eka and echÿu in particular. I had some hypothesis concerning the difference, but in trying to find proof of them in the corpus, I recognised that examples in favour often came from a single speaker and could not be confirmed with data from the others,corpus|) thus they remain speculative for the time being. It would thus definitely be necessary to do some video-recorded elicitation with each of the speakers, analyse the results for each of them individually, and check the results with their usage in larger portions of text, before possibly arriving at a more general classification. Eka and echÿu do not resemble the nominal demonstratives found in Baure or Terena in form, but they share some traits with the demonstrative and pronominal system found in Trinitario.Mojeño Trinitario|( Since I believe the Trinitario system may shed some light on the Paunaka one, I will provide a short comparison. The information about Trinitario is based on the descriptions
summary:
Paunaka has three nominal demonstratives, eka, echÿu, and nechÿu, which can function both pronominally and adnominally without changing form, with adnominal demonstratives always preceding the noun. There are no articles to contrast with them, and while eka and echÿu appear to have partly developed into definite articles, speakers differ in which form they generalize, making their exact functional distinction unclear.

Nechÿu is used in spatial contexts, while the usage of eka and echÿu varies considerably across speakers: Juana prefers eka, Miguel prefers echÿu, and María S. uses demonstratives less often overall. Because of this speaker variation and lack of consistent evidence, the author concludes that firm generalizations about the distinction between eka and echÿu are not yet possible.

text: by . Paunaka has two third person markersperson marking|( for verbs, ti- and chÿ-. They do not distinguish number or gender, but are used according to transitivity of the verb and person of the object (see ). On nouns, only chÿ- is used to mark third person possessors (see ). Like Paunaka, Trinitario has a third person marker ti-, which occurs in similar contexts as the Paunaka one.person marking|) However, in addition to ti-, Trinitario does not only have a single contrasting third person marker, but a whole set of different ones which distinguish gender, number and non-humanness. To give but one example, the feminine singular third person marker is su-. Person markers can also occur as free forms in Trinitario. They function as articles in this case, so su is the feminine singular article, and it is also analysed as the third person singular feminine root. Third person pronouns are derived from third person roots by prefixing e-, thus the third person singular feminine pronoun is esu. Turning back to Paunaka now, the demonstrative echÿu seems to be derived by the same principle; a prefix e- is attached to a third person root chÿ, which can also act as a third person marker on verbs and nouns (chÿ-). The difference to the Trinitario system is a) that chÿ- never occurs as a free form, b) that the Paunaka form also occurs adnominally (hence its analysis as a nominal demonstrative, not as a personal pronoun) and c) that a vowel u is added to the end of the demonstrative. In addition, the Paunaka demonstrative lacks the specificity in gender and number, but this is due to the presumed root chÿ not expressing this difference. As for the ending in u, this could actually be cognate to the demonstrative suffix -ro of Trinitario considering that the vowel *o of the common ancestor of both languages changed to u in Paunaka and that *r was lost . Demonstratives are construed with a prefix p- in Trinitario, to which a person root is added. Eight different demonstrative suffixes can be added optionally. Together with two other suffixes, -ro forms a subset. This subset works as “a speaker-centered distance-oriented three-term system” , with -ro being the marker that encodes medial distance. This also fits with the medial nominal and adverbial demonstrativeadverb!demonstrative adverbdemonstrative!demonstrative adverb nechÿu in Paunaka, which only takes a different prefix (see below). Turning to eka now, we can also find some similarities with Trinitario. Eka does not include a person marker, but just like echÿu, it has a prefix e-. The morpheme -ka is reminiscent of Trinitario -ka, which is the demonstrative suffix encoding proximate distance. This analysis is fostered by the form of the proximate adverbial demonstrativeadverb!demonstrative adverbdemonstrative!demonstrative adverb being naka ‘here’ in Paunaka. It seems thus plausible that eka encodes proximate and echÿu medial distance or that they once encoded this distinction and lost it at some point. If there was a medial demonstrative, a third demonstrative encoding distal distance would also be expected, but there is none in Pauanaka. According to , distance-neutral demonstratives are cross-linguistically rare, but do occur. Mojeño Trinitario|) Although their basic deictic functions thus remain unclear for the time being, it is noticeable that both eka and echÿu have further grammaticalisedgrammaticalisation|( into various directions. Both are used to introduce relative clauses,relative relation but echÿu is clearly preferred in this context (see ). Eka can be used as a complementiser, although this is only a marginal strategy in complementation (see ). Eka is also used as a filler in hesitation, especially by Juana, but generally, the question word chija ‘what, who’ more commonly fulfils this function. All three usages, relativisation, complementationcomplement relation and hesitation, are common in the grammaticalisation path of nominal demonstratives .grammaticalisation|) Furthermore, the demonstrative eka or more precisely the demonstrative demonstrative|( morpheme ka may have played a role in word formation. First, there is the non-verbal existential copulacopula|( kaku.non-verbal predication|( According to , non-verbal copulas can develop from demonstratives in identificational usage (i.e. uses of the kind “this is ...” or “here/there is ...”). The syllable ku, which is added to ka could be related to the locational suffix -uku, which can attach to personal pronouns (see above). The copula is mainly used to encode the existence of something (like Spanish haber), but also with reference to location (like Spanish estar), the latter is illustrated by ( -kaku-1), which is a statement by Juana about her daughter. kaku Espanya\\ kaku Espanya\\ exist Spain\\ ‘she is in Spain’ copula|) Second, apart from the existential copula, there is also a non-verbal predicate kapunu ‘come’. This one has probably arisen from the very same morpheme ka together with the associated motion marker -punu (see ). I suspect that it emerged as a presentational predicate (“here comes ...”), but has by now been extended to all contexts in which the action of coming is predicated to a third person referent, e.g. a questioninterrogative clause as in ( -kapunu-1), which comes from Juana telling me about the life of her sister. Some soldiers asked her sister about her husband. “¿kapunu pima?”\\ kapunu pi-ima\\ come 2sg-husband\\ ‘“did your husband come?”’ non-verbal predication|) In addition, ka also appears in the question word kajane ‘how many’, together with the distributive marker -jane (see ), as well as in the demonstrative adjective kana ‘this size’, which is always accompanied by a gesture showing the size (see ).demonstrative|) The demonstrative eka cannot be used if the referent is in a spatial relation to the rest of the clause. Echÿu is sometimes used together with a locative-marked noun by Miguel, but not so much by the other speakers. Instead of this, they mostly resort to nechÿu, which can be used together with a locative-marked noun or without one, the latter being the case in ( -DEMc). This example comes from Juana explaining the advantage of a fixed post in the market of Concepción, where she used to sell food. kuina tetukapu mutepa nechÿu\\ kuina
summary:
Paunaka has two third person markers, ti- and chÿ-, which do not mark number or gender and are used according to transitivity and object person; on nouns, only chÿ- marks third person possessors. Trinitario has a similar ti-, but also a larger set of third person forms that distinguish gender, number, and non-humanness, and its third person roots can also appear as free forms functioning as articles and as bases for pronouns.

The passage then compares Paunaka demonstratives eka and echÿu with Trinitario forms, suggesting that they may reflect proximate and medial deixis, though Paunaka lacks a clear distal counterpart. It also argues that these demonstratives have grammaticalized further, being used in relative clauses, complementation, hesitation, and even in the formation of non-verbal predicates such as the existential copula kaku and the predicate kapunu.

Nechÿu often refers to an item or object, but it can also refer to a place as in ( -DEMc) above. It is then usually place nounsplace noun that are combined with or anaphorically taken up by nechÿu, i.e. nouns that prototypically refer to places excluding toponyms . Nauku and naka mostly denote places expressed by both toponyms and place nouns. Consider ( -4), in which nechÿu is combined with a noun. Whether it is an adverb or a nominal demonstrative is not clear, it could be both. Translation by a nominal demonstrative sounds better in this case, but this does not tell us anything about the word class of the original language. The example comes from a story by Miguel about a lazy man, who does not make his field. As a consequence, his family has nothing to eat anymore, so he finally climbs a cusi palm (Attalea speciosa) and cuts off his limbs pretending they were cusi racemes. From up on the top of the palm, he tells his son to put the supposed raceme (the second leg he has cut off) into his basket. “pue ¡pinukaji nechÿu sÿkikÿyae!”\\ pue pi-nuka-ji nechÿu sÿki-kÿ-yae\\ well 2sg-put.irr-imp demc basket- -loc\\ ‘“well, put it into that basket!”’ Nechÿu is not used with exophoric referents that are very close to the speaker or far away as far as I can tell. In ( -4) above, nechÿu is used to indicate a location close to the addressee: The basket supposedly stands on the ground, thus close to the son. The demonstrative thus indeed seems to be related to medial distance. When used anaphorically, however, no distance distinctions are made as far as I can tell. I gloss nechÿu as ‘demc’ in this grammar, a gloss that suggests it is part of a paradigm together with the nominal demonstratives. This was a decision taken at some point, motivated by the similarity to echÿu, and by the fact that it often refers to items not to locations. However, I must admit at this point that I am insecure about this analysis. I suggest that there is considerable overlap in adverbial and nominal functions in this case, and propose there is a continuum from more nominal to more adverbial demonstratives, in which nechÿu occupies a middle position, see . A few more examples with nechÿu follow to illustrate the exophoric use of the demonstrative. In ( -1) and ( -5), it refers to something that is close to the speaker but not within the current interactional space. In ( -1), nechÿu occurs with the locative-marked NP nuinekÿyae chubiu bia ‘at the door of the church’. It most often refers to items or places at a medial distance, can be used both exophorically and anaphorically, and is sometimes even used with temporal meaning in the expression **tukiu nechÿu**. The author therefore glosses it as **demc** but remains uncertain about the analysis.

summary: The passage explains that the adverb **nauku** ‘there’ introduces a location into the discourse, the oblique topic pronoun **nebu** then refers back to that location in the next clause, and once the location has become topical, it is taken up again by the demonstrative **nechÿu**. In the example, all three forms are translated as “there” in English, but they play different discourse roles in marking the same location.

( -INDEF2) comes from Juana, who told me about her personal domain to speak Paunaka in the past: the way to the field she walked together with her sister María S. chija echÿu bimu cheiku chenekÿ bichujijikÿubÿu bitupubu asaneti\\ chija echÿu bi-imu chÿ-eiku chenekÿ bi-chujiji-kÿu-bu bi-tupu-bu asaneti\\ what demb 1pl-see 3-along? way 1pl-talk-am.conc.tr-mid 1pl-find-mid field\\ ‘what we saw along the way we talked about walking (until) we reached the field’ ( -INDEF2) is also from Juana. She was telling me about the journey of her grandparents back home from Moxos, where they had bought cows. juchubu kaku eka mÿiji tinikujane baka\\ juchubu kaku eka mÿiji ti-niku-jane baka\\ where exist grass 3i-eat-distr cow\\ ‘where there was grass, the cows ate’ It is relatively common cross-linguistically to use “bare interrogatives” as indefinite pronouns, i.e. interrogative pronouns that do not carry any derivational device . In this scenario, the indefinite use is always secondary to the interrogative use according to , which is why chija and juchubu are primarily analysed as question words throughout this work (see ). I also follow in presenting juchubu as an indefinite pronoun while it could also be considered an indefinite adverbadverb in a stricter sense. Use of the indefinite pronouns is relatively rare in Paunaka and they are usually accompanied by a relative clauserelative relation to provide some additional information (see also and Footnote in that section), thus the construction structurally resembles a content question including a question word very much, a sign that use of the question words as indefinite pronouns is not fully grammaticalised.grammaticalisation However, regarding the use of chija, a word of caution is necessary: speakers also use ¿chija? as a filler in hesitation (‘what was it?’), and it is thus not always clear which function the word has in a specific clause.question word|) This is the case in ( -INDEF1), which I elicited from María S. in order to speak about Juana, who was making her house in Concepción at that time. Although chija could well be an indefinite pronoun here semantically, intonation sets it apart from the rest of the sentence and it is preceded by a false start so it is probably rather to be analysed as a filler here: tisemaiku ti- ¿chija? tisuachi chubiupai\\ ti-semaiku ti- chija ti-isua-chi chÿ-ubiupai\\ 3i-search 3i- what 3i-weed.irr-3 3-plot\\ ‘she is looking for ¿what was it? someone to weed her plot’ In the other examples I give here chija is not set apart from the rest of the sentence by intonation, pauses or false starts, thus I am fairly confident that we are dealing with the indefinite pronoun rather than with any other use of the word. There may be more examples of the indefinite use that I have mistakenly taken to represent the use as filler. ( -INDEF3) includes the negative particle kuina. It is taken from María S.’s story about the two hunters who meet the devil in the woods. One man feeds the devil with the meat they hunted, but the devil does not fill up, thus finally, the man has to admit: “kuinabutu chija nenikapi”\\ kuina-bu-tu chija nÿ-nika-pi\\ neg-dsc what 1sg-feed.irr-2sg\\ ‘“there isn’t anything left that I could give you to eat”’ The next example also contains kuina and comes from the recordings made by Riester. Juan Ch. talks about his life in Retiro. kuina chija baejumikine, micha bubiu nakaja\\ kuina chija bi-a-ejumi-kene micha bi-ub-i-u naka-ja\\ neg what 1pl-irr-remember-emph2 good 1pl-be-subord-real here-emph1\\ ‘there is nothing to think about (i.e. complain about?), our living here is good’ It is possible that chija needs to be accompanied obligatorily by further material to be made more precise, this would explain why Juana adds echÿu in the following example. summary: Paunaka uses the interrogative words **chija** ‘what, who’ and **juchubu** ‘where’ as indefinite pronouns meaning ‘something/someone’ and ‘somewhere,’ respectively, but this use is secondary to their primary interrogative function. The indefinite use is relatively rare and often accompanied by a relative clause or other added material, suggesting it is not fully grammaticalised; **juchubu** can sometimes stand alone, while **chija** may be hard to distinguish from a hesitation filler.

text: adjective|( In this section, adjectives, numerals and quantifiers are described. The latter two are often subsumed under the former, but they differ from adjectives in some ways. There are only very few adjectives, since most property concepts are expressed by stative verbsstative verb ( ). Thus adjectives constitute a minor category in Paunaka. They express value, dimension, colour and shape. They are seldom used attributively in Paunaka, most of the time they occur as predicates. They are easily distinguished from verbs, since subject indexes do not precede the stem.person marking|( Indexes following the stem do not show up very frequently either, but this may be directly connected to adjectives having primarily third person referents. Occurrence of third person markers that follow the stem is very restricted in general (see ). The only adjective taking person markers from time to time is micha ‘good’ and the adjectives derived from it. The person marker follows the adjective in this case, which is just what we expect in non-verbal predication, see .person marking|) Micha and its derivations are also easily distinguishable from |( when negated,negation a verbal formverb of the word occurs, which makes micha suspicious of having been derived from a stative verb originally. As for other adjectives, a possibility to distinguish them from nouns is their behaviour when combining with classifiersclassifier|( (see ). If an adjective combines with a classifier, this classifier expresses a property (mostly shape) of the referent and thus it provides additional information about the referent. Nouns can also combine with classifiers, but the process resembles compounding and the product of the process is a new noun denoting a new referent. Adjectives are thus much more flexible in combining with a classifier than nouns, and they share this flexibility with the subgroup of descriptive stative verbsstative verb that can also take classifiers ( ). There are words, however, which are ambiguous as to whether they are nounsnoun|) or should rather be analysed as adjectives.classifier|) Numeralsnumeral|( are often defined as a subclass of adjectives, but there are features that distinguish them from adjectives in general. This is probably due to different functions of adjectives and numerals: “Whereas an adjective indicates a property of a noun, a numeral is not a property of the object itself but of a set of objects, often a nonce-property” . In Paunaka, the most important difference is that numerals often occur attributively, while adjectives can in general occur attributively, but do not do so very frequently. Nonetheless, numerals can also be used as predicates. The only numeral of presumably Paunaka origin is chÿnachÿ ‘one’, all numbers higher than ‘one’ have been borrowedborrowing from Spanish with different degrees of integration into Paunaka. The word for ‘other’, punachÿ is very similar to chÿnachÿ in the way it is composed. It is thus also treated in the section about numerals.numeral|) Both words probably contain the general classifier -na, which is also found on the adjectives (mu)temena ‘big’ and kana ‘this size’. Quantifiersquantifier are also described in this chapter, although they were priorly analysed as adverbs because they do not frequently modify nouns, but are more often used predicatively or adverbially. However, adjectives do not often occur as nominal modifiersmodification either. Semantically, quantifiers come close to numerals,numeral since both provide information about a quantity. The most frequently used quantifiers are loansborrowing from Bésiro. In the NP,noun phrase both quantifiersquantifier and numeralsnumeral can only precede the noun,word order while adjectives can also follow it, although the latter case could possibly be described as a kind of modification by a relative clause (see ). describes adjectives in more detail, is about numerals and the word for ‘other’ and discusses the quantifiers found in Paunaka.
summary:
The passage describes adjectives, numerals, and quantifiers in Paunaka, noting that adjectives form a small class because most property concepts are expressed by stative verbs. Paunaka adjectives typically occur as predicates rather than attributively, are distinguished from verbs by the absence of subject indexes, and can be distinguished from nouns by their more flexible combination with classifiers. 

Numerals and quantifiers are partly similar to adjectives but differ in distribution and function: numerals more often occur attributively and can also be predicative, while quantifiers are closer semantically to numerals but are more often used predicatively or adverbially. The text also notes that most numerals above ‘one’ are borrowed from Spanish, and many quantifiers are loans from Bésiro.

text: There are only a few adjectives in Paunaka, thus is dedicated to describing the ones that occur, while examines the different usages of adjectives as predicates, attributes, adverbs, and secondary predicates.
summary: Paunaka has only a small number of adjectives, so the discussion focuses on the adjectives that do occur. It also examines how adjectives are used as predicates, attributes, adverbs, and secondary predicates.

text: The most important adjectives are micha ‘good’, some derivations of micha, (mu)te\-mena ‘big’ and the demonstrative adjective kana ‘this size’. The most frequent among them is micha ‘good’. One example with it is ( -1), which is a statement by Miguel after having looked at a puzzle game that shows a story about a boy and his squirrel. michayu chÿnÿnÿikiu eka aitubuchepÿimÿnÿ\\ micha-yu chÿ-nÿnÿik-i-u eka aitubuchepÿi-mÿnÿ\\ good-ints 3-live-subord-real dema boy-dim\\ ‘the life of the little boy is very good’ Micha usually does not take a person marker,person marking|( with one exception: when meeting another person, people use a greeting formula including micha and a second person index. Literally, this is a questionpolar question about the condition of the other. The formulaic answer is without a person marker; see ( -micha-1), which is a little lecture of this convention (in Spanish) that Juana gave to Swintha. yo primero “¿michabi?” y usted me contesta “micha”\\ yo primero micha-bi y usted me contesta micha\\ I first good-2sg and you me answer good\\ ‘me first “¿michabi?” (= are you doing fine?) and you answer “micha” (= fine)’ person marking|) A number of other adjectives have been derivedderivation|( from micha; these are michana ‘nice’, which probably includes the general classifier, a further derivation michanabÿke ‘beautiful, pretty, handsome’ used in reference to people, which additionally takes the noun -bÿke ‘face’,incorporation michaniki ‘delicious’, which probably includes the verb stemverbal stem -nik(u) ‘eat’, and michamue ‘of sunny weather, sky without clouds’, which presumably includes the same sequence -mu that is also found in anÿmu ‘sky’ (as opposed to anÿke ‘up, above’). The proposed composition of these derived adjectives is found in ( -1) to ( -1), interlinear glosses of these words are usually not given in this detail in the remainder of this work. In ( -1), Juana talks about the house of an acquaintance in Austria. michana ubiae puru teka\\ micha-na ubiae puru teka\\ good- house mere brick\\ ‘the house is nice, (it has) mere bricks’ In ( -1), María S. corrects my use of michana in reference to a baby. michanabÿke\\ micha-na-bÿke\\ good- -face\\ ‘she is pretty’ ( -Pred-2) is a statement by María S. about the fish Juana is talking about. ja, michaniki\\ ja micha-nik-i\\ afm good-eat-?\\ ‘yes, it is delicious’ ( -1) was elicited from Juana. michamue\\ micha-mu-e\\ good- ?-?\\ ‘the weather (lit.: sky) is nice’ derivation|) A verbal form is preferredverb|( when these concepts are negated,negation see ( -micha-IRR-1) and ( -2). Since there are no lexical antonyms, this happens relatively frequently. I would suggest that micha originated as a stative verb in the first place, but in positive statements, person markers were lost at some point, which then led to a hybrid behaviour of the form. In ( -micha-IRR-1), Juana talks about her mother. i tanÿma kuina tamicha chiyuikia mimi\\ i tanÿma kuina ti-a-micha chi-yuik-i-a mimi\\ and now neg 3i-irr-good 3-walk-subord-irr mum\\ ‘and by that time my mother couldn’t walk well (lit.: her walking was not good) anymore’ ( -2) is about the school building in Santa Rita, which was in a miserable state. A new building was thus constructed. kuina tamichana echÿu, tikebupu echÿu\\ kuina ti-a-michana echÿu ti-kebu-pu echÿu\\ neg 3i-irr-nice demb 3i-rain-dloc demb\\ ‘it wasn’t good, it dripped in’ verb|) I have also found one example in which michanabÿke takes a first person index preceding the stem in a positive sentence, another proof for the semi-verbal behaviour of these adjectives. In this example, ( -2), Juana cites the water spirit whom their grandparents met on their way back home from Moxos, where they had bought some cows. The water spirit wanted to lure away Juana’s grandfather from his wife by appearing to him at night and telling him his wife was ugly and she was beautiful. It is not clear to me why Juana used the reportive -ji on the connective chijikiu ‘however’, since I believe this word belongs to the quoted speech. “chÿjikiuji bien nimichanabÿke”, dice\\ chÿjikiu-ji bien ni-michanabÿke dice\\ however-rprt well 1sg-beautiful she.says\\ ‘“however, I am very beautiful”‘ she says On the other hand, I have also found one non-verbal form of micha with irrealis RS in the corpus, which is presented in ( -micha-IRR-2). There are a few more examples with derived forms taking the non-verbal irrealis marker, like the one in ( -1). ( -micha-IRR-2) was produced by María S. and directed to me to say farewell. ¡michaina pibÿbÿkupunia!\\ micha-ina pi-bÿbÿkupun-i-a\\ good-irr.nv 2sg-fly.back-subord-irr\\ ‘may your flight back be good!’ ( -1) comes from Juana. There had been heavy rainfalls and the road where she lived was very muddy, but the forecast had announced that rain would stop for a while. Note that Juana incorrectly uses the incompletive marker -kuÿ here instead of the discontinuous marker -bu, but she corrected herself in the utterance that immediately followed. michamuenatu te tajaitu kuinakuÿ tikeba\\ michamue-ina-tu te tajaitu kuina-kuÿ ti-keba\\ of.good.weather-irr.nv-iam seq tomorrow neg-incmp 3i-rain.irr\\ ‘the weather will be nice now, tomorrow it won’t rain anymore’ In summary, micha and its derivations have a verbalverb and a non-verbal form. Choice is sensitive to reality status, with realis triggering a non-verbal and irrealis a verbal realisation. However, the correlation is not perfect, there are a few counter-examples in the corpus. A second relatively frequent adjective is temena/mutemena ‘big’. Both forms can be used interchangeably without any difference in meaning. Juana clearly prefers temena, Miguel mutemena and María S. seems to use both equally frequently. The last syllable na probably goes back to the general classifier -na (see ), it detaches when another classifier is added (see below). ( -1) is an example of the form mutemena used by María S. in making jokes with Swintha. The other examples in this section all include the shorter form temena. aja, mutemena pichubatÿi\\ aja, mutemena pi-chubatÿi\\ afm big 2sg-buttocks\\ ‘yes, your butt is big’ When the collectivecollective|( marker is attached to the adjective (as well as to other adjectives and verbs that end in na), the last syllable is usually repeated. summary: The passage describes several important adjectives, especially *micha* ‘good’, *temena/mutemena* ‘big’, and the demonstrative adjective *kana* ‘this size’. It shows that *micha* and its derivatives often behave partly like verbs: they can appear in verbal and non-verbal forms, with realis contexts tending to trigger non-verbal realization and irrealis contexts triggering verbal realization, though there are some exceptions. It also notes that *temena* and *mutemena* are interchangeable in meaning, with the final *-na* probably related to a general classifier.
