Both were elicited from Juana. temekiji anibÿ\\ teme-ki-ji anibÿ\\ big- -col mosquito\\ ‘the mosquitos are big’ temepuneji\\ teme-pune-ji\\ big-leaf-col\\ ‘big leaves’ Kanademonstrative adjective|( ‘this size’ is a demonstrative adjective that is always accompanied by a gesture showing the size. One example is ( -whip), which comes from Miguel, who was speaking about the whip of his teacher back in the old days when he went to school in Altavista. kaku echÿu asotera chija bitÿpi echÿu, kana echÿu, chimusuji eka baka\\ kaku echÿu asotera chi-ija bi-tÿpi echÿu kana echÿu chi-musuji eka baka\\ exist demb whip 3-name 1pl-obl demb this.size demb 3-skin dema cow\\ ‘he had what we call an azotera (= whip), it was of this size (showing with hands), made from cowhide’ As is the case with (mu)temena, the last syllable of kana is repeated when a collective marker is added, see ( -kana-1) from Juana, where she speaks about some shells she needs for polishing a clay pot. kananaji micha sipÿ\\ kana-na-ji micha sipÿ\\ this.size-rep-col good shell\\ ‘very big like this, the shells’ adjective|) Apart from the adjectives presented up to here, there are a few more words that express qualities, and it is sometimes hard to decide whether they are nouns or adjectives. Consider the expressions of age such as chubui ‘old man; old (male)’ and juberÿpu ‘old woman; old (female)’ as well as sepitÿ or chepitÿ ‘child, offspring; small, little’. I treat chubui and juberÿpu as nouns in this grammar, and sepitÿ/chepitÿ as noun or adjective, depending on the context. I admit there is ambiguity in the decisions I made. There are simply no good criteria to arrive at a clear decision. Like adjectives, chubui, juberÿpu and sepitÿ/chepitÿ often occur predicatively. However, they also frequently head an NP.head In addition to these criteria, sepitÿ/chepitÿ can also take the limitative marker -jiku and is then often used adverbially. In reference to non-singular participants, speakers may also use sese-ji instead of sepitÿ, which is probably derivedderivation from the same root se. This word, however, is usually realised as sesejinube with the fixed meaning ‘children’, while other more adjective-like uses are very rare. Some examples that point to the words for ‘small’ being adjectives are given below. In ( -1), Juana uses sepitÿ to contrast small and big clay pots. sepitÿ i temena\\ sepitÿ i temena\\ small and big\\ ‘small ones and big ones’ ( -2) is a statement by María S. about a tortoise. sepitÿmÿnÿ chikebÿke\\ sepitÿ-mÿnÿ chi-kebÿke\\ small-dim 3-eye\\ ‘its eyes are small’ In ( -1), María S. makes use of sese-ji- in speaking about some fruits that still have to ripen. sesejikuÿmÿnÿ nikechubi\\ sese-ji-kuÿ-mÿnÿ ni-kechu-bi\\ small-col-incmp-dim 1sg-say-2sg\\ ‘they are still very small as I said to you’ ( -2) was elicited from Juana and comes from the same context as ( -big-3) above. It seems that the general classifier shows up on this form together with an incorporated noun.incorporation|( Due to lack of more examples with classifiers or nouns being attached to the stem, I cannot make any judgements about this being grammatical or not. It seems strange though considering that other adjectives usually drop -na when they combine with another classifier or noun. sesepunenaji\\ sese-pune-na-ji\\ small-leaf- ?-col\\ ‘very small leaves’ incorporation|) Other adjectives are enui ‘green, not ripe, raw’ and the borrowedborrowing colour terms asuru ‘blue’ and amariyo ‘yellow’. All of them occur extremely infrequently in the corpus and none of them takes classifiers.classifier The reason to treat them as adjectives is a purely semantic one. The terms for ‘white’ -kipÿpa and ‘black’ -pisÿ are stative verbs. The term for ‘red’, tisi, is most probably a verb, too (thus its form is actually ti-(i?)si 3i-be.red). It is shorter than other colour terms, and it never occurs with reference to a first or second person in the corpus (and attempts to elicit such forms failed). However, Mojeño Trinitario has a cognate form -itsi, which is clearly a verb (Rose 2021, p.c.). Kachu- ‘big and round’, possibly related to kana ‘this size’, occurs twice in the corpus and takes a classifier or inalienably possessed noun,incorporation the latter is the case in ( ) which comes from Juana who produced it in elicitation with some pictures. isijibÿ, kachujibÿ eka tarupe\\ isijibÿ kachu-jibÿ eka tarupe\\ flower big.round-flower dema flower.sp\\ ‘a flower, the taropé (Dorstenia brasiliensis) has a big and round blossom’
summary: The passage describes how some adjective-like forms in the language combine with collective markers, classifiers, or incorporated nouns, but not always in a straightforward way. Repetition appears to occur automatically with the collective marker in forms like *(mu)temena* and *kana*, rather than adding a clear meaning of its own, while some adjectives lose *-na* when combined with classifiers or body-part terms. It also notes that several words for age, size, and color are difficult to classify consistently as nouns, adjectives, or verbs, with some used predicatively, some as noun heads, and some—especially color terms—treated as stative verbs or verbs.

text: Adjectives are used predicativelyattributive clause|( most of the time, which is evident from the examples given above. If there is a noun in the sentence to which the property is predicated, the adjective usually comes first, then comes the NP. ( -Pred-3) and ( -Pred-1) provide two examples of this. Adjectives are also often the only constituent of a clause. In ( -Pred-3), Juana speaks about a bird of prey that once stole her dog. temena echÿu sia\\ temena echÿu sia\\ big demb hawk.sp\\ ‘the hawk is big’ ( -Pred-1) comes from a listing of different crops by María C. michanikiyuku echÿu papayu\\ michaniki-yu-uku echÿu papayu\\ delicious-ints-add demb papaya\\ ‘papayas are delicious, too’ attributive clause|) Adjectives are seldom used attributivelymodification|( in free speech. One spontaneous example with an attributive adjective is ( -ATTR-1). Juana talks about the making of pasture by the people from Santa Rita in exchange for the construction of their reservoir. i echÿu max temenanaji yÿkÿke kapunu makina, motosierra chibu\\ i echÿu max temena-na-ji yÿkÿke kapunu makina motosierra chibu\\ and demb more big-rep-col tree come machine chain.saw 3top.prn\\ ‘and the biggest trees, a machine came, a chain saw more precisely’ An example including the demonstrative adjective kana used as an attribute is ( -new-ATTR-1). summary:
Paunaka has only one apparently native numeral, chÿnachÿ ‘one,’ whose form may be analyzable into elements related to person marking, a classifier, and possibly a restrictive or limitative suffix. This numeral is used not only for counting but also with indefinite-article-like meanings, limitative forms, and an exclamatory expression, and it can combine with tense/aspect/modality markers.

All numerals above ‘one’ are borrowed from Spanish. Some of these borrowed numerals, especially ‘two’ and often ‘three,’ may take the suffix -chÿ, while higher numerals show this less consistently; ‘two’ is also phonologically adapted into Paunaka as ruschÿ.

The passage distinguishes several quantifiers by degree and countability: *pario* ‘some/a bit’ and *pariki* or *musume* ‘many/a lot’ for countable items, *chama* ‘much, a lot’ mainly for non-countable things, and *pasayu* as a less frequent alternative. text: adverb|( Adverbs typically form a large heterogeneous class. They have been described as “a ‘catch-all’ category” that lumps together “ ny word with semantic content (i.e., other than grammatical particles) that is not clearly a noun, a verb, or an adjective” . Adverbs typically modify, but unlike adjectives, they do not primarily modify nouns but verbs, adjectives,adjective other adverbs, nouns and full clauses . The adverbs of Paunaka are not marked for personperson marking or for number and they do not take the locative marker -yae, either. They cannot occur as arguments of a verb and they are never modifiedmodification by a nominal demonstrative. This definition excludes some locative words which are often used adverbially, but are rather analysed as nouns due to their ability to occur with the locative marker or as an argument of a verb. -1.3ptAdverbs can be subdivided into subclasses depending on their semantics. There are spatial ( ), temporal and aspectual ( ), and modal ( ) adverbs. The different subclasses of adverbs can take different modal, temporal, aspectual and/or other markers.
summary:
Adverbs are a heterogeneous class often defined as words with semantic content that are not clearly nouns, verbs, or adjectives. In Paunaka, they are uninflected for person or number, do not take the locative marker -yae, cannot function as verb arguments, and are not modified by nominal demonstratives; this excludes some locative words that are better analyzed as nouns.

Adverbs are classified semantically into spatial, temporal/aspectual, and modal subclasses, and these subclasses may take different modal, temporal, aspectual, or other markers.

text: locative|( Locative adverbs provide clues about the spatial setting of an event. They definitely comprise the demonstrative adverbsadverb!demonstrative adverb|(demonstrative!demonstrative adverb|( naka ‘here’ and nauku ‘there’, i.e. not here, (far) away, see ( ). What exactly is perceived as “here” varies, as it does in other languages, and largely depends on the situational “engagement area” of a speaker, i.e. the space that she is currently focused on by paying attention to this space and acting in it . In addition, there is another demonstrative, nechÿu glossed as ‘demc’, with the approximate meaning of ‘in that place, there’, i.e. in an identifiable place of mostly medial distance. Nechÿu has nominal and adverbial properties. This has been described in more detail in . The locative adverbs are given in . In ( ), Juana uses two demonstrative adverbs. She speaks about a relocation within the city of Santa Cruz after her grandson finished his premilitary service. tukiu nauku tanÿma bibÿsÿu naka\\ tukiu nauku tanÿma bi-bÿsÿu naka\\ from there now 1pl-come here\\ ‘from there we came here now’ The demonstrative adverbs (including nechÿu) can be used on their own or be accompanied by a noun phrase that specifies the exact location. In ( ), the location meant by naka is shown by a gesture, thus no NP co-occurs. Naka refers to the belly of the María C. in this case, where a sorcerer had introduced a frog. ani naka peÿ\\ ani naka peÿ\\ look here frog\\ ‘look, here a frog’ In ( ) María C. specifies what she means by naka with a prepositional phrase. On the other hand, none of them is modified by nominal demonstratives in the corpus, which might be a hint that they are adverbs rather than nouns. summary: Locative adverbs in the language indicate spatial setting and include demonstratives such as naka ‘here’, nauku ‘there, away’, and nechÿu ‘in that place’, whose exact meaning depends on the speaker’s engagement area and the situation. These forms can occur alone or with a noun phrase or prepositional phrase specifying location, and nauku may either refer to an unspecified distant place or, when origin is relevant, to a specific place outside the speaker’s current sphere. The passage also notes that some other spatial words, such as nujekÿ ‘inside’, nekupai ‘outside’, anÿke ‘up’, and apuke ‘down/ground’, do not fit neatly into noun or adverb categories, since they show mixed nominal and adverbial behavior.

text: temporal/aspectual|( Temporal and aspectual adverbs comprise those words that provide information about the temporal setting of an event, its internal constituency or its relation to another event. lists the temporal and aspectual adverbs. In addition, there are a few more words referring to times of the day that are probably rather nouns than adverbs, although they are used adverbially most of the time. Among them are mane ‘morning’, tose ‘noon, midday’, kupei ‘afternoon’ (also used with the meaning ‘late’ as its equivalent tarde in Spanish), yuti ‘night’. Mane, kupei and yuti can be modified by a nominal demonstrative, but this happens rarely. Tose occurs with the locative marker -yae once in the corpus. The word for ‘day‘, tijai, is a stative verb, and so are the words derivedderivation from it, e.g. tijaikenekÿu ‘dawn’, tajaitu ‘tomorrow’ or tajaibÿti with the idiomatic meaning ‘see you tomorrow/another day'. Theiamitive|( adverb metu ‘already’ is used very frequently and probably the source for the iamitive marker -tu (see ). Just like the iamitive marker,iamitive|) metu can be used both when an event is completed, ( ), and when it is ongoing at the moment in question, ( ), with or without a connotation of earliness. Thus, depending on the specific context and the aktionsart of the predicate, ‘now’ is sometimes a more appropriate translation than ‘already’. Metu always precedes the predicate. ( ) was elicited from María S. and refers to an imagined pot. nimutu metu terabajikutu\\ ni-imu-tu metu ti-rabajiku-tu\\ 1sg-see-iam already 3i-break-iam\\ ‘when I saw it, it was already broken’ ( ) is a statement by Juana about herself. nÿti metu juberÿpunÿtu\\ nÿti metu juberÿpu-nÿ-tu\\ 1sg.prn already old.woman-1sg-iam\\ ‘I am old already/now’ Equally frequent is tanÿma ‘now’. This adverb might have originated from a stative verb, the initial t being a fixed third person marker, and -nÿma an associated motion marker (see ). However, the word is totally lexicalised. When a morpheme is added, especially -yu, the first syllable is usually dropped today, resulting in a form nÿmayu. In the recordings by Riester, we find the full form tanÿmayu. Nÿmayu is punctual and best translated as ‘just’. ( ) is a statement by María S. which refers to me having changed the position of my chair a bit because the sun was shining on me. When I was sitting in the shade again, she said: michatu tanÿma\\ micha-tu tanÿma\\ good-iam now\\ ‘now it is good’ ( ) comes from Juana and refers to the work the people of Santa Rita did for a lady from Germany in exchange for the construction of the reservoir. juu nÿmayu tijaipai tiyununubetu techikanube\\ juu nÿmayu ti-jai-pai ti-yunu-nube-tu ti-echika-nube\\ intj just 3i-be.light- 3i-go-pl-iam 3i-fell.tree.irr-pl\\ ‘oh, when it just began to dawn (lit.: there was just light on the ground), they already went to fell trees’ The adverb (u)chuine is used if the point in time is not considered as “now” because the event expressed by the verb is completed, but it is still perceived as something in the very recent past, as in ( ). The word is only used to refer to points in time of the current day.past reference It may be derivedderivation from the uncertain future marker uchu ‘some day (perhaps, in an uncertain future)’ (see ), at the same time it resembles the adverb ukuine ‘yesterday, some day in the recent past’, which also refers to a recent past, but less recent than the current day, see ( ). The translation with ‘yesterday’ is not very precise, since ukuine can also refer to the day before yesterday or another day in the recent past. However, most of the times it is used to refer to the day preceding the current day. ( ) is a statement by Juana about her daughter including uchuine. uchuine chÿnachÿtu ora tichujiku tukiu nauku\\ uchuine chÿnachÿ-tu ora ti-chujiku tukiu nauku\\ just.now one-iam hour 3i-speak from there\\ ‘just an hour ago she talked from there (on telephone)’ ( ) contains ukuine and also comes from Juana, who tells me about the source of her knowledge about her brother’s health. chikuetea chijinepÿi ukuine\\ chi-kuetea chi-jinepÿi ukuine\\ 3-tell 3-daughter yesterday\\ ‘his daughter told it yesterday (or a few days ago)’ In addition, (u)kuinebu refers to points in time in an intermediate pastpast reference which may be some days ago, but also some weeks or months ago, as in ( ), which was recorded in April and the event that Juana is referring to happened some months ago: some friends of the daughter who live in Argentina came to visit her over New Year and brought some coffee as a present. nauku Argentina tupununube uikuinebu\\ nauku Argentina ti-upunu-nube uikuinebu\\ there Argentina 3i-bring-pl some.time.ago\\ ‘they brought it from Argentina some time ago’ The adverbs tanÿma and (u)chuine can be intensified by a marker -paiku/a, which narrows the possible time frame. ( ) comes from Miguel who told us a story, while we sat to eat and relax a bit on our visit to Altavista. ... tiyuna paseana nenabi biti tanÿmapaiku\\ ti-yuna pasea-ina nena-bi biti tanÿma-paiku\\ 3i-go.irr stroll-irr.nv like-1pl 1pl.prn now-punct\\ ‘... he will go on a jaunt like we are doing right now’ In ( ), María S. asks me about my arrival in Santa Rita that day. ¿chuinepaiku pitupunubu?\\ chuine-paiku pi-tupunubu\\ just.now-punct 2sg-arrive\\ ‘you have just arrived?’ The adverb maneiku ‘soon’ is probably derivedderivation from mane ‘morning’. It is used very infrequently. One example is given in ( ), where Juana makes a statement about my departure to Germany being close in contrast to Swintha’s, who had plans to stay a bit longer. asi max temprano piyunupuna, maneiku piyuna\\ asi max temprano pi-yunupuna maneiku pi-yuna\\ so more early 2sg-go.back.irr soon 2sg-go.irr\\ ‘so you go back earlier, you go soon’ Janeka ‘never’ seldom shows up in the corpus, but one example from Juana is given below. It is not clear to me why she uses realis RS here. She speaks about the pot she was going to make with the clay she had just collected.
summary: The passage describes temporal and aspectual adverbs that locate events in time, characterize their internal structure, or relate them to other events. It highlights several time-of-day words that are often used adverbially, and it notes that adverbs such as *metu* ‘already’, *tanÿma* ‘now’, *(u)chuine* ‘just now/recently today’, and *ukuine* / *(u)kuinebu* ‘yesterday/recently/long ago’ differ in how recent or completed the relevant event is, with some forms able to be intensified to narrow the time frame.

It expresses that something that has been expected is completed after a time span that is considered (too) long, as in ( ), where Juana’s daughter finally calls her boss to accompany her to the airport and speak to the people in charge to put in a good word for her sister who had arrived to Spain without a valid visa. abane chichujiku te tiyununubetu\\ abane chi-chujiku te ti-yunu-nube-tu\\ finally 3-speak seq 3i-go-pl-iam\\ ‘finally she spoke to him and they went (to the airport)’ temporal/aspectual|)
summary: The passage explains two temporal expressions: **janeka**, meaning “never,” as in an example glossed ‘nobody ever breaks it,’ and **abane**, meaning “finally.” **Abane** indicates that an expected event is completed after a time span felt to be too long, illustrated by an example where someone finally speaks and then goes to the airport.

text: modal|( Modal meanings are seldom expressed by adverbs, since most information of this kind is marked on the predicate or more rarely other constituents of the clause (see ). However, a few modal adverbs are used in Paunaka and they are given in . Repente is a loanborrowing from Spanish de repente ‘maybe’ (also ‘suddenly’, which is also another meaning of the Paunaka word, but less frequently). It is more or less synonym with the uncertainty marker (-)kena, which expresses uncertainty (see ). Kena is phonologically bound to another word most of the time, and it can also attach to repente. Repente has some variants pente and depente, but they are less frequent than repente. ( ) offers one example of the adverb, which comes from Miguel when talking with María C. about her husband, who was ill. pero repentekena michaupunu punachina semana\\ pero repente-kena micha-upunu punachÿ-ina semana\\ but maybe-uncert good-reg other-irr week\\ ‘but maybe he has recovered (lit.: is good again) next week’ Theavertive|( adverb nakayenetu/nakayenetÿini ‘almost’ is complex,derivation at least as its ending is concerned. It contains either the iamitive marker -tu or the avertive marker -tÿini (see for iamitive aspect and for avertive modality). As for the rest of the word, naka could derive from the demonstrative adverb (see above), and yene could relate to the deductive marker -yenu ( ), but this is speculative. In any way, the difference between both variants of the adverb is that nakayenetu is proximate, i.e. the event is temporally close and realisable, while nakayenetÿini is avertive, i.e. the event was imminent but did not occur. ( ) is one example of the proximate use of the adverb. Juana answers my question here, when they were going to eat. nakayenetu toseina binika\\ nakayenetu tuse-ina bi-nika\\ almost noon-irr.nv 1pl-eat.irr\\ ‘we will eat just before noon’ ( ) gives one example of the avertive version of the adverb. Juana was searching for the Paunaka name for ‘deer’, there must have been one and it must have sounded similar to yÿnÿ ‘jabiru’ (a bird: Jabiru mycteria). nakayenetÿini chija eka nikecha yÿnÿ\\ nakayenetÿini chi-ija eka ni-kecha yÿnÿ\\ almost 3-name dema 1sg-say.irr jabiru\\ ‘I would have almost said yÿnÿ (i.e. jabiru) is its name’ avertive|) modal|) adverb|) The following section describes prepositions.
summary:
The passage says that modal meanings in Paunaka are usually expressed on the predicate rather than by adverbs, but it identifies a few modal adverbs. Among them, **repente** is a Spanish loan meaning ‘maybe’ (also ‘suddenly’) and is largely synonymous with the uncertainty marker **-kena**, which can even attach to **repente**; the adverb has less frequent variants **pente** and **depente**.  

It also describes the avertive adverb **nakayenetu/nakayenetÿini** ‘almost,’ whose ending likely contains the iamitive or avertive marker, though the rest of its form is speculative. The two variants differ in meaning: **nakayenetu** is proximate, referring to something temporally close and still possible, while **nakayenetÿini** is avertive, referring to something that was imminent but did not happen.

text: preposition|( oblique|( There are four words that can be analysed as prepositions, they are given in . These prepositions are used to mark constituents as obliques (see ). They encode an instrument, a causer,instrument/cause source, benefactive,beneficiary aim or resultaim/result, recipient or a comitative relation. Typical examples for the prepositions are given in ( -preps.1) to ( -preps.4). As illustrated by these examples, prepositions are always placed before the NPnoun phrase|( they are related to. Nonetheless, not all of them necessarily occur together with an NP: if they take a first or second person marker,person marking|( no NP shows up with the preposition, and if they take a third person marker, an NP is optional. The source preposition tukiu is never marked for person. Consequently, it always occurs together with a noun or an adverb. The comitative preposition -aj(i)echubu is always marked for person. The instrument/cause preposition -keuchi is normally person-marked and only rarely drops a third person index. As regards (-)tÿpi, first and second person markers are obligatory, while the third person marker usually alternates with an NP, although sometimes there is both a third person index on the preposition and an NPnoun phrase|) following it, especially if the referent is human.person marking|)animacy In addition to the prepositions presented in this section, Paunaka makes use of a few words that express specific spatial relations to a referent. This is often achieved by using adpositions in other languages, but in Paunaka these words are better analysed as relational nouns,relational noun|( since they obligatorily take the locative marker to specify that a spatial relation is expressed (see ). If a noun is juxtaposed to the relational noun, it can be regarded its possessor. The possessor noun does not take the locative marker. In contrast to relational nouns, the locative marker is never attached to the prepositions, not even to tukiu, which is used to mark source expressions, i.e. a spatial relation. However, the noun that tukiu relates to can take the locative marker. This is illustrated in ( ) and ( ). In ( ) the locative marker is attached to the noun following the preposition and the preposition itself is unmarked. In ( ), the locative marker is attached to the relational noun and its possessor is unmarked.relational noun|) ( ) was produced by Miguel in talking with Juan C. about their past. ja bibÿsÿupunu tukiu Turuxhiyae sinkuenta i dos\\ ja bi-bÿsÿupunu tukiu Turuxhi-yae sinkuenta i dos \\ afm 1pl-come from Altavista-loc fifty-two \\ ‘well, we came from Altavista in 52’ ( ) also comes from Miguel and refers to the picture in the frog story in which the dog stands on a log (and the boy leans over that log). tijipuikutuji chÿineyae echÿu yÿkÿke\\ ti-jipuiku-tu-ji chÿ-ine-yae echÿu yÿkÿke\\ 3i-jump-iam-rprt 3-top-loc demb tree\\ ‘it has jumped on top of the log, it is said’ The degree of grammaticalisation of the prepositions differs with the verbal origin being still recognisable in the instrument/cause preposition -keuchi and the comitative -aj(i)echubu, while the sources of the prepositions (-)tÿpi and tukiu are not clear. This will be explained in more detail in the sections that follow. The source preposition tukiu is described in , the many different functions of the general oblique marker (-)tÿpi are illustrated in , the instrument and cause preposition -keuchi is described in , and finally is dedicated to the least grammaticalised adpostion, the comitative marker -aj(i)echubu.
summary:
Paunaka has four prepositions that mark oblique constituents and can express roles such as instrument, cause, source, benefactive, recipient, comitative, and aim/result. These prepositions normally precede the noun phrase they relate to, but person marking can replace or optionally accompany an NP depending on the preposition; the source preposition tukiu never takes person marking, while the comitative and instrument/cause markers usually do, and (-)tÿpi shows mixed behavior.  

The language also has relational nouns for spatial relations, which obligatorily take a locative marker, unlike prepositions, whose own form never carries locative marking; in such constructions, the noun linked to tukiu may take the locative marker, or a noun may function as the possessor of a relational noun. text: source|( The preposition tukiu introduces source expressions and thus occurs a lot in sentences describing motion events. It never takes a person marker.person marking ( ) was provided by María S. and referred to a present I gave her. tukiu Alemania pupunu\\ tukiu Alemania pi-upunu\\ from Germany 2sg-bring\\ ‘you brought it from Germany’ The initial t of the preposition could be a hint that it derivesgrammaticalisation from a verb inflected with the third person marker ti-, u we also find in the defective verb -ubu ‘be, live’. The sequence kiu resembles what we find in deranked verbs, a thematic suffix + subordinate marking, but then again, deranked verbs rather take the third person marker chÿ- instead of ti- (see ). Tukiu is usually preposed to a noun or a locative adverb adverb|(, especially naka ‘here’ and nauku ‘there’. Locative adverb and noun also often combine to yield a more precise source expression. If there is a noun in the source expression, it can take the locative marker -yae, but this is not always the case. Adverbs never take this marker.adverb|) In ( ), the toponymtoponym|( noun in the source expression bears the locative marker. The example is from María C.’s account about her life. She was once very ill and went to San Pedrito crawling, where they extracted two frogs from her belly. Note that she does not use the verb for ‘crawl’ in this sentence, but resorts to a collocation with a Spanish origin, kuatrupie from a cuatro pies ‘on hands and knees’, which is used adverbially. kuatrupie niyunu San Pedrito tukiu Arubeituyae\\ kuatrupie ni-yunu San Pedrito tukiu Arubeitu-yae\\ on.hands.and.knees 1sg-go San Pedrito from Arubeito-loc\\ ‘on hands and knees I went to San Pedrito from Arubeito’ ( ) has a source expression in which the toponym (i.e. a noun) occurs without a locative marker. It was produced by Juana while sitting at her house in Concepción. She informed me about the plans of the inhabitants of Santa Rita to participate in the public appearance of Evo Morales in Concepción in 2015. aja las ocho naka kapununubeina titupunapunube tukiu Santa Rita\\ aja las ocho naka kapunu-nube-ina ti-tupunapu-nube tukiu Santa Rita \\ intj at eight o’clock here come-pl-irr.nv 3i-arrive.irr-pl from Santa Rita \\ ‘yes, at eight o’clock they will come here, they will arrive from Santa Rita’ toponym In ( ), the source is expressed with the adverb nauku ‘there’. This sentence stems from Juana. I had been waiting for her at the zoo, when she had just arrived home from elsewhere. las dies nibÿsÿu tukiu nauku, nubiuyae\\ las dies ni-bÿsÿu tukiu nauku nÿ-ubiu-yae\\ at ten o’clock 1sg-come from there 1sg-house-loc\\ ‘at ten I came home from there, to my house’ In the source expression of ( ), we have both the adverb nauku and a complex locative expression containing the relational noun -chuku ‘side’. The sentence comes from María S., who told me about her life. The family had once lived more remote from where Santa Rita is located today. Only José remained in this remote location, the other siblings moved away. bijechikutu tukiu nauku chukuyae Kose\\ bi-jechiku-tu tukiu nauku chi-chuku-yae Kose\\ 1pl-move-iam from there 3-side-loc José\\ ‘we moved from there close to José’s’ In ( ), Juana combines naka with a toponym. She compares the coffee from Argentina she received as a present to the coffee from Bolivia here. max michaniki eka tukiu naka Bolivia\\ max michaniki eka tukiu naka Bolivia\\ more delicious dema from here Bolivia\\ ‘the one from here, from Bolivia is better’ The source preposition is also often used to encode sources of non-motion events. It might be the case that this is due to influence of Spanish, which would also make use of the source preposition de to encode these cases. Two examples of this use are given below, both were produced by Juana. In the first of these examples, the source is a source of knowledge, not of motion along a path. It comes from Juana’s account about her encounter with two old Paunaka ladies, who first did not recognise that she understood them talking in Paunaka. In ( ), Juana cites what one of the ladies said to her after Juana had introduced herself to them. “ja'a nichupuikubane pia tukiu Turuxhiyae”\\ ja'a ni-chupuiku-bane pi-a tukiu Turuxhi-yae\\ afm 1sg-know-rem 2sg-father from Altavista-loc \\ ‘“yes, I know your father from Altavista in the old days”’ ( ) is from the story about the fox and the jaguar. The jaguar has already drowned in a pond at this point of the story. Some months later, approximately in August, the fox comes back to speak with the skeleton of the jaguar. The pond has fallen dry by that time. tibukubutu echÿu ÿne tukiu nechÿu kurichiyae\\ ti-buku-bu-tu echÿu ÿne tukiu nechÿu kurichi-yae\\ 3i-finish-mid-iam demb water from demc pond-loc\\ ‘the water had vanished (lit.: finished) from the pond’ source|) The following section is dedicated to the general oblique marker (-)tÿpi, which is the most frequent preposition.
summary: The preposition **tukiu** introduces source expressions and is common in motion-event descriptions, typically appearing before a noun or locative adverb such as *naka* ‘here’ and *nauku* ‘there’. Source nouns may optionally take the locative marker **-yae**, though adverbs do not, and the preposition is also used with non-motion sources such as sources of knowledge or disappearance, possibly under Spanish influence.

text: general oblique|( The preposition (-)tÿpi is the one found with the largest array of different functions and is thus simply glossed ‘obl’ for ‘oblique’. It is often used with constituents that have the semantic role of a benefactive,beneficiary but also with aims or results,aim/result recipients,recipient temporal expressions, and sometimes also with goals. The preposition is also used to introduce purpose clauses. In general, (-)tÿpi can be found in most of the contexts in which the speakers would use the prepositions para or por (both among other things mean ‘for’), when speaking Spanish. As for its origin, there is a stative verb -tÿpina ‘be straight, be correct’, but the similarity to the preposition may be coincidental. If the preposition is in some way related to the verb, the semantic connection has become opaque. In what follows, I give examples for the many different uses of (-)tÿpi. Among the most frequent are the expression of benefactivesbeneficiary|( and results or aims.aim/result To illustrate these uses, compare the following two examples, in which (-)tÿpi is used once to mark a benefactive constituent in ( ) and once to mark a result or aim in ( ). summary:
The preposition (-)tÿpi is a highly general oblique marker with many functions, including benefactive/beneficiary, aim or result, recipient/addressee, temporal expression, and sometimes goal. It is also used to introduce purpose clauses and appears in contexts where Spanish would use *para* or *por*.

The passage illustrates that (-)tÿpi can mark recipients when verbs cannot directly index them, attach affected participants in existential clauses, and express relational meanings such as price, age, and time. Its possible connection to the verb -tÿpina ‘be straight, be correct’ is uncertain and the semantic link, if any, is opaque.

The text also suggests that **-keuchi** is grammaticalized and probably derives from a verbal root plus suffixes, with its person marking and realis form no longer freely changeable.

The passage argues that **-aj(i)echubu** is a comitative form in an intermediate stage of grammaticalization: it still shows verbal properties such as middle marking and reality-status inflection, but it also behaves like a preposition because it uses special third-person marking and is not fully verbal. The corpus examples show that the form can function more preposition-like, with the companion expressed after it and sometimes the verb alone marking plural joint action, but there are also cases where **-aj(i)echubu** acts more like a verb by agreeing with the clause’s person/number and indexing the accompanee.

text: connective|( In the grammaticography of standard average European (SAE) languages, words with a linking function are often divided into the class of conjunctions (or particles) and the class of adverbs.adverb A number of words have a clause linking functioncomplex sentence|( in Paunaka, but as for their part of speech classification,word class this is less clear than it might be in some SAE languages, and this is why they are called “connectives” in this grammar. They are all discussed together in this section. As for tÿpi ‘obl’ (or: ‘for’), this is a preposition rather than an adverb or a conjunction, but it still has a linking function and is thus included in this description. lists the connective words of Paunaka. At least one example of the use of each of these connectives is given in this section. Many connectives have been borrowedborrowing|( from Spanish: the three typical SAE coordinating conjunctions pero ‘but’, o ‘or’ and i ‘and’ can be found in Paunaka,coordination but also the subordinating consecutive/temporal entonses ‘so, thus, then’, temporal depue ‘afterwards, then’ and causalcause porke ‘because’.subordination This is not surprising given that all connectives are prone to being borrowed, since they fulfil an important role in managing the processing of discourse and speaker-addressee interaction in general, which leads to less attention towards the actual form used and finally to long-term borrowing . As for masa ‘lest’, this connective could also be of Spanish origin, deriving from más ‘more’, which is sometimes also used as an adversative connective ‘but’. Masa is used exclusively in apprehensional clauses (and together with the frustrative marker in warningsadmonitive) today, but it seems to be the case that it was used in adversative coordination in former times (see ). However, masa could also be related to Mojeño Ignaciano machu ‘caution, beware of...’ (Rose 2021, p.c.).borrowing|) Most connectives do not only link clauses, but also connect a piece of information to the previous discourse, i.e. they occur at the beginning of intonationallyintonation independent clauses, sometimes after a pause . The connective nechikue (or less frequently nechukue) is possibly related to the demonstrative nechÿu ‘demc’ (see ). It presents an event as a consequenceconsecutive of another, preceding event. One example is given in ( ), where Miguel speaks about how the family moved from Altavista to Santa Rita (not directly, but moving to several other villages and settlements elsewhere, before settling down there): nauku echÿu ÿne sepitÿjiku kuina chitupuna bitÿpi, nechukue biyunuku naka \\\ nauku echÿu ÿne sepitÿ-jiku kuina chi-tupuna bi-tÿpi nechukue bi-yunuku naka Naranjito\\ there demb water small-lim1 neg 3-reach.irr 1pl-obl therefore 1pl-go.on here Naranjito\\ ‘there was little water, it wasn’t enough for us, therefore we went on to Naranjito’ There is another consecutive connective, entonses, a loanborrowing from Spanish entonces ‘so, thus, then’. Its consecutive force is weaker than that of nechikue, but stronger than that of sequential te ‘then’. It introduces events that happen subsequently to previously mentioned events. However, these events are not only connected temporally, but the second one is also a consequenceconsecutive from the other. On the other hand, the event introduced by nechikue is most often temporally subsequent to the priorly mentioned event, but not necessarily so . In ( ), Miguel uses entonses. summary:
In Paunaka, clause-linking words are grouped under the label “connectives” because their part-of-speech classification is less clear than in standard average European languages; the section also includes the preposition tÿpi because it has a linking function. Many connectives are borrowings from Spanish, including pero, o, i, entonses, depue, and probably masa, reflecting the tendency of connectives to be borrowed in discourse management.

The passage then describes several connectives and their uses: nechikue marks consequence, entonses marks a weaker consecutive relation, te marks sequence, depue refers back to earlier discourse and can be combined with i, kue introduces conditional and temporal clauses, and che(je)puine marks cause. Most connectives can link clauses as well as connect a clause to prior discourse, often appearing at the beginning of intonationally independent clauses.

Like chijikiu, it can introduce independent clauses, but it can also link two clauses to form a complex sentence, which is the case in ( ). This example comes from Miguel telling me about the beginning of settlement in Santa Rita. nebutu naka bipajÿkiu pero kuinauku eka ÿneina bitÿpi\\ nebu-tu naka bi-pajÿk-i-u pero kuina-uku eka ÿne-ina bi-tÿpi\\ 3obl.top.prn-iam here 1pl-stay-subord-real but neg-add dema water-irr.nv 1pl-obl\\ ‘from that point on we stayed here, but there was no water for us either’ The connective masa ‘lest’ is used to form apprehensionalapprehensional|( clauses. ( ) is given here to exemplify this. It comes from the same description as ( ) above and provides the answer to my question why Juana puts totaí oil on her head. ja tÿpi eka betuka bichÿtiyae masa eka tayutu eka bimukiji; masa takipÿpa\\ ja tÿpi eka bi-etuka bi-chÿti-yae masa eka ti-a-yu-tu eka bi-muki-ji masa ti-a-kipÿpa\\ afm obl dema 1pl-put.irr 1pl-head-loc lest dema 3i-irr-be.ripe-iam dema 1pl-hair-col lest 3i-irr-be.white\\ ‘well, for this we put it on our heads, lest our hair gets ripe (i.e. grey); lest it gets white’ apprehensional|) The positive counterpart of masa ‘lest’ is tÿpi, which is a preposition to mark different kinds of obliquesgeneral oblique (see ), but can also be used to introduce purpose clauses, in which case it can be translated as ‘to, in order to’. Two examples follow. In ( ), the connective i introduces a new intonation unit and thus attaches the clause to the preceding discourse.
