summary: The passage describes several Paunaka connectives used to mark clause relations: che(je)puine and Spanish loan porke ‘because’ for cause, chijikiu ‘however’ and borrowed pero ‘but’ for contrast, masa ‘lest’ for apprehensional clauses, tÿpi ‘to, in order to’ for purpose clauses, and borrowed i ‘and’ and o ‘or’ for coordination. It notes that some borrowed connectives can introduce independent clauses or complex sentences, and illustrates their use with narrative examples before moving on to the next chapter on nouns.

text: noun|( This chapter is about nouns and NPs in their primary, referential use. Nouns can also act as predicates, which is described in . First of all, the composition of simplex and complex noun stems is discussed in and . There are different processes for derivingderivation a complex noun from a nominal root, among them repetition, compounding and addition of classifiers.classifier Nominalisationnominalisation of verbs is a marginal strategy. Three different classes of nouns can be distinguished by their interaction with possession marking: inalienable, alienable and non-possessable nouns. Possession marking with these three types of nouns is the topic of . The second main division in nouns concerns human and non-human nounsanimacy and their possibilities to combine with plural and other number markers. This is described in . There is no grammatical gender. Nominal irrealis is the topic of . This process is comparable to the better-known nominal tense marking, but in nominal irrealis marking, the referent is non-existent but presupposed. “Deceased”deceased marking is a category marked on kinship terms and personal names in reference to people who have passed away (see ). This could be considered a case of specialised nominal tense. The diminutive is discussed in . It occurs not only on nouns, but also on verbs and other parts of speech,word class but it most often relates to a referent, not to predication. There is no core-case marking (flagging). A few prepositionspreposition encode oblique relations, and there is a general locative marker -yae. In order to express more specific spatial notions, special locative noun stems are used in juxtaposition with a noun referring to the ground. This is the topic of . Information on the NP is given wherever it seems relevant to the topic discussed, but summarises all this information and provides a unified description of the NP. A schema of the noun including all markers that can attach to it in referential use is given in . The locative marker occurs in two different slots. This is related to the fact that it precedes the diminutivediminutive marker and follows the plural marker, while the diminutive always precedes the plural marker. Unfortunately, there are no examples in the corpus in which all three (diminutive, plural and locative) occur on the noun. agglutination
summary: The chapter surveys nouns and noun phrases in their primary referential function, including the structure of simplex and complex noun stems and the main processes for deriving complex nouns, such as repetition, compounding, classifier addition, and marginal verbal nominalisation. It also describes noun classes based on possession, animacy, and number marking, notes the absence of grammatical gender and core-case marking, and discusses nominal irrealis, deceased marking, diminutives, and locative expression. A unified NP description is provided, including the ordering of affixes, with particular attention to the fact that the locative marker occupies two slots relative to plural and diminutive marking.

text: nominal stem|( Compared to verbs, nouns have significantly less internal complexity. The great majority of simplex (i.e. non-derived non-composite) noun stems are di- or trisyllabic. In addition, there are a few mono- and tetrasyllabic stems. Some of the latter have a specific phonological structure (see ). Table shows some non-possessed simplex noun stems with different numbers of syllables. Among nouns, we find many loans from Spanish,borrowing|( especially nouns denoting objects and concepts that were introduced to the area by karay in different points in time, such as baka ‘cow’ from vaca, arusu ‘rice’ from arroz, anyo ‘year’ from año, kupeta ‘gun’ from escopeta, etc. Some of them are phonologically more integrated than others, which may be a hint that they are older. In addition, there are also a number of nouns borrowed from BésiroBésiro|(. When they are similar to Paunaka’s native nouns in phonemic and syllabic structure, they were mostly not recognised by me, since I do not speak Bésiro. As far as I can tell from checking a word list with 705 entries by and the vocabulary lists compiled by , they are surprisingly low in number, but a more in-depth study may reveal that there are actually more loans. A number of nouns with a Spanish origin must have entered Paunaka via Bésiro, easily detectable if they contain the sounds and , which are not part of the phonemic inventory of native Paunaka words. One of these loans is remonixhi ‘lemon’ from Bésiro nermónixhi from Spanish limón. The Bésiro noun contains the prefix n-, which is preposed to nominal roots starting with a vowel and the “general case” suffix -xhi . Both are typical for Bésiro nouns. While the prefix is detached in Paunaka – and the first two sounds metathesised again, reflecting the Spanish original –, the suffix is maintained. This cannot be considered a general pattern though, and there is only a small number of nouns with final xhi (or similar sounds) in Paunaka. Most loanwords are integrated differently. Bésiro|) Two animal terms that are widespread in the area are found in Paunaka as well, where they have the specific forms takÿra ‘chicken, hen’ and kabe ‘dog’. Merÿ ‘plantain’ and patabi ‘sugarcane’ are probably borrowed from Guarayu.borrowing|) Besides borrowing, new lexemes are created by word formation processes. This is the topic of the following section.
summary: Paunaka noun stems are generally simpler than verbs: most simplex nouns are di- or trisyllabic, with only a few mono- and tetrasyllabic stems. The noun lexicon includes many Spanish borrowings, especially for introduced objects and concepts, as well as some loans from Bésiro and a few from other languages; some loanwords show clear phonological integration or evidence of passing through Bésiro. Besides borrowing, the passage notes that new nouns are also created through word-formation processes.

text: There are several processes that produce complex nouns in Paunaka, but none of them is very productive. A few nouns with repeated syllables are found (see ). Compoundingcompounding is largely restricted to plant parts (this is the topic of ). Attachment of classifiersclassifier to a noun or verb stem is similar to compounding (this is discussed in ). A different derivational pattern is found with some parts of body parts (see ). Finally, some nouns are derived from verbs with nominalisers (see ).
summary: Paunaka has several processes that form complex nouns, but none is highly productive. These include a few reduplicated nouns, compounding largely restricted to plant parts, classifier attachment to noun or verb stems, some body-part-related derivations, and nouns derived from verbs with nominalizers.

text: Some noun stems contain repeated syllables, but this is hardly productive, and thus does not fall under the concept of reduplication ( ; ). shows some noun stems with repeated syllables. Repetition of more than one syllable is extremely rare. One example with repetition of the last two syllables is pichikurakura ‘thrush-like wren’, a bird species with the scientific name Cam\-py\-lo\-rhyn\-chus turdinus, which seems to be named after the sound it makes when singing. Another one is pasipasi ‘sand fly sp.’, which might be onomatopoetic,onomatopoeia too, considering the buzzing sound these insects make. This is the complete list of nouns with more than one repeated syllable I found in the corpus. As for pasipasi, it is also one of the few examples of full repetition. Most other cases of full repetition are disyllabic words, like the endearment forms mimi ‘mum, mother’ and yeye ‘granny, grandmother, old lady’. In most cases, there is no corresponding noun without the repeated syllable. However, corresponding to two words at the bottom of the table, -tabubuji and yÿkÿkekeji, there are also yÿkÿke ‘tree, wood, stick’ and -tabu ‘branch, twig’. Both words including the repetition express a multitude of branches and twigs in the crown of a tree. Repetition is probably triggered by the collective marker in this case (see ). There is also repetition of the general classifier on adjectives if the collective marker is added, see .
summary: Repeated syllables in noun stems are mentioned as very rare and not productive, so they are not treated as reduplication. The passage gives a few examples, including longer repeated forms such as *pichikurakura* and *pasipasi*, as well as full repetition in disyllabic words like *mimi* and *yeye*, often without a nonrepeated counterpart. In a few cases, repetition seems linked to collective meaning, especially when used with nouns for branches or twigs, and it may also be triggered by the collective marker.

text: compounding|( Compounding is not very productive in Paunaka, the only exception being compounds of a plant name and a plant part, especially leaves of plants. The plant name occurs in N1 position and it modifiesmodification the plant part in N2 position. The nouns in N2 position are always inalienably possessed,inalienability as in ( ). In addition, some seeds of plants can be expressed by compounds, as in ( ). As for other plant parts, speakers rather use complex NPsnoun phrase with a possessedpossession form of the plant part followed by the plant name, as in ( ), which is from Juana’s telling of the frog story. When the collective marker is added, -pÿi is detached from most forms, but it has completely lexicalisedlexicalisation with the words -jinepÿi ‘daughter’ and -sinepÿi ‘grandchild’, i.e. these words are never found without -pÿi. Consequently, they do not take the collective marker (see ). The first part of -jinepÿi, *jine, has cognates in other Southern Arawakan languages, the addition of -pÿi is an innovation that is only found in Paunaka. endearment|) Finally, a lot of lexicalisedlexicalisation compounds are found among body part terms, especially for bones and hair . While -jiyu ‘body hair’ can also occur in non-compound forms, the sequence -chupu/-chupea, which is found in compounds denoting bones, is never used as a non-compound lexeme. In body part compounds, strikingly, the order of modifiermodification and modified noun seems to be reversed, with N1 being the semantic head. However, we cannot be sure, how these body parts were perceived originally, so, instead of ‘face hair’, the beard could have also been perceived as ‘hair face’, i.e. the part of the face with hair, so that the question which part is the semantic head cannot be resolved here. ( ) lists a few examples for compounds with -jiyu and ( ) with -chupu. Both -jiyu ‘hair’ and -chupu ‘bone’ (in this specific case with the slightly different form -chupea) can also be combined in the word for eyebrow, literally ‘hair bone face’ (or ‘hairy part of the boney part of the face’), see ( ). compounding|)
summary:
Compounding in Paunaka is generally unproductive, except for compounds combining a plant name with a plant part, especially leaves, where the plant name occurs first and modifies an inalienably possessed noun. Some plant seeds are also expressed by compounds, but other plant parts are more often described with complex noun phrases using a possessed form of the part plus the plant name.

The collective marker -pÿi is usually detachable, but it has become fully lexicalized in *-jinepÿi* ‘daughter’ and *-sinepÿi* ‘grandchild’, which never occur without it and do not take the collective marker. Many lexicalized compounds also occur among body-part terms, especially for bones and hair, and in these forms the modifier-noun order may appear reversed, though the original semantic structure is sometimes unclear.

text: derivation|(classifier|( Classifiers can derive nouns from other nouns and verbs.verb They are often completely lexicalisedlexicalisation|( on the noun and cannot be detached. There is, for example, the word pair mutepa ‘dust, earth’ and muteji ‘loam, mud’. Both must derive from a stem *mute, but there is no such noun (or verb) in the language – at least not synchronically.lexicalisation|) A list of all classifiers I could identify is given in . ( ) and ( ) list words in which the derivational process is still transparent, because the stemsnominal stem are also found without classifiers. The nouns in ( ) are results of the combination of a noun with a classifier, while ( ) lists two nouns which are derived from verb stems with the help of classifiers. There are also some idiosyncratic forms. The word ÿneumu may be composed of ÿne ‘water’ and -umu, the classifier for liquids. Its meaning, however, is ‘inside the water’. This word seems to be quite old, it was possibly already used in the Proto language of the Bolivian ArawakanSouthern Arawakan languages, considering that we find a similar word in Old Mojeño,Mojeño languages <uneamukû> ‘inside of the water’ , although this one includes the boundedness classifier <-kû> – whose cognate form -kÿ is also found in the corpus on ÿneumu once. The latter is a reflex of Proto-ArawakanArawakan languages *-Vku . It expresses boundedness, i.e. nouns with this classifier are perceived as having boundaries, as a kind of “container”. It is a special case of classifier, since it is often used in locative expressions only, see , but also found lexicalisedlexicalisation with some nouns outside of such contexts, e.g. the word chenekÿ ‘way, path’ occurs with -kÿ in locative and non-locative contexts. I have claimed elsewhere that the two word formation processes of compounding two noun stems and combination of a noun with a classifier can be seen as two ends of a continuum, where nouns have a more concrete lexical meaning and can typically occur on their own (or with a person marker if they are inalienably possessed), and classifiers have a broader meaning, mostly based on shape, and can never stand on their own, which makes them more reminiscent of derivational affixes,affix yet with a relatively concrete meaning. classifier|)
summary: The passage explains that classifiers can derive nouns from other nouns and verbs, and that many such forms are fully lexicalised, so the classifier cannot be separated from the noun. It gives examples of transparently derived nouns, idiosyncratic lexicalised forms, and the boundedness classifier -kÿ/-kû, which is often used in locative expressions but also appears in some lexicalised nouns. It concludes that compounding two noun stems and combining a noun with a classifier form a continuum between more concrete lexical items and more abstract derivational elements.

subsection: Derivation of parts of body parts
text: There is one derivational prefix ke-, which attaches to a few body part terms to derive a part of this body part . The process is not productive and restricted to the nouns listed in ( ). The same derivation pattern seems to be at work in derivation of the word ‘tail’ from ‘wing’ as in ( ), although the semantic relationship between those animal body parts is not the same as for the human body parts in ( ), since a tail is not a part of the wings. An animal does not even necessarily have to have wings in order to have a tail. chisi – chikeisi\\ chÿ-isi chi-ke-isi\\ 3-wing 3-der-wing\\ ‘its wing(s) – its tail’
summary: The passage describes a derivational prefix ke- that attaches to a small, fixed set of body-part nouns to form a term meaning “a part of that body part.” This process is not productive and is restricted to the listed nouns. A similar pattern appears in the derivation of ‘tail’ from ‘wing,’ though the semantic relation is different because a tail is not literally part of a wing.

text: nominalisation|( A few nouns result from nominalisation with the suffix -kene, they are listed in ( ). All of them are inalienably possessedinalienability and given here with the first person plural possessor. They are objective nouns , i.e. the patientpatient/theme is nominalised. In addition, further nouns that may or may not contain the nominaliser are kuchepukene ‘sorcerer’, -akene/-ekene ‘non-visible side’, in both cases no form without -kene is known to me. The word tijaikenekÿu ‘dawn’ is derived from tijai ‘it is light, day’, seemingly with -kene and the translocative concurrent motion markerassociated motion -kÿu, but this does not make much sense to me, since this marker usually encodes motion away from the scene (‘the light that is going’?). Note that tijai is formally a verb, although used like a noun in most cases (see ). One further example of a nominalised verb form used referentially (as S of a non-verbal predicate) has been found in the data collected by Riester: ( ), which is about scarcity of food due to a drought. We can conclude that nominalisation is a very rare process of word formation in Paunaka. This is because speakers rather use headless relative clausesrelative relation in those contexts in which a nominalised verb would be expected in other languages. nominalisation|)derivation|)nominal stem|) We will leave the inner constituency of nouns now and have a look at nominal inflection, starting from the next section, which is about possession marking.
summary: The passage says that nominalisation with the suffix **-kene** produces only a few nouns, all of which are inalienably possessed and denote the patient/theme of the event. It notes a handful of additional forms that may include the nominaliser, but concludes that nominalisation is **very rare in Paunaka**, since speakers usually use headless relative clauses instead of nominalised verbs in contexts where other languages would use them.

text: inflection|( possession|( person marking|( Possession is marked on the head noun, i.e. the noun denoting the possessed. Possessed nouns take a person marker, which precedes the noun stemnominal stem and indexes the possessor as in ( ). pimuse\\ pi-muse\\ 2sg-mother.in.law\\ ‘your (sg) mother-in-law’ The person markers are given in .possessor|( They are identical to the ones that index subjectssubject on verbs,verb with the only difference being that two third person markers are available for verbs, which are connected to differential object marking (see ), while nouns have only one third person marker. There is no gender distinction in the third person, neither is the marker is specified for number. When a humananimacy third person plural possessor is to be expressed, the plural marker -nube is added. The first person singular and the third person markers have allomorphs, both including a distinction between a high front and a high central vowel. The allomorphs with the front vowel predominantly occur when the following syllable contains an /i/ or /u/, the ones with the central vowel before syllables with /ÿ/, /ɛ/ and /a/, but this distribution is a tendency rather than an absolute rule. With only one exception to my knowledge, only the markers containing the central vowel can precede a vowel-initial syllable, although in most cases, the vowel of the person marker is deleted in such cases (see ). person marking|) In most contexts with third person plural possessors, there are also several possessed items, as in ( ). This becomes apparent from the context in which these nouns are used. One exception is the noun -ubiu ‘house’. There is often only one house for various people, see ( ) . chiyumaji – chiyumajinube\\ chi-yumaji chi-yumaji-nube\\ 3-hammock 3-hammock-pl\\ ‘his/her hammock – their hammocks (or, less likely: their hammock)’ chubiu – chubiunube\\ chi-ubiu chi-ubiu-nube\\ 3-house 3-house-pl\\ ‘his/her house – their house (or: their houses)’ If the possessed noun is non-human,animacy the plural marker unambiguously relates to the possessor, but when it comes to possessed kin, it is often less clear whether the possessor or the possessed kin is pluralised. A detailed discussion about the ambiguity of plural marking concerning possessed kin with third person possessors is postponed to .possessor|) Nouns can be divided into three different classes according to how they interact with possession: there are inalienable, alienable and non-possessable nouns, see , and below. Roughly, the first of them must be possessed, the second ones can be possessed and the third ones cannot be possessed. This tripartite division is very typical for Arawakan languages ( ; ) and in addition, the existence of a class of inalienable nouns is common in Amazonian languagesAmazonian language in general .
summary:
Possession is marked on the head noun by a person marker preceding the noun stem, which indexes the possessor, and these markers are identical to those used for subject marking on verbs except that nouns have only one third-person marker. Third-person possession does not distinguish gender or number, though plural human possessors can be expressed with the plural marker -nube, and plural marking with possessed kin may be ambiguous between possessor and possessed.  

Nouns are divided into three possession classes: inalienable, alienable, and non-possessable, meaning that some nouns must be possessed, some may be possessed, and others cannot be possessed. This three-way distinction is described as typical of Arawakan languages and consistent with broader Amazonian patterns.

text: inalienability|( Inalienable nouns obligatorily express a possessor. This is related to the fact that in inalienable possession, there are “inextricable, essential or unchangeable relations between ‘possessor’ and ‘possessed’” . According to , there is an implicational hierarchy among semantic groups that are conceived as inalienably possessed cross-linguistically. The hierarchy is given in . The semantic groups of nouns that are inalienably possessed in Paunaka are kinship terms, body parts, plant parts (to some extent), spatial relations, and some culturally basic items, so that Paunaka fully confirms the hierarchy. All inalienable nouns obligatorily express the possessor by a person markerperson marking|( preceding the possessed noun. An example with a kinship term is given in ( ). It was elicited from Juana. nimu piati ukuine\\ ni-imu pi-ati ukuine\\ 1sg-see 2sg-brother yesterday\\ ‘I saw your brother yesterday’ person marking|) The noun -ati ‘brother’ is used to refer to male siblings of females and the term -etine ‘sister’ to refer to female siblings of males. If the reference is to a sibling of the same sex as the possessor, the noun -piji, glossed here as ‘sibling’, is used, see ( ). The example also comes from Juana and is about her daughter who did not go to the airport to pick up her sister. kuina tiyuna chipiji\\ kuina ti-yuna chi-piji\\ neg 3i-go.irr 3-sibling\\ ‘her sister didn’t go’ Whether the referent is a male or a female person is only recoverable by the context. An example with the kinship term -etine ‘sister’ is given in ( ). It comes from Isidro, who greeted me. ¿michabi?, netine\\ micha-bi nÿ-etine\\ good-2sg 1sg-sister\\ ‘how are you, my sister?’ The noun for ‘God’, bia, is also a kinship term, it consists of the noun -a ‘father’ and the first person plural markerperson marking|( bi-, so literally it means ‘our father’, though this seems to be intransparent to the speakers. In order to mark the difference between ‘our father’ and ‘God’, it looks as if the Paunaka re-analysed the noun stem -a ‘father’ as -ÿa as in ( ). But this is only true for the first person plural, the second person singular is still pia (pi-a ‘your father’). If the stem were regular *-ÿa, the second person singular should be *pÿa. In general, speakers rather avoid the first person plural form and speak of ‘my father’, nÿa (nÿ-a), instead. Bÿa only showed up in elicitation. The same is true for the second person plural form, for which I could elicit ÿa, but only after some contemplation about what the form could be.person marking|) bia – bÿa\\ bi-a bi-ÿa?\\ 1sg-father 1sg-father\\ ‘God – our father’ Some kinship terms have suppletive endearment forms,endearment|( which are free, non-possess\-able nouns used both as vocatives and referentials. The possessed forms on the other hand are never used as vocatives. gives the forms. The female ones, mimi ‘mum’ and yeye ‘granny’ are used a lot, the latter can be used in respectful reference to any older indigenous female person. Taita ‘dad’ can also be used with non-kins, but occurs only rarely. endearment|) Most body-part terms are inalienably possessed , one example is given in ( ). It comes from María C. who was worried that her chicha would soon be finished. tikuti nemua neamÿnÿ ÿne\\ ti-kuti nÿ-emua nÿ-ea-mÿnÿ ÿne\\ 3i-hurt 1sg-belly 1sg-drink.irr-dim water\\ ‘my stomach hurts when I drink water’ Plant parts are semantically closely related to body parts. These parts usually occur with a third person possessor possessor|( in Paunaka. The possessor is the plant in this case, which follows the possessed part, see ( ) and ( ). chipuneji kÿjÿpi\\ chi-pune-ji kÿjÿpi\\ 3-leaf-col manioc\\ ‘leaves of a manioc, manioc leaves’ chimusuji merÿ\\ chi-musuji merÿ\\ 3-skin plantain\\ ‘banana peel’ A third person possessor is also chosen, when no possessor is lexically expressed, as in ( ), which has chÿi ‘its fruit’. María S. gives an explanation about a plant here. takujibÿ eka te kanainatu chÿi te puero binika\\ ti-a-kujibÿ eka te kana-ina-tu chÿ-i te puero bi-nika\\ 3i-irr-have.flower dema seq this.size-irr.nv-iam 3-fruit seq can 1pl-eat.irr\\ ‘it blossoms and once its fruits have this size (showing with hands), we can eat them’ possessor|) Among the culturally basic items that are inalienably possessed in Paunaka are -sane ‘field’, -mÿu ‘clothes’, -etea ‘language’, and also some parasites like -kane ‘worm’ and -ine ‘louse’. The word for ‘house’, -ubiu, originated as a deranked verb, but acquired characteristics of a noun like being able to combine with the locative marker (see ). It is also inalienably possessed. As for other nouns which typically fall into the class of inalienables, the word for ‘arrow’ is not remembered by the speakers and a word for ‘village’ does not exist. ( ) was produced by Isidro to answer Swintha’s question whether he would go to his field the next day. tajaitu niyunupunuka nisaneyae\\ tajaitu ni-yunu-punuka ni-sane-yae\\ tomorrow 1sg-go-reg.irr 1sg-field-loc\\ ‘tomorrow I will go to my field again’ ( ) comes from Miguel who was looking at a little wooden toy figure and identified it as female. chimÿu tÿnai entonses apimiyapÿimÿnÿ\\ chi-mÿu ti-ÿnai entonses apimiyapÿi-mÿnÿ\\ 3-clothes 3i-be.long thus girl-dim\\ ‘its garment is long, so it is a girl’ Another semantic subclass of nouns that has been identified as a typical member of the inalienable class is spatial relations . There is indeed a small class of relational nounsrelational noun|( in Paunaka, which can take the locative marker. They express some specific spatial relations and are juxtaposedjuxtaposition to the noun denoting the ground. The latter acts as the possessor of the relational noun. There is also a number of free spatial nouns like anÿke ‘up, above’, apuke ‘ground, down’ and pÿkÿjÿe ‘middle’ which are never possessed. Here is one example of a spatial relation that is inalienably possessed by the noun referring to the ground, more examples are given in . ( ) comes from an elicitation session with Juana and María S. with playmobil toys. chÿupekÿ mura chipÿtapaikutu\\ chÿ-upekÿ mura chi-bÿtupaiku-tu\\ 3-place.under horse 3-make.fall-iam\\ ‘it is under the horse, it throw it down’ relational
summary: Paunaka inalienable nouns obligatorily express a possessor, usually by a person marker preceding the noun, and the language fits the cross-linguistic hierarchy of inalienably possessed semantic classes. These include kinship terms, most body parts, some plant parts, spatial-relational nouns, and several culturally basic items such as ‘field,’ ‘clothes,’ ‘language,’ and some parasites. The passage also notes special possessive patterns for kinship terms, plant parts, and relational nouns, including cases where the possessor is understood from context or by the noun’s semantics.

text: noun|) As can be seen from the previous examples, ( ), ( ), and ( ) to ( ), if the possessor is expressed lexically, word order in the NPnoun phrase is always possessed – possessor. Free nouns can be derivedderivation|( from inalienables by addition of the suffix -ti, see ( ) and ( ). This is the only “non-possessed” suffix in the language. nisane – asaneti\\ ni-sane asane-ti\\ 1sg-field field-npossd\\ ‘my field – field’ nimukiji – mukitiji\\ ni-muki-ji muki-ti-ji\\ 1sg-hair-col hair-npossd-col\\ ‘my hair – hair’ Apart from asaneti ‘field’, non-possessed forms of inalienable nouns are not very frequent in my data. The non-possessed suffix seems to be lexicalisedlexicalisation on the alienably possessed noun yubuti ‘axe’, i.e. it is not detached, when the noun is marked for possession.derivation|) There is no prefix for an unspecified possessor. Instead of deriving a non-possessed form or marking an unspecified possessorpossessor|( on the inalienable noun, Paunaka speakers resort to a different strategy: a third person or a first person plural markerperson marking|( can be used to express a more general reference of a noun. Plant parts, for instance, are never marked as non-possessed in the corpus. They take a third person marker by default, even when the part is detached from the plant. The same is true for the noun chÿeche ‘meat’ (chÿ-eche 3-flesh, lit.: ‘his/her/its flesh’), note that the same noun is used to refer to flesh as a body part, e.g. nÿeche ‘my flesh’ (nÿ-eche 1sg-flesh). The use of a third person marker to indicate a general possessor was also the solution the PDP team chose for the production of a poster with body part terminology for the speaker community . Although it was generally agreed on by the speakers that this was correct, we later found out that for general reference to body parts, such as in school books, medical descriptions etc., people rather use the first person plural marker bi-, consider ( ), which comes from Juana who was telling me about the medical use of the soursop. jaja upichai tÿpi bikÿna\\ jaja upichai tÿpi bi-kÿna\\ afm medicine obl 1pl-heart\\ ‘yes, it is medicine for our heart’ person marking|) possessor|) inalienability|)
summary:
In Paunaka, when a possessor is overtly expressed in the noun phrase, the order is always possessed noun followed by possessor. Free nouns can be formed from inalienable nouns with the suffix -ti, which is the only non-possessed suffix in the language, though such forms are rare and may be lexicalized on certain nouns like *yubuti* ‘axe’.  

Paunaka has no prefix for an unspecified possessor; instead, speakers use person marking to express general reference. In particular, plant parts and some body-part terms typically take a third-person marker by default, while first person plural marking can also be used for more general references such as “our heart.”

text: alienability|( Alienable possession is “less permanent and inherent” than inalienable possession . Nouns denoting manipulable objects usually belong to the class of alienable nouns and this is also true for Paunaka. Loansborrowing from Spanish (and less often Bésiro) are also typically alienable, even the ones denoting friends and kins – those latter ones usually show up in the derived, inalienable form (see below). Grammatically, alienability is reflected by the fact that these nouns are free forms in the first place, but can be marked as possessed. There are two different sub-classes of alienably possessed nouns. A small number of nouns can be marked for possession directly, i.e. the only difference between a possessed and an unpossessed form is the presence of a person marker indexing the possessor.person markingpossessor|( Some examples are given in . ( ) has a possessed form of -yumaji ‘hammock’, which does not take the possessed suffix. Compare with ( ), in which the word occurs in non-possessed form. ( ) comes from María C., who was afraid that her hammock would get wet because it was about to rain. kaku niyumaji nekupai\\ kaku ni-yumaji nekupai\\ exist 1sg-hammock outside\\ ‘my hammock is outside’ ( ) was a question by Juana directed to me. ¿pisachu pibena yumaji?\\ pi-sachu pi-bena yumaji\\ 2sg-want 2sg-lie.down.irr hammock\\ ‘do you want to lie down in the hammock?’ The larger number of alienable nouns takes the suffix -ne to derivederivation|( a possessable form. This form can be considered inalienable, since it obligatorily takes a person markerperson marking for the possessor. Two nouns in , kasune ‘trousers’ and pusane ‘bag’ also end in -ne in their non-possessed form. Both are borrowedborrowing from Bésiro or Proto-Chiquitano, pusane derives from Proto-Chiquitano */pɨtsaná-ʂɨ/ , and kasune from Bésiro <kasuná-x>, which is itself a loan from Spanish calzón ‘pants, underpants, shorts’ . Thus in both cases the syllable ne can be considered part of the root. Nouns derived with -ne take a person marker to index the possessor just like other inalienable nouns.possessor|) According to , -ne is the most common possessive suffix among the Arawakan languages. It is the only one that Paunaka productively makes use of. This is mentioned here explicitly because some other Arawakan languages have more than one. ( ) and ( ) show inalienable nouns in their non-possessed and possessed forms follow. tÿmuepa – nitÿmuepane\\ tÿmuepa ni-tÿmuepa-ne\\ knife 1sg-knife-possd\\ ‘knife – my knife’ sÿki – nisÿkine\\ sÿki ni-sÿki-ne\\ basket 1sg-basket-possd\\ ‘basket – my basket’ derivation|) The overwhelming number of nouns belonging to the class of alienables are loansborrowing from Spanish denoting either objects or people with a kinship or other social relation to the possessor. ( ) shows a borrowed kinship term, -kumare with and without possession marking occurring in a single sentence. It comes from Juana who was talking about the trip to Europe. echÿu nikumarene nauku Concecion, kumare Nacha, kuina tisacha tiyuna, tÿbaneyu\\ echÿu ni-kumare-ne nauku Concecion kumare Nacha kuina ti-sacha ti-yuna ti-ÿbane-yu\\ demb 1sg-fellow-possd there Concepción fellow Nacha neg 3i-want.irr 3i-go.irr 3i-be.far-ints\\ ‘my fellow there in Concepción, fellow Nacha, doesn’t want to go, because it is very far’ ( ) has the Spanish loan kama from cama ‘bed’, which denotes an object. It comes from Isidro who was describing a picture of a puzzle game. timuku eka chikamaneyae\\ ti-muku eka chi-kama-ne-yae\\ 3i-sleep dema 3-bed-possd-loc\\ ‘he sleeps in his bed’ If attributive verbsattributive prefix (see ) are derivedderivation from alienable nouns, the possessed form of the noun is used as in ( ), which comes from elicitation with María S. nikupanakune\\ ni-ku-panaku-ne\\ 1sg-attr-basket-possd\\ ‘I have a basket (on the back)’ alienability|)
summary: Alienable possession in Paunaka is used for nouns whose referents are less permanent or inherent, especially manipulable objects and many borrowings from Spanish or Bésiro, including some kinship and social terms. These nouns are free forms but may be marked as possessed either directly by a person marker or, more commonly, by the suffix -ne, which obligatorily takes possessor marking and is the only productive possessive suffix in Paunaka. When attributive verbs are derived from alienable nouns, the possessed form of the noun is used.

text: non-possessability|( Paunaka has a number of non-possessable nouns, which cannot take person markers.person marking Some of them can be possessed indirectly, they “require an additional grammatical element joining the two constituents” (i.e. the possessed and the possessor) . This is achieved by using a possessable noun including the possessor marking in juxtaposition to the non-possessable noun. The possessed noun always precedes the non-possessable one in this case, which can be seen in ( ) from Isidro describing a puzzle game on which a boy plays with a squirrel. chipeu mase\\ chi-peu mase\\ 3-animal squirrel\\ ‘his squirrel’ mentions that non-possessable nouns in Arawakan languages “may include astronomical bodies, natural phenomena, harmful animals and personal names”. In Paunaka, at least some speakers allow a possessed form of astronomical bodies if used in a metaphorical context, e.g. in talking to one’s lover, see ( ), which was elicited from Miguel. nÿjaikene\\ nÿ-jaike-ne\\ 1sg-star-possd\\ ‘my star’ This shows that non-possessability is for semantic reasons and does not have to do with morphological properties of the noun in question. explains that it is common sense among speakers of Amazonian languagesAmazonian language that some items simply cannot be possessed, but the principles underlying are language and culture specific. The most important group of non-possessable nouns in Paunaka is animals. Besides harmful animals as predicted by , this also includes pets, but not parasites like lice and worms, which are inalienably possessed. As has already been shown in ( ) above, the indirect strategy to express possession of animals includes the inalienable noun -peu ‘domestic animal’ as a relational noun relational noun|(. This noun carries the person markerperson marking and the noun denoting the specific animal follows. Another example is given in ( ). It comes from María S., who was complaining that her chicken get stolen when she leaves her house. kuina dejaunubeina nipeu takÿra\\ kuina dejau-nube-ina ni-peu takÿra\\ neg leave-pl-irr.nv 1sg-animal chicken\\ ‘they don't leave my chicken alone’ (i.e. they steal them) ( ) comes from Miguel telling Alejo the frog story. He describes the picture on which the boy stands on the stone. pero kapunuji echÿu chipeu kabemÿnÿ\\ pero kapunu-ji echÿu chi-peu kabe-mÿnÿ\\ but come-rprt demb 3-animal dog-dim\\ ‘but his dog is coming, it is said’ This pattern, i.e. the expression of possession of an animal by juxtaposition of a possessed noun ‘domestic animal’ and the name of the specific animal, is shared with Terena, the Mojeño languages, and Baure (cf. ; ; Rose 2021, p.c.; ). In the Mojeño languages, however, the cognate nouns only denotes rideable animals. TrinitarioMojeño Trinitario uses a more general relational noun for possession of non-rideable animals . Paunaka also has a general relational noun -yae (cognate to the Mojeño one). It is semantically unspecific and identical in form with the locative marker. In ( ) the relational noun occurs in juxtaposition to the noun uneku ‘town’. According to Miguel, who provided this example in elicitation, this is the correct way to express the notion of one’s town. According to María S., however, ‘town’ cannot be possessed at all. niyae uneku\\ ni-yae uneku\\ 1sg-grn town\\ ‘my town’ According to the analysis by for the TrinitarioMojeño Trinitario equivalent of Paunaka’s -yae, it first arose as a general relational noun before spreading to other contexts. As such, it has cognate forms in other Arawakan languages ( , and consider also the “possessive -ya-” of Tariana, ). Note that also considers that the Baure locative marker -ye, another cognate of Paunaka’s -yae, could be a nominal root. Since function and morphosyntactic contexts are relatively different in current Paunaka, I use two different glosses for -yae. If it occurs in possession contexts together with a person marker,person marking I call it general relational noun, abbreviated grn in following , in those contexts where it is attached to a noun, I call it a locative marker, abbreviated loc (for locative marking see ). In current Paunaka, the general relational noun is found in genitive predication (see ), but it can also occur in contexts of attributive possession. Possession of crops can be expressed in this way. I first came across this in one of the recordings of the 1960s by Riester, see ( ). akomoraupuna niyaemÿnÿ arusu\\ akomorau-puna ni-yae-mÿnÿ arusu\\ accommodate-am.prior.irr 1sg-grn-dim rice\\ ‘I will go to store away my rice’ Elicitation showed that crops can either be marked as possessed in this way or by using the alienable possession strategy explained above (see ). Which strategy is used for which crop may depend on frequency and speaker. ( ) is another example of a crop that was spontaneously marked for possession by using the general relational noun -yae in elicitation: niyae ucheti\\ ni-yae ucheti\\ 1sg-grn chili\\ ‘my chili’ Instead of using one of the relational nouns -peu or -yae, speakers may also use other possessable nouns in juxtaposition to the non-possessable ones. Consider ( ), where the natural resource of water is marked as possessed by a preceding possessed noun that simultaneously acts as a measure term for the mass noun. The noun tapiki is borrowed from Spanish tapeque or Proto-Chiquitano tapiki ‘travel supplies’ . This example also comes from elicitation with María S. pitapikine ÿne\\ pi-tapiki-ne ÿne\\ 2sg-travel.supplies-possd water\\ ‘your travel supplies of water’ relational noun|) non-possessability|) possession|) The next section is about number marking on nouns.
summary: Paunaka has several semantically defined non-possessable nouns that cannot take person marking directly, especially animals, though some can be possessed indirectly by juxtaposing them with a possessable relational noun or other possessable noun. The main indirect strategy uses nouns like -peu ‘domestic animal’ and -yae ‘general relational noun’ before the non-possessable noun, and speakers differ in how broadly these forms can be used, including for crops, towns, or even metaphorical uses such as “my star.”

text: Plural marking is obligatory with humananimacy|( referents. There is one plural marker -nube, which is largely restricted to human nouns (see ). In addition, the distributive marker -jane can be used to signal non-singularity of non-human referents, usually animate ones.animacy|) It is described in . The collective marker -ji is used with nouns of two different semantic classes: things which are little individuated, since they occur in masses or swarms and kinship terms with the plural marker (used for both plural kin and plural possessors) (see ). Although distributives and collectivescollective are not part of the number system according to , they are certainly semantically related, since they also provide information about quantity. This is why they are all subsumed under the heading of “number” here. All three markers are also found on verbsverb (see ).
summary: Plural marking is obligatory with human referents, with the plural marker **-nube** largely restricted to human nouns. Non-singularity of non-human, usually animate referents can be expressed by the distributive **-jane**, while the collective **-ji** is used with nouns referring to masses or swarms and with kinship terms. Although distributives and collectives are not always treated as part of the number system, they are grouped under “number” here because they also convey quantity, and all three markers occur on verbs as well.

text: plural|( The plural marker -nube is obligatory with non-singular human nouns.animacy An example of such a constellation is given in ( ), where the noun (a)pimiya ‘girl, young woman’ takes this marker. Juana is speaking about the production of traditional clay pots here. i tanÿma kuina tanabunube pimiyanube\\ i tanÿma kuina ti-ana-bu-nube pimiya-nube\\ and now neg 3i-make.irr-dsc-pl girl-pl\\ ‘and today the young women don’t make them any more’ ( ) comes from Miguel who was happy that Swintha knew a word he had forgotten because: tiyÿsebÿkeunÿnube eka aitubuchepÿinube naka unekuyae\\ ti-yÿsebÿkeu-nÿ-nube eka aitubuchepÿi-nube naka uneku-yae\\ 3i-ask-1sg-pl dema boy-pl here town-loc\\ ‘the boys here in town asked me (about it)’ The noun aitubuche ‘boy, young man’ in ( ) is a loan from Bésiro, and the plural marker can also be used with Spanish loans. An example is ( ) with a plural-marked version of the noun kristianu ‘person’, borrowed from the Spanish noun cristiano ‘Christian person’. The sentence comes from the recordings of the 1960s with Juan Ch., who introduced his playing the flute with a few words. ¡esamu!, kristianunube\\ e-samu kristianu-nube\\ 2pl-hear person-pl\\ ‘listen, people!’ The Spanish word gente ‘people’ is borrowed as a countable noun jente ‘man’ into Paunaka. ( ) shows an occurrence of this noun with the plural marker. It comes from Juana telling about the work of the people of Santa Rita in exchange for the construction of their reservoir. tropanube eka jentenube trabakunube\\ tropa-nube eka jente-nube trabaku-nube\\ pack-pl dema man-pl work-pl\\ ‘the men worked in packs’ Two nouns contain the plural marker as lexicalisedlexicalisation|( part of the stem.nominal stem One is mu\-pÿi\-nube ‘devil’. The noun is composed of the privativeprivative|( marker mu-, the body-part term -pÿi ‘body’ and the plural marker, signifying thus ‘the ones without body’, a term that presumably goes back to pre-Christian belief in spirits. The other noun is seunube ‘woman’. I cannot offer any explanation why the plural marker lexicalised with the rootnominal root *seu. The plural of seunube ‘woman’ is seunubenube ‘women’, see ( ). Juana counts the Supepí siblings here. trexenubechÿ seunubenube i ruxhnubechÿ jentenube\\ trexe-nube-chÿ seunube-nube i ruxh-nube-chÿ jente-nube\\ three-pl-3 woman-pl and two-pl-3 men-pl\\ ‘the women are three and the men are two’ lexicalisation|) There is also one plural-only noun: sesejinube ‘children’. The corresponding singular forms are either sepitÿ ‘small, child’ or the gender-specific (a)pimiya ‘girl, young woman’ and aitubuche ‘boy, young man’, see ( ) and ( ) above. Plural is usually marked on both the noun and the verb if the noun conominatesconomination a subject or object index. There is thus a kind of agreement in number between verb and noun, see ( ) and ( ) above. The plural marker -nube does not occur on non-human nounsanimacy|( with few exceptions. First, anthropomorphic characters in narratives can take the plural marker. However, in my data I only found this for verbs (see ).The reason for this is that there is hardly any story in which two or more animals or other anthropomorphic characters would be of the same species or kind, so that there is not much possibility for plural marking on a noun referring to them (like ‘the foxes’). Of course, they could also be denominated by another noun that does not specify the species like ‘the friends’, but this is not the case in the stories I collected. There is one interesting example from a story told by María S. about how the tortoise obtained its carapace, in which there is a mismatch between plural marking on the verb and distributive marking on the noun, see ( ); however, this cannot be generalised. \ea \begingl \glpreamble te chisamunubetuji eka ubechajane\\ \gla te chi-samu-nube-tu-ji eka ubecha-jane\\ \glb seq 3-hear-pl-iam-rprt dema sheep-distr\\ \glft ‘then the sheep heard it, it is said’ \endgl \trailingcitation \xe Second, a few inanimate nouns occasionally take the plural marker. The noun anyo ‘year’, a loanborrowing from Spanish año, is such a case, which can be seen in ( ), where Juana talks about her mother who was ill for a long time. tibenunukubu yumaji anyonube\\ ti-benunuku-bu yumaji anyo-nube\\ 3i-lie-mid hammock year-pl\\ ‘she lay in the hammock for years’ Furthermore, the noun ubiae ‘house’ can take the plural marker when reference is to multiple houses, see ( ). This noun is a special case, though, because it derivesderivation from a verb (-ubu ‘be, live’), thus the use of the plural marker may be a relict of subject number marking. Juan C. talks about his village, San Miguelito de la Cruz, in this example. kakiu nechÿu pario ubiaenube\\ kakiu nechÿu pario ubiae-nube\\ exist.subord? demc some house-pl\\ ‘there are some houses’ In addition, ubiae can also take the distributive marker -jane as in ( ), where Miguel talks with Alejo and Polonia about the current state of Altavista. i tanÿmatu echÿu ubiaejane kuinabutu\\ i tanÿma-tu echÿu ubiae-jane kuina-bu-tu\\ and now-iam demb house-distr neg-dsc-iam\\ ‘and now the houses do not exist anymore’ There are not many occurrences of ubiae with the plural marker in my corpus and even less with the distributive marker, which is connected to the fact that non-human nouns do not have to be marked for number at all.animacy|) The nominal demonstratives can take the plural marker, when used pronominally, as in ( ), which was elicited from Miguel. If they modify the noun, there is usually no plural marking on the demonstratives, see also . echÿunube tichujijikubunube\\ echÿu-nube ti-chujijiku-bu-nube\\ demb-pl 3i-talk-mid-pl\\ ‘they are chatting’ plural|)
summary:
The passage describes the plural marker **-nube** in Paunaka, noting that it is obligatory with non-singular human nouns and often appears on both nouns and verbs when the noun functions as subject or object. It is generally not used with non-human nouns, though there are a few exceptions such as anthropomorphic characters, the loanword **anyo** ‘year’, and **ubiae** ‘house’ in reference to multiple houses.

The text also notes a few lexicalized forms containing -nube, such as **mu-pÿi-nube** ‘devil’ and **seunube** ‘woman’, as well as the plural-only noun **sesejinube** ‘children’. Finally, nominal demonstratives can take plural marking when used pronominally, but usually not when they modify a noun.

text: distributive|( The plural marker cannot be used with non-human nouns,animacy but there is another marker, -jane, used mainly to express plurality of animals, as in ( ). It was produced by Miguel, but in the story he was telling, it is uttered by the jaguarundi, who warns his companion, the drunken fox, to stop singing lest he calls the attention of the dogs. While the fox and the jaguarundi are anthropomorphic characters and thus subject of plural marking, the dogs are not; they behave like dogs and they do not speak but bark. Use of a distributive form makes clear that there are several dogs that could harm them, thus marking the situation extremely dangerous. “¡tch xhhh, kaku kabejane naka, kaku kabejane naka!”\\ tch xhhh kaku kabe-jane naka kaku kabe-jane naka\\ intj intj exist dog-distr here exist dog-distr here\\ ‘“shh, shhh, there are dogs around here, there are dogs around here!”’ The marker is called “distributive marker” in this grammar, although this term might be a bit misleading. According to , the primary function of distributive marking on nouns is to “spread (distribute) various entities over various locations or over various sorts (types)”. In current Paunaka, the function of the distributive is rather to express overtly that there are various non-humans tokens,animacy|( since number of non-human entities does not have to be specified at all. I had priorly just glossed the marker as a non-human plural until I noticed that there are a few cases in which -jane occurs together with -nube. In these cases, there would be a semantic mismatch if -jane was analysed as a non-human plural marker. I have found three such cases. First of all, there is a question word kajane ‘how many’ and a quantifying stative verb -kijane ‘be many’, where the marker is a lexicalisedlexicalisation part of the stem. Both add the plural marker when they refer to quantities of humans. In addition, -jane also shows up in the plural form pujane(nube) ‘others’ of the singular form punachÿ ‘other’. Distributives encode distinctiveness or individuation of referents , each member of a group is perceived individually in contrast to perceiving plurality as a unit. I suppose this may have once been the primary function of -jane, and this is still well visible in the question word kajane ‘how many’. Asking for a number presupposes that each member of a group is counted individually. Nonetheless, the primary function of the distributive marker in current-day Paunaka is plural-marking of non-human referents.plural It is never attached to human nouns nor to verbs in reference to humans. Among the possible non-human referents, it is more commonly found with animate than with inanimate nouns and bigger, more individuated animals, like dogs, cows, and to a lesser extent pigs, are more likely to be marked by the distributive than smaller and less individuated animals like chicken and fish.animacy|) In ( ), the distributive marker attaches to baka ‘cow’. The example comes from Juana who was telling me about the journey of her grandparents back home from Moxos. They had bought cows there. It is a long way from Moxos to the Chiquitania, which the grandparents went by foot. They slept in huts or temporary shelters and let the cows in enclosures they found along the way. kaku eka bakayayae eka bakajane\\ kaku eka bakaya-yae eka baka-jane\\ exist dema enclosure-loc dema cow-distr\\ ‘the cows were in the enclosure’ Contrary to the plural marker, -jane usually occurs only once in a clause, either on the predicate or on the NP conominatingconomination subject or object, with some exceptions. Which factors determine the choice of either predicate or NPnoun phrase taking the distributive marker remains to be investigated. Thus, there is usually no agreement in -jane between the NP and the predicate, although a few counterexamples exist. All examples in this section show the use on the NP. ( ) is another example with dogs, it comes from Juana who was telling me about her own dogs. tichaneikune eka kabejane\\ ti-chaneiku-ne eka kabe-jane\\ 3i-care.for-1sg dem dog-distr\\ ‘the dogs protect me’ ( ) is an example of the distributive marker on the word for ‘pig’ and was elicited from Miguel. tibÿjaneupuku ÿbajane\\ ti-bÿ-jane-u-pu-uku ÿba-jane\\ 3i-go.in-distr-real-dloc-add pig-distr\\ ‘the pigs also go inside’ In ( ), there are two inanimateanimacy nouns with plural referents, the ‘stones’ and the ‘adobe bricks’; however, only the first one takes the distributive marker. The example comes from Miguel who told me about the construction of the school building in Santa Rita a long time ago. entonses bisemaikutu echÿu maijane banautu echÿu arubi\\ entonses bi-semaiku-tu echÿu mai-jane bi-anau-tu echÿu arubi\\ thus 1pl-search-iam demb stone-distr 1pl-make-iam demb adobe\\ ‘thus we looked for stones, we made adobe bricks’ An example from Juana with two inanimateanimacy distributive-marked nouns is ( ), in which the flower boxes they have in Cotoca, a small city famous for its ceramics, are compared to jars. kaku echÿu maseterojane nena yÿpijanemÿnÿ\\ kaku echÿu masetero-jane nena yÿpi-jane-mÿnÿ\\ exist demb flower.box-distr like jar-distr-dim\\ ‘there are flower boxes that look like jars' distributive|)
summary: In current Paunaka, the marker **-jane** is mainly used to mark plurality of **non-human** referents, especially animate and more individuated animals such as dogs and cows, while it is never attached to human nouns or to verbs referring to humans. Although it is called a distributive marker, the passage argues that its present primary function is overt non-human plural marking; its older distributive sense of distinguishing members individually is still visible in forms like *kajane* ‘how many’.

text: collective|( The marker -ji, which can best be interpreted as a collective marker, since it is found on a number of nouns that occur in uncountable collections or groups like -mukiji ‘hair’ and mÿiji ‘grass’. summary:
The marker **-ji** is interpreted as a **collective marker**, used with nouns referring to uncountable collections or groups, such as hair, grass, branches, leaves, fruits, and small fish that occur in swarms. The passage notes that -ji can be difficult to distinguish from a homophonous classifier in some cases, but the collective does not apply to soft-mass classifiers.

The marker also appears on **kinship terms** when the possessed kin and/or possessor is plural, though its distribution is complex. In some cases plural marking refers only to the possessor or only to the possessed kin, while in other cases both plural and collective marking occur; elicitation suggests that for some speakers the collective is required with third-person plural possessors and plural possessed kin.

text: nominal irrealis|( Nominal irrealis is a category that has not been widely described up to now. It is reminiscent of the better-known category of nominal tense (aka nominal temporal markers cf. ) – a relatively widespread feature in South American languages ( ; ). Nominal irrealis is marked by attaching -ina to the noun in question. The very same marker also figures as an irrealis marker in non-verbal predication. There is sometimes considerable overlap between both functions (see ), but there are also enough cases in which nominal irrealis can well be distinguished from predication. These cases are described in this section. In nominal irrealis, -ina indicates that an entity is non-existent or that it has not come into existence yet. This is in compliance with the function it fulfils in predication (see ). Regarding syntax, I have found irrealis-marked objectsobject and obliques,oblique but no irrealis-marked subjects. Consider ( ) from Juan C. Irrealis marking is due to the non-existence of a pair of trousers in the possession of the speaker here, because his patrón refused to give him one. Before the land reform of 1952, many people in the Chiquitania worked in a debt-bondage relation on the haciendas of big landowners, patrones, who were supposed to “pay” their workers in kind (see ). Depending on the character or mood of the patrón, people were often paid badly or not paid at all. kuina tipunakane nikasuneina\\ kuina ti-punaka-ne ni-kasune-ina\\ neg 3i-give.irr-1sg 1sg-trousers-irr.nv\\ ‘he didn’t give me my supposed trousers’ Note that, if the pair of trousers in question existed, the object would not be marked for irrealis. Imagine, for example, a situation, in which a child wants to put on a pair of trousers, but the mother refuses to give it to her because it has just been washed and is drying, or because the child is supposed to wear that pair of trousers on Sunday service. In this situation, which was described to Miguel in elicitation, the statement of the child would be as in ( ) and use of irrealis on the object would be incorrect. nÿenu kuina tipunakane nikasune\\ nÿ-enu kuina ti-punaka-ne ni-kasune\\ 1sg-mother neg 3i-give.irr-1sg 1sg-trousers\\ ‘my mother didn't give me my trousers’ ( ) is from the personal account about Juana’s daughter who once wanted to emigrate to Spain to live with her sister as a nanny. The plan never worked out, this is why irrealis and frustrative is used on the predicate (see ). The irrealis on the oblique noun with the function of functive complies with this reading: the job as an attendant was never accomplished despite the strong expectation of the people involved. i tiyunaini arsaroremÿnÿina tÿpi chisobrinonemÿnÿ\\ i ti-yuna-ini arsarore-mÿnÿ-ina tÿpi chi-sobrino-ne-mÿnÿ\\ and 3i-go.irr-frust attendant-dim-irr.nv obl 3-nephew-possd-dim\\ ‘and she would have gone as an attendant of her nephew’ In ( ), the field that is talked about by Miguel has not been made at all because the main character of the story is a lazybones who prefers swinging in his hammock and playing the flute to the hard physical work of wresting a field from the woods. kuinaji tana pario chisaneina\\ kuina-ji ti-ana pario chi-sane-ina\\ neg-rprt 3i-make.irr some 3-field-irr.nv\\ ‘he didn't do anything for his (supposed) field, it is said’ The previous examples have shown the use of the nominal irrealis to express non-existence in absolute terms. Moreover, the non-existence of the entity marked with -ina was contrary to the expectation of the people involved in all cases. This can be called the “negative use”negation of nominal irrealis. The other semantic context found to be expressed by nominal irrealis is future reference. ( ) is from a story by Miguel about ants and trees and their relation to humans: Trees are sad, when a boy is born because once he grows up, he fells trees for making his field. The irrealis-marked object chisaneina ‘his (future) field’ has not come into existence by the reference time of the clause, which is the birth of the boy. chejepuine echÿu aitubuchepÿi tijÿkatu, tiyunaji tebitaka chisaneina\\ chejepuine echÿu aitubuchepÿi ti-jÿka-tu ti-yuna-ji ti-ebitaka chi-sane-ina\\ because demb boy 3i-grow.irr-iam 3i-go.irr-rprt 3i-clear.irr 3-field-irr.nv\\ ‘because once the boy has grown up, he will go and clear his future field, it is said’ Irrealis nouns also occur in purposive expressions. In ( ) the aim of the action is additionally marked by the oblique preposition tÿpi. It comes from María S. niyunu niyÿbamukeikupu arusu tÿpi niyitÿina\\ ni-yunu ni-yÿbamukeiku-pu arusu tÿpi ni-yÿti-ina\\ 1sg-go 1sg-husk-dloc rice obl 1sg-food-irr.nv\\ ‘I went to husk rice (in machine in town) for my (future, not yet made) food’ Nominal irrealis specifies the non-existence of the entity in question, be it absolute or only at reference time. It is not related to the semantics of RS marking of the predicate and should therefore be independent of RS marking of the predicate. Nonetheless, I have found only two examples of irrealis-marked objects in combination with a realis predicate in my corpus. Both come from Juana, and both are about houses. In ( ), although the action of building the house is completed as signalled by the realis predicate and the general past setting of the story, the irrealis marker on the object is used to express that one of the main characters (Jesus in this case) does not live in the house by reference time, it is his future house,future reference the one where he is going to live after marrying his wife. tanau chubiuna\\ ti-anau chÿ-ubiu-ina\\ 3i-make 3-house-irr.nv\\ ‘he made his house (where he was going to live)’ In ( ), Juana speaks about ongoing construction of the future house of one of her daughters. ja’a puakenechÿ tanaunube chubiunubeina\\ ja’a pu-akene-chÿ ti-anau-nube chÿ-ubiu-nube-ina\\ afm other-non.vis.side-3 3i-make-pl 3-house-pl-irr.nv\\ ‘yes, on the other side (of the street) they are making their future house’ Last, non-verbal irrealis is also frequently found on temporal nouns or adverbstemporal/aspectual to trigger a future reading,future reference as in ( ), which comes from Juana, who was talking about a visit of her brother at
summary: The passage describes nominal irrealis, marked by the suffix **-ina**, which indicates that a noun refers to something non-existent or not yet existent, and it overlaps with the same marker used for irrealis in non-verbal predication. In the corpus, it appears on objects and obliques but not subjects, and it is used both for the absolute absence of an entity and for future reference, including in purposive expressions and some cases where a realis predicate co-occurs with an irrealis-marked noun.

This can be seen in ( ), in which the irrealis marker only occurs on the modifier punachÿ ‘other’, but not on the noun semana ‘week’. The sentence comes from Miguel who was talking about Swintha here. punachina semana tiyunupunukatu\\ punachÿ-ina semana ti-yunu-punuka-tu\\ other-irr.nv week 3i-go-reg.irr-iam\\ ‘next week she will leave again’ The whole construction in ( ) resembles the local Spanish expression la otra semana ‘the other week’, which can refer either to the preceding or coming week. summary: The passage explains that in complex noun phrases, nominal irrealis is marked only once rather than by agreement between the noun and its modifier, as shown by irrealis appearing on the modifier but not on the noun in “next week.” It also notes that Paunaka uses this marking to distinguish a coming week from a preceding week, unlike the Spanish expression *la otra semana*, and contrasts nominal irrealis, which concerns non-existence, with the next section’s markers for ceased existence, specifically death.

text: deceased marking|( This section is about different possibilities to express on a noun that a person is deceased. Three different markers can be used in this case, -ini, -kue and -bane, which occur with different types of nouns. Only the last of them is also used with other parts of speechword class as a remote past marker. provides a summary of the three forms used for deceased marking. It is not uncommon among Arawakan languages to mark on a human noun that the referent is deceased ( ; ; ; ; ; ; ), and this is also found in non-related languages in AmazoniaAmazonian language (e.g. in Mosetén, see , and Hup, see ). As for Arawakan languages, states that “Wise (1988a) reconstructs one other classifier: *mini meaning ‘dead, past, abandoned’, which in most northern languages retains a suffix similar to -mi, and in most southern languages a suffix similar to -ni. A fuller form was found in Maipure -mine and Baré -amini”. The Paunaka marker that relates to this is -ini. This deceased marker attaches to kinship terms, sometimes to the referential forms, but mostly to the endearment/vocative formsendearment|( (see in ). ( ) and ( ) show its use on endearment forms. ( ) comes from Juana who was talking about what she did with her grandmother in the old days. micha echÿu yeyeini\\ micha echÿu yeye-ini\\ good demb granny-dec\\ ‘my late granny was a good person’ ( ) is also from Juana. It comes from her account about their grandparents’ journey to Moxos to buy cows. beintechÿ baka chiyÿseie chÿchÿini\\ beintechÿ baka chi-yÿseie chÿchÿ-ini\\ twenty cow 3-purchase grandpa-dec\\ ‘it were twenty cows that my late grandpa bought’ endearment|) Paunaka’s deceased marker is -ini is identical in form to the frustrativefrustrative|( marker (see ). It is unclear to me at this stage of research whether -ini should be described as one polysemous marker or as two homophonous markers. For the time being, I opt for an analysis of two homophonous markers with different glosses (dec for ‘deceased’, frust for ‘frustrative’). According to the analysis of , frustrative is often extended to the expression of discontinuous past, i.e. a past situation that was interrupted counter to the expectation of the speaker. Deceased people, obviously, belong to a discontinuous past.past reference Although the fact that people die may not be unexpected – at least if they are old –, the death of a beloved person causes pain and sorrow for the bereaved people, and frustrative is also connected to negative emotions (see ). However, even in the examples given by , it is in most cases not the frustrative alone that establishes a discontinuous past reading, but the frustrative together with another specialised marker. Comparing the form of the Paunaka deceased marker with other Arawakan languages Arawakan languages|( reveals that a lot of languages have a cognate form to express the meaning of ‘deceased’, and besides Paunaka, only the Mojeño languages and Terena have an identical (or homophonous) or similar form for frustrative marking. Arawakan languages|)frustrative|) In the examples ( ) and ( ), it is only the deceased marker on the noun that specifies that the people referred to have passed away. The deceased marker is also found on a noun kuineini ‘deceased’, and often this noun precedes the noun referring to the deceased person. The deceased marker (or one of the other markers described below) can be added to the noun as in ( ) or be left out as in ( ). In that case, kuineini is the only expression of ceased existence of the person in question. ( ) is from an account of Miguel about the history of Santa Rita. The founder of Santa Rita is the grandfather of the Supepí siblings and their father was among the twelve families that came to live in the village in the 1950s. kapunutu kuineini taitaini pero kapununube dose familia\\ kapunu-tu kuineini taita-ini pero kapunu-nube dose familia\\ come-iam deceased dad-dec but come-pl twelve family\\ ‘my late father had come (here), but twelve families came (altogether)’ ( ) is from a listing by María C. of people she knew who were killed by sorcery. nechÿu kapunu kuineini kupare Tieko\\ nechÿu kapunu kuineini kupare Tieko\\ demc come deceased fellow Diego\\ ‘next came late fellow Diego’ Alternatively to -ini, the remote markerremote past|( -bane (see ) can also be used on human nouns to signal that the referent is deceased. It is mainly attached to referential kinship terms. These nouns occur with -bane much more often than with -ini. The noun -enu ‘mother’ is even exclusively combined with -bane in my corpus and never with -ini. One example of -bane on kinship terms is given in ( ), in which Juana tells me about the move of her late parents to Altavista. te tiyununubetu tanÿma eka nÿabane nÿenubane te tijechikunubetu chukuyae patrun nauku Turuxhiyae\\ te ti-yunu-nube-tu tanÿma eka nÿ-a-bane nÿ-enu-bane te ti-jechiku-nube-tu chi-chuku-yae patrun nauku Turuxhi-yae\\ seq 3i-go-pl-iam now dema 1sg-father-rem 1sg-mother-rem seq 3i-move-pl-iam 3-side-loc patrón there Altavista-loc\\ ‘now my late father and my late mother went (away), they moved close to their patrón there in Altavista’ Another example is ( ) from Juan C. telling about the various relocations in his life. I could not find out where Trion is or was, I suppose it is among the places that were renamed or abandoned. kuineini niuchikubane tiyunu naka Trion\\ kuineini ni-uchiku-bane ti-yunu naka Trion\\ deceased 1sg-grandfather-rem 3i-go here Trion\\ ‘my late grandfather went to Trion’ In ( ) María C. uses all three strategies described so far, -bane on a referential kinship term, -ini on an endearment form and an additional kuineini preposed to it. She describes her exact kinship relation to the Supepí siblings here. ja chÿenujinube ekanube chipijibane kuineini mimini\\ ja chÿ-enu-ji-nube eka-nube chi-piji-bane kuineini mimi-ini\\ afm 3-mother-col-pl dema-pl 3-sibling-rem deceased mum-dec\\ ‘yes, their mother was the late sister of my late mother’ As stated above, -bane is also used as a general remote past marker (see ).
summary: The passage describes three Paunaka markers used to indicate that a human referent is deceased: -ini, -bane, and the noun kuineini, which can be added to or replace the marker. The marker -ini occurs mainly on kinship terms and endearment/vocative forms, while -bane is used especially on referential kinship terms and is the form most often found with nouns such as ‘mother’; it is also used as a general remote past marker on other parts of speech.

text: It is then mainly associated with predicates (or with the whole proposition). In some cases, use of -bane with nouns can possibly be analysed as a nominal pastnominal tense|( marker with the meaning ‘former, ex-, old’. In most cases, however, it is not possible to distinguish a predicative and a referential use of the marker. This is reminiscent of the overlap of predicative and referential use of the non-verbal irrealis marker (see ), but in the case of the remote marker, ambiguity is enhanced by the fact that it can float in the clause in predicative use: it mostly occurs on the predicate, but not always. Consider ( ) and the two translations given. One suggests a predicative use of the marker, the other one a referential use. The example comes from a story by María S. about how the tortoise got its carapace: the tortoise does not want to leave her house in the story in order to pay homage to newborn Jesus. As a consequence, she is punished by having her house fixed on her back. nechikue tepajÿku tanÿma chitapu chubiubane\\ nechikue ti-epajÿku tanÿma chi-tapu chÿ-ubiu-bane\\ therefore 3i-stay now 3-scales 3-house-rem\\ ‘therefore her carapace stays now, which was her house before’\: ‘therefore her carapace stays now, (which is) her former house’ Another example, in which -bane could be analysed as a nominal past marker is ( ). Altavista does not exist anymore, at least not as a big estate dedicated to agriculture based on forced labour. Juana told me that her father had found two of the cows her grandparents had been deprived of by karay somewhere in the pampa and took them to Altavista, where he lived at that time. kapunu nÿabane te chumu nauku Turuxhiyaebane\\ kapunu nÿ-a-bane te chÿ-umu nauku Turuxhi-yae-bane\\ come 1sg-father-rem seq 3-take there Altavista-loc-rem\\ ‘my late father came and took them to old Altavista’ remote past|) nominal tense|) There is yet a third marker that can be used to signal the ceased existence of people. This marker, -kue, is almost exclusively attached to proper names in my data, i.e. it does not occur with kinship terms or other human nouns, and proper names do not occur with any of the other two markers previously described (both statements with one exception each). It is thus glossed ‘dec.pn’, a deceased marker for proper names. The marker is probably of Tupi-Guarani origin, since it is very similar phonetically to the nominal past marker found in some of these languages: Guarayu has a past marker -kwer (Bischoffberger 2017, p.c.), Guarasu uses -kwe/-we as a “disconnected” marker, which marks nominal past among other things , in Bolivian Guaraní, the deceased marker is -gwe/-kwe , and Paraguayan Guaraní has a nominal (or referential) past marker -kue . An example is given in ( ). It comes from María C. Note that she omits the third person marker here, something she does frequently. tupunubu kuineini Pernatokue\\ tupunubu kuineini Pernato-kue\\ arrive deceased Fernando-dec.pn\\ ‘late Fernando arrived’ I want to conclude this section with ( ), which comes from Juana. She was thinking about which tale she could tell us (when we had asked her to tell one). She considers telling one story her brother told her, who was a very good storyteller. chÿkueteabane taita Tubusiukue\\ chÿ-kuetea-bane taita Tubusiu-kue\\ 3-tell-rem dad Tiburcio-dec.pn\\ ‘late Tiburcio told it in the old days’ deceased marking|) The following section is about diminutives, both marked on the noun and on other parts of speech.
summary: The passage describes three markers used to express past or ceased existence: **-bane**, which is mainly associated with predicates but can sometimes be analyzed as a nominal past marker meaning ‘former, ex-, old’; **-kue**, a deceased marker used almost exclusively with proper names; and **-kue** is likely of Tupi-Guarani origin based on its similarity to related forms in other languages. It also notes that the predicative and referential uses of **-bane** are often difficult to distinguish, and that this ambiguity is increased because the marker can float within the clause rather than appearing only on the predicate.

text: diminutive|(derivation|( Paunaka has one diminutive marker, -mÿnÿ. It can occur on nouns and verbs,verb as in ( ), which was elicited from María S. and shows both of this. The diminutive also occasionally occurs on words belonging to other classes. tibebeikubumÿnÿ michimÿnÿ\\ ti-bebeiku-bu-mÿnÿ michi-mÿnÿ\\ 3i-lie-mid-dim cat-dim\\ ‘the little cute cat is lying (on a chair)’ The form of the diminutive marker, -mÿnÿ, reminds me of the diminutive found in Guarayu. Guarayu has mini among other diminutives, which can be added to verbs and adjectives, in addition to nouns . Paunaka’s diminutive marker is also similar to the TrinitarioMojeño Trinitario one -samini and proposed that both forms are cognates. Note however, that Paunaka’s /ɨ/ is a reflex of *u of a common ancestor language, and the process of fronting did not take place in the Mojeño languages . If the forms are cognates, we have to assume an unconditioned shift from *i to /ɨ/ in Paunaka. The same holds for the hypothesis that the Paunaka diminutive is related to the Guarayu form. In Guarasu, another Tupi-Guarani language closely related to Guarayu, there is a diminutive marker -m\' ɨ nɨ , which is identical to the Paunaka one, but we do not know whether the languages were in contact. Besides the basic meaning of smallness, the diminutive marker can also express emotional values like affection and compassionendearment and attenuation, often for reasons of politeness or modesty. This extension from the core meaning has been reported to occur very frequently cross-linguistically . Even if the diminutive is not attached to a noun, but to an adjectiveadjective or a verb,verb it is associated with a noun (or its referent) in most cases. Sometimes it can also attenuate the verb’s meaning. It is, however, often impossible to distinguish diminutive notions belonging to the referent from purely predicative attenuation, because a small, modest or pitied referent usually causes little action. In many cases, I just do not know what the speaker exactly wanted to express with the diminutive. This is why I decided not to treat the diminutive in different chapters -- unlike other markers of transcategorial morphology like the person and number markers, the non-verbal irrealis and the remote past marker, where the different functions are more easily distinguished (at least in some cases). To compensate for this, the subsections on diminutive marking are ordered by word class. First, examples of diminutives on nouns are given in , while discusses use of the marker on verbs. In , occurrences of -mÿnÿ with other parts of speech are presented. The use of diminutives is not only very common in Paunaka, but also in Bolivian Spanish, where it has largely the same functions , but not the same distribution, i.e. it cannot be used on verbs.
summary: Paunaka has a single diminutive marker, -mÿnÿ, which can occur on nouns and verbs and occasionally on other word classes; it is also associated with the noun or referent even when attached to adjectives or verbs. Besides indicating smallness, it can convey affection, compassion, endearment, attenuation, or politeness, and the author notes that its exact function is often difficult to separate between referential and predicative meanings. The form is compared with diminutive markers in related languages, but the proposed cognate relationships are uncertain because of problematic sound correspondences.

text: Sometimes, the diminutive marker -mÿnÿ clearly expresses its core meaning of smallness. This is often the best interpretation, when it is added to inanimate nouns. An example is ( ) from Miguel. The woman, a character of a narrative, brings some food to her husband, who is supposed to be working in the woods.
