After the woman has discovered the deception of her husband, who had pretended he was making a field, the man decides to sacrifice himself by cutting off his limbs. He takes his little son with him, so that the latter can carry his limbless father and throw him into a well from where the lazy man rises as a comet. chumuji chichechapÿimÿnÿ\\ chÿ-umu-ji chi-chechapÿi-mÿnÿ\\ 3-take-rprt 3-son-dim\\ ‘he took his little son, it is said’ The diminutive can also be used for a small amount of something. Consider example ( ), in which María C. describes that she only has little corn left to prepare chicha, her preferred beverage, though it cannot be excluded that the speaker also uses the diminutive to express self-pity about that fact. kakumÿnÿ amukemÿnÿ te tibukapu echÿu te kuinabu nea aumue\\ kaku-mÿnÿ amuke-mÿnÿ te ti-buka-pu echÿu te kuina-bu nÿ-ea aumue\\ exist-dim corn-dim seq 3i-finish.irr-mid demb seq neg-dsc 1sg-drink.irr chicha\\ ‘there is little corn and when it will be finished, then I cannot drink chicha anymore’ Finally, there are also cases, in which no smallness is involved and the only possible reading is one of emotional evaluation. This is the case in ( ), where María C. feels pity for herself. nÿti juberÿpunÿmÿnÿ\\ nÿti juberÿpu-nÿ-mÿnÿ\\ 1sg.prn old.woman-1sg-dim\\ ‘poor me, I am an old woman’ Affection is not necessarily for the referent of the noun that bears the diminutive marker, but can also be for the possessor of that noun. Juana’s speech is full of diminutives in reference to the old ladies, and in ( ), she adds one to a possessed item, the walking cane of one of the ladies. kaku chibastunemÿnÿtu, mhm, chiyuikiumÿnÿ\\ kaku chi-bastun-ne-mÿnÿ-tu mhm chi-yuik-i-u-mÿnÿ\\ exist 3-cane-possd-dim-iam intj 3-walk-subord-real-dim\\ ‘she already had a cane, mhm, for walking’

summary: The diminutive on verbs has largely the same functions as on nouns and can also weaken the force of the verb. It may indicate smallness, cuteness, or empathy, may refer to the subject or object, and can soften meanings in contexts such as slight change, polite imperatives, or modest self-presentation.

subsection: Diminutives on other parts of speech
text: Diminutives can also occasionally be added to other parts of speech. They can attach to the few adjectives that exist in Paunaka, and infrequently also to pronouns and demonstratives (usually the nominal demonstratives, but one time in the corpus also to the demonstrative adverb naka ‘here’). Because of the emotional value of the diminutive, -mÿnÿ can also be added to the adjectiveadjective|( (mu)temena ‘big’. This is the case in ( ). It is not clear, though, whether Juana uses the diminutive to express her pity for some, already grown, ducks that died in her absence, because none of her family members fed them, or to attenuate the meaning of the predicate as ‘big, but small’ = ‘biggish’. pero temenanajimÿnÿtu\\ pero temena-na-ji-mÿnÿ-tu\\ but big-rep-col-dim-iam\\ ‘but they were already big, the poor ones’\: ‘but they were already biggish’ adjective|) ( ) is a statement by María C. about herself, in which the diminutive is added to the first person singular pronoun,personal pronoun because she pities herself. nÿtimÿnÿ baichane, kuina nÿana kuina nenuina\\ nÿti-mÿnÿ baicha-ne kuina nÿ-a-ina kuina nÿ-enu-ina\\ 1sg.prn-dim orphan-1sg neg 1sg-father-irr.nv neg 1sg-mother-irr.nv\\ ‘poor me, I am an orphan, I don’t have a father, I don’t have a mother’ In ( ), a numeral carries the diminutive for attenuation. The sentence comes from María S. chÿnamÿnÿchÿ nipeu ÿba\\ chÿna-mÿnÿ-chÿ ni-peu ÿba\\ one-dim-3 1sg-animal pig\\ ‘I have a single pig’ derivation|) While the diminutive can thus attach to various parts of speech,diminutive|) the locative marker, which is described in the following section, exclusively occurs with nouns.
summary: In Paunaka, the diminutive suffix *-mÿnÿ* can occasionally attach not only to nouns but also to a few adjectives, pronouns, demonstratives, and even numerals. Its use often expresses emotional nuance or attenuation, as in forms meaning ‘poor me’ or ‘biggish,’ though the locative marker discussed next is restricted to nouns.

The marker attaches exclusively to nouns that express spatial relations in a clause, more precisely relations of place, goal, and source. It is not found on adverbs. In slow speech, the marker is pronounced -yae, but it can be reduced to -ye or -ya in rapid speech. ( ) is an expression of a place, ( ) presents the locative marker on a goal, and ( ) on a source expression. ( ) comes from Juana, who was telling me how hard it was to obtain water before the reservoir was made in Santa Rita. bupunu ÿne Santa Rita\\ bi-upunu ÿne Santa Rita \\ 1pl-bring water Santa Rita \\ ‘we brought water to Santa Rita’ ( ) is a comment from María S. about her siblings who moved away from Santa Rita. depue tepajÿkunubetu uneku\\ depue ti-epajÿku-nube-tu uneku\\ afterwards 3i-stay-pl-iam town\\ ‘then they stayed in town’ If the verb in a goal expression is -yunu ‘go’, it is also not uncommon that the locative marker is missing on the noun denoting the goal, as in ( ) from Clara. In ( ), there is contact from above (‘on’), in ( ) the spatial relation is one of closeness and can be translated with ‘at’, and in ( ), the figure (i.e. the subject of the clause) is inside a location (‘in’). It referred to a pig which I had asked for, since it was suddenly not in the yard anymore. tiyunu tisemaiku yÿtie atajauyae\\ ti-yunu ti-semaiku yÿtie atajau-yae\\ 3i-go 3i-search food water.reservoir-loc\\ ‘it (the pig) went to look for food at the reservoir’ ( ) was elicited from Miguel. kaku kÿjÿpi ubiaeye\\ kaku kÿjÿpi ubiae-yae\\ exist manioc house-loc\\ ‘there is manioc in the house’ The locative marker alone thus expresses the most expected spatial relations and its interpretation as ‘on’, ‘at’ or ‘in’ largely depends on the spatial dimensions of the noun denoting the ground (i.e. the location) and the habits or properties of the figure . In order to be more specific or for the expression of unusual relations, speakers can make use of two different strategies: either a more precise locative noun is derived from the noun denoting the ground or a complex NPnoun phrase is used
summary:
The passage describes a general locative marker, -yae, which attaches to nouns expressing spatial relations of place, goal, and source, but not to adverbs. It can be reduced in rapid speech, is sometimes omitted in certain contexts such as with toponyms or after the verb ‘go’ in goal expressions, and may also appear with human nouns or in instrumental-like uses. 

Its main function is to mark ordinary spatial relations, with meanings like ‘on,’ ‘at,’ or ‘in’ depending on the noun and context, though it can extend to some nonspatial uses such as knowledge “in the head” or words “in” a language. When speakers need greater precision or unusual spatial relations, they use either a more specific locative noun derived from the ground noun or a complex noun phrase.

summary: The passage describes how Paunaka expresses containment and other spatial relations using derived container nouns, locative stems, and possessed relational nouns. Complete “inside” relations can be marked with the bounded classifier -kÿ or the locative stem -j(ÿ)ekÿ, while other spatial relations use inalienably possessed relational nouns such as ‘under,’ ‘side,’ ‘top,’ and ‘non-visible side,’ with the locative marker often attached. Body-part terms are used only for spatial relations with animate, real possessors and do not extend metaphorically to inanimate referents.

Their status is somewhat unclear because they may also function as adverbs; they usually stand alone as the ground rather than appearing with another noun, and they generally do not take the locative marker except in a few cases.

text: noun phrase|( modification|( The typical NP minimally consists of a noun or a pronoun.head Nouns can optionally be modified, pronouns are never modified. NPs can also do without a noun or pronoun. In this case, only the “modifier” is present . In this section, only those NPs consisting of a noun and a modifier are considered which form a single syntactic unit and act as an argument in the clause . There are no discontinuous NPs in Paunaka. Modifiers are nominal demonstratives,nominal demonstrative adjectives,adjective numerals,numeral relative clauses,relative relation and other nouns. The status of quantifersquantifier as modifiers of nouns is not totally clear. Relative clauses are discussed in detail in will thus not be considered here. shows the word order in the NP. The following examples show those types of modifiers which precede the noun. ( ) has a nominal demonstrative and a noun. It comes from Miguel’s narration of the story about the fox and the jaguar. demonstrative + noun:\echÿu kupisaÿrÿ\\ ti-yunu-tu echÿu kupisaÿrÿ\\ 3i-go-iam demb fox\\ ‘the fox had already gone’ In ( ), the word for ‘other’ acts as a nominal modifier. Juana speaks about the plans of her landlord. ‘other’ + noun:\punachÿ kuartojane naka\\ ti-ana punachÿ kuarto-jane naka\\ 3i-make.irr other room-distr here\\ ‘he wants to make other rooms here’ ( ) exemplifies the use of a numeral as a modifier. María S. tells her husband here that I have three children (which is not true, I have only two, thus I corrected her, but this is not of importance for the use of the modifier). numeral + noun:\treschÿ chichechajinube chijinepÿinube\\ kakutu treschÿ chi-checha-ji-nube chi-jinepÿi-nube\\ exist-iam three 3-son-col-pl 3-daughter-pl\\ ‘she has three sons and daughters by now’ In ( ), there is an adjective adjective|( and a noun. summary: Paunaka noun phrases minimally consist of a noun or pronoun, though nouns may be modified while pronouns are not, and there are also noun phrases made up only of a modifier. The passage describes several kinds of noun-noun modification in which the modifier specifies a type, including measure terms with what is measured and material nouns with the object made from them. It also explains that some nouns, especially animals, require relational nouns for possession, and that number, diminutive, and locative markers usually appear only once in an NP, typically on the head noun, though they can occasionally be distributed across modifiers and heads.

The text further notes that NPs usually contain no more than two modifiers, though more complex combinations do occur, such as numeral-plus-adjective or demonstrative-plus-“other”-plus-type noun constructions. Double plural marking is reported as rare.

chapter: The verb and morphology on predicates
text: verb|( Verbs can be fairly complex in Paunaka; however, the only categories that are obligatorily marked on verbs are person/numberperson marking and reality status (RS). Complexity can increase through derivational processesderivation inside the stem and through addition of inflectional formatives.inflection There are also processes at the edge of the verb stem,verbal stem which can be considered borderline cases between derivation and inflection. Two main classes of verbs, stativestative verb|( and activeactive verb, can be distinguished by a different strategy of RS marking.reality status The position of the subject marker is identical in stative and active verbs, i.e. the person marker encoding the subject always precedes the verb stem.person marking shows the template of a stative verb. Contrary to active verbs, the position of the markers following the stem could not be established because there are few examples in which two or even more of them are combined. Thus all markers that have been found on stative verb stems in the corpus are simply given in alphabetical order. agglutination Stative verbs are intransitivevalency and encode typical stative relations like colour, knowledge, emotion, and temperature. There are simple and derived stative verbs. Interestingly, the incorporation of body part terms into active verb stems often results in stative verb stems. The stems of stative verbs do not carry a thematic suffix. Realis RSrealis is not marked on stative verbs, while irrealis is marked by a prefix a-, which directly precedes the stem. There are also a number of active verbsactive verb that encode stative relations, all of them are deponent middle verbs,middle voice i.e. they only occur in the middle form (see ).stative verb|) , a slightly adapted repetition of in , shows the template of an active verb, including morphology inside and outside of the stem. As has been mentioned before (see ), the position of the optative markers could not be established because there are simply not enough examples in the corpus. Superscript numbers show different possible positions for some markers. sidewaysfigure Template of an active verb sidewaysfigureagglutination Active verbsactive verb can be intransitive, transitive or ditransitive.valency Many, but not all of them, have a thematic suffix that marks the stem boundary.reality status|( Realis RSrealis is signalled by absence of any marker including irrealis inflection; note that irrealis can be marked on different markers, but generally only once. The default/realis realisation of these markers is with a vowel u. In irrealis RS, u changes to a. In some cases, there is also a proper suffix -a that signals irrealis RS that alternates with a suffix -u for realis RS. A more elaborate explanation follows in .reality status|) Paunaka has no passive, but there is middle voice. TAME marking is optional and not restricted to verbs. The markers expressing these categories are also found on non-verbal predicatesnon-verbal predication and sometimes on other constituents in the clause. Another category is associated motion (AM), the expression of motion events that happen before, simultaneously with and possibly also after the event expressed by the verb. Related to this category is the expression of associated path and repetitive. The remainder of this chapter is organised roughly by verb structure, from inner to outer processes: to deal with verb stems including derivations inside and at the edge of stems. This is followed by sections on the most important inflectional categories, person/number in and reality status in . AM markers are discussed in . This is followed by a section on the middle voice in . TAME marking is the topic of . Finally, some degree markers are presented in . Similarly to TAME markers, they do not only attach to verbs (although one of them, the additive marker, is deeply integrated into the verb structure as will become apparent).
summary: Paunaka verbs are structurally complex, but the only categories obligatorily marked on verbs are person/number and reality status (RS), with further complexity coming from derivation, inflection, and some borderline stem-edge processes. The language distinguishes stative and active verbs: stative verbs are intransitive, lack a thematic suffix, and mark irrealis with prefix **a-** while realis is unmarked, whereas active verbs may be intransitive, transitive, or ditransitive and mark realis/irrealis through alternations such as **u ~ a** or suffixes **-u / -a**. Paunaka has no passive but does have middle voice, and TAME, associated motion, and degree markers are optional and can also occur on non-verbal predicates or other clause constituents.

text: stative verb|( intransitive|( Stative verb stems express emotion, cognition, temperature, colour, consistency, taste and some other properties, qualities and non-permanent states. They are composed a bit differently from active ones, since they never include a thematic suffix and do not take aktionsart suffixes. Unlike in other Arawakan languages, however, stative verbs index subjectssubject just like active verbs .person marking The main difference lies in a different location for irrealis marking: stative verbs take an irrealis prefix, while realis is completely unmarked. A small number of stems are stative by their inflection for irrealis preceding the verb stem, see , but transitive by their ability to either be combined with an object NPnoun phrase or even index an object by a person marker.person marking They are further described in .
summary: Stative verb stems express emotions, cognition, temperature, color, consistency, taste, and other non-permanent properties or states. Unlike active verbs, they do not take thematic or aktionsart suffixes, but they do index their subject like active verbs; their main inflectional difference is that stative verbs mark irrealis with a prefix while realis is unmarked. A small set of stems are stative in irrealis marking but transitive because they can combine with an object NP or index an object with a person marker.

text: verbal root|( Most stative verbs are or appear to be underived or “simplex”. However, it is possible that they are the result of non-productive or singular derivational processes. We can sometimes recognise semantic similarities between phonologically similar stems, e.g. -kutiu ‘be ill’ must be derived from -kuti ‘hurt’ (which is also stative), -michainu ‘be pleased’ from the adjective micha ‘good’, and -(i)chuna ‘know, be capable’ is certainly related to the active verb -chupu ‘know (a fact)’, but there are no regular patterns underlying these derivations. A number of stative verb stems start with the syllable ku. There is indeed a derivational process to derive stative verbs from nouns that includes a prefix ku-attributive prefix (see ), but not in every case is the derivation transparent such that the part of the verb stem following ku would be recognisable as an independent stem. The verb -pisÿ ‘be black’ seems to be borrowedborrowing from Bésiro, and it inflects like an ordinary stative verb. shows some additional stative verbs. Many of them describe properties, both of prototypically human and prototypically inanimate referents; others describe states. verbal root|)
summary: Most stative verbs appear to be underived or “simplex,” though some may reflect irregular, non-productive derivational processes. The passage notes a few possible relationships between similar stems and explains that while there is a derivational process using the prefix ku to form stative verbs from nouns, this derivation is not always transparent. It also suggests that -pisÿ ‘be black’ is borrowed from Bésiro and observes that many stative verbs describe properties or states.

However, to my knowledge, only two of them have a counterpart without this final sequence, and it is not possible to derive new words with this root.nominal root All verbs that end in -umi denote emotions and feelings that are typically associated with humans. The root probably derives fromlexicalisation an obsolete noun with the meaning ‘heart’; this noun had the form -omiri in Old MojeñoMojeño languages (Rose 2021, p.c.). Note that some Baure verbs denoting emotions and physical feelings include a root -’in(o) that is also found in the noun etko’in ‘heart’ , and it is quite possible that Paunaka once had the same pattern of word formation. lists the verb stems that end in -umi.
summary: A few stative verbs end in the sequence **-umi**, and only two of them have a counterpart without this final sequence, so this root is no longer productive for forming new words. All verbs ending in **-umi** denote human emotions or feelings, and the root is probably related to an obsolete noun meaning “heart,” comparable to the Old Mojeño form **-omiri**.

text: attributive prefix|( Verbs can be derived from nouns with the prefix ku-, which directly precedes the nominal stem. The prefix goes back to Proto-Ara\-wa\-kan *ka- and has cognates in many Arawakan languages . The prefix is probably related to the homophonous causative prefix. Both have in common that they increase valency by one participant . For causative derivations see . Only possessable nounspossession can be combined with ku- (see ). In the case of alienable nouns, the derived form including the possessed marker -ne is chosen, see ( ) and ( ) below. The meaning of attributive verbs is classically described as ‘have X, be with X’, but in Paunaka, some attributive verbs have more active meanings (‘make X, do with X’), and a small number of attributive verbs can even be used transitively, though they remain stative by position of irrealis marking. To start with, consider some examples which show the classical, possessive function of the attributive prefix: ( ) to ( ). In ( ), Miguel is talking about Federico, whom he had jokingly called a relative of theirs (the men in Santa Rita usually do not have beards). tikujiyumama biparientene\\ ti-ku-jiyumama bi-pariente-ne\\ 3i-attr-beard 1pl-relative-possd\\ ‘our relative has a beard’ ( ) comes from María S., who could not cultivate her field in 2018 because of problems with her knee. kuina nakuesanebu\\ kuina nÿ-a-ku-esane-bu\\ neg 1sg-irr-attr-field-dsc\\ ‘I don’t have a field anymore’ ( ) comes from Miguel explaining a word to me: pÿsi, ‘spirit of the hill’. pÿsi chija bitÿpi echÿu tikubiunube naka chiyikikeyae\\ pÿsi chi-ija bi-tÿpi echÿu ti-ku-ubiu-nube naka chiyikike-yae\\ pÿsi 3-name 1pl-obl demb 3i-attr-house-pl here hill-loc\\ ‘pÿsi we call the ones who have their houses in the hills (i.e. the owners of the hills)’ In ( ), the derived verb does not have a stative meaning, but rather indicates a change of state. Note that the connective che(je)puine ‘because’cause sounds more like mapuine or bapuine in all of his speech. mapuine takukane uchu i chibuka chikane kuinabu binikeneina\\ chejepuine ti-a-ku-kane uchu i chi-buka chi-kane kuina-bu bi-ni-kene-ina\\ because 3i-irr-attr-maggot uncert.fut and 3-finish.irr 3-maggot neg-dsc 1pl-eat-nmlz-irr.nv\\ ‘because then it may get maggots and if the maggots finish it, we do not have any food anymore’ In ( ) and ( ), the meaning of the derived verb is active, ‘do X’. In ( ), María C. speaks about the old days in Altavista, when she had to work at night. yuti nikuyuine pan de arroz\\ yuti ni-ku-yui-ne pan de arroz \\ night 1sg-attr-bread-possd rice bread \\ ‘at night I baked rice bread’ ( ) is an utterance by the drunken fox in the story of the fox and the jaguarundi as told by Miguel. “nÿsachutu eka nakusunine”\\ nÿ-sachu-tu eka nÿ-a-ku-suni-ne\\ 1sg-want-iam dema 1sg-irr-chant-possd\\ ‘“I want to sing now”’ The attributive verb -kuyae ‘have, possess, own’ is always realised with a third person markerperson marking following the stem. The owner is a spirit in this case. kaku tikuyaechÿ\\ kaku ti-ku-yae-chÿ\\ exist 3i-attr-grn-3\\ ‘there is an owner’ In an elicitation session on possessive questions,content question María S. also used the third person marker -chÿ on the attributive verb in many of the questions she formed, like the following: ¿chija tikupeuchÿ?\\ chija ti-ku-peu-chÿ\\ what 3i-attr-animal-3\\ ‘who is the owner of the animal?’ In the same elicitation session, she also formed some possessive verbs without the attributive prefix. This happened more than once, which is why I find it worth mentioning here, though I cannot say whether other speakers would accept such a verb form. ¿chija tipeuchÿ?\\ chija ti-peu-chÿ\\ what 3i-animal-3\\ ‘who is the owner of the animal?' On the other hand, I have also heard the attributive verb with ‘house’, taking the thematic suffix, which is a suffix of active verbs (see ). This may be a special case though because the noun for house, -ubiu, derives fromlexicalisation a verb (see ). Note that the final /u/ of the noun gets lost in the attributive verb. ( ) shows the use of the attributive verb including the thematic suffix. Juana had just told me that a relative of hers lives in a huge house, in which the rooms downstairs are rented: i nauku anÿke nebu chubiu tikubiku\\ i nauku anÿke nebu chÿ-ubiu ti-ku-ubiku\\ and there up 3obl.top.prn 3-house 3i-attr-reside?\\ ‘and up there, there is the flat of the owner of the house’ In general, though not always having stative semantics, attributive verbs are intransitive. Usually, they cannot take person markersperson marking to index an object. In the few cases in which an object is logically possible, it can be expressed periphrastically, as in the case of the verb -kuetea ‘tell’ from -etea ‘language, word’, where the addressee is expressed by an oblique form. In ( ), Clara uses such a construction. She was addressing Swintha, helping her formulate what she wanted to say: that Federico already told us about the death of María C.’s husband. tikuetea etÿpi\\ ti-ku-etea e-tÿpi\\ 3i-attr-language 2pl-obl\\ ‘he told you’ attributive prefix|)
summary:
The prefix **ku-** derives verbs from nouns and likely goes back to Proto-Arawakan *ka-; it may be related to the homophonous causative prefix because both increase valency by one participant. It combines only with possessable nouns, while alienable nouns require the possessed marker **-ne**, and the resulting attributive verbs can mean ‘have X’ or ‘be with X,’ though some also have more active senses like ‘make X’ or ‘do X.’  

Although attributive verbs are generally intransitive and usually do not index an object with person marking, some special forms show third-person marking, occasional use without the prefix, or even the thematic suffix of active verbs. The text also notes that **-kuyae** ‘have, possess, own’ always appears with a third-person marker and may be referential rather than predicative.

text: A peculiarity of the verbal root -ÿ ‘be long’ is that it cannot occur on its own, but needs some additional material that specifies the kind of length that is expressed by the stem. All stems presented in are lexicalisedlexicalisation and only occur with the third person marker ti- ‘3i’. In addition, there is the verb stem -ÿnai ‘be tall’, which most probably consists of the root -ÿ, the general classifier -na and an i of unknown origin. This verb can also be inflected for first and second person as in ( ). nÿti nÿjÿku micha, nÿnai\\ nÿti nÿ-jÿku micha nÿ-ÿnai\\ 1sg.prn 1sg-grow good 1sg-be.tall\\ ‘I grew well, I am tall’ The -nai part of this verb can be replaced by body-part nouns to specify that a specific body part is long, see ( ), or the body-part noun is placed before na and i is dropped as in ( ). It is not clear at this point whether both forms are grammatical. summary:
The verbal root **-ÿ** ‘be long’ cannot appear by itself and must be combined with additional material that specifies what kind of length is meant. Most stems are lexicalised and occur only with the third-person marker **ti-**, but the related stem **-ÿnai** ‘be tall’ can also be inflected for first and second person and is likely formed from **-ÿ**, the classifier **-na**, and an element **i** of unknown origin.

The **-nai** part can be replaced by body-part nouns to indicate that a particular body part is long, or a body-part noun can be placed before **na** with **i** omitted. The passage notes that it is unclear whether both constructions are grammatical, since one was elicited and the other was produced spontaneously.

summary:
Some active verb stems are identical to the verbal root and therefore do not take a thematic suffix; these simplex verbs may be mono- or disyllabic, and some may begin with an additional initial *i*. Because stem-initial high front vowels merge with the person-marker vowel, an initial *i* is only detectable when a stative derivation exists, as in *-imu* ‘see’ and its stative form *-imubÿke* ‘see well’.  

The passage also notes that some of these stems mark irrealis not by changing final *u* to *a*, but by adding *-a*. Comparison with Mojeño Trinitario suggests that at least some of these stems formerly had an extra final syllable, with cognates such as *-imo’o* ‘see’, *-iso’o* ‘weed’, and *-iyo’o* ‘cry’.

subsection: Verb stems with a thematic suffix
text: verbal stem|( derivation|( thematic suffix|( There are two thematic suffixes in Paunaka, -ku and -chu, which both have cognate forms in the other Southern Arawakan languages. Thematic suffixes are only found on active verbs, which is why calls the TrinitarioMojeño Trinitario cognates, which she suggests are allomorphs, an “active suffix”. argues that the Baure cognate of -ku is an absolute suffix, which interacts with transitivity, and the cognate of -chu is an applicative. Paunaka’s -chu could also be interpreted as an applicative applicative|( marker, but contrary to Baure, we do not find many verb roots that can take both suffixes. The only exception of an active verb I know of is the root -su ‘write’, which can be combined with the extension applicative suffix -i and -ku into the stem -suiku ‘write’, as well as with the suffix -chu into -suchu ‘write something’. This pair of verb stems suggests an interpretation of -chu as an applicative. Additional support comes from the derivation of active from stative verbs, e.g. -jÿchu ‘light (fire)’ from -ijÿe ‘burn’ and -eimachu ‘cook until done’ from -ima ‘be cooked, done’, but this kind of active verb stem derivation also seems to be used very infrequently. I thus decided to call both suffixes ‘thematic suffixes’, -ku being glossed as ‘th1’ and -chu as ‘th2’.applicative|) lists verb stems that are usually realised with the thematic suffix -ku and list verb stems with -chu. The thematic suffix -ku occurs much more frequently than -chu. If Spanish loansborrowing|( are verbalised, it is usually the suffix -chu that is attached to the stem. Loan verb integration by this suffix is also found in Mojeño Trinitario and Baure . ( ) shows a verb borrowed from Spanish. The verbal root -ayurau, derived from the Spanish participle ayudado ‘helped’, takes the thematic suffix -chu to yield the stem -ayurauchu ‘help’. tayurauchunÿ\\ ti-ayurau-chu-nÿ\\ 3i-help-th2-1sg\\ ‘she helps me’ borrowing|) The suffix -chu is also found in some irregular derivations, e.g. the pluractional -paikechu ‘all die’ from -paku ‘die’ and equally -kupaikechu ‘kill all’ from -kupaku ‘kill’.thematic suffix|)
summary: Paunaka has two thematic suffixes on active verbs, -ku and -chu, both cognate with forms in other Southern Arawakan languages. Although -chu can be analyzed as applicative-like in some cases, the evidence is limited, so the author treats both as thematic suffixes; -ku is much more frequent, while -chu is especially common in verbalized Spanish loans and some irregular derivations.

text: aktionsart|(extension applicative|( The extension applicative suffix -i (‘ext’) directly precedes the thematic suffixes,thematic suffix usually -ku, sometimes also -chu. This suffix is completely lexicalisedlexicalisation with the verb stems and thus hard to grasp. The term “extension applicative” comes from who describes a cognate form of this suffix for Baure. According to her analysis, the suffix has at least two functions: first, it can decrease the valency of a transitive verb by deriving a durative form, and second, it can change the semantic role of the object . In Paunaka, verbs with the extension applicative suffix can be transitive or intransitive. Many of them are atelic,telicity but not all of them. There is a huge number of verbs which take the marker, so many that I first thought I was dealing with a (morpho-)phonological rule (prepalatalisation) rather than with a morpheme. There are, however, a number of verbs that are never realised with -i. Some verb stems with the extension suffix and the thematic suffix -ku are listed in . Only a few related verbs differ in presence or absence of -i, which makes the analysis very difficult. The pairs I have found in the corpus are given in . Among them, we find some that suggest a durative derivation, like -samu ‘hear’ and -samuiku ‘listen’, so this speaks for an analysis as an aktionsart suffix. Others rather differ in involvement of a human being in the event, although this human being is not always involved in the same type of stem, i.e. either the one without or the one with the applicative, and it does not necessarily have to be realised as an object, as e.g. in the pair -umu ‘take’ (whose object can be human or non-human) and -umeiku ‘steal’, whose object is usually non-human, but a human is necessarily involved as the victim of the theft. It is thus not precisely an applicative which changes the semantic role of the object. extension applicative|)
summary: The suffix -i, called the extension applicative, precedes the thematic suffixes and is highly lexicalized with verb stems, making it difficult to analyze. Although it may reduce valency by deriving durative forms and alter object semantics, in Paunaka it appears with many verbs that can be transitive or intransitive, and only some verb pairs suggest a clear durative or semantic contrast.

text: intensive aktionsart|( The suffix -ji shows up on many verb stems whose semantics includes an intensive degree, and so it can be analysed as an aktionsart suffix. It is only found on active verbs with the thematic suffix -ku and directly precedes it. Just as is the case with extension applicative -i, there are not many verb stems that can be realised with or without the suffix, so that it is hard to determine the exact meaning of it. It is also possible that the sequence ji is just part of the verb root, especially with the shorter, trisyllabic stems. There is also a homophonous classifier-ji for soft masses (see ), which has to be distinguished from the aktionsart suffix. Both occur in different slots, theoretically, but in all actual verb forms found in the corpus, they both directly precede the thematic suffix, so that knowledge about position inside the stem does not help in this case. lists some verbs which do or may contain the intensive suffix -ji. Verb stems that can be realised with or without the aktionsart suffix are listed in . They all include more changes than absence vs. presence of the aktionsart suffix. The same statement made for the extension applicative also holds for the intensive aktionsart suffix: in general, it either always forms part of the stem or never, with only few exceptions. intensive aktionsart|)aktionsart|)
summary:
The suffix **-ji** appears on many verb stems with an intensive meaning and can be analysed as an **aktionsart suffix**, but its exact function is hard to pin down because few stems occur both with and without it. It occurs only on **active verbs with the thematic suffix -ku**, directly before that suffix, though in some shorter trisyllabic stems **ji** may simply be part of the root.  

A homophonous **classifier -ji** for soft masses must be distinguished from this suffix, but in actual corpus forms both occupy the same visible position before the thematic suffix. Overall, most verbs either consistently include the intensive suffix as part of the stem or never do, with only a few exceptions.

text: reduplication|( In some of the verb stems of Paunaka, we find a syllable of the verbal root reduplicated. These verbs often encode iterative or durative, and sometimes intensive events, so that reduplication seems to encode the same semantic notion as the applicativeextension applicative and aktionsart intensive aktionsart suffixes -i and -ji (see and ). As far as I know, there is only one verb root with more than one reduplicated syllable, which is -musimusiku ‘blink, wink’ (with a related noun -musipa ‘eyelash’). The great majority of verb stems are instances of partial reduplication of a single syllable. Verbs with a reduplicated root syllable almost exclusively take the thematic suffix -ku. Some of these verb stems are listed in , including two that repeat the syllable twice. Only a handful of verbs are also found without the reduplicated syllable. They are listed in . In addition to the forms in Tables and , where the reduplicated syllable belongs to the verbal root, reduplication is also found on the last syllable of the verb stem in continuouscontinuous|( marking. The reduplicated syllable is followed by the extension suffix -i and the thematic suffix thematic suffix|( -ku, and the whole sequence -CViku stands for continuous aspect. Note that it is not always clear whether we are dealing with reduplication of a root or a stem syllable, since they are identical for all those verb stems that do not end in a thematic suffix. For those verbs, it is not clear whether the form derived by reduplication + -i + -ku should be analysed as continuous forms or as verbs with a reduplicated stem syllable and the extension applicative suffix with the latter triggering the addition of the thematic suffix -ku. All “continuous” verbs derived from verbs without a thematic suffix show a high degree of lexicalisationlexicalisation|(, while in most cases where there is a thematic suffix on the underived verb stem (and thus the continuous marker is -kuiku),thematic suffix|) the continuous form seems to be used for inflectionalinflection|( rather than derivational purposes, e.g. progressive marking, mirroring the use of Spanish gerunds. Continuous marking often but not always goes along with middle voice (see ). It is sometimes also found on non-verbal predicates.non-verbal predication shows the most frequent lexicalised continuous forms. An example of the inflectional use of the continuous is given in ( ). lexicalisation|) The example comes from Juana and refers to her little parrot, which we were watching. tinikukuikumÿnÿ tikunipa\\ ti-niku-kuiku-mÿnÿ ti-kunipa\\ 3i-eat-cont-dim 3i-be.hungry\\ ‘it is eating, it is hungry’ continuous|) inflection|) Another process that optionally but frequently includes reduplication on the edge of a verb stem is concurrent motion markingassociated motion (see ). This can probably be considered a case of automatic reduplication, where the presence of a marker triggers reduplication on another morpheme without reduplication itself adding any meaning . However, as rightly remark, “it may be hard to determine that the involved reduplication does not contribute in any way to the meaning of the resulting construction”. summary: Paunaka verb stems often show partial reduplication of a syllable from the root, and these forms typically express iterative, durative, or sometimes intensive meanings, overlapping with the functions of certain suffixes. Reduplication also appears in continuous marking, where a repeated syllable plus -i and -ku forms a continuous aspect marker, though many such forms are lexicalized and some are better analyzed as inflectional, sometimes with middle voice or even on non-verbal predicates. The passage also notes reduplication in concurrent motion marking and in an allomorph of the regressive/repetitive marker, though in these cases the repeated syllable may not belong to the verb stem itself.

summary: Most classifiers in the passage are more often attached to stative than active verb stems, but some transitive verbs also take classifiers, where the classifier can refer to the object or to an oblique, such as a goal or location. The morphemes -pai and -e are treated as classifiers rather than directionals because they can occur with both transitive and intransitive verbs, and -pai can even derive nouns, though they primarily refer to obliques. The author tentatively concludes that some classifiers may promote obliques to object status in related languages, but for Paunaka the evidence is not yet sufficient to confirm this.

The passage explains that Paunaka allows incorporation of noun stems into active verb stems, but this is now rare and occurs mainly with body-part terms. Incorporation can trigger possessor raising, as when the possessor of the incorporated body part appears as the direct object, and some incorporated forms have become lexicalized or semantically extended into stative verbs.  

It also notes two exceptions: one verb incorporates the noun for ‘seed’ to mean ‘husk,’ and the relational noun ‘top’ can be incorporated as -ne, apparently the only relational noun found in verb incorporation.

text: valency|( Many active verbsactive verb|( are ambitransitive,ambitransitivity i.e. they can be used intransitively and transitively without any overt change of the verb stem. Only the choice of the third person markerperson marking (see ) possibly sheds light on the valency. There are also some verbs that are stativestative verb by their stem, but can be used transitively nonetheless. Furthermore, two affixes increase the valency of an active verb: causative and benefactive. Both of them do not occur very frequently in my corpus. Valency of active verbs can be decreased by reciprocal marking, which expresses that the participants act on each other. Paunaka has no reflexive marker proper, but reflexive is one of the functions of the middle markermiddle voice -bu, see . All processes described in this section are found on the edge of verb stems, i.e. following or replacing the thematic suffix (if the verb in question has one, see and ). They arguably derive new stems that are the locus of RS marking.reality status This sets them apart from middle voice, which is clearly marked outside the verb stem, following the RS marking. Therefore, I decided to describe causative, benefactive, and reciprocal here as derivational processesderivation and provide an extra section for middle marking.middle voice While the causative markers precede the verb stem, benefactive and reciprocal follow.
summary:
Many active verbs in Paunaka are ambitransitive, meaning they can be used both transitively and intransitively without any overt change in the verb stem, and some stative verbs can also be used transitively. Valency can be increased by causative and benefactive affixes and decreased by reciprocal marking; reflexive meaning is expressed by the middle marker -bu rather than by a dedicated reflexive marker.  

These valency-changing processes occur at the edge of the verb stem and are treated as derivational, because they likely create new stems that host reality-status marking. This contrasts with middle voice, which is marked outside the verb stem and follows reality-status marking; causative markers precede the stem, while benefactive and reciprocal markers follow it.

summary: Paunaka transitive verbs are often ambitransitive: a non-human third person object may be omitted when it is contextually accessible or when a general statement is intended, but the same verb can also appear with an overt NP object. In intransitive uses, third person subjects take the prefix ti-, while in transitive uses some verbs alternate between ti- and chÿ-, though others like -piku ‘fear’ always take chÿ-; the verb -niku ‘eat’ is especially notable because its causative meaning ‘feed, give food’ has the same form as the non-causative, making the two sometimes difficult to distinguish.

The passage explains that while stative verbs are usually intransitive, some can take objects either through an added noun phrase or verbal complement without object indexing, as in **-(i)chuna** ‘be capable, know’. It also discusses **-kuye** ‘be like this,’ the most frequent transitive stative verb, which behaves as an anaphoric demonstrative verb and often closes discourse topics. In the corpus it usually appears with third-person indexing, can stand as a clause by itself, and has related forms such as **chikuyena/kuyena** meaning ‘how?’ or ‘why?’.

text: active verb|(causative|( derivation|( In causative derivations, one participant, the causer, is added to the semantic structure of the verb. The causer is expressed as the subject argument of the predicate. The agent of the non-causative verb becomes the causee of the causative verb and is expressed as the object. I have only found causative derivations of intransitive verbs in the corpus, the majority of them being active verbs. Causative derivation is not very productive. Nonetheless, two different causative prefixes could be identified, ku- and mi-. Both of them have cognates in several other Arawakan languages . claimed for Baure that the cognate causative prefix ko- derives causative states, while verbs derived with the cognate prefix imo- express caused actions. I cannot confirm this same distinction for Paunaka. However, my impression is that the prefix ku- is predominantly used with telictelicity verb stems. Causative verbs derived with mi- have only been found in Juana’s speech in the corpus. Both derivations are rare so that I do not want to make any absolute claims about them here. The prefix ku- is found on the highly lexicalisedlexicalisation verb -kupaku ‘kill’ from -paku ‘die’, as in ( ), which was elicited from José. tikupakubi ue\\ ti-ku-paku-bi ue\\ 3i-caus1-die-1pl water.spirit\\ ‘the water spirit kills us’ Another example with the causative prefix ku- is given in ( ), which comes from Juana’s description of one picture of the frog story , where some bees (or wasps) chase the dog and the frightened boy falls from the tree. The causative verb -kubenupu usually means ‘fell (trees)’, while -benupu means ‘fall down’, but is more often used with the more specific meaning ‘be born’. i naka tikijane jane, aa, chikubenuputu\\ i naka ti-kijane jane aa chi-ku-benupu-tu\\ and here 3i-be.many wasp intj 3-caus1-fall.down-iam\\ ‘and here are a lot of wasps, ah, they have made him fall’ ( ) is an example with the transitive verb -kurabajiku ‘break’, a causative derivation of -rabajiku ‘break (intr.)’. It was elicited from María S. and referred to an imagined broken pot. eka ÿba tikurabajikuchÿ\\ eka ÿba ti-ku-rabajiku-chÿ\\ dema pig 3i-caus1-break-3\\ ‘the pig broke it’ Other causative verb stems derived with ku- that I found in the corpus include -kuchepaku ‘wake up (tr.)’ from -chepaku ‘wake up (intr.)’, -kujapÿku ‘fill (tr.)’ from -japÿku ‘fill (intr.)’ and -kurÿrÿku ‘make burn, light fire’ from -rÿrÿku ‘burn’. The use of the other causative prefix, mi-, is illustrated by the following examples. As has been stated above, all of them come from Juana. The verb in ( ) builds on the verb stem -benu ‘lie down’ (which is related to -benupu ‘fall’ in ( ) above). Juana tells about her sister, who was severely injured and put into the hammock by her son. chimibenu yumaji\\ chi-mi-benu yumaji\\ 3-caus2-lie.down hammock\\ ‘he laid her down in the hammock’ Other verbs that take mi- are -mijÿku ‘raise, bring up’ from -jÿku ‘grow’ and -mikuchu ‘bathe so.’ from -kubu ‘bathe, take a bath’. The resulting verb is active and carries the thematic suffix -chu (see ). nimikumÿuchabÿti\\ ni-mi-ku-mÿu-cha-bÿti\\ 1sg-caus2-attr-clothes-th2.irr-prsp\\ ‘I am going to dress him’ verb|) Speakers often prefer a periphrastic expression for causative relations.manipulative verb|( If volition and movement is involved in the action, i.e. cause and effect take place in different locations , they use a complement construction including the manipulative verb -bÿche(i)ku ‘send, order’, one example of which is given here. It was elicited from Miguel. More examples can be found in . nibÿchekabi pisupa\\ ni-bÿcheka-bi pi-isu-pa\\ 1sg-order.irr-2sg 2sg-weed-dloc.irr\\ ‘I will send you to weed’ manipulative verb|) The other possibility is preferred if no volition is involved. It builds on the instrument and cause prepositioninstrument/cause -keuchi (see ). Consider ( ), which is about making something fall, just like ( ) above. It also comes from a description of the frog story, but this sentence was produced by Miguel and referred to another picture, the one on which the dog has made the beehive (or: wasp nest) fall. tibÿtupaikubutu chikeuchi echÿu kabe eka chubiu eka jane\\ ti-bÿtupaikubu-tu chi-keuchi echÿu kabe eka chÿ-ubiu eka jane\\ 3i-fall.down-iam 3-ins demb dog dema 3-house dema wasp\\ ‘the wasp nest fell down because of the dog’ A similar example comes from María S. who had just stated that smoking is bad and now provides the reason: chepuine bikutiu chikeuchi bijibÿkia\\ chepuine bi-kutiu chi-keuchi bi-jibÿk-i-a\\ because 1pl-be.ill 3-ins 1pl-smoke-subord-irr\\ ‘because we get ill by smoking’ causative|)
summary:
The passage describes causative derivation in which an added causer becomes the subject and the original agent of the non-causative verb becomes the object. In the corpus, causatives are rare and occur only with intransitive verbs, mostly active ones, though two prefixes are identified: ku- and mi-, with ku- more common and mi- found only in Juana’s speech.  

Examples show that ku- can derive verbs such as ‘kill,’ ‘make fall,’ and ‘break,’ while mi- appears in forms meaning ‘lay down,’ ‘raise,’ ‘bathe,’ and other derived verbs, including a double derivation. Speakers often prefer periphrastic causative constructions instead, using either the manipulative verb meaning ‘send, order’ when volition and movement are involved, or the instrument/cause preposition when no volition is involved.

text: active verb|(applicative|(benefactive|( The benefactive marker occurs on the edge of the stem of active verbs, following the thematic suffix -- if the verb stem in question includes one -- but preceding or fusing with RS marking.reality status The benefactive marker thus has the realis form -inu and the irrealis form -ina. It has cognates in the other Southern Arawakan languages. In benefactive derivation, added SAP participants are indexed by a person marker following the stem, i.e. as the object of the active verb. ( ) has a second person plural subject and a first person singular object. The sentence comes from Juana who cited her deceased sister here, who was in prison and demanded to see her daughter. “¡epuninane nijinepÿimÿnÿ!”\\ e-epun-ina-ne ni-jinepÿi-mÿnÿ\\ 2pl-take-ben.irr-1sg 1sg-daughter-dim\\ ‘“take my daughter to me!”’ In my data, the added participant is always a recipient. Verbs of the type ‘do instead of somebody else doing it’ or ‘do because it is good for somebody’ are absent, so that the suffix could be called a recipient applicative more precisely. The marker -inu is not found to encode any malefactive relations, i.e. actions that are done to the detriment of the recipient. It is due to the relation with other Arawakan languages that I prefer the term benefactive nonetheless. Benefactive verbs with a third person subject always take the third person marker chÿ-,person marking|( no matter whether the themepatient/theme is animate or inanimate and whether a first or second person recipientrecipient|( is indexed. This marker is reserved for 3>3 relationships on transitive and ditransitive (non-subordinate) verbs (see ). Note that non-derived ditransitive verbs take the marker chÿ- if they also take a third person object object|( marker -chÿ (see ), but not if they have an SAP object. Benefactive verbs do not take the marker -chÿ though. We can therefore state that there is a kind of double object marking on benefactive verbs, but they do not behave like other ditransitive verbs regarding person marking.person marking|) In ( ) we find a benefactive derivation of the verb -upunu ‘bring’. The recipient is marked by a person index as the object of the verb and the third person marker chÿ- is used obligatorily, also with inanimate themes,patient/theme a photo in this case, which we had brought to María C. Apparently, she had already been waiting for this photo. metu nÿmayu chupuninunÿnube\\ metu nÿmayu chÿ-upun-inu-nÿ-nube\\ already just 3-bring-ben-1sg-pl\\ ‘they just finally brought it to me’ Another example with double object marking is ( ), which was elicited from Clara. chiyÿseikinubi\\ chi-yÿseik-inu-bi\\ 3-buy-ben-2sg\\ ‘he bought it for you’ object|) ( ) illustrates a benefactive derivation with a first person subject and a third person recipient object. The latter is not marked on the verb. The theme objectpatient/theme is expressed by an NP, the benefactive recipient is not expressed overtly at all, and it is the benefactive verb itself that provides the information that there is a recipient. The example is an excerpt from Juana’s citation of what Miguel’s daughter had told her. “i netukinu pan”\\ i nÿ-etuk-inu pan\\ and 1sg-put-ben bread\\ ‘“and I served him some bread”’ recipient|) Only very few verb stems take the benefactive suffix in spontaneous speech, though a few more could be elicited from Clara and Miguel; the latter provided the verb forms in ( ). tisipuikinane, tiyÿtikinane\\ ti-sipuik-ina-ne ti-yÿtik-ina-ne\\ 3i-pay-ben.irr-1sg 3i-set.on.fire-ben.irr-1sg\\ ‘he/she will pay for me, he/she will cook for me' verb|) Juana would not produce benefactive verbs in elicitation, but rather found other ways of expressing a benefactive relation, as in ( ) and ( ): eka nipiji tiyÿseiku, tiyÿseiku nauku, kapunu tipunÿ\\ eka ni-piji ti-yÿseiku ti-yÿseiku nauku kapunu ti-pu-nÿ\\ dema 1sg-sibling 3i-buy 3i-buy there come 3i-give-1sg\\ ‘my sister bought it, she bought it there, she came and gave it to me’ metu pisutu nitÿpi\\ metu pi-isu-tu ni-tÿpi\\ already 2sg-weed-iam 1sg-obl\\ ‘you already weeded for me’ Especially the general oblique preposition (-)tÿpi of this last example is used a lot to encode benefactive relations,beneficiary much more than any derived benefactive verb (see for more information on the preposition).benefactive|)applicative|)
summary:
The passage describes a benefactive suffix on active verbs, with realis form **-inu** and irrealis **-ina**, which occurs at the stem edge and can follow the thematic suffix or fuse with reality-status marking. In the author’s data, the added participant is always a **recipient**, and benefactive verbs show unusual person marking: a third-person subject takes **chÿ-** obligatorily, while the recipient is indexed as the object, producing a kind of double object marking.  

The suffix is relatively rare in spontaneous speech, and speakers often express benefactive meanings instead with other constructions, especially the general oblique preposition **(-)tÿpi**. Although the suffix could more precisely be called a recipient applicative, the author retains the term **benefactive** because of its cognates in other Southern Arawakan languages.

text: active verb|( reciprocal|( Paunaka’s reciprocal marker is rarely found in natural discourse, but the speakers have no difficulty in producing reciprocal forms in elicitation. The form of the marker is -kuku, irrealis -kuka.reality status It goes back to Proto-ArawakanArawakan languages *-kaka , and cognates are also found in all other Southern Arawakan languages . The reciprocal marker is either added after the thematic suffix thematic suffix|( -ku or replaces it, depending on the speaker. thematic suffix|) Since the additive marker -uku/-uka (see ) can also directly follow the stem-closing suffix, many verbs have a sequence kuku or kuka which is not related to the reciprocal marker. The reciprocal marker can only be attached to transitive verb stems. Third person subjects then always take the person marker ti- regardless of animacy, and chÿ- is not possible (compare ).person marking This is a clear sign that valency of the verb decreases if the reciprocal marker is added. Consider the following pair of examples: In ( ), the speaker uses the marker chÿ- to indicate that a third person acts on another third person. In ( ), chÿ- is not possible. Both examples were elicited from Juana. eka kabe chinijabaku takÿra\\ eka kabe chi-nijabaku takÿra\\ dema dog 3-bite chicken\\ ‘the dog bit the hen’ tinijabakukuku kabe\\ ti-nijabaku-kuku kabe\\ 3i-bite-rcpc dog\\ ‘the dogs are biting each other’ The reciprocal marker can also be used on verbs with a first person plural marker as in ( ), which was also elicited from Juana. bipitanÿkukuka\\ bi-pitanÿku-kuka\\ 1pl-embrace-rcpc.irr\\ ‘we embrace each other’ The following example ( ) with a reciprocal marker was produced spontaneously by María S., who was making fun of an embracing couple by stating that they should rather go fishing. bupuna echÿu tipitanÿikukunube tepuikanube\\ bi-upuna echÿu ti-pitanÿi-kuku-nube ti-epuika-nube\\ 1pl-bring.irr demb 3i-embrace-rcpc-pl 3i-fish.irr-pl\\ ‘let’s bring the ones that embrace each other so that they fish’ If the verb -eu ‘hit, fight’ is combined with the reciprocal marker, the collective marker -ji is added. This seems to be peculiar to this one verb, since it is not found in other reciprocal derivations. One example is given in ( ), which was elicited from María S. teukukujinube chajechubu chÿa\\ ti-eu-kuku-ji-nube chÿ-ajechubu chÿ-a\\ 3i-fight-rcpc-col-pl 3-com 3-father\\ ‘with his father, they were fighting with each other’ If we compare examples ( ) and ( ) above, we see that the reciprocal marker can occur in two different possible slots: that of the thematic suffix,thematic suffix|( which usually closes the stem, thus replacing this suffix, and the one following the thematic suffix. There are a few more markers that can occur either in the place of the thematic suffix or in a position following it, namely the associated motionassociated motion|( markers and the distributive marker, but their treatment is postponed.thematic suffix|) Since they do not affect the valency of a verb, if we adopt the view that derivation and inflection can be seen as a continuum , then causative, benefactive and reciprocal markers are clearly on the derivational side, but AM markers and especially the distributive marker can be placed a little further to the inflection side.associated motion|) valency|) reciprocal|) active verb|) derivation|) verbal stem|) The following two sections deal with the most important inflectional categories of the verb, person ( ) and reality status ( ).
summary: Paunaka’s reciprocal marker is -kuku (irrealis -kuka), a reflex of Proto-Arawakan *-kaka, and it is rarely used in natural discourse but can be readily produced in elicitation. It attaches only to transitive verbs, reduces valency, and can appear either in the thematic-suffix slot or after the thematic suffix; in one verb, -eu ‘hit, fight,’ it combines with the collective marker -ji. The passage also notes that causative, benefactive, and reciprocal markers are clearly derivational, while associated motion and distributive markers are closer to inflection because they do not affect valency.

chapter: The verb and morphology on predicates
text: inflection|( person marking|( Verbs take the very same person markers as nouns do: on nouns they index possessors and subjects in non-verbal predication (see and ), on verbs they index subjects and objects.argument|( The occurrence of the same set of person markers on nouns and verbs is common among Arawakan languages ( ; ). There is, however, one person marker that only occurs with verbs in Paunaka, the third person marker ti-, which is also found in the Mojeño languages. It is described in detail in . summarises the subjectsubject|( and objectobject|( indexes found on verbs. object|) Subject markersalignment|( precede the verb stems of both main classes, which are stativestative verb and activeactive verb. The latter includes both intransitive and transitive verbs. Indexing the subject is in general obligatory on all verbs, but in rapid speech, person markers are sometimes dropped. This partly depends on the speaker -- both Marías drop person markers more often than other speakers do --, and partly on the marker – the one most likely to be dropped is the third person marker ti-. An NPnoun phrase referring to the subject can co-occur, but this is not necessary, thus the NP can be defined as an optional conominalconomination and the person markers as cross-indexes according to the terminology used by .subject|) First and second person objectsobject are indexed by a person marker following the stem.verbal stem In this regard, Paunaka is a typical Arawakan languageArawakan languages exhibiting nominative-accusative alignment.alignment|) Third person markers that follow the stem occur rarely and only under specific circumstances, which will be discussed in . The index chÿ-, however, expresses 3>3 relationships on verbs. That means that in general, third person singular objects are only indexed on the verb if there is also a third person subject, i.e. jointly with the subject by chÿ-. This marker is used obligatorily if the object is human, but it is optional with non-human objects.object Both third person markers ti- and chÿ- are underspecified for number. The plural, distributive or collective marker can be used to encode that a third person subject or object is non-singular. The following sections describe subject and object marking in more detail, starting in with the description of how first and second person arguments are indexed. Subsequently, I attend to the third person in , with being devoted to third person plural indexing. provides an overview of the contexts in which a third person marker can follow a verb (or other) stem.
summary: Paunaka uses the same set of person markers on nouns and verbs: on nouns they index possessors and subjects in non-verbal predication, while on verbs they index subjects and objects. Subject markers are normally obligatory and precede both stative and active verb stems, whereas first- and second-person objects are marked after the stem, giving the language a nominative-accusative pattern; third-person marking is more restricted, with ti- and chÿ- used in specific contexts and both being unspecified for number.

summary: Every verb obligatorily takes a subject marker, and first/second person subject indexes occur before the stem on both transitive and intransitive verbs, including active and stative intransitives. First/second person objects are also obligatorily marked, but their indexes follow the stem; they are formally similar to the subject markers, have different allomorphs in some environments, and cannot be replaced by or co-occur with personal pronouns.

text: object|( subject|( There are two different third person indexes on verbs, ti- and chÿ- (also realised as chi-). Only the latter also occurs on nouns, where it indexes a possessor (see ); ti- is attached to verbs exclusively. The marker ti- only indexes the subject, while chÿ- is used to encode two third person arguments, a subject and an object. The gloss chosen for ti- is ‘3i’ and for chÿ-, it is ‘3’. Both indexes do not distinguish gender and are underspecified for number, but there are other means to express plurality of an argument (see ). Third person markers follow a stem only marginally, see . Let us first have a look at ti-.animacy|( This marker is obligatory with intransitive verbs and with transitive verbs with SAP objects, and it can also be used with many transitive verbs that have non-human third person objects, see ( )--( ). ( ) has a stative intransitive verb. It comes from Juana speaking about her son-in-law. That fact that the subject is a male person is thus deduced from the context; this information is not given by the third person marker. tikutiu\\ ti-kutiu\\ 3i-be.ill\\ ‘he is ill’ In ( ) from the same speaker, there is a middle verb, which is also intransitive, and ti- clearly relates to the conominated female person. i titupunubu nijinepÿi\\ i ti-tupunubu ni-jinepÿi\\ and 3i-arrive 1sg-daughter\\ ‘and my daughter arrived’ ( ) has a transitive verb with a first person singular object and was elicited from María S. The imagined third person subject was a dog in this case, but it was not conominated. tinijabakunÿ\\ ti-nijabaku-nÿ\\ 3i-bite-1sg\\ ‘it bites me’ In ( ), there is a first person plural object. It comes from María S. who speaks about smoking. tikupakabi\\ ti-kupaka-bi\\ 3i-kill.irr-1pl\\ ‘it can kill us’ If there is a non-human third person object as in ( ), ti- may also be used. summary:
The passage distinguishes two third person verbal indexes in Paunaka: **ti-**, which attaches only to verbs and indexes the subject, and **chÿ- / chi-**, which can mark both a third person subject and object and also occurs on nouns as a possessor marker. Neither marker distinguishes gender or number, and **ti-** is obligatory with intransitive verbs and with transitive verbs whose object is a speech-act participant, while **chÿ-** is obligatory when a human third person object is involved.

It also shows that **ti-** may appear with some transitive verbs whose objects are non-human third persons, whereas **chÿ-** is used when a third person acts on another third person, including rare cases with inanimate subjects and animate objects. Nonetheless, since the stone plays an important role in the story, she knows the story well and her brother Miguel, who was co-telling the story, also knows it well, it is also possible that the NP is indeed definite, referring to ‘the stone (that we all know)’. Compare ( ) with the intransitive verb with ( ) and ( ) with transitive verbs. ( ) comes from María S. who told me the story about the two hunters who meet the devil in the woods. One of them interacts with the devil and is taken away to be eaten in the end, while the other hides away in a tree and stays there until the devil leaves the scene. He does not try to save his friend: janeka tiyuna, tipiku\\ janeka ti-yuna ti-piku\\ never 3i-go 3i-be.afraid\\ ‘he never went, he was afraid’ ( ) and ( ) both come from Juana describing pictures of the frog story. In the first example, it is the boy who feels fear, in the second one the dog. In both cases, there is a concrete thing that they fear. chipiku jane\\ chi-piku jane\\ 3-be.afraid wasp\\ ‘he fears the wasps’ chipiku ÿne\\ chi-piku ÿne\\ 3-be.afraid water\\ ‘it is afraid of the water’ Some transitive verbs are preferably used with chÿ-, among them -umu ‘take’, -imu ‘see’, and -tupu ‘find, meet’. Others are rather indexed with ti- like -anau ‘make’ and -yÿseiku ‘buy’. This is certainly connected to frequency effects: ‘make’ and ‘buy’ hardly ever take humananimacy objects, while ‘take’, ‘see’, and ‘find, meet’ can readily have human objects and are thus often realised with chÿ- for that reason. By extension, chÿ- is then also used with non-human objects more frequently. This is not absolute, though, since speakers may still opt for the the other marker as in ( ) above where -umu is combined with ti- or ( ) below, in which -anau is combined with chÿ- . There are not only differences among verbs, but also differences between the speakers: Juana generally produces more forms with chÿ- than Miguel. But even if she often uses chÿ-, she may also opt for ti-. When she once told me a story about her grandparents’ journey to Moxos to buy some cows, she used ti- on most of the verbs that describe an action of her grandparents upon the cows, as in ( ). However, prompted by questions about some words that I did not understand, she re-told the story some days later, adding the description of how her grandparents met an evil spirit on their way back home, and this time she used the marker chÿ- more often for describing actions of her grandparents upon their cows, as in ( ). The cows can be considered definitedefiniteness in both examples. i enteraukena kuje ke te kapupununubetu te tupunanubetu baka\\ i enterau-kena kuje ke te kapupunu-nube-tu te ti-upuna-nube-tu baka\\ and whole-uncert moon that seq come.back-pl-iam seq 3i-bring.irr-pl-iam cow\\ ‘and it took them a whole month to come back and bring the cows’ kapupunutu niuma chupunu chipeu baka\\ kapupunu-tu ni-uma chÿ-upunu chi-peu baka\\ come.back-iam 1sg-grandfather 3-bring 3-animal cow\\ ‘my grandfather came back and brought his cows along’ An important difference between the two examplesreality status|( is that the verb in ( ) is realis, while in ( ), it is irrealis. Irrealis is among the factors that signal low transitivity . However, it is not the case that every irrealis verb with a non-humananimacy object would take ti-. Consider , which comes from the same speaker and has an irrealis verb that takes the index chÿ- (and is also one of the relatively few examples of the verb -anau ‘make’ taking this marker). Juana speaks about her daughter in Spain, who still owns a plot in Bolivia that she could use for building a house. kapunuina chana chubiuna\\ kapunu-ina chÿ-ana chÿ-ubiu-ina\\ come-irr.nv 3-make.irr 3-house-irr.nv\\ ‘if she comes, she can make her future house’ A few more examples in the corpus combine an irrealis verb with chÿ-: consider ( ), which was produced by María S. in elicitation and has two clauses that give information about sown and planted crops using the same verb. Strikingly, in the first clause the realis verb is indexed with ti-, and in the second clause the negated irrealis verb carries the marker chÿ-. jaja ja amuke tebuku, pero kÿjÿpi kuina chebuka\\ jaja ja amuke ti-ebuku pero kÿjÿpi kuina chÿ-ebuka\\ afm afm corn 3i-sow but manioc neg 3-sow.irr\\ ‘yes, yes, he sowed corn, but he did not plant manioc’ Thus irrealis as the only decisive factor for choosing one or the other marker can definitely be ruled out.reality status|) I would rather suggest that several factors are involved, and more profound knowledge about discourse structure is needed to explain each and every choice. How different factors trigger the choice of one or the other of the two third person indexes is summarised in . object|)
summary:
The passage argues that neither definiteness nor irrealis status alone determines the choice between the third-person markers chÿ- and ti-, since both markers can occur with definite or indefinite objects and with realis or irrealis verbs. Instead, the distribution seems to depend on several interacting factors, including verb semantics, object animacy, frequency, discourse context, and speaker-specific usage.

It also notes that some verbs show preferences for one marker or the other: chÿ- is common with verbs like ‘take,’ ‘see,’ and ‘find,’ while ti- is more often used with verbs like ‘make’ and ‘buy.’ However, these patterns are not absolute, and speakers may vary in how often they use each marker.

chapter: The verb and morphology on predicates
text: Both third person markers are underspecified for number, i.e. both singular and plural subjects take ti- and chÿ-. However, the plural marker, the distributive marker, and the collective marker can be attached to the verb to indicate that one of the participants is non-singular. All of them also occur on nouns (see ). It is not uncommon among Arawakan languages to have a third person marker that is not specified for number and a separate marker expressing plural. In Danielsen’s ( ) sample, 15 out of 38 languages have “separate gender/person and plural marking”, while 17 do not show this distinction, and for six languages, the question remains unclear.
summary: Both third person markers are underspecified for number, so singular and plural subjects alike take ti- and chÿ-. Non-singularity can instead be marked on the verb by a plural, distributive, or collective marker, which also appears on nouns. The passage notes that this kind of separate person/gender and plural marking is common in Arawakan languages, with Danielsen’s sample showing this pattern in 15 of 38 languages.

chapter: The verb and morphology on predicates
subsubsection: Third person plural subject marking with -nube
text: plural|(subject|( If the third person plural subject is human,animacy the marker -nube is added to the verb obligatorily. The following examples show third person plural subjects on different kinds of verbs with different valency and different types of objects. In ( ), there is an intransitive verb and thus ti- is used. It comes from an utterance by Miguel. tikujemunubetu\\ ti-kujemu-nube-tu\\ 3i-be.angry-pl-iam\\ ‘they were already angry’ The verb in ( ) has a third person plural subject acting on an SAP object. The marker indexing the SAP object always precedes the plural marker. The example comes from the recordings by Riester with Juan Ch. The patrones are the ones who might kill their workers if they tried to escape. tikupakabinube\\ ti-kupaka-bi-nube\\ 3i-kill.irr-1pl-pl\\ ‘they would kill us’ In ( ), there is a third person plural subject. It is not a human subject in this case, but an anthropomorphic fox and jaguarundi are acting, the two main characters of a story. They see a pot with strong chicha, the third person singular inanimate objectanimacy of this clause (and they decide to get drunk). In this example, Miguel chose the index chÿ- to encode the 3>3 relationship. An example with a humananimacy third person plural subject acting on a non-human third person object being encoded by the ti-marker has already been given in ( ) above. pero chimukunubeji echÿu barerekiji tijapÿkubu isipau\\ pero chi-imu-uku-nube-ji echÿu barereki-ji ti-japÿku-bu isipau\\ but 3-see-add-pl-rprt demb pot-rprt 3i-fill-mid strong.chicha\\ ‘but they also saw a pot filled with strong chicha’ subject|)

In the examples, **ti-** marks an intransitive verb, while on transitive verbs the marker indexing an SAP object precedes the plural marker; for 3>3 relations, **chÿ-** may be used, as in the story example with anthropomorphic fox and jaguarundi.

chapter: The verb and morphology on predicates
subsubsection: Third person plural object marking with -nube
text: object|( Not only humananimacy third person plural subjects, but also human third person plural objects can be encoded by -nube. It is thus not always clear which of the arguments is the plural participant. In this respect, Paunaka differs from the Mojeño languages, where the plural marker can only relate to the subject . If the subject is an SAP, the only participant to which -nube can refer is obviously the object, as in ( ), which is taken from an utterance by Juana. nichupuikunube\\ ni-chupuiku-nube\\ 1sg-know-pl\\ ‘I met them’ However, if both subject and object have third person referents, ambiguity arises. Only context and general knowledge can clarify which one is the plural argument. In the following example, Juana describes a photo to my colleague Swintha on which my husband is carrying both my daughters in his arms. It is therefore clear that a singular subject acts on a plural object. chakachunube chima\\ chÿ-akachu-nube chi-ima\\ 3-lift-pl 3-husband\\ ‘her husband lifts them’ The next example from Miguel is sufficiently clear because of world knowledge: it is the patrón, the liege lord, who was supposed to pay his many workers; any other interpretation would be odd. kuina chisiupuchanube eka patron\\ kuina chi-siupucha-nube eka patron\\ neg 3-pay.irr-pl dema patrón\\ ‘the patrón didn’t pay them’ On the other hand, in ( ), the subject is plural. Juana had just narrated that her brother felt dizzy and fell. It was thus only a single person who was lifted and taken away and the plural marker must thus refer to the subject. chakachunube chumunubeji nauku\\ chÿ-akachu-nube chÿ-umu-nube-ji nauku\\ 3-lift-pl 3-take-pl-rprt there\\ ‘they lifted him and took him there, it is said’ It is also possible that both subject and object are plural as is the case in ( ), which has two conominal NPs that encode subject and object. The first NP only consists of a modifier, but this is nothing special in Paunaka. Both NPs are marked for plural. It is not important in this case to which of the arguments the plural marker belongs; it could be any of the two. There is no double plural marking on verbs. The sentence comes from Juana who told me what her daughter in Spain had said to her. This daughter wanted to convince Juana to visit her. “pujanenube chumunube chÿenujinube”\\ pu-jane-nube chÿ-umu-nube chÿ-enu-ji-nube\\ other-distr-pl 3-take-pl 3-mother-col-pl\\ ‘“others take their mothers (to Spain for a visit)”’ object|) plural|)
summary: The passage explains that in Paunaka, the plural marker **-nube** can refer either to a plural subject or a plural object, unlike in the Mojeño languages where it only marks the subject. When one argument is a speech-act participant, **-nube** must refer to the object, but with two third-person arguments the plural role is often ambiguous and must be resolved by context or world knowledge. It also notes that if both subject and object are plural, the marker may belong to either argument, and verbs do not show double plural marking.

chapter: The verb and morphology on predicates
subsubsection: Third person plural subject marking with -jane
text: distributive|(subject|( If the third person plural subject is non-human,animacy the marker -jane can be used optionally to establish plural reference. ( ) shows this with three verbs. It was produced by Juana and is about some ducklings that we were watching. tiyunujane kosinayae tinikupajane teajane ÿne\\ ti-yunu-jane kosina-yae ti-niku-pa-jane ti-ea-jane ÿne\\ 3i-go-distr kitchen-loc 3i-eat-dloc.irr-distr 3i-drink.irr-distr water\\ ‘they go into the kitchen to eat and drink water’ The distributive marker -jane can occur in two different morphological slots of the verb. First, it can attach to the complete verb stem including the thematic suffix thematic suffix|( (see ), and the other possibility is to replace the thematic suffix by -jane. Obviously, this possibility only exists for verbs that have a thematic suffix. If the distributive marker deletes the thematic suffix, the reality status suffix follows the distributive marker (see ( ), ( ) and also ). In order to compare both forms directly, consider the following two examples with the verb -niku ‘eat’. In ( ), the full verb stem -niku including the thematic suffix -ku is used and folowed by -jane. The example is from the same context as ( ) above; the ducklings were approaching us, coming back from eating grass somewhere. ( ) shows the use of the distributive marker in the slot that is usually occupied by the thematic suffix. Thus only the rootverbal root -ni shows up here. The example comes from elicitation with María S. which aimed at finding out whether there is a difference between the verbs for ‘eat’ and ‘feed’. tinikujane mÿiji\\ ti-niku-jane mÿiji\\ 3i-eat-distr grass\\ ‘they ate grass’ tinijaneutu\\ ti-ni-jane-u-tu\\ 3i-eat-distr-real-iam\\ ‘they already ate’ It is tempting to analyse the latter form as the older, more conservative one and the one in which the distributive follows the thematic suffix as an innovation which regulates the pattern by making distributive marking more reminiscent of plural marking. Nonetheless, since we do not have any old texts to compare with, this remains speculative. In any case, María S. prefers the form without thematic suffix, while the other speakers prefer the other one. When asked, all speakers accept both forms. There is no difference in meaning according to them, and I could not find any difference either. Another example with the distributive marker produced by María S. is given in ( ): the verb stemverbal stem is -yuiku ‘walk’, but the thematic suffix -ku is deleted, and -jane is inserted in the slot. It comes from elicitation and is about some recently hatched chicks. tiyuijaneatu\\ ti-yui-jane-a-tu\\ 3i-walk-distr-irr-iam\\ ‘they are about to walk’ If the object is an SAP, the object marker follows the distributive marker. Only the form of the verb in which -jane deletes the thematic suffix has been found in the corpus.thematic suffix|) Note that there is not necessarily agreement in number between the conominalconomination subject and the verb. summary: The passage explains that the distributive marker **-jane** can optionally mark plural reference when a third-person plural subject is non-human, and it may appear either on the full verb stem or in the slot of the thematic suffix, with speakers accepting both forms and reporting no meaning difference. It also notes that **-jane** is usually attached to either the verb or the noun, more often the verb, and that with SAP objects the distributive is often not realized on the verb; examples show its use with intransitive and transitive verbs, including cases with non-human animate plural subjects.
