summary: The distributive marker can optionally index non-human third-person plural objects, but only when the referents are animate. In this use, it signals a higher degree of individuation, which is context-dependent because animals may be viewed either as individual beings or not. An example is given of a second-person subject acting on a non-human animate plural object marked by **-jane**.

Since all property verbs are intransitive, the collective marker always refers to the subject. There are not many examples in the corpus and they all refer to fish. Although they fill different slots in the verb template, both often just occur on the right edge of the actual verb form. It might thus be possible that I mistakenly took as a reportive marker which was indeed a collective marker in some cases. There is one active verb on which the collective marker is found apparently. summary:
The collective marker **-ji** can encode non-singularity on verbs, especially on some stative property verbs when the subject is a mass or swarm; in these cases it always refers to the subject, not the object. The corpus contains few examples, mostly involving fish, and agreement in collective marking between verb and noun is optional rather than required.  

The text also notes that **-ji** is hard to distinguish from the reportive evidential because they have the same form, though they occupy different template slots. One rare example shows **-ji** on an active verb, **-eu** ‘hit, fight,’ together with the reciprocal marker, in a meaning like ‘they were fighting with each other.’

chapter: The verb and morphology on predicates
subsection: Third person markers following the stem
text: object|( Third person markers that follow the stem only rarely occur on verbs, but there are some exceptions. First of all, the ditransitive verb -punaku ‘give’ may possibly take -chÿ as a marker to index a recipient or theme.patient/theme There are two examples in the corpus that point to this. However, those two examples are not totally clear for several reasons (grammatical structure, pronunciation, lexicon) and there are not enough contrastive examples to compare with. I give one of them here nonetheless, but acknowledge that the issue needs additional research. ( ) is not clear in structure regarding use of irrealis and realis and the function of chija as an indefinite pronoun or hesitation marker. In addition, I could also not determine the exact meaning of the verb -yubunu. My colleague Lena S. elicited the sentence ‘I will give a present to my mother’ from Juana. The latter needed several attempts to formulate an adequate Paunaka translation, one of them containing the verb -punaku ‘give’ with the third person marker -chÿ: niyunabÿti nipunakumÿnÿchÿ chija eka niyubuniachÿ\\ ni-yuna-bÿti ni-punaku-mÿnÿ-chÿ chija eka ni-yubun-i-a-chÿ\\ 1sg-go.irr-prsp 1sg-give-dim-3 what dema 1sg-be.worth?-subord-irr-3\\ ‘I am about to go to give her her present’ (jxx-e191021e-2) Third person markers that follow the stem most frequently occur on speech verbs,speech verb|( or more precisely on one specific speech verb, -kechu ‘say’. This verb is used in connection with direct speech. The verb with -chÿ may precede or follow the quoted speech and both third person indexes, ti- and chÿ- occur on these verbs, as well as SAP indexes. One example with a speech verb following the direct speech is given below. Juana cites the husband of her sister in this case, who was a criminal and treated his family badly. “¡patÿkemiu!”, chikechuchiji chichechapÿi\\ pi-a-tÿkemiu chi-kechu-chi-ji chi-chechapÿi\\ 2sg-irr-be.quiet 3-say-3-rprt 3-son\\ ‘“shut up!” he said to his son, it is said’ Speech verbs have been identified as a special type of trivalent verbs in Mojeño Trinitario . This is probably also the best analysis for the Paunaka verb -kechu, and it relates to the probable possibility of -punaku ‘give’ taking third person markers after the stem (see above). Let us have a closer look at -kechu ‘say’. First of all, this verb can be used without any object index. The subject can be first, second or third person, and in the latter case, the marker ti- is used relatively consistently as in ( ), in which Clara cites what her brother José had said to her the day before. “niyuna nisemaika kringanube”, tikechu\\ ni-yuna ni-semaika kringa-nube ti-kechu\\ 1sg-go.irr 1sg-search gringa-pl 3i-say\\ ‘“I am going to search for the gringas”, he said’ A first or second person addresseeaddressee|( can be indexed on the verb as an object. If the agent is a third person, ti- is used to index the subject. This can be seen in ( ), where Miguel tells me what his fellow said to him when he decided to teach him to calculate. tikechunÿ: “Miyel, nimesumeikapi echÿu”\\ ti-kechu-nÿ Miyel ni-mesumeika-pi echÿu\\ 3i-say-1sg Miguel 1sg-teach.irr-2sg demb\\ ‘he said to me: “Miguel, I am going to teach it to you”’ When there is a third person addressee, the third person marker -chÿ is normally used.addressee|) ( ) provides one example, here in combination with a first person singular marker that indexes the agent. It comes from Miguel’s account about the past of Santa Rita. He narrates how he talked with brother Bendelín, who helped in constructing the school of the village. entonses nÿjakupu nikechuchÿ “bueno...”\\ entonses nÿ-jakupu ni-kechu-chÿ bueno\\ thus 1sg-receive 1sg-say-3 well\\ ‘so I accepted, I told him: “well...”’ Strikingly, if the agent is a third person, too, we usually find both chÿ- and -chÿ on the verb, as in the introductory example ( ) above. Given the fact that chÿ- already indexes two third person participants, it seems that three arguments are encoded in this case: the agent, the addressee and possibly the utterance. Since -chÿ indexes the addressee if there is an SAP agent, I would suggest that it also encodes the addressee in this relation and chÿ- encodes agent and utterance. ( ) offers a second example of the constellation with apparently three third person arguments being encoded. It comes from a different speaker than ( ), has an agent that is conominated (instead of the addressee) and also shows the speech verb preceding the quoted speech. Miguel starts to tell me here what the patrón said to Marco Choma, one of the founders of Santa Rita, when he finally let the indigenous people free in the 1950s. entonses chikechuchÿ echÿu chipatrone: “bueno...”\\ entonses chi-kechu-chÿ echÿu chi-patron-ne bueno\\ thus 3-say-3 demb 3-patrón-possd well\\ ‘so the patrón said to him: “well...” To complete the picture: There are also a few occurrences of the verb -kechu taking chÿ- without any index following the stem and a few more where we find the prefix ti- being combined with -chÿ. This is mainly true for Miguel’s speech, but sometimes also found with Juana. An example is given in ( ). It comes from Miguel’s story about the lazy man. This is the moment that the wife of the lazybones finds out that he was betraying her when he said he was going to work in the woods to supply them with food: i titupunubuji echÿu chiyenu i tikechuchÿji: “aja chikuyeje echÿu pitrabakune”, tikechuchi\\ i ti-tupunubu-ji echÿu chi-yenu i ti-kechu-chÿ-ji aja chi-kuye-ja? echÿu pi-trabaku-ne ti-kechu-chi\\ and 3i-arrive-rprt demb 3-wife and 3i-say-3-rprt intj 3-be.like.this-emph1? demb 2sg-work-possd 3i-say-3\\ ‘and his wife arrived there, it is said, and said to him, it is said: “aha, this is your work”, she said to him’ In terms of its meaning, the verb form in ( ) seems to be an equivalent to the ones in ( ) and ( ) above. However, it is this precisely this construction, i.e. the combination of the markers ti- and -chÿ, that we sometimes also find with other verbs. speech verb|) As for these verbs, the -chÿ sometimes also occurs in focusfocus|(
summary: Third-person markers that follow the stem are rare on verbs, but they do occur, especially with the ditransitive verb *-punaku* ‘give’ and, more clearly, with the speech verb *-kechu* ‘say’. For *-kechu*, the person marking suggests a special trivalent structure: *ti-* typically indexes a third-person subject, while *-chÿ* normally indexes a third-person addressee, and in some cases both markers appear together when all participants are third person. The passage notes that some examples remain ambiguous and that the analysis, especially for *-punaku*, requires further research.

chapter: The verb and morphology on predicates
text: reality status|( While tense and aspect play a minor role in Paunaka (see ), reality status (RS) is obligatorily expressed on every predicate, and in addition, there is nominal irrealis marking on nouns. In all cases of non-verbal reality status marking, -inanon-verbal irrealis marker expresses irrealis and realis is unmarked. On verbs, irrealis is associated with a and realis is marked by the absence of irrealis marking, but associated with u on active verbs, as can be seen in ( ), in which the stem of the realis verbverbal stem in ( -realirr.1) ends in u and this vowel changes to a in the irrealis form of ( -realirr.2). A more detailed explanation is given below in . RS has been defined by as “a grammatical category with the binary distinction of realis and irrealis”, where the notion of realis marks a “perceived certainty of the factual reality of an event's taking place, while irrealis is used to identify that an event is perceived to exist only in an imagined or non-real world” . The validity of RS as a unifiable category has been doubted severely (see e.g. ; ); however, has demonstrated that RS is a significant category in Nanti, an Arawakan languageArawakan languages of the Kampan branch. have shown that this is equally true for some of the Southern Arawakan languages. On predicates, realis RS encodes non-hypothetical non-future events, while irrealis expresses an array of functions. It is found on predicates with future reference, in negative clauses,negation in hypothetical constructions, to mark imperative and polite directives,directive speech act obligation, possibility and ability, optatives and is also found on verbal complements of certain complement-taking verbs (see ). In addition, it can express habitual events in procedural texts and is sometimes, but not always, also used to express habitual events in the past.past reference The system is thus consistent with the findings by illustrated in , with two differences. First, in expressions of uncertainty both RS can occur in Paunaka. There is a special uncertainty marker -kena (see ), so that there is no need to express uncertainty with an irrealis predicate. RS then rather provides information about the temporal reference or polarity of the event that is marked as uncertain.uncertainty Second, habitualhabitual|( is at least partly encoded by irrealis in Paunaka, while argues that encoding of habitual vs. non-habitual belongs to another category, i.e. temporal definiteness. In Nanti, the argument goes, the “habitual construction crucially takes realis marking, in accord with our notional definition of realis and irrealis, since habitual constructions denote repeated realisation of some situation” . Nanti has a specialised marker to encode habitual, and as I have argued, markers specialised for a certain kind of unrealness interact with RS and may thus have an influence on the encoding of it (see Footnote ). The question whether or not temporal definiteness should be considered a semantic parameter that triggers differential RS marking should therefore be addressed again in a cross-linguistic study of RS marking. Habitual is among the “additional semantic contexts where, in at least some languages, irrealis marking has saliency” as suggested by .habitual|) Last but not least, in addition to the semantic contexts cited in the literature on RS, some speakers of Paunaka also produce irrealis verb forms when they are asked to translate Spanish verbs or clauses in elicitation sessions. Of course, the predicates in these translation tasks often refer to events that are not actual, not realised so that translation with an irrealis verb form is a logical consequence in some situations, at least for some of the speakers. The remainder of this section is dedicated to discussion of the formal expression of RS on verbs in and the semantics of the RS system in . For marking RS on non-verbal predicates, see and for nominal irrealis see . Paunaka’s RS marking on verbs is typical for a Southern Arawakan language, both regarding the shape and behaviour of markers as well as the semantic parameters that trigger irrealis marking .
summary:
Paunaka obligatorily marks reality status on every predicate, with realis unmarked in non-verbal contexts and irrealis marked by -ina; on active verbs, realis forms are associated with -u and irrealis with -a. The system distinguishes realis events as non-hypothetical and non-future, while irrealis covers future reference, negation, hypotheticals, directives, obligation, possibility, ability, optatives, some complement clauses, and sometimes habitual or past habitual events.

The passage also notes two special points: uncertainty is marked by a separate form -kena, so RS does not itself encode uncertainty, and habituality in Paunaka may be partly expressed by irrealis, unlike analyses that treat habituality as a separate category. Overall, Paunaka’s RS system is presented as typical of Southern Arawakan languages.

chapter: The verb and morphology on predicates
subsection: Form of the reality status markers
text: On verbs, irrealis is associated with the vowel a. Stative verbsstative verb|( take a prefix a- that is inserted directly before the verb stem,verbal stem see the following example, where the verb in ( -prefix.1) is unmarked and the verb in ( -prefix.2) takes the irrealis prefix. stative verb|) Active verbsactive verb|( take a suffix -a which replaces the last vowel u of the verb stemverbal stem in most cases as in the following example, where ( -yunu.1) shows an active verb with realis RS and ( -yunu.2) has the same verb with irrealis RS. I decided not to separate the irrealis marker from the stem or suffix by a dash in my analysis and not to overtly gloss realis RS at all for reasons that will become apparent in the discussion below. fusion|(One peculiarity of RS marking is that a number of grammatical markers attract the irrealis suffix, i.e. the reciprocal, continuous, additive, and associated motion associated motion|( (AM) and related markers (see in the introduction to this Chapter). This is also why the status of realis marking on active verbs is less clear. There is an association between realis and the final vowel u of the verb stem and the markers mentioned above. Some of these markers can be inserted between the last vowel of the verb stem minus the thematic suffix and the reality status marking, i.e. they replace the thematic suffix. The final vowel of these markers is then either realis u or irrealis a, see ( ), where this is exemplified with the prior motion marker. However, instead of replacing the thematic suffix,thematic suffix|( all of the markers mentioned above can also follow the thematic suffix. Irrealis is only marked once in this case, i.e. on the marker that follows the thematic suffix. I will continue to exemplify this with the prior motion marker here. Thus in ( ), we have a verb with a stem ending in u and an AM marker ending in a, resulting in a clash between RS markings if u were understood as a proper marker of realis: There is no neat way to capture the complexities of realis marking in active verbs in the glosses, since u seems to be a hybrid of default vowel and realis marker proper. My practical solution is as follows: I consider each and every verb stem to have two realisations, a default one and an irrealis one. The same is true for the reciprocal, continuous, additive, and AM and related markers.associated motion A verb has realis RS in the absence of any irrealis marking. The irrealis vowel a is not considered a separate suffix because suffixes or – more generally speaking – markers starting with a vowel usually form a diphthongvowel sequence with a preceding vowel rather than deleting it (except when they attach to a diphthong, but then it is the first vowel of the marker that vanishes). I would thus consider irrealis marking to be a case of incipient fusionfusion|) in an otherwise strictly agglutinative language. The analysis adopted here differs in this point from the one proposed by for Trinitario,Mojeño Trinitario which has a lot of vowel elision in general. In Paunaka, a verb including a thematic suffix + AM markerassociated motion would thus be analysed as follows: pinikupuna\\ pi-niku-puna\\ 2sg-eat-am.prior.irr\\ ‘you will go to eat’ However, in cases where a can not be analysed as replacing a default vowel and in addition u acts as a proper marker of realis, these vowels are glossed as separate suffixes as in ( ) and ( ) above.active verb|) After this discussion of the form of the RS markers, the following section presents different semantic parameters that trigger either realis or irrealis marking.
summary: The passage explains that irrealis marking in Paunaka is associated with the vowel **a**: stative verbs take a prefix **a-**, while active verbs take a suffix **-a** that usually replaces the final stem vowel **u**. It also notes that several grammatical markers, including reciprocal, continuous, additive, and associated motion, can attract irrealis marking, making realis marking on active verbs somewhat unclear and suggesting an incipient case of fusion rather than a fully separate suffix.

chapter: The verb and morphology on predicates

It comes from María C., who was listing names of crops for me to learn some vocabulary. aa chermuya biniku, chÿi\\ aa chermuya bi-niku chÿi\\ intj cherimoya 1pl-eat fruit\\ ‘ah, we eat cherimoya, it is a fruit’ realis|) The difference between ( ) and ( ) as opposed to ( ) is that the former two examples describe actions that are done habitually, when certain things are prepared. ( ) on the other hand is not about the habitual eating of cherimoya fruits in their season, but it is used in this case to describe one property of the fruit, its edibility. There may be certain differences here between speakers, or use of either realis or irrealis may depend on how concrete speakers imagine certain actions at the moment of speaking. While the description of how something is made or how it works is relatively abstracted from a real situation, personal habits are more concrete as in the following example from María S. nijibÿku niyunu asaneti\\ ni-jibÿku ni-yunu asaneti\\ 1sg-smoke 1sg-go field\\ ‘I smoke when I go to the field’ Irrealis can also be used to describe habitual events in the past.past reference However, habitual past events are also often described with realis predicates and one speaker can even switch back and forth between realis and irrealis in accounts about the past. This may again be dependent on how much the speaker generalises the event or is remembering a concrete situation, even if the event happened habitually. This is hard to prove though, because we do not have direct access to their cognition. One example in which irrealis is used for an event in the past that occurred repeatedly is ( ), which comes from an account about what Juana used to do with her late grandmother, when she was much younger. puna tijai biyuna bepueikupa\\ puna tijai bi-yuna bi-epueiku-pa\\ other day 1pl-go.irr 1pl-fish-dloc.irr\\ ‘another day we would go to fish’ habitual|)
summary:
The passage explains that **realis** is used for non-future events and often marks present or past reference, while **irrealis** is used for future events and is frequently supported by temporal adverbs such as *tomorrow* or *yesterday*. When no lexical time marker is present, speakers rely on context to determine whether the clause is realis or irrealis.

It also shows that **irrealis** can express habitual actions, especially in procedural descriptions, where it may overlap with obligation, whereas **realis** can describe general customs, habits, or properties. Habitual past events may be expressed with either form, and speakers sometimes alternate between them depending on how abstract or concrete they construe the event.

chapter: The verb and morphology on predicates
text: In Paunaka, all positive declarativedeclarative clause non-future clauses take realis predicates. An example is ( ), where Juana describes a picture of the frog story; for another example see ( ) above. tiniku, teumÿnÿ ÿne\\ ti-niku ti-eu-mÿnÿ ÿne\\ 3i-eat 3i-drink-dim water\\ ‘it (the dog) is eating, it is drinking water’ Negation,negation|( on the other hand, triggers irrealis marking as in ( ), which has a stative verb and therefore takes an irrealis prefix. Juana speaks about her son-in-law here, who is ill. kuina tajimama\\ kuina ti-a-jimama\\ neg 3i-irr-be.strong\\ ‘he is not strong’ ( ) has a negated active verb. It is a statement by Clara who had asked María C. for a word in Paunaka that she did not remember. María C. did not remember either. kuina pichupabu\\ kuina pi-chupa-bu\\ neg 2sg-know.irr-dsc\\ ‘you don’t know it anymore’ There is no general “doubly irrealis construction”doubly irrealis construction|( in declarative clauses,declarative clause though a doubly irrealis construction is possibly found in prohibitive clauses,directive speech act!prohibitivenegation!prohibitive see below. Thus, a verb with future reference and negative polarity marks irrealis in a way identical to a verb that has future reference or negative polarity only. Paunaka is thus ambiguous to the extent that there is no way to mark on the predicate that there is negation and another semantic parameter triggering irrealis. ( ) is an example of a predicate that takes irrealis for two reasons, negative polarity and future reference. It was elicited from María S. tajaitu kuina nÿnika\\ tajaitu kuina nÿ-nika\\ tomorrow neg 1sg-eat.irr\\ ‘I won’t eat tomorrow’ -0.9ptThere is also one kind of lexically expressed doubly irrealis construction, which regards negative abilitive sentences. While in positive statements, irrealis alone is sufficient to encode this modality, in negative statements, speakers often add the non-verbal ability predicate puero ‘can’, borrowedborrowingknowledge/ability predicate from the Spanish modal verb poder, possibly via Besɨro (see ). This, however, is not mandatory. An example without puero is given below. It was produced by Miguel making jokes with Swintha, who had asked him to give away his house: kuina nÿpunaka eka nubiu, kuina tamichana\\ kuina nÿ-punaka eka nÿ-ubiu kuina ti-a-michana\\ neg 1sg-give.irr dema 1sg-house neg 3i-irr-be.nice\\ ‘I can’t give away my house, it is not in a good condition’ In ( ), puero is used in addition to the irrealis verb. This example comes from Juana talking about her ill son-in-law. kuina puero tiyuika\\ kuina puero ti-yuika\\ neg can 3i-walk.irr\\ ‘he cannot walk’ doubly irrealis construction|) negation|)
summary:
In Paunaka, positive non-future declarative clauses take realis predicates, while negation triggers irrealis marking. The language does not generally show a separate “doubly irrealis” form in declaratives, so predicates with both future reference and negation are marked with the same irrealis form as either feature alone.

A special case concerns negative abilitive sentences: speakers often add the borrowed modal predicate *puero* ‘can’ alongside the irrealis verb, though this is optional.

chapter: The verb and morphology on predicates
text: Most hypothetical predicates are found in conditional clausestemporal overlap/condition|( in my corpus (see also ). The antecedent clause often contains a connective kue ‘if, when’, but it can also be unmarked. The predicate of the antecedent clause is irrealisirrealis|( in most cases. The predicate of the consequent clause is also irrealis in deontic, hypothetical, futurefuture reference or counterfactual constructions.counterfactuality Some of these cases are exemplified in ( ) and ( ). ( ) comes from Miguel and refers to the fact that María C.’s husband, being severely ill, cannot stay at home alone if she leaves for a day or so. kue piyuna tiyunauku echÿu\\ kue pi-yuna ti-yuna-uku echÿu\\ if 2sg-go.irr 3i-go.irr-add demb\\ ‘if you go, he has to go, too’ In ( ), Juana cites what her daughter in Spain promised her. kue pibÿsÿa, mimi nipabentecha nubiu, te biyunupunatu nauku\\ kue pi-bÿsÿa mimi ni-pabentecha nÿ-ubiu te bi-yunupuna-tu nauku\\ if 2sg-come.irr mum 1sg-sell.irr 1sg-house seq 1pl-go.back.irr-iam there\\ ‘if you come, mum, I will sell my house, and then we go back there’ irrealis|) However, if the consequence clause is realis,realis|( we are rather dealing with a temporal clause as in ( ), a statement by Juana about the arroyo close to Santa Rita. kue tijinupatu tÿpi enero, juu tijapÿkutu\\ kue ti-jinupa-tu tÿpi enero juu ti-japÿku-tu\\ if 3i-flow.irr-iam obl January intj 3i-fill-iam\\ ‘if water flows in January, huu, it fills’ realis|) temporal overlap/condition|) Counterfactual conditional predicatescounterfactuality|( with past reference additionally take a frustrative mark\-er (see also ). There is one personal account in which Juan tells how her daughter once travelled to Spain to help her sister care for her children. The whole journey turned out to be in vain because she was rejected at the airport, since she did not have a valid visa. Several predicates in this account are marked with irrealis and frustrative because they refer to hypothetical and counterfactual ideas about what one daughter would have done in Spain, and what the other daughter should have done to prevent her sister from being deported. ( ) is a remark about other people who were expelled, too. i pujanenube tiyunanubeini trabakunubeina nauku \\ i pu-jane-nube ti-yuna-nube-ini trabaku-nube-ina nauku \\ and other-distr-pl 3i-go.irr-pl-frust work-pl-irr.nv there\\ ‘and others would have gone to work there’ counterfactuality|)
summary: Most hypothetical predicates occur in conditional clauses, which may be introduced by *kue* ‘if, when’ or left unmarked; the antecedent clause usually has irrealis marking, and the consequent clause is also irrealis in deontic, hypothetical, future-reference, or counterfactual constructions. If the consequence clause is realis, however, the construction is treated as temporal rather than conditional. Counterfactual predicates with past reference additionally take a frustrative marker, as shown in examples describing unrealized or prevented events.

In these cases, the realis/irrealis contrast reflects another semantic feature such as hypotheticality or past reference, as shown by examples where uncertainty is expressed about future knowledge or a possible past event.

text: irrealis|( The term speaker-oriented modality refers to “those cases in which the speaker gives someone an order or gives someone permission” . It comprises various directives as well as expressions of permission . The only directivesdirective speech act|( explicitly mentioned by as taking irrealis marking are imperativesimperative and polite directives or exhortatives,hortative and speaker-oriented modality is never expressed by realis verbs according to his study. I start with the constructions mentioned by and then move on to other constructions that have been subsumed under the term speaker-oriented modality: prohibitives, hortatives, admonitives, and permissives . Imperativesimperative|( can simply be formed as second person irrealis predicates, as in ( ). An imperative marker can be added, but the predicate remains irrealis (see ). Whether the imperative is to be understood as a command or polite directive mainly depends on intonation. ( ) was produced by Juana who had given me some chicha. ¡pea!\\ p-ea\\ 2sg-drink.irr\\ ‘drink!’ imperative|) There is a special particle jaje ‘hort’ for hortatives.hortative This particle need not be accompanied by a predicate if it is clear from the context what the request is, but if there is an extra predicate, it has irrealis RS, as in ( ). The example comes from Miguel’s story about the cowherd and the spirit of the hill. The latter had taken away the cows, but invites the cowherd to come with him to look for the cows here. “¡jaje biyuna bimupajane echÿu bakajane!"\\ jaje bi-yuna bi-imu-pa-jane echÿu baka-jane\\ hort 1pl-go.irr 1pl-see-dloc.irr-distr demb cow-distr\\ ‘“let’s go and see the cows!”’ Note that in both imperative and hortative constructions the event expressed by the predicate remains to be fulfilled, so that they may be understood as a subclass of temporally unrealised event. Optativeoptative is expressed by -yuini or -jÿti. I have only found these markers in combination with irrealis predicates, but they are not very frequent in general (see ). irrealis|) There is no special permissive construction as far as I know that would be different from an imperative. There is no general agreement on how to form prohibitivesdirective speech act!prohibitive|(negation!prohibitive|( among the speakers. While some of them simply use standard negation constructions, others employ constructions with a different negativenegative particle|( particle. Two speakers, Juana and María C., use a special negative particle naka ‘proh’ accompanied by a realis predicate, but one of them also used irrealis predicates in an elicitation session, when I asked for more examples with the prohibitive particle. Given the fact that the prohibitive construction with the realis predicate was not elicited and that there are doubly irrealis constructionsdoubly irrealis construction including negation and another semantic parameter in Nanti and Terena that include a realis-marked predicate (see above), I believe that the construction with the realis predicate may be the conservative one and the use of irrealis an extension of its use in standard negation. ( ) is a prohibitive sentence elicited from María C. ¡naka piyuyuikubu!, ticheneikabi piuse\\ naka pi-iyuyuiku-bu ti-cheneika-bi pi-use\\ proh 2sg-cry-mid 3i-care.for.irr-2sg 2sg-grandmother\\ ‘don’t cry! your grandmother will take care of you.’ The prohibitive negator naka was verified by a third speaker, María S., who herself uses the negator masaini in prohibitives, which is probably composed of the apprehensional connective masa ‘lest’ and the frustrative -ini. Masaini is also used in warnings, i.e. it has an admonitive admonitive|( flavour.negative particle|) In both cases, the predicate of masaini-constructions is sometimes realis and sometimes irrealis in my corpus, similar to prohibitive constructions with naka. As far as I can tell, this is free variation that may have to do with an extension of the use of irrealis in standard negation. I could not find any other semantic parameter that could have an influence on the choice of either realis or irrealis in these constructions, but note that there are only a few of them. Two examples of masaini being combined with realis predicates are given below. ( ) was elicited from María S. and shows the prohibitive use of masaini peculiar to this speaker. ¡masaini pekubu!\\ masaini pi-ekubu\\ adm 2sg-laugh\\ ‘don’t laugh!’ ( ) is rather a warning. It was elicited from Miguel. Just a moment earlier, he had used an irrealis predicate in almost the same sentence. ¡masaini tinijabakubi kabe!\\ masaini ti-nijabaku-bi kabe\\ adm 3i-bite-2sg dog\\ ‘be careful, the dog may bite you!’ |) See for more examples of negative imperatives and related constructions.negation!prohibitive|)directive speech act!prohibitive|)directive speech act|)
summary:
Speaker-oriented modality in the language includes commands, permissions, and related directives, and it is generally marked with irrealis rather than realis forms. Imperatives are formed as second-person irrealis predicates, hortatives use a special particle jaje, and optatives use -yuini or -jÿti, while permissive constructions are not clearly distinct from imperatives.

Prohibitives show variation across speakers: some use standard negation, others use a special negative particle naka, and one speaker uses masaini, which also appears in warnings. In these prohibitive and admonitive constructions, both realis and irrealis predicates occur, which the author interprets as free variation or an extension of irrealis in negation.

chapter: The verb and morphology on predicates
text: Agent-oriented modality refers to the expression of “those cases in which the agent of a clause is influenced in some way in performing the action described in the clause” by “internal and external conditions” . According to , obligation and need (called necessity by ) are expressed by irrealis predicates. In Paunaka, obligation and need may be expressed simply by an irrealis predicate,irrealis|( see ( ) to ( ), all of them coming from Juana. In ( ) she expresses her faith in God and duty as a Catholic. baejumi micha bia bakukene\\ bi-a-ejumi micha bia bi-a-kukene\\ 1pl-irr-remember good God 1pl-irr-pray\\ ‘we have to believe in God and pray’ The following example was elicited from Juana, because I wanted to express my pity for some groups of children from different schools who had a sports competition in the blazing sun. takubijainube\\ ti-a-kubijai-nube\\ 3i-irr-play-pl\\ ‘they have to play’ ( ) comes from the creation story. The silk floss tree has swallowed the complete supply of corn, thus Jesus decides that it has to be felled to get the corn back. “bikutataka eka mupuÿ”\\ bi-kutataka eka mupuÿ\\ 1pl-fell.irr dema silk.floss.tree\\ ‘“we have to fell this silk floss tree”’ Additionally a Spanish loan phraseborrowing tiene ke from tiene que ‘must’, also used in Bésiro, is occasionally used by some of the speakers. This makes the notion of obligation more explicit. Although it is a third person singular expression in Spanish (‘he/she/it has to’), it is not restricted to third person in Paunaka. Tiene ke is always followed by an irrealis predicate as in the statement in ( ), which comes from Clara who is speaking about washing a wound here. tiene ke chikipucha xhabuji\\ tiene ke chi-kipucha xhabu-ji\\ must 3-wash.irr soap-rprt\\ ‘she should wash it with soap, it is said’ The other semantic notions that are subsumed under agent-oriented modality are ability, desire/willingness, and root possibility; the latter “is related to ability, but also takes external factors into account” . Desire is usually expressed by want-verb constructions in Paunaka, which are dealt with in . Ability and root possibility can indeed be expressed by irrealis marking, as is the case in ( ) taken from the narrative of the fox and the jaguar told by Miguel and Juana. The fox had just boasted about the many different jumps he knows, while the jaguarundi only knows one jump, but a very effective one, with which he can escape into trees, for instance, as Miguel states. tikutijikatu chÿnajiku chijipuikiu, ¡bruj!\\ ti-kutijika-tu chÿna-jiku chi-jipuik-i-u bruj\\ 3i-flee.irr-iam one-lim 3-jump-subord-real idph\\ ‘he can escape with only one jump, bruh!’ irrealis|) In addition, there are also constructions containing the non-verbal predicate puero ‘can’, a loan from Spanish, but mostly puero is used when an ability or a possibility is negatednegationknowledge/ability predicate (see above). Ability in the sense of capability can also be expressed by the stative verb -ichunaknowledge/ability predicate ‘be capable, know’, which is followed by realis complements if no other factor (e.g. negation, hypotheticality) triggers irrealis marking. This is logical, since the notion of capability is expressed by an extra predicate (see discussion in Footnote ), so that the realis complement can express the “perceived certainty of the factual reality” . One example is ( ) from Juana, who is speaking about her children here. tichunanube tubuejinube\\ ti-ichuna-nube ti-ubueji-nube\\ 3i-be.capable-pl 3i-swim-pl\\ ‘they can swim’ modality|)
summary: The passage explains that Paunaka often uses irrealis predicates to express agent-oriented modality, including obligation, need, ability, and root possibility. Obligation and need may appear with irrealis marking alone or with the Spanish loan phrase *tiene ke* “must,” which is followed by an irrealis predicate; ability and root possibility can also be marked by irrealis, though ability may alternatively be expressed by the loan *puero* “can” or by the stative verb *-ichuna* ‘be capable, know’ with a realis complement.

text: future reference|( Relative future is used to refer to those cases in which two events are set into a relation, in which the first has past time referencepast reference in relation to the moment of speaking, but the event encoded by the second predicate is not realised by the reference time defined by the first predicate. used the term “prospective construction”, but I prefer “relative future” because “prospective" was used to denote a specific type of aspect by . Relative future is inherent in purposive constructions as well as some types of complementation. -2.8ptIrrealisirrealis|( is typically found on the purpose verb in purposive constructions. There are various ways to form them (see , , , and ). One example is given below. It comes from Juana who told me about the work the people of Santa Rita did in exchange for their reservoir. The women brought the men chicha. tumunube aumue tÿpi teanube nauku\\ ti-umu-nube aumue tÿpi ti-ea-nube nauku\\ 3i-take-pl chicha obl 3i-drink.irr-pl there\\ ‘they brought them chicha to drink’ irrealis There are two construction types to express purpose of motion.purpose|( Both of them have in common that the purpose verb can be irrealis, but also realis if the motion verb also has realis RS. This is discussed in detail in , but two examples of a motion-cum-purpose construction are given below. In ( ), the purpose verb is irrealis, in ( ) it is realis. It is not clear what triggers the choice of realis or irrealis complementscomplement verb in those cases. It might be the case that a different perspective is taken: while irrealis complements focus on the fact that the event is not completed by the reference time of the main verb, realis complements emphasise the fact that the whole event composed of the main and the complement verb is over by the moment of speaking. The context of ( ) is a description of the journey of Juana’s grandparents; the whole setting is in the past, but within this past there is a relative future, i.e. the acquisition of the cows. tiyununube Monkoxi tiyÿseikupanube chipeunube baka\\ ti-yunu-nube Monkoxi ti-yÿseiku-pa-nube chi-peu-nube baka\\ 3i-go-pl Moxos 3i-buy-dloc.irr-pl 3-animal-pl cow\\ ‘they went to Moxos in order to buy cows’ future reference|) On the other hand, in the recording from which ( ) is taken, a recording by Riester with Juan Ch., the general topic is a supply of food in the present to which the event of hunting in the past made a contribution. The RS of the complement verb would probably have been different for a detailed description of the different sub-events that resulted from the hunting expedition. uchuine tijaikenekÿutu niyunu ninÿupu\\ uchuine tijaikenekÿu-tu ni-yunu ni-nÿu-pu\\ just.now dawn-iam 1sg-go 1sg-lie.in wait-dloc\\ ‘today in the early morning I went to lie in wait (for animals)’ purpose|) In complementation, some complement verbscomplement verb obligatorily take irrealis RS, regardless of the RS of the main predicate. This is described in more detail in . One example is ( ) with a desiderative verb with realis RS and the complement in irrealis. This is logical given that the event of the complement is hypothetical at the time of reference of the main verb. The sentence was elicited from José. tisachu tinijabakabi echÿu kabe\\ ti-sachu ti-nijabaka-bi echÿu kabe\\ 3i-want 3i-bite.irr-2sg demb dog\\ ‘the dog wants to bite you’ reality status|) In the following section, I will turn to a category that is still relatively unknown, although publications on this topic have been increasing during the last two decades. This is associated motion, the morphological expression of motion events together with a non-motion predicate.
summary: The passage explains that relative future refers to cases where one event is past relative to the speech moment, but another event has not yet occurred by the reference time established by the first. This is common in purposive constructions and some complements, where purpose verbs often take irrealis marking, though realis may also occur in motion-cum-purpose constructions; the choice appears to depend on perspective, with irrealis highlighting incompletion at the reference time and realis emphasizing that the combined event is complete by the speech moment. Some complement verbs obligatorily require irrealis regardless of the main predicate, as in desiderative constructions, and the section then turns to associated motion.

chapter: The verb and morphology on predicates
section: Associated motion, associated path, and regressive/ repetitive
text: associated motion|( In addition to having motion verbs, Paunaka possesses some means to express motion through morphemes attached to other verbs, e.g. the marker -punu, which encodes motion prior to the event expressed by the verb, as in ( ) from elicitation with Miguel. The first scale thus definitely holds for Paunaka: All markers encode motion of the subject, motion of the object being restricted to two specific verbs. The second scale also holds for Paunaka; however, Paunaka has more fine-grained expressions for concurrent motion than for prior motion. It shares this characteristic with Trinitario.Mojeño Trinitario This chapter concludes with , which deals with the different possibilities to mark regression and repetition on predicates, with the regressive marker definitely being derived from the prior motion marker.
summary: Paunaka can express motion not only with motion verbs but also with attached morphemes such as **-punu**, which marks motion occurring before the event described by the verb. The language primarily encodes motion of the subject, with motion of the object limited to two specific verbs, and it has more detailed ways to express concurrent motion than prior motion, a pattern it shares with Trinitario.

chapter: The verb and morphology on predicates
section: Associated motion, associated path, and regressive/ repetitive
text: Both -(CV)kÿu and -(CV)kÿupunu can be clearly defined as AM markers, because they are not used for any other purpose than AM marking. They both encode concurrent motion, i.e. motion that happens simultaneously with the action expressed by the predicate, but differ in deixis. The marker -(CV)kÿu consists of a sequence kÿu that is attached to the reduplicatedreduplication last syllable of the verb stem in the majority of cases. Since most active verb stems end in the thematic suffix -ku, the most frequent form of the concurrent motion marker is -kukÿu, but there are also cases in which another last syllable is reduplicated as is the case in ( ) below. The reduplicated syllable may also be dropped so that the bare form -kÿu shows up, but there are only very few occurrences of this in the corpus. The marker -(CV)kÿu is used to express concurrent translocative motion, i.e. motion away from the deictic centre. It attaches to non-motion verbs, active and stative ones alike. ( ) shows the marker attached to an active non-motion verb. There is no (other) motion verb in this clause, the only marker of motion being the AM marker, which encodes that the actions of talking and moving (walking in this case) happen simultaneously. The sentence comes from Juana’s description of their grandparents’ journey to Moxos and back home. They had bought cows in Moxos. chichujikukukÿunube chipeunube baka\\ chi-chujiku-kukÿu-nube chi-peu-nube baka\\ 3-speak-am.conc.tr-pl 3-animal-pl cow\\ ‘they went talking to their cows’ In addition, the marker can also attach to manner of motion verbs,motion predicate|( where it adds a certain translational reading, as in the following example from the same story as the prior example. There were heavy rainfalls and the grandparents came to an arroyo, which they had to cross swimming. tubuejijikÿubu pasaunube\\ ti-ubueji-jikÿu-bu pasau-nube\\ 3i-swim-am.conc.tr-mid pass-pl\\ ‘swimming they went and passed (the arroyo)’ The verb -ubueji ‘swim’ in the example above is a stative verb and could therefore arguably be defined as a verb that expresses a stative location ‘be in water’ rather than motion ‘swim’. However, the AM marker also attaches to clearly active manner of motion verbs like -bÿbÿku ‘fly’ in ( ) and -yuiku ‘walk’ in ( ). ( ) comes from the story by Miguel about a lazy man. At the end of the story, he sacrifices himself, cutting off his arms and legs, and lets his son throw him into a pond. From there, he rises to the sky as a comet, which comes back every year. kada anyo kue pimua echÿu pasauna chikuyeni tibÿbÿkukukÿu anÿke...\\ kada anyo kue pi-mua echÿu pasau-ina chi-kuye-ni ti-bÿbÿku-kukÿu anÿke\\ each year if 2sg-see.irr demb pass-irr.nv 3-be.like.this-deict 3i-fly-am.conc.tr up\\ ‘every year, when you see something passing by there like moving and flying above...’ motion predicate|) The AM marker in the previous example expresses that the flight follows a certain route, which is also encoded by the Spanish loan pasau, which has several translations into English, of which ‘pass by’ is the most accurate here. Compare this example to ( ), where Juana does not emphasise a route but rather the ability of the bird to fly, and thus does not use the concurrent AM marker on the predicate. i echÿu yÿnÿ tibÿbÿku anÿke\\ i echÿu yÿnÿ ti-bÿbÿku anÿke\\ and demb jabiru 3-fly up\\ ‘and the jabiru flies up in the sky’ The focus on route is prevalent in the following example, where Miguel describes the motion of a wooden toy cow that I move along my notebook, not randomly, but following a route from one point on the notebook to another. mm, tiyuikukukÿu\\ mm ti-yuiku-kukÿu\\ intj 3i-walk-am.conc.tr\\ ‘hm, it goes walking’ Irrealis is expressed on the AM marker rather than on the verb stem. The irrealis form of the marker is -(CV)kÿa as can be seen in ( ) (second verb in the example), where irrealis is due to future reference of the predicate. Both can attach to non-motion verbs as well as manner-of-motion verbs, where they indicate that the action occurs simultaneously with motion and often add a route or translational reading; irrealis is marked on the AM marker itself in -(CV)kÿa for -(CV)kÿu, while no irrealis cases are reported for -(CV)kÿupunu.

This is surprising, since addition of -punu to motion verbs usually denotes a movement back to a place, but I have indeed encountered examples with -bÿsÿupunu, in which no return is implied. summary:
The marker -punu (irrealis -puna) primarily expresses prior motion relative to the predicate, and it can also function as a directional or purpose marker when combined with another motion predicate. It attaches to both verbal and some non-verbal stems, often causing the thematic suffix -ku to drop, and it appears with motion verbs that are lexicalised with the marker, including forms meaning motion toward or away from the deictic center.  

The passage notes that some verbs with -punu have no clear meaning difference from their unmarked counterparts, though the marked forms may be preferred; for example, -bÿsÿupunu and -bÿsÿu both mean ‘come’ in the cited examples. By contrast, -yunupunu is lexicalised as ‘go back,’ with the point of origin usually being the speaker’s home or another previously left location.

summary: The passage argues that **-punu** has several related functions: on non-motion verbs it marks prior motion without specifying direction, while on motion verbs it expresses regressive deixis and may also indicate motion toward the deictic center. In clauses containing another motion predicate, **-punu** appears to mark purpose, and the author suggests these uses may be widening into a purpose marker, possibly under Spanish influence. The passage also mentions a separate imperative particle **pana** ‘come!’ that may be historically related to an older irrealis form.

text: In addition to the concurrent and prior AM markers, there is possibly also a subsequent motion marker -nÿmu/-nÿma. This marker appeared once Juana’s account of her grandparents’ journey and was translated by her as ‘sleep in a hut, on the way’. This translation could imply subsequent motion because sleeping on the way, on a long journey that takes several days, implies that one moves on the next day. timukunÿmunube juchubu kaku ÿne\\ ti-muku-nÿmu-nube juchubu kaku ÿne\\ 3i-sleep-am.subs?-pl where exist water\\ ‘they spent the night where water was (and went)’ Mojeño Trinitario has a cognate marker -numo, which is analysed as a subsequent motion marker by . Among the translations for the suffix she found in the grammar by , there is ‘do on the way’ besides subsequent motion ‘do and go’. In current Trinitario,Mojeño Trinitario speakers translate the morpheme as ‘do sth. first’, which is also the translation found for the IgnacianoMojeño Ignaciano cognate -numa . ( ) is from an elicitation session, in which I asked María S. whether some verbs with added -nÿmu were possible and what they meant. I asked for the form nikubunÿmu ‘I bathe (and go)’, and María S. produced the following sentence to provide me with an example of how the form could be used. It contained an explicit motion verb that encoded motion back home after the action of the verb marked with -nÿmu is completed. niyunupunatu ubiayae nikubunÿmutu\\ ni-yunupuna-tu ubiae-yae ni-kubu-nÿmu-tu\\ 1sg-go.back.irr-iam house-loc 1sg-bathe-am.subs?-iam\\ ‘I will go back to the house now, I have bathed now (and go)’ With other verbs, the speaker rather provided a translation that included ‘over there’ (which does not exclude the possibility that it is a subsequent motion marker) and she would not accept all examples that I tried to produce with this marker. It is in any case a rare marker and does not seem to be included in the (very) active repertoire of grammatical morphemes of the speakers.
summary:
The passage suggests that -nÿmu/-nÿma may be a subsequent motion marker, though the evidence is limited and somewhat uncertain. It is glossed in one example as involving sleeping “on the way,” and related markers in Mojeño Trinitario and Mojeño Ignaciano are analyzed or translated as expressing subsequent action or “do sth. first.”  

Speaker judgments indicate that -nÿmu is rare and not fully productive in current use: it was accepted only in some elicited contexts, often with added explicit motion verbs or locative meanings, and does not seem to be part of the active everyday grammatical repertoire.

The dislocative attaches to the purpose verb in this case, as in ( ), where María S. describes a duty of her life as a child and adolescent. biyuna bisupa\\ bi-yuna bi-isu-pa\\ 1pl-go.irr 1pl-weed-dloc.irr\\ ‘we had to go to weed’ motion-cum-purpose construction|) In addition, the dislocative marker is lexicalisedlexicalisation with a number of motion verbsmotion predicate and possibly also with some non-motion verbs. The general motion verb -yunu ‘go’ has a variant -yunupu ‘go to’ derivedderivation with this suffix. I found it very hard to come to grips with it until I finally understood that a) my assumption that the marker occurred on certain stative verbs was simply false and resulted from some misheard forms and b) my main consultants on this topic, Juana and María S., use the marker quite differently. I will explain this in more detail below. In the preliminary stage of analysis, I decided to name the marker “dislocative”, following the terminology of , who uses the term to describe a morpheme in Lowland Chontal of Oaxaca (Tequistlatecan). According to , “the dislocative is oriented to the Goal or ending point of motion away”. It is “concerned with situating the event at a not-here location”. Since this definition holds for some of the constructions found with the marker, I will stick to the term, although in other contexts “intentional” or “purposive” would be a better gloss. Although the dislocative marker occurs in different kinds of motion expressions, it does not by itself encode motion (although motion may be implied in its use by María S.). It rather highlights the path or goal of a motion event or adds such a component. It could therefore be defined as belonging to a category of “associated path”, although this term was originally used to cover the functions of some grammatical markers that encode AM plus some more path-related meanings . Despite highlighting a path or a goal, it is not a directional either, since it does not encode any specific direction, but rather the existence of a direction with an endpoint. In the remainder of this section, I give an overview of the different kinds of occurrences and functions of the dislocative. It is not itself a marker of motion; rather, it highlights or adds a path or goal component, sometimes functioning like an applicative, as in forms derived from -yunu ‘go’ such as -yunupu ‘go to,’ which require an explicit goal.

It is most commonly found in motion-cum-purpose constructions, where a motion verb combines with a second verb marked for dislocation, but it can also appear in a few rarer cases with non-motion verbs like ‘rain’ when direction toward a goal is important. text: object|( Paunaka does not have special markers that encode the motion of the object, unlike other South American languages . Nonetheless, there is one verbal root -ne that is combined with either -punu or -pu, the result being verb stems that encode the motion of the object. The root -ne is not used on its own, nor is there any verb stem *-neku or *-nechu. The verb -nekupu ‘see somebody coming’ is composed of the root -ne, the thematic suffix -ku and the dislocative marker -pu and expresses cislocative concurrent motion of the object. One example is given in ( ), which is about the appearance of the spirit of water before Juana’s grandparents on their journey home from Moxos. nenayuji eka chinekupunubeji echÿu pariki chikebÿkeji\\ nena-yu-ji eka chi-nekupu-nube-ji echÿu pariki chi-kebÿke-ji\\ like-ints-rprt dema 3-see.coming-pl-rprt demb many 3-eye-rprt\\ ‘it seems that they saw a pair of eyes approaching them, it is said’ If the object is an SAP, it is indexed on the verb as in ( ), which was elicited from María S. nÿnekupubi\\ nÿ-nekupu-bi\\ 1sg-see.coming-2sg\\ ‘I see you coming’ If the root -ne combines with -punu ‘am.prior’, there is no thematic suffix on the verb stem. The verb -nepunu ‘see somebody going’ expresses translocative concurrent motion of the object. However, the verb is also translated as ‘see somebody over there’ by the speakers. Distance could be the more important information in this verb in comparison to motion, although the latter is probably also part of its semantics. When María S. was asked in an elicitation session what the object of the verb could be doing “over there”, the first thing that came to her mind was motion away from the scene (going to the toilet or going to wash clothes). ( ) is from an account of the imagined theft of a young woman in the recordings from the 1960s by Riester. Juan Ch. fears that the grandfather of the woman could catch them, therefore he proposes: bumupaika tanÿma, kuina chinepunabu\\ bi-umu-paika tanÿma kuina chi-nepuna-bu\\ 1pl-take-punct.irr now neg 3-see.going.irr-dsc\\ ‘we’ll take her quickly now, so that he doesn’t see her going anymore’ There are no other monoverbal constructions, to my knowledge, that express associated motion of the object. Strikingly, while -punu is normally more closely connected with cislocative motion and -pu with translocative motion (see previous , , and ), in combination with the root -ne and encoding the motion of the object, the directions reverse: -nekupu encodes cislocative motion and -nepunu translocative motion. object|)
summary: Paunaka lacks general special markers for object motion, but it does have a verbal root -ne that combines with -ku/-pu or with -punu to form stems expressing motion of the object. The form -nekupu means ‘see somebody coming’ and encodes cislocative concurrent motion, while -nepunu means ‘see somebody going’ and encodes translocative concurrent motion, though speakers may also understand it as ‘see somebody over there.’ Notably, these combinations reverse the usual directional association of -pu and -punu: with -ne, -pu marks cislocation and -punu marks translocation.

summary:
The passage contrasts two related verbs: **-yunupunu**, which marks a return to a more permanent base or home and foregrounds the act of returning, and **-yunupunuku**, which is used for returning to a less permanent place and emphasizes departure from the current location. Examples show that speakers choose between them depending on whether the endpoint is a home-like basis or a temporary stay, with emotional importance often lying in the leaving rather than the arriving.

It then explains that the **regressive marker** on stative predicates expresses restoration of a previous state, such as something becoming neat again or someone recovering health. On motion and other active verbs, it can indicate undoing a prior action or moving away from a place again, and it can also mark a repeated action in a new situation.

Most of the middle verbs in have reduplicatedreduplication rootverbal root syllables. These verbs can also be used without the middle marker. However, forms without the middle marker occur less frequently and if asked, speakers state that the middle form sounds better. Although this longer duration is among the meanings expressed by reduplication, the middle marker may be used with the same function here. Strikingly, it is used on verbs expressing change in body posture with the same effect as in Paunaka: the change in body posture is expressed by a simple verb, and the resulting body posture state by the addition of the marker, but contrary to Paunaka, Baure does not reduplicate any syllable of the verb stem . The way the semantic pairs of change in body posture and static body posture are expressed in Paunaka also run counter to the expected distribution of the middle marker as supposed by , i.e. the verbs expressing the change should be the ones that receive middle marking according to her analysis. However, states that it is actually “physical states” that are expressed by the deponent middle verbs, and this is also reflected in the examples she gives, e.g. Fula (West Atlantic Niger-Congo) behaves like Paunaka in that the body posture verbs are middle-only verbs and the change in posture verbs are mostly active . She further argues that “the middle, when in contrast with the active, cross-linguistically displays an association with various kinds of noneventuality*, e.g. with atelic, nonpunctual, and/or irrealis temporomodal categories of the verb” . The atelictelicity and nonpunctual association also seems to play a role for at least some of the middle verbs in Paunaka, but RSreality status is totally independent from it. Most of the deponent or high-frequency middle verbs belong to one of the classes that mentions as being typical of middle marking. However, the opposite is not true: very few of the potential verbs with middle semantics are middle-marked in Paunaka. Apart from the semantic class of posture verbs, which are quite consistently associated with middle marking, there is no clustering of the middle forms among a certain semantic class. summary: In Paunaka, the middle marker attaches only to active verb stems and is used to express reflexive and anticausative readings; it has two allomorphs, -bu after realis /u/ and -pu after irrealis /a/, with distribution determined by reality status. The language also has deponent middle verbs and some high-frequency middle verbs, many of which are intransitive, sometimes lexicalized, and often associated with longer duration or certain posture-state meanings. The passage further notes that while some middle verbs fit cross-linguistic expectations for middle voice, the relation between middle marking and semantics is limited, and reality status is independent of the middle’s aspectual or semantic uses.

TAME categories are expected to be expressed on verbs, but as has been stated in , TAME markers can attach to various parts of speechword class in Paunaka. However, it is true that they are primarily (but not exclusively) found on predicates -- verbal and non-verbalnon-verbal predication ones alike. Predication is mainly associated with verbs, and this is why these markers are described in this place. Compare ( ), in which the iamitive marker -tu occurs on a verb, with ( ), which has a non-verbal predicate with the same aspect marker. nanautu nÿkÿiki\\ nÿ-anau-tu nÿkÿiki\\ 1sg-make-iam pot\\ ‘I’ve already made the (clay) pot’ chubuitu kuineini chÿchÿini Marku Choma\\ chubui-tu kuineini chÿchÿ-ini Marku Choma \\ old.man-iam deceased grandpa-dec Marco Choma \\ ‘my late grandfather Marco Choma was already old’ Since there is a fully-fledged discussion of non-verbal predication in , I will only give a very brief summary of non-verbal predication -verbal predication|( Verbal predicates can be distinguished from non-verbal ones by two features: the place of subject indexingperson marking|( and a different irrealis marker. Concerning the first one, if a subject is indexed on a non-verbal predicate, it always follows the word stem, i.e. it occurs in the position that verbs reserve for object marking. It is important to know, however, that not in all kinds of non-verbal predication is a subject indexed. Most importantly, third person subjects cannot be marked on non-verbal predicates at all. This is in analogy to the third person marker -chÿ occurring only sparsely and under specific conditions on verbs (for third person object marking see ).person marking|) Second, while realis RS is not marked on non-verbal predicates, there is a special irrealis marker -ina,non-verbal irrealis marker which shows up whenever a non-verbal predicate occurs in a context that triggers irrealis marking. Thus inflection for irrealis RS is just as obligatory as with verbal predicates. It is only expressed by other means. Among non-verbal predicates are some words that encode dynamic events. Most of them have a Spanish origin, since Spanish verbs are often borrowedborrowing as participles and then integrated into Paunaka as non-verbal predicates. Nonetheless, the word kapunu ‘come’ is also a dynamic non-verbal predicate, and it is of Paunaka origin. This word is only used with third person referents. Since it may not always be clear that we are dealing with non-verbal predication, I mention it whenever a non-verbal predicate occurs in one of the examples of this section. They may also appear twice in a clause, on the predicate and on another word. Most of them occur in a position relatively far from the verb stem,verbal stem but the discontinuous marker and especially the incompletive marker appear in slots a little closer to the stem. The discontinuous marker seems to be possible in two different slots. For a schema of an active verb which shows the positions of the TAME markers, see in or in the introduction to this chapter. For a short discussion and a few examples of possible orders of TAME markers with respect to other morphemes, see . Most TAME markers are always phonologically attached to the predicate (or other word in the clause), i.e. they enter into its prosodic structure and can alter stress assignment. The uncertainty marker kena and the remote (past)remote past marker bane can also occur as free forms. They precede the predicate in this case. It explains that verbal and non-verbal predicates differ in subject indexing and irrealis marking, and that TAME markers may also attach to the negative particle or adverbs, sometimes appearing more than once in a clause. text: aspect|( Paunaka has a handful of aspect markers, which are summarised in . These include iamitive, discontinuous, incompletive, prospective, and continuous. They are described in to , respectively. All of them do not only attach to verbs, but also to non-verbal predicatesnon-verbal predication and to adverbsadverb and some can also attach to the negative particle kuina. A morphologically marked distinction between the two most basic aspect categories, perfective and imperfective,perfective/imperfective is absent. Paunaka’s aspect markers all act on event boundaries, closely interacting with the aktionsart aktionsart|( of the predicate. That is, if there is an event boundary because the verb is telic,telicity|( the aspect marker will situate the event with respect to this boundary. If there is no such boundary, the aspect marker introduces a boundary to situate the event with respect to it. The boundary introduced can be the initial or the final boundary of the event. There is also interaction with negation. This is illustrated in Figures and . summary: Paunaka has a small set of aspect markers, including iamitive, discontinuous, incompletive, prospective, and continuous, and these can attach not only to verbs but also to non-verbal predicates, adverbs, and sometimes the negative particle *kuina*. The language lacks a morphological perfective/imperfective distinction, and its aspect markers work by locating events relative to boundaries, interacting closely with the predicate’s aktionsart and sometimes with negation. In atelic contexts, such as with iamitive *-tu*, context determines whether the initial or final boundary is interpreted.

text: iamitive|( The most frequent of the tense and aspect markers of Paunaka is the omnipresent iamitive marker -tu. The term “iamitive” is related to the better-known perfect. According to , iamitive markers are “aspectotemporal markers that seemingy overlap with both the perfect and ‘already’”. Thus, a sentence like ( ) can have various translations into English depending on the context. tipakutu\\ ti-paku-tu\\ 3i-die-iam\\ ‘she is dead (already/now)’ \: ‘she has died (already/now)’ In his thesis, described iamitives in some Southeast Asian languages in detail. Subsequently, proposed that the iamitive is a distinct gram type in a larger grammatical space that also includes perfects in the traditional sense and many other gram types that overlap in their uses. A new gram type, though with the name “new situation”, was also proposed by , in analysing iamitive-like markers in Kiranti languages (reflected by the optional addition of “now” in the translation of ( )). Others have argued against gram status of the iamitive. Among them is , who states that the differences from “traditional” perfects can still be explained within the functional realm of the perfect if we acknowledge that the perfect has distinct peculiarities in tenseless languages. I am agnostic as to the question whether the iamitive is a distinct gram type or should better be defined as a peculiar expression of the perfect gram or even be dismissed at all and be replaced by a more encompassing definition of perfect. I simply use the term “iamitive” here because the characteristics of the Paunaka marker fit relatively well the description of iamitive given by . The iamitive is generally optional in Paunaka, in the sense that it does not enter into any obligatory binary distinction iamitive vs. non-iamitive, though its use is highly favoured in some situations. This should be kept in mind, when reading the following lines. According to , iamitives share with perfects the property of marking “the current relevance of a previous event”, but they differ from perfects in how they interact with the aktionsart of a verb. This becomes apparent when considering stative verbs,stative verb|( since “certain types of states are particularly likely to be marked by iamitives, notably states that are the outcome of some natural process, such as ‘be ripe’ or ‘be grown up’” . Such states result from a “unidirectional development” of a “natural course of events” . This is exactly what we find in Paunaka. On stative predicates, the iamitive marker -tu expresses, first, that the state holds at reference time, and second, that it is the result of some previous change,resultative i.e. that there existed a time prior to reference time in which the state did not hold. This is the main difference between an iamitive and a perfect, since the perfect does not imply that the state encoded by a stative verb currently holds . The iamitive marker is -tu in Paunaka and it is certainly related to the adverb metu ‘ready, already’. ( ) provides an example of a iamitive marker on a stative verb that encodes the result of a prior change of state, i.e. the hair colour of an elderly man, which has changed from black to grey or white, with the latter being expressed by the verb -yu ‘be ripe’ in Paunaka. The example was elicited from Isidro. tiyutu nimukiji\\ ti-yu-tu ni-muki-ji\\ 3i-be.ripe-iam 1sg-hair-col\\ ‘my hair is already white’ In the same situation, Miguel proposed an answer containing the stative verb for ‘white, clear’, see ( ). However, this is not the way the colour of elderly people’s hair is usually referred to in Paunaka. All the same, the iamitive marker equally attaches to the verb here. pisururutu\\ pi-sururu-tu\\ 2sg-be.clear-iam\\ ‘you are already white’ ( ) is about a ripe fruit and also builds on the verb -yu ‘be ripe’. As in ( ) above, the iamitive marker is used on the verb. It also attaches to kana ‘this size’, which is a demonstrative adjective and thus we have an example of non-verbal predication here. The adjective is always accompanied by a gesture showing the actual size. The sentence comes from a correction session with María S. (it slightly differed from the one she had originally produced). kanainatu chÿi te tayutu binikatu\\ kana-ina-tu chÿi te ti-a-yu-tu bi-nika-tu\\ this.size-irr.nv-iam fruit seq 3i-irr-be.ripe-iam 1pl-eat.irr-iam\\ ‘once the fruit has this size, then it is ripe and then we can eat it’ Although it is highly common to attach a iamitive marker to a stative predicate that can be analysed as encoding the result of a process, this is not obligatory. In the following example, no iamitive is used on the verb -yu ‘be ripe’, possibly because the change of state is backgrounded here, the more important information being the actual state of being ripe as a precondition for the chicken eating the fruit. The sentence comes from María S., too. kuina chinijanea, kuina, abÿrÿsÿi si kue tayu chinijanea\\ kuina chi-ni-jane-a kuina abÿrÿsÿi si kue ti-a-yu chi-ni-jane-a\\ neg 3-eat-distr-irr neg guava yes if 3i-irr-be.ripe 3-eat-distr-irr\\ ‘they (the chicken) don’t eat it, no, guavas, yes, they eat if they are ripe’ If the stative verb does not encode the endpoint of a natural development per se, then such a reading is added by the iamitive marker.stative verb|) It can, for example, combine with the non-verbal existential copula kaku, and in this case, it expresses that something has come into existence by reference time that has not been there before. This can be seen in the following example ( ). The context is as follows: Miguel and I had paid José a visit and when we came back to the village, we were bitten by some small ticks. Miguel made a comment that there were many ticks, and María S. reacted with a question, which can rather be read as an expression of surprise than as a request for information. Apparently, she was surprised that the tick season had already started, since she had not noticed any ticks up to this point. ¿kakutu
summary:
The passage describes the Paunaka marker **-tu**, called an **iamitive**, which is frequent but optional and related to the adverb **metu** ‘ready, already.’ The author notes that iamitives are debated as a grammatical category, but uses the term because Paunaka fits the description well, and emphasizes that on stative predicates the marker signals both that the state currently holds and that it resulted from a prior change, unlike a traditional perfect.  

The marker is especially common with stative verbs describing outcomes of natural processes, such as ‘be ripe’ or changes in hair color, and it can also occur on non-verbal predicates. If a stative verb does not itself imply a natural endpoint, the iamitive adds a reading of newly attained existence or change, as with an existential construction indicating that something has come into being by reference time.

It typically refers to a persistent state after the end of an event, though it can also occur with shorter or reversible states, and in a few cases may target the end of an event itself. The marker may attach to the predicate, the negative particle, or both without a change in meaning, and it is distinct from the homophonous middle marker.

The incompletive marker **-kuÿ** means ‘still, (not) yet’ and can appear in both positive and negative sentences. In positive clauses it marks an event or state as ongoing at reference time but implies that it will end later, with strong stative overtones: it is used mainly with reversible states, nouns or adjectives denoting a starting point in development (such as ‘boy’ or ‘this size’), and active verbs only when they are understood statively rather than as ongoing actions.

summary: The passage explains that the prospective marker **-bÿti** is used to indicate temporally prior events that must be completed before another event can occur, and this is especially clear when the order of events is explicitly stated. It occurs mainly with **irrealis predicates**, but can also combine with **realis predicates** to express the same kind of temporal sequencing from a present or past perspective. The marker also appears in a farewell formula, where it conveys the idea that another day must come before meeting again.

text: continuous|( As was explained in , continuous marking can be analysed as a derivational processderivation if it applies to the root of a verb.verbal root However, if it applies to the stem of the verb,verbal stem it is often used in a way that resembles aspect marking. In both cases, continuous marking signals duration of an action or state, and derivational and aspectual usage certainly overlap. This section only presents examples with verbs that are not lexicalised with continuous marking. All of them have realis RS. Continuous marking is achieved by reduplication of the last syllable of the stem and an addition of iku, most probably the extension applicative and the thematic suffix (see and ). Its citation form in text is thus -CViku, and in the interlinear analyses of examples, CV is replaced by the actual syllable showing up on the word. A continuous predicate encodes that the event was begun at some point and is ongoing at reference time. It is thus sometimes related to a second more punctual event, but this is not necessarily expressed overtly. The relation between two events is very clear in ( ), which comes from the recordings by Riester with Juan Ch. The punctual event is the sudden awareness of a gray brocket and the ongoing event is the animal’s eating. It serves as a background for the punctual event. uchuine mane nisimuku unya chinikukuiku chipuneji kÿjÿpi nisaneyae\\ uchuine mane ni-simuku unya chi-niku-kuiku chi-pune-ji kÿjÿpi ni-sane-yae\\ just.now morning 1sg-find gray.brocket 3-eat-cont 3-leaf-col manioc 1sg-field-loc\\ ‘today in the morning, I found a gray brocket eating manioc leaves on my field’ A similar example was produced by Juana when telling me about how a criminal in-law of hers was finally arrested. The additive marker on the second predicate is used because the man who was eating had also arrived only recently. tinikukuikuji kapunukunube suntabunube\\ ti-niku-kuiku-ji kapunu-uku-nube suntabu-nube\\ 3i-eat-cont-rprt come-add-pl soldier-pl\\ ‘he was eating, it is said, when the soldiers came, too’ More often, no second event is overtly expressed. In ( ), Juana speaks of an ongoing listening on the telephone, a call she received from her daughter in Spain. nisamuikukuiku telefonoyae\\ ni-samuiku-kuiku telefono-yae\\ 1sg-listen-cont telephone-loc\\ ‘I was listening on the telephone’ A continuous form of the verb may also show up in elicitation when the original sentence in Spanish contains a progressive, which was the case in the following example from José. tanÿma eka kabe tanÿmapaiku timajaikukuiku\\ tanÿma eka kabe tanÿma-paiku ti-majaiku-kuiku\\ now dema dog now-punct 3i-bark-cont\\ ‘now the dog is barking right now’ ( ) comes from Juana. It is a citation of an old lady whom she once met in Candelaria, and who at first did not recognise that Juana could also speak Paunaka. When Juana could not stop laughing about something she said, it began to dawn on her. “tekukuikubuyuju eka pimiya”\\ ti-eku-kuiku-bu-yu-ju eka pimiya\\ 3i-laugh-cont-mid-ints-? dema girl\\ ‘“this girl is laughing”’ The continuous marker does not only attach to active predicates like the ones above, but also to statives.stative verb ( ) builds on a stative verb, and ( ) on an adjective. Considering these examples, it becomes clear why the marker is cited as -CViku: final syllables other than the thematic suffix -ku are involved here. Both examples come from María C. In ( ), she provides information about her having been ill. entero eka mane nekujimamaikumÿnÿ\\ entero eka mane nÿ-kujima-maiku-mÿnÿ\\ whole dema morning 1sg-have.fever-cont-dim\\ ‘the whole morning, I had fever’ In ( ), she states that she is fairly well (on a totally different occasion). This could also be considered a case of derivation rather than inflection, since this expression is highly conventionalised: the continuous marker is attached to the adjective micha ‘good’, whenever a statement about health is made. michachaikune pario\\ micha-chaiku-ne pario\\ good-cont-1sg some\\ ‘I am fairly well’ With continuous marking, the discussion of aspect is completed.aspect|) The next section is about tense.continuous|)
summary: Continuous marking in this language can function either derivationally, when it applies to a verb root, or more aspectually, when it applies to the stem; in both cases it expresses duration and overlap between derivational and aspectual uses. It is formed by reduplicating the last syllable of the stem and adding *iku* (citation form -CViku), and it indicates that an event began earlier and is ongoing at reference time, sometimes with an overt second event but often without one. The marker is not limited to active verbs: it also appears with stative verbs and adjectives, including conventionalized expressions about health.
