text: tense|( Tense is a marginal category in Paunaka, since temporal information is usually conveyed by RS status realis is used for past and present reference,past reference irrealis for future reference (in positive clauses). Nonetheless, two tense markers add more information to this general distinction, the remote (past)remote past marker -bane and the particle uchu used to specify an uncertain and in most cases also remote future.uncertain future They are listed in . Neither tense marker is obligatory. The remote (past) marker is usually phonologically attached to a word, i.e. it forms part of its prosodic contour, while the uncertain future marker does not. It is the only TAME marker that is always realised as a separate phonological word and is thus orthographically represented as an independent word, too. This is the peculiarity of the uncertain future marker. The remote (past) marker has a different peculiarity: in combination with the stative verb rootverbal root -ÿ ‘be long’, it does not refer to a remote point in time,remote past but to a remote point in space (distance).
summary: Tense is a marginal category in Paunaka, since temporal reference is usually expressed by realis for past and present and irrealis for future in positive clauses. Two optional tense markers add further distinctions: the remote past marker **-bane**, which is usually phonologically attached to a word and can indicate spatial remoteness with the stative root **-ÿ** ‘be long’, and the particle **uchu**, which marks an uncertain and usually also remote future and is always realized as a separate phonological word.

text: remote past|( past reference|( According to the classification by , Paunaka can be defined as a language with one remoteness degree in the past, i.e. a language that has one “morpho-syntactic marker for a past tense that specifically refers to remoteness”. In Paunaka, this marker, -bane, is the only past marker, and it does not contrast with a morpho-syntactic expression for recent past. Recent past or a past reading in general is induced from realis RS (see ) and the general linguistic and non-linguistic context. The remote marker is not obligatory. Besides marking remote past, it also occurs in one expression of spatial distance, which is why I decided to gloss it as “remote” (‘rem’) and not “remote past”. The marker is used in fictional narratives to establish a temporal distance between the events in the narration and now. A typical start for a story as Miguel tells them is ( ). The first sentence presents the main character to the addressee. It typically contains the non-verbal existential copula kaku, which carries the remote marker -bane to create a gap between reference time, the time the story takes place, and utterance time (the “now" of that moment). In addition, the reportive marker -jievidentiality (see ) encodes that what is told was not witnessed by the speaker himself. kakubaneji chÿnachÿ jente bakeronu\\ kaku-bane-ji chÿnachÿ jente bakeronu\\ exist-rem-rprt one man cowherd\\ ‘once upon a time, there was a man who was a cowherd, it is said’ Outside of fiction, “remote” refers to the time of the speakers’ childhood and adolescence or the time before or when they moved to the villages of Santa Rita and San Miguelito de la Cruz, or at least this is what their use of the marker suggests. In ( ), Juan C. describes one of the different temporary locations of residence in his life before he came to San Miguelito de la Cruz and made his home there. The time he is referring to is his childhood, which is perceived as being long ago, and this is signalled by the use of the remote marker on the verb of the second clause. nauku nijÿkiu, no ve, pero komo nikechu kuina bitibuabane\\ nauku ni-jÿk-i-u no ve pero komo ni-kechu kuina bi-tibua-bane\\ there 1sg-grow-subord-real right but like 1sg-say neg 1pl-sit.down.irr-rem\\ ‘there I grew up, you know? but as I said, we didn’t settle down there (and all that happened a long time ago)’ ( ) also comes from Juan C. It is his answer to the question whether he went to school in Altavista. aa niyunubane\\ aa ni-yunu-bane\\ afm 1sg-go-rem\\ ‘yes, I went (long ago)’ ( ) was elicited from María S. Since the person who made the house in this example is unknown, it follows that its construction must have happened long ago. kuina bichupa chija tanaubanechÿ eka ubiae\\ kuina bi-chupa chija ti-anau-bane-chÿ eka ubiae\\ neg 1pl-know.irr what 3i-make-rem-3 dema house\\ ‘we don’t know who made this house (long ago)’ In ( ), Juana reports what happened to their grandparents’ cows, which they had bought in Moxos in order to breed cattle. It was some karay who took their cows away. chibejiupununubebane chipeunube baka\\ chi-bejiu-punu-nube-bane chi-peu-nube baka\\ 3-take.away-am.prior-pl-rem 3-animal-pl cow\\ ‘they came to take away their cows (long ago)’ Although the remote marker is mostly used on predicates, it sometimes occurs on another word in the clause, especially adverbial demonstratives and personal pronouns, but still refers to the event as a whole, as is shown in ( ), which comes from Miguel in telling me about the history of Santa Rita. kaku echÿu xhikueramÿnÿ nakabane\\ kaku echÿu xhikuera-mÿnÿ naka-bane\\ exist demb school-dim here-rem\\ ‘there was a small school here long time ago’ In addition to giving information about the temporal setting of the event, -bane can also be used for deceased marking and possibly as a nominal past marker. In this function, it mostly attaches to kinship terms. Deceased marking is described in . In ( ), -bane is used on the copula to express remote past temporal reference and on a kinship term to express that the person in question is deceased. It is from a description by María S. of how the Supepí family moved to the place where Santa Rita is located nowadays from the place where the village was situated before. depue kakukuÿbane nÿenubane primero nubiu nauku\\ depue kaku-kuÿ-bane nÿ-enu-bane primero nÿ-ubiu nauku\\ afterwards exist-incmp-rem 1sg-mother-rem first 1sg-house there\\ ‘afterwards my late mother was still in my first house there long ago’ The remote marker -bane is certainly related to the adverb abane ‘finally’, with one example given below in ( ). In this utterance, Juana expresses that her daughter finally followed her advice to ask her boss for help in order to save her sister from being deported from Spain before ever having entered the country. abane chichujiku te tiyununubetu\\ abane chi-chujiku te ti-yunu-nube-tu\\ finally 3-speak seq 3i-go-pl-iam\\ ‘finally she spoke to him and they went’ It also sometimes occurs in isolation, i.e. not phonologically bound to a word, but this is very rare. ( ) gives one example of this. It is a statement by María C. about her consumption of alcohol in former times. bane pimiyakuÿne neu, bariente\\ bane pimiya-kuÿ-ne nÿ-eu bariente\\ rem girl-incmp-1sg 1sg-drink liquor\\ ‘long ago, when I was still a young woman, I drank, liquor’ All examples given up to this point illustrate the temporal function of -bane.past reference|) Nevertheless, when it is added to the stative verbal rootverbal root -ÿ ‘be long’, it expresses spatial remoteness (see also ). The complete verb form is tÿbane and means ‘it is far away’. In my data, most of the clauses containing tÿbane do not contain anything other than the verb. However, in ( ), there is a subject. In this utterance, Juana thinks about the reason why the flight to Germany is that expensive. tÿbane Alemania\\ ti-ÿ-bane Alemania\\ 3i-be.long-rem Germany\\ ‘Germany is far away’ There is also mÿbane ‘it is near’ with the non-productive privative prefix on the same
summary:
Paunaka has a single past-remoteness marker, **-bane**, which does not contrast with a separate recent-past form; instead, past interpretation in general comes from realis status and context. The marker is optional and is used mainly to show that an event is temporally distant, especially in fictional narratives and in references to childhood, earlier life, or deceased relatives, though it can also attach to non-predicative elements and is sometimes used as a nominal past marker.

The same marker also appears in one spatial expression, where it marks remoteness in **tÿbane** ‘it is far away,’ showing that its basic meaning is “remote” rather than only “remote past.”

text: uncertain future|( Unlike the other markers described in this section, the uncertain future marker uchu is a particle which is usually realised as an independent word. It is not phonologically bound to the preceding word, i.e. it neither affects stress assignment nor does the first vowel /u/ fuse into a diphthong with a preceding vowel. However, as for the latter feature, there are a few exceptions in the corpus, which come from Juana and apply to inflected verbs ending in /i/, as in ( ) below. Uchu always follows the word to which it refers. This may be a verb, a non-verbal predicate or some other constituent of the sentence. The particle exhibits the same floating characteristics as the other tense and aspect markers. There is no restriction as to the position of the particle inside the sentence except for the fact that it never appears sentence-initially. It cannot occur on its own either. These features set this marker apart from adverbsadverb and are the reason why I analyse it as a particle. As for its semantics, uchu is used to describe that a future event is assumed to happen, but not for sure. There is a certain insecurity about the event’s fulfilment, possibly because the exact date is not known to the speaker and the event even may not happen at all. This being so, uchu is always combined with irrealis RS. Usually it is used when an event is assumed to happen in the remote future, as in ( ), a statement by Juana following my explanation that I had plans to come back to Bolivia, but no idea when that would be. nikichupapi uchu\\ ni-kichupa-pi uchu\\ 1sg-wait.irr-2sg uncert.fut\\ ‘I will wait for you (whenever you may come back)’ ( ) comes from the same recording session. Juana was wondering when we, i.e. Swintha and I, could come back to Bolivia after the Paunaka Documentation Project had finished and thus asked me. As in ( ), there is reference to a very uncertain future, since it was not clear at all whether we would come back and when that would be. ¿juchubu uchu ebÿsÿupupunuka?\\ juchubu uchu e-bÿsÿu-pupunuka\\ where uncert.fut 2pl-come-reg.irr\\ ‘when may you come back?’ In ( ), uchu targets a future that is not actually believed to come; the sentence is rather meant as a joke to express how much María S. suffered from the strong sun. fuerte sache, tikupakane uchu\\ fuerte sache ti-kupaka-ne uchu\\ strong sun 3i-kill-1sg uncert.fut\\ ‘the sun is strong, one day it will kill me’ ( ) was elicited from Juana. I aimed at eliciting the irrealis marker on nouns. However, I got the uncertain future marker in addition to it, since a remote and uncertain future is expressed here. nijinepÿi taichunatu tisuika profesuruina uchu\\ ni-jinepÿi ti-a-ichuna-tu ti-suika profesuru-ina uchu\\ 1sg-daughter 3i-irr-be.capable-iam 3i-write.irr teacher-irr.nv uncert.fut\\ ‘when my daughter will know how to write, one day she will be a teacher’ The particle uchu is not very frequent among the speakers I worked with, but it is found much more in the recordings made by Riester in the 1960s. If we consider these recordings, it becomes clear that uncertainty is much more important than remoteness because uchu is sometimes used to refer to events that might happen very soon, and it can even be accompanied by a definite date, see ( ). Salt was among the things that people received weekly in exchange for working for their patrón, but depending on the patrón’s mood, it was not guaranteed that they really always got what they were supposed to get. sabaru uchu bibeamÿnÿtu kuyepa\\ sabaru uchu bi-bea-mÿnÿ-tu kuyepa\\ Saturday uncert.fut 1pl-take.away.irr-dim-iam salt\\ ‘on Saturday, we can possibly take salt’ I want to conclude this section with an example that I particularly like. It also comes from the recordings by Riester. Juan Ch. complains here about the amount of pastureland he and others have to reclaim for their patrón. nikuchabueji portrero, chibu kuchabueji, nenayu binika mÿiji uchu\\ ni-kuchabueji portrero chibu kuchabueji nena-yu bi-nika mÿiji uchu\\ 1sg-work pasture 3top.prn work like-ints 1pl-eat.irr grass uncert.fut\\ ‘I am working for the pasture, this is what I work, it seems we’re going to eat grass in the future’ uncertain future|) tense|) The next section is about modality and evidentiality.
summary:
The uncertain future marker **uchu** is a particle that usually appears as an independent word and is not phonologically bound to the preceding word, though it occasionally fuses with a preceding /i/ in a few corpus examples. It follows the constituent it refers to, cannot occur sentence-initially or on its own, and is analyzed as a particle because of its floating behavior.

Semantically, **uchu** marks a future event as expected but not certain, often implying uncertainty about whether or when it will happen, and it is always combined with irrealis marking. While it is often used for remote future events, older recordings show that it can also refer to soon-to-happen events or even be used with a definite date when the event is only considered possible.

text: modality|( “Modality is consideration of alternative realities mediated by an authority” . In this section, the expression of modality and evidentiality is discussed. As for modality, states that “ here is hardly any grammatical category which has been given more diverging definitions, and under the label of which a wider range of phenomena has been studied”. He further states that “ odality traditionally has been viewed as a semantic, rather than syntactic or morphological, category" . While there are certainly ways to express all or most of the modalities that have been proposed in the literature, I limit my discussion here to the modalities and evidentialities that are expressed by specific morphological means in Paunaka. All markers described throughout this section are summarised in . Two kinds of modality can be distinguished in Paunaka. One type is concerned with the expression of non-realisation or counter-to-fact notions. The other type is epistemic modality. “Epistemic modality is concerned with what is known about the actual world” . It indicates how speakers judge the proposition in terms of how much they are committed to the truth . frustrative|) Evidentialityevidentiality on the other hand is concerned with the source of information . We can thus state that both epistemic modality and evidentiality are concerned with responsibility the speaker takes for the truth/certainty/correctness of the proposition. starts with a description of markers that relate to non-realised counterfactualcounterfactuality events, is concerned with epistemic modality, and finally the only morphological expression of evidentiality in Paunaka is described in .
summary: The passage introduces modality and evidentiality in Paunaka, noting that modality is a widely debated category and that the discussion is limited to meanings expressed by specific morphological markers. It distinguishes two kinds of modality: counterfactual or non-realized events, and epistemic modality, which concerns a speaker’s commitment to the truth of a proposition. Evidentiality is defined as the source of information, and the text emphasizes that both epistemic modality and evidentiality relate to the speaker’s responsibility for the proposition’s truth or certainty.

text: counterfactuality|( The markers described in this section do not merely encode non-realisation (as was proposed as an overarching term for some of the functions described here by ). Non-realisation is expressed by irrealis RS in Paunaka, which is analysed as belonging to a separate grammatical category “reality status” following , see for more information. The important point is that besides non-realisation, there is a notion of counterfactuality or counter-expectation inherent in all of the categories described here, the most frequent of them being frustrative,frustrative|( as in ( ). The frustrative marker is attached here to the non-verbal copula kaku. In this example, Juana states that there would have been time to intervene when her daughter was deported to Bolivia because of having travelled to Spain without a valid visa. However, that time was not used and the opportunity passed by unused. kakuini tiempo\\ kaku-ini tiempo\\ exist-frust time\\ ‘there would have been (enough) time’ As for combination with RS, frustrative and avertive have been found with realis and irrealis predicates, optative only with irrealis ones. Frustrative markers are very widespread among the languages of South America . The term has been used by several scholars working on Amazonian languages,Amazonian language but often “rather on the basis of an intuitive understanding of the word frustrate, along with some comparison with other languages known to the authors” . This multifaceted usage of the term is reflected in the definition given by : “A frustrative refers to an event that did not have the expected outcome or was finished unsuccessfully. The action can be left unfinished, or be finished but not as expected, or be done in vain. It involves emotive frustration on part of the speaker, but not necessarily so”. The very vague definition and broad usage of the frustrative category has been criticised by who state that in South American linguistics, “the umbrella term ‘frustrative’ has been used for non-realized TAM categories almost on an ‘anything goes’ principle”. They propose five distinct categories of non-realisation instead: apprehensional, avertive, frustrated initiation, frustrated completion, and inconsequential.frustrative|) As for the category “apprehensional”apprehensional, this is cross-linguistically most often expressed by subordinate clauses , and this is also the case in Paunaka, where apprehensional clauses are introduced by a specific connective masa ‘lest’ ( ), so that I will not further consider it here. The avertive “involves past verb situations that almost took place but did not” and it has four different properties: non-realised verb situation as a whole, imminence, pastness, and perfectivity . There is indeed a marker in Paunaka that comes close to this definition. Morphosyntactic means to express frustrated initiation are absent, but frustrated completion is possibly realised by the same marker as avertive. Frustrated completion has the properties of non-realised completion of verb situation, pastness and imperfectivity of prefinal stage . Turning now to the category “inconsequential”, frustrative|( “it is about the lack – or the lack of completeness, or stability -- of the expected, or wished-for results/consequences -- of a verb situation that has itself been realized in the past” . This definition is not so far from the one given by for the frustrative: “Frustrative is a grammatical marker that expresses the non-realisation of some expected outcome implied by the proposition expressed in the marked clause”. However, Overall’s frustrative is not restricted to past events, and he identifies five possible extended functions of the frustrative: evaluative, incompletive or action narrowly averted, discontinuous past, counterfactual conditional, and narrative effect . Given the possibility of semantic extensions, his definition works well for the Paunaka morpheme, and I thus decided to use the term "frustrative” throughout this work. The basic function of frustrative, the non-realisation of an expected outcome, is expressed by the Paunaka marker, as well as counterfactual notions and it seems to be possible to use it for negative evaluation, too. This is explained in more detail below. The avertive marker is indeed a compoundcompounding of two distinct TAME markers, the iamitive and the frustrative. Another complex marker including the frustrative is the optative, or rather one of the two optative markers, and it probably also forms part of the non-productive complex marker -buini. It discusses the debated and broad use of “frustrative” in South American linguistics, notes related categories such as apprehensional, avertive, frustrated initiation, frustrated completion, and inconsequential, and concludes that the author will use “frustrative” because it best fits Paunaka’s marker and its extended functions. The passage explains that the Paunaka frustrative marker signals that an expected or intended outcome did not occur and is often associated with the speaker’s disappointment, annoyance, or negative evaluation. It can appear on existential clauses, in counterfactual clauses, and on desiderative verbs, and it is not restricted to past events.

text: There are two markers of epistemic modality in Paunaka, one used to express uncertainty and the other one to express a deduction, with the first one being much more frequent than the other. Both of them can combine with realis as well as irrealis predicates, i.e. epistemic modality is independent of reality status. Uncertainty uncertainty|( The uncertainty marker -kena reflects the speaker’s uncertainty about the proposition. It is thus a marker of speculative modality or possibility . Other names for markers with the same or related semantics include dubitative and potential , but I prefer the neutral “uncertainty”, which includes both a dubitative and a potential reading, and does not make any claim as to why the speaker is uncertain about the proposition. The marker -kena occurs very frequently. One example is ( ), which comes from Miguel. The context is as follows: Juan C. had talked about the singing of frogs at night. Miguel was surprised to hear about this, because apparently he had never heard frogs at night, and so he considers why this could be. He uses -kena to signal that what he proposes is a speculation, i.e. that he might be fast asleep so that he completely misses the sounds at night. ( ) is from the same context as ( ) and ( ) above: Juana’s encounter with the two old ladies in Candelaria, who do not recognise in the beginning that Juana speaks Paunaka and understands them. At this point of the story, they finally realise this fact. Juana’s laughing about their comments in Paunaka lets them conclude that she is a speaker, too, that she must be related to them in some way. Note that the predicate of the first clause is a noun, while the second one is a verb. “kumade, ¡biparienteneyenu eka pimiya, chisamuyenu paunaka!”\\ kumade bi-pariente-ne-yenu eka apimiya chi-samu-yenu paunaka\\ fellow 1pl-relative-possd-ded dema girl 3-hear-ded Paunaka\\ ‘“fellow, this girl must be our relative, she must understand Paunaka!”’ ( ) also comes from Juana. She has never been to school and her geographical knowledge is limited to the facts she needs to know in daily life (which is not to say that it is in general limited knowledge, as her capacity to remember places of utility is extraordinary). Nonetheless, she knows from her daughter who once went to Spain that the journey takes a whole day, so she deduces that Spain must be far away. entero tijai chÿbÿbÿkiu, pucha tÿbaneyenu\\ entero tijai chÿ-bÿbÿk-i-u pucha ti-ÿbane-yenu\\ whole day 3-fly-subord-real damn 3i-be.far-ded\\ ‘her flight took a whole day, damn it must be far’ Finally, ( ) is an example with the deductive marker on a noun. It comes from Miguel, who described the things he saw in one of the pictures of the frog story to his brother José. He had previously identified the bed with its long, adorned bedposts as a church, but then realised it was only a bed (and further that the picture depicted a room or house). aa nakaku eka ¡kamajayenutu!\\ aa naka-uku eka kama-ja-yenu-tu\\ intj here-add dema bed-emph1-ded-iam\\ ‘aa here is also this what must have been a bed!’ deductive|) modality|)
summary: Paunaka has two epistemic modality markers: one for uncertainty and one for deduction, with the uncertainty marker being much more frequent. Both markers can occur with either realis or irrealis predicates, showing that epistemic modality is independent of reality status.

text: evidentiality|( Paunaka has one evidential marker -ji, which is used as a reportive (or reportative) and hearsay marker. This means that the event was not witnessed by the person who speaks. It was reported to her by another person. It may also be the kind of information a person has picked up somewhere without necessarily knowing the source, such as rumors or the like. Alternative names for the function conveyed by the reportive marker include secondhand and quotative, but quotative was defined by as an evidential with “overt reference to the quoted source”. According to , a system with only one evidential that is a reportive is frequent in Arawakan languages and the most widespread, both in South America and worldwide. The Paunaka reportive is used largely in the same way as the related markers in Baure and the Mojeño languages (cf. ; ; ; ). In narratives, we find it in most clauses. It usually attaches to the predicate, as in ( ) and ( ), but may instead or in addition be attached to other constituents of the clause as well, as is the case in ( ). ( ) is the start of a story told by Miguel. The reportive marker is attached to the non-verbal copula kaku ‘exist’, which in addition also carries a remote past marker -bane. kakubaneji ruschÿnubeji jente tiyununube tichubikupunube\\ kaku-bane-ji ruschÿ-nube-ji jente ti-yunu-nube ti-chubiku-pu-nube\\ exist-rem-rprt two-pl-rprt man 3i-go-pl 3i-stroll-dloc-pl\\ ‘once upon a time, there were two men who went hunting (lit.: strolling around), it is said’ ( ) also comes from Miguel. He was looking at the frog story book and told Alejo the story that develops throughout the book. It is remarkable that he uses a reportive marker here, because he was actually witnessing what was going on. However, the proceedings in a picture book are of course not real, and Miguel’s re-narration of the story thus definitely falls into the realm of the genre of fiction, so that the use of reportive markers is adequate. echÿu aitubuchepÿimÿnÿ chimumukuji\\ echÿu aitubuchepÿi-mÿnÿ chi-mumuku-ji\\ demb boy-dim 3-watch-rprt\\ ‘the little boy is watching it (the dog), it is said’ An example that comes from a story told by María S. is ( ). tisachuji tinika kesuji isini\\ ti-sachu-ji ti-nika kesu-ji isini\\ 3i-want-rprt 3i-eat.irr cheese-rprt jaguar\\ ‘the jaguar wanted to eat cheese, it is said’ In fictional stories, -ji is found frequently on utterance verbs that mark direct speech. It has been reported to occur “extremely frequently” on verbs of utterances in narratives in Baure , as well as in Mocoví (Guaycuruan), which takes as evidence that the reportive also has a quotative function. Although the reportive can also function as a quotative on reported direct speech, as is the case in example ( ) below, it is not a tautology to have it on utterance verbsspeech verb|( in fiction. I believe it is not used for quotative function in these cases. Quoting direct speech normally presumes that the speaker has listened to the original utterance, and in fact, the reportive marker does usually not occur on utterance verbs in Paunaka, when a speaker quotes direct speech that she has witnessed. The direct speech of fictional stories, however, is nothing that has been witnessed by the narrator. The reportive marker is used to create a certain distance to the quoted speech in this case. One example of this is ( ), which comes from the story about the fox and the jaguar told by Miguel. At this point in the story, the jaguar has just asked the vulture whether the fox was still there (the vulture was supposed to guard the fox). The answer of the vulture is then accompanied by a speech verb bearing the reportive marker. “kakukuÿ”, tikechuji echÿu sÿmÿ\\ kaku-kuÿ ti-kechu-ji echÿu sÿmÿ \\ exist-incmp 3i-say-rprt demb vulture \\ ‘“he is still here”, the vulture said, it is said’ speech verb|) The reportive marker is not solely used in fiction. It is also used when people speak about what other people have done or said without having witnessed this themselves. Thus ( ) comes from Juana telling me about her grandparents’ encounter with a water spirit, a big snake, on their way back from Moxos where they had bought cows. She has not personally witnessed this, so she uses a reportive marker several times here: on the non-verbal similative particle nena ‘be like’,similative clause on the verb and on the conominal object. Note that while an encounter with a spirit may sound fantastic to some readers, something belonging to the genre of myths and narratives, this is not the case for many people in the Chiquitania, who deeply believe that spirits exist. They are the owners of particular places in the landscape. nenayuji eka chinekupunubeji echÿu pariki chikebÿkeji\\ nena-yu-ji eka chi-nekupu-nube-ji echÿu pariki chi-kebÿke-ji\\ like-ints-rprt dema 3-see.coming-pl-rprt demb many 3-eye-rprt\\ ‘it seems that they saw a pair of eyes approaching them, it is said’ In ( ), Juana speaks about a place, where some people go to fish, but she has never been to. The word komunida (Span. comunidad) denominates an indigenous village and/or its inhabitants. kaku komunidaji nauku\\ kaku komunida-ji nauku\\ exist community-rprt there\\ ‘there is a village, it is said’ Paunaka’s reportive marker is occasionally used with the function of a quotative, where the source of the quoted reference is usually obvious from the context. Consider ( ), which was a Paunaka translation of a Spanish utterance by my colleague Swintha. piti pikupauchaji\\ piti pi-kupaucha-ji\\ 2sg.prn 2sg-use.irr-rprt\\ ‘she says: “you can use it”’ further notes that the TrinitarioMojeño Trinitario reportive can occasionally be used with a meaning of ‘pretend’ (Span. fingir). I have not encountered an exact equivalent of this meaning in Paunaka, but in the recordings of the 1960s by Riester, the reportive twice combines with the frustrativefrustrative|( to convey a meaning of an ironic or sarcastic ‘so-called’, as in ( ), where the speaker complains that the pututu soup he gets from the patrón is like chicha, i.e.
summary: Paunaka has a single evidential marker, -ji, which primarily functions as a reportive or hearsay marker: it indicates that the speaker did not witness the event directly and learned about it from others or indirectly. It is used very frequently in narratives, especially with predicates and speech verbs, and can also occur with quoted speech to create distance from reported discourse, though it is not the usual marker for direct quotations of witnessed speech. The marker is also used in non-fiction contexts when speakers describe events, sayings, or places they have not personally experienced.

text: degree marker|( There is a small number of miscellaneous markers that have not been described up to here, because they do not fit neatly into any category that has been mentioned so far. They are possibly best analysed as focus markers, but not in the sense that they simply mark the focus in a clause. They all add more specific information. Rose (2021, p.c.) proposes the term “degree markers”, which I will adopt in my description. All of these markers occur with words of different classes.word class The intensifier is described in . It usually attaches to predicates and can be translated with ‘very’ in most of the cases. In , the additive marker is discussed, which comes close in function to the English adverb ‘also’. It expresses that an action or a participant is added to the discourse. is about the two limitative markers, which are similar in function to the adverbs ‘only’ and ‘just’. Finally, provides some examples of the emphatic markers.
summary: The passage introduces a small set of miscellaneous markers that do not fit neatly into earlier categories and are tentatively treated as “degree markers,” though they may also be analyzed as focus markers in a broader sense. These markers add specific information and occur with different word classes, including an intensifier meaning roughly “very,” an additive marker like “also,” two limitative markers similar to “only” and “just,” and emphatic markers.

The only exception to its predicative distribution is the lexicalized adverb **nÿmayu** ‘just, only when,’ which is historically derived from *tanÿma* ‘now’.

summary: The passage describes a single additive marker, **-uku**, which can attach to predicates and some other constituents and means ‘also/too/as well’; when negated, it can also mean ‘neither’. text: limitative|( There are two limitative markers, -jiku and -yÿchi, which translate as ‘only, just’, but just like the Spanish equivalent nomás , they can also be used in contexts that do not precisely or primarily mark delimitation. They are thus also often used to emphasise that something is the way it is expressed as against imagined possible objections of the interlocutor. Both markers attach to different parts of speech and both can have wide or narrow scope. In the latter case, the markers usually attach directly to the word over which they have scope, though a few counterexamples to this general tendency exist. According to the speakers, -jiku and -yÿchi can be used interchangeably. However, there are a few words that habitually combine with -jiku but not with -yÿchi: mÿbanejiku ‘close, near’ and sepitÿjiku ‘small’, which usually occur with -jiku, but are sometimes also used without it, and chinajiku ‘only one, alone’, which derives from chÿnachÿ ‘one’. The following three examples show the usage of -jiku ‘lim1’ with wide or proposition scope. The statement in ( -2) is made by Miguel, who had explained before that he is afraid of being operated on and he might just go blind. repentekena suturubÿkejikunÿ\\ repente-kena suturubÿke-jiku-nÿ\\ maybe-uncert blind-lim1-1sg\\ ‘maybe I am just going blind’ ( -1) is from a story about the fox and the jaguar. The jaguar has caught the vulture and wants to eat him as a punishment for letting the fox escape, but the vulture escapes due to the jaguar's stupidness and while flying up, he defecates into the jaguar’s mouth and the jaguar eats his excrement instead. Thus in this specific case, -jiku could also have scope over the noun only, but chances are that to express such a meaning, the limitative marker would have been attached to the noun instead of the verb. chinikujikutu chisikuji\\ chi-niku-jiku-tu chi-sikuji\\ 3-eat-lim1-iam 3-excrement\\ ‘now he only ate his excrement’ Another case of -jiku being used with proposition scope is ( -4) from Miguel, where he tells me about the old school building of Santa Rita whose thatched roof was rotting away: tibÿrujikutu echÿu sakiji\\ ti-bÿru-jiku-tu echÿu sakiji\\ 3i-be.rotten-lim1-iam demb satintail.sp\\ ‘the satintail (Imperata brasiliensis) was just rotten’ In ( -3), -jiku has narrow scope over the predicate. The sentence comes from Juana and the machine she speaks of was brought to make the reservoir in Santa Rita. chupunu echÿu makina echÿu tikurumejikujiku\\ chÿ-upunu echÿu makina echÿu ti-kurumejiku-jiku\\ 3-bring demb machine demb 3i-pierce-lim1\\ ‘he brought the machine that only drills’ Another example of -jiku exhibiting narrow scope is ( -5), where the marker is attached directly to the noun. María C. states here that she only knew her mother when she was a child, because her grandmother had already passed away and her father died when she was still very young. nÿenujiku nichupuiku\\ nÿ-enu-jiku ni-chupuiku\\ 1sg-mother-lim1 1sg-know\\ ‘I knew only my mother' The following examples include -yÿchi ‘lim2’, the first three of them having wide scope. ( -1) is a comment by Juana about her feelings when speaking to her daughter in Spain on the telephone. nichÿnumiyÿchi kue tichujika\\ ni-chÿnumi-yÿchi kue ti-chujika\\ 1sg-be.sad-lim2 if 3i-speak.irr\\ ‘I only get sad when she talks’ ( -4) comes from Miguel telling me about how it came to be that he went to school. Some other children had invited him to the classes, but he did not tell his parents about his plans to attend: niyunuyÿchi\\ ni-yunu-yÿchi\\ 1sg-go-lim2\\ ‘I just went’ ( -2-3) comes from María S. She produced this sentence as a contrast to what she had said before, that there is a small football field for children nowadays and that children in general play a lot. Thus, although the limitative marker is attached to the adverbial here, it has scope over the whole proposition. maneyÿchi biyunu asaneti\\ mane-yÿchi bi-yunu asaneti\\ morning-lim2 1pl-go field\\ ‘we just went to the field in the mornings’ The following examples show the use of -yÿchi with narrow scope. In ( -2), María S. explains to me that her field is close to her house in comparison with other people that have fields further away from the village. nÿti nakayÿchi nisane\\ nÿti naka-yÿchi ni-sane\\ 1sg.prn here-lim2 1sg-field\\ ‘I have my field just here’ ( -5) comes from María C. talking about sorcerers and the people they killed. She contrasts seeing the things that happened with just talking about them. nechukue nimu kuina nichujikayÿchi nÿatiyubi\\ nechukue ni-imu kuina ni-chujika-yÿchi nÿ-ati-yu-bi\\ therefore 1sg-see neg 1sg-talk.irr-lim2 1sg-brother-ints-2sg\\ thus I saw it, I am not only talking (i.e. gossiping), my dear brother’ One final example of -yÿchi being used for emphasis is ( -6) from Juana, where she affirms a statement I had made when we were speaking about the former patrón of Retiro after listening to the recordings Riester made with Juan Ch. in the 1960s. ja ¡pariki maruyÿchi!\\ ja pariki maru-yÿchi\\ afm many bad-lim2\\ ‘yes, (he was) very bad!’ limitative|) This leads us to the topic of the next section.
summary:
The passage describes two interchangeable limitative markers, **-jiku** and **-yÿchi**, both glossed as meaning ‘only, just,’ though they can also function more broadly to emphasize a statement against possible objections. Either marker may have wide or narrow scope, with narrow scope usually shown by direct attachment to the word it modifies, although some exceptions occur.  

It also notes a few fixed or preferred combinations, such as **mÿbanejiku** ‘close, near,’ **sepitÿjiku** ‘small,’ and **chinajiku** ‘only one, alone,’ which tends to derive from ‘one.’ Several examples illustrate both markers used with proposition scope and with narrower scope over nouns, predicates, or adverbials.

text: emphatic|( There are two emphatic markers. One of them has a longer and a shorter allomorph. The longer one is -ja’a and only occurs at the end of words. It was primarily used by Juan Ch., who attached it to demonstrative adverbs in the recordings from the 1960s. However, Juana sometimes attaches the long form to the mirative particle jimu ‘you see, you know, right?’ (see Footnote in ). The shorter allomorph -ja can be followed by other markers and is more frequent today. The emphatic marker is used to emphasise, stress or particularly point out something. It is difficult to find a good translation into English. In the Spanish variety spoken in the region, the particle pues (pronounced pue) comes close. The emphatic marker can also occur as a separate phonological word (realised as ja, ja’a, jaja and the like), usually at the beginning of an utterance. In this case, it marks affirmation and is glossed as such (‘afm’). ( -1) is an example of the longer allomorph. It comes from Juan Ch., who had just previously mentioned that they should leave Retiro and let the woods take over that place. kue kuina repente bipakamÿnÿ nakaja’a\\ kue kuina repente bi-paka-mÿnÿ naka-ja’a\\ if neg maybe 1pl-die.irr-dim here-emph1\\ ‘if not, we will maybe just die here’ ( -2) comes from Juana’s account of her encounter with the two old Paunaka ladies in Candelaria. She reveals here that she is a speaker, too. Note that the additive marker is irregularly given as -kuku here, probably because it cannot be properly integrated phonologically, since there are already two vowels preceding it. nichujikuja, yeye, jimu eka nÿenu paunaka nÿakuku paunaka\\ ni-chujiku-ja yeye jimu eka nÿ-enu paunaka nÿ-a-uku? paunaka\\ 1sg-speak-emph1 granny mir dema 1sg-mother Paunaka 1sg-father-add? Paunaka\\ ‘I really speak (Paunaka), granny, you know, my mother is Paunaka, my father is Paunaka, too’ ( -3) comes from Miguel’s story about the lazybones. In the beginning of the story, his wife asks him to make a field to supply them with food. “panajachÿu pario eka pisaneina kuina binikukeneina"\\ pi-ana-ja-chÿu pario eka pi-sane-ina kuina bi-niku-kene-ina\\ 2sg-make.irr-emph1-demb some dema 2sg-field-irr.nv neg 1pl-eat-nmlz-irr.nv\\ ‘“make something for your field, we do not have any food”’ One example of an emphatic marker as an affirmative particle is ( -4). It is an affirmation by Juana of a statement I made before about a dog that was eating bread. ja tiniku yui\\ ja ti-niku yui\\ afm 3i-eat bread\\ ‘yes, it eats bread’ The second emphatic marker is -kene.focus|( It is homophonous with the nominalisernominalisation (see ), but is sometimes also realised as -kine. It occurs rarely, which is why had not previously distinguished it from the (equally rare) nominaliser. However Rose (2021, p.c.) analyses the cognate and equally homophonous forms -giene of TrinitarioMojeño Trinitario as two different morphemes, a nominaliser and an intensifier. Since an analysis that distinguishes two morphemes also makes sense in the Paunaka case, I follow her analysis here. -1.9ptBaure has no cognate form to my knowledge, but in Terena, a particle kene/keno is described as a connective which functions as an adversative (‘but’), but is also used “to enumerate the phases of a process or the individuals of a group” , where it indicates a switch from one topic to the other, where the new topic is a new subject. This particle could be cognate with the Paunaka marker. As for Paunaka, I have found -kene being attached a few times to the verb -anau ‘make’. In this case, it always indicates either focus on the subject or topicalisation of it. An example is given in ( -s1). This sentence was produced by Juana who was talking with María S. and wanted to resume the topic of the conversation after some disruption by other people speaking about different things. no che nanakene nikuaji nÿpuipuna\\ no che nÿ-ana-kene ni-kuaji nÿ-pui-puna\\ intj 1sg-make-emph2- 1sg-net 1sg-fish-am.prior\\ ‘why, no, as for me, I make my net and go fishing’ If the verb including -kene is combined with the topic pronoun chibu, there is subject focus and the sentence resembles a cleft construction (see ). ( -s2) is such a case. María C. states here that she recognises who bakes the bread I was talking about (in order to take the turn in the conversation with me). chibu chanaukine\\ chibu chÿ-anau-kene\\ 3top.prn 3-make-emph2\\ ‘she is the one who makes it’ Indication of subject focus is also the function of the marker in ( -c1). Thematically, this example is also about the patrón, whom Juan Ch. cannot imagine working like the workers do. Apparently, the patrón claimed that he could do it. sachu chanaukene\\ sachu chÿ-anau-kene\\ want 3-make-emph2\\ ‘HE wants to do it’ Almost all of the other instances of -kene I have found in the corpus also include the emphatic marker -ja (see above) and iamitive -tu (see ), resulting in a sequence -kenejatu. They usually contain a kind of affirmation of something that was previously said or implicit in the context and have a flavour of certainty or conviction about the truth of the statement. Additionally, they can also indicate that the discourse topic is definite and not considered worth discussing further. Consider ( -strange), in which we find the sequence -kene-ja-tu twice: on the manner demonstrative verb -kuye ‘be like this’ and on the copula kaku. summary: The passage describes two emphatic markers in Paunaka: a first marker with a long allomorph -ja’a, which only appears word-finally, and a shorter, more frequent form -ja that can occur before other markers; both are used to emphasize or affirm statements. The second marker, -kene (also -kine), is rare and homophonous with a nominaliser, but in the corpus it mainly marks subject focus or topicalisation and often adds a sense of affirmation, certainty, or discourse continuation, sometimes combining with -ja and -tu in the sequence -kene-ja-tu.

text: This chapter is about different kinds of simple clauses. With “simple clauses” I refer to main clauses that only contain a single finite verb or non-verbal predicate.non-verbal predication Clause combination and complex predicates are described in Chapter . The simple clauses described here relate to different types of speech acts: declarative, directive and interrogative. Declarative clauses are the topic of and , the difference being that the first is about those with verbal predicates and the latter about the ones with non-verbal predicates. Both sections include a discussion on the expression of arguments, word order and negation: in these topics form subsections, but in they are integrated into different subsections, which are ordered by semantic type. is about imperatives and other directives, such as the prohibitive and hortative. deals with different types of interrogative clauses.
summary: This chapter describes simple clauses, defined as main clauses with a single finite verb or a non-verbal predicate, and excludes clause combination and complex predicates. It covers simple clauses according to speech-act type: declaratives, directives, and interrogatives. Declaratives are treated separately for verbal and non-verbal predicates, with discussion of argument expression, word order, and negation; the chapter also includes imperatives and other directives such as prohibitives and hortatives, as well as different kinds of interrogative clauses.

text: declarative clause|( The verbal declarative clause minimally consists of an inflected verb.finite verb Core argumentsargument|( are indexed on the verb,person marking except for third person objectsobject which are not always marked. NPsnoun phrase|( can co-occur, i.e. they are conominal.conomination|( provides information on the expression of subjects and on the expression of objects. There is no flagging of core arguments on nouns. Oblique NPs can be marked by the locative marker or prepositions; this is the topic of . Typically only one core argument is conominated, either a subject or an object, and this argument usually follows the verb. The most basic word ordersword order|( are thus V, VS and VO. Obliques mostly follow the verb, and also the S or O argument, as far as it is conominated. The preverbal slot is associated with highlighting. Both subject and object NPs can occur in this slot as well as obliques.obliquenoun phrase|) We thus also find SV and OV orders. In the rare cases that the subject as well as the object is conominated, the most frequent word orders are VOS and SVO. VSO is also possible; OVS, however, is highly exceptional.word order|) Information on possible word orders is provided in . It would certainly be worth to examine information and discourse structure of Paunaka to learn more about the conditions that trigger conomination of participants and their position in the clause. I have some preliminary thoughts on this issue that I share in this section, but did not undertake a full analysis.
summary:
The verbal declarative clause minimally consists of an inflected finite verb, with core arguments indexed on the verb; however, third-person objects are not always marked. NPs can co-occur with the verb as conominals, and there is no case flagging on core noun arguments, while oblique NPs may be marked by the locative marker or prepositions.  

Typically only one core argument is conominated, either the subject or the object, and this argument usually follows the verb, giving the basic orders V, VS, and VO; preverbal position is associated with focus and allows SV, OV, and other less common orders, including VOS, SVO, and rarely VSO, with OVS highly exceptional.

The passage describes object marking in Paunaka verbs. First- and second-person objects are obligatorily indexed on the verb, with the marker following the verb stem, and in ditransitives the indexed object is the recipient; personal pronouns do not normally co-occur with these indexes, though a person-marked preposition -tÿpi can very rarely accompany an emphasized SAP object.

text: oblique|( In this work, obliques are defined as per as nominal constituents that modify a verb or clause. According to this definition, obliques are adjuncts, but the issue is not totally clear for Paunaka. Obliques are never required syntactically by any verb. They are neither indexed on the verb in verbal declarative clauses nor obligatorily expressed by an NP (or PP). Nonetheless, a few verbs highly favour the overt expression of an oblique, first and foremost the motion verbmotion predicate -yunu ‘go’, as exemplified in ( ) from María C., but also -etuku ‘put’ and to a lesser extent -kuetea ‘tell’. This is because these verbs semantically require a goal or addressee. It could thus be argued that the obliques of these verbs are (optional) arguments. tiyunu kampoyae\\ ti-yunu kampo-yae\\ 3i-go countryside-loc\\ ‘she went to the countryside’ It has been argued that the distinction between arguments and adjuncts is possibly not a crosslinguistic but a language-particular one . Concerning Paunaka, there is no general difference in the expression of those kinds of obliques that are semantically entailed and other constituents that seem to be completely optional by the semantics of the verb, i.e. those that clearly qualify as adjuncts, and I do not know of any test that would unambiguously set apart arguments from adjuncts in Paunaka. This is why I decided not to distinguish them in the analysis for the time being. Thus, obliques comprise spatial, temporal, benefactive,beneficiary instrumental, cause,instrument/cause and comitative relations, and depending on the specific kind of relation, they can take the general locative markerlocative marker|( -yae (see ), or they can be marked by a preposition (see ). summary:
The passage defines obliques in Paunaka as nominal constituents that modify verbs or clauses and are generally adjuncts, since they are never syntactically required, never indexed on the verb, and not obligatorily expressed. However, some verbs such as ‘go,’ ‘put,’ and ‘tell’ often favor overt obliques because they semantically require a goal or addressee, making the argument/adjunct distinction difficult to apply consistently in this language.  

Obliques can express spatial, temporal, benefactive, instrumental/cause, and comitative relations, and they may be marked by the locative suffix -yae, by a preposition, or sometimes remain unmarked, especially with motion-goal expressions. The passage also introduces the oblique topic pronoun nebu, used with locative and temporal relations and often preceding the verb.

text: word order|( conomination|( Paunaka has a wide range of possible word orders regarding nominal expressions of arguments: VS, VO, SV, OV, VOS, VSO, SVO. If we consider the argument indexes on the verb, however, the order is rigid: subject indexes always precede the verb stem,verbal stem i.e. the order is s-V for intransitive verbs. First and second person object indexes always follow the verb stem, yielding s-V-o. Third person objects are either indexed by a marker that encodes 3>3 relationships on verbs or remain unmarked, thus we have s+o-V or s-V argument orders on verbs with third person objects.person marking It is common that only one core argument is conominated and the most basic word orders can thus be considered VS and VO. It is also very common that a clause contains nothing but a verb if subject and, if applicable, object participants are well-established in discourse. V and VS sentences are mainly found with intransitive verbs and are related to topictopic|( continuity, topic establishment and topic change. VO order is typical for transitive verbs. This is connected to the subject being an established topictopic|) and the object providing new information, i.e. having the role of focus . For convenience, the word order types of the discussed sentences are placed above the examples in this section. Word orders of material that is not relevant for the discussion is given in parenthesis; this is usually other juxtaposed sentences that I did not want to omit, because intonation suggested that they closely belonged to the sentence I want to discuss or because I believe they are indicative for information structure. Let us start with two examples that contain nothing more than the inflected verb. ( ) represents the answer Juana gave to my (stammered) question after her relation to her grandchildren. The grandchildren are established as participants by my question, so they do not need to be conominated by an NP. They are encoded by the plural marker on the verb. The first person subject participant is expressed by the index preceding the verb stem. If both subject and object are conominated, we mostly find VOS or SVO order. There are also some examples of VSO in the corpus. As for OVS, however, it was only found in elicitation contexts, though it was not rejected as being completely wrong, given that the relations between the participants were sufficiently clear. I will provide examples for all orders. ( ) and ( ) have VOS order, ( ) and ( ) are examples for SVO, ( ) and ( ) show VSO order. An example from elicitation with OVS order is ( ). ( ) comes from María C. talking about Clara. Our visit at her place caused a delay in her work. ( ) is an example of SVO order. Juana and I had been looking at the frog story and she had identified the bird that flies from the tree as a hawk. We go on with the next page, but Juana digresses from the task in order to tell me about the hawk and an experience with another bird of prey that stole her dog. The hawk has been mentioned shortly before, but it is not topical. In order to indicate that the topic changes to the hawk again, the NP is positioned before the verb. SVO:\sia tiniku takÿra\\ eka sia ti-niku takÿra\\ dema bird.sp 3i-eat chicken\\ ‘the hawk eats chicken’ In ( ) the object is a headless relative clause (see ). It comes from the story about the two men who meet the devil in the woods as told by Miguel. The devil approaches shouting. It is important in the development of the story that only one of the men answers the devil and this importance is highlighted by placing the NP in preverbal position. SVO:\chinachÿ echÿu chikompanyerone chijakupu echÿu tiyÿbui\\ i chinachÿ echÿu chi-kompanyero-ne chi-jakupu echÿu ti-yÿbui\\ and one demb 3-companion-possd 3-receive demb 3i-shout\\ ‘and one of the companions answered the one who shouted’ ( ) is an example of VSO order. It comes from Juana telling the frog story and describing the picture on which the dog is running away from the beehive that has fallen down and the bees chase it. VSO:\jane eka kabe\\ chi-nisapiku-tu jane eka kabe\\ 3-sting-iam wasp dema dog\\ ‘the wasps sting the dog’ ( ) is another example of VSO order, where the subject is a proper name. It remains to be checked whether VSO order is (more) usual if subjects are expressed by proper names, there are very few examples of such constellations in the corpus. In any case, this sentence was produced by María S. in elicitation, she first used a first singular index, when I asked her to translate the sentence, but repeated it with her own name to be put like this in this work. Here you are, María. VSO:\Maria yumaji\\ ti-ana-tu Maria yumaji\\ 3i-make.irr-iam María hammock\\ ‘María is making a hammock’ One of the very few examples of OVS orders was produced by Juana, when Swintha asked her to describe a photo that showed me with my two daughters lying on top of me. However, a lot of hesitation marks accompany this sentence, so it is very probable that it might be taken as a mistake or probably as left dislocation of a topical object (the picture they had been looking at before also showed my daughters and me). OVS:\ÿ chakachu chÿenujinube\\ ruschÿ-nube-chÿ chÿ-akachu chÿ-enu-ji-nube\\ two-pl-3 3-lift 3-mother-col-pl\\ ‘the two of them, her mother lifts them’ A different sentence with OVS order was produced by me in elicitation with María S. I asked her whether it was correct and she confirmed it; however, when she repeated the sentence, her intonation indeed suggested that it was a case of left dislocation. She would not accept such a sentence if both object and subject were animate,animacy i.e. when I tried to elicit OVS order with a cat being the subject and a mouse being the object of the verb
summary: Paunaka allows many surface word orders for full nominal arguments, including VS, VO, SV, OV, VOS, VSO, SVO, and occasionally OVS, but the order of verbal person indexes is much more rigid: subject indexes precede the verb stem, first- and second-person object indexes follow it, and third-person objects may be marked or unmarked. The passage argues that the basic clause types are VS and VO, with verb-only clauses common when participants are already established in discourse; VS is associated mainly with intransitive clauses and topic continuity, while VO is typical of transitive clauses where the subject is topical and the object introduces new information. Among clauses with overt subject and object, VOS and SVO are most common, VSO is also attested, and OVS is rare and often questionable or linked to left dislocation.

It is thus not totally clear whether the NP nijinepÿi ‘my daughter’ in the third clause refers to the subject or the object, since both participants are Juana’s daughters. I would opt for an analysis as an object, because the topical subject of this clause is the same as the one in the preceding clause, there is thus topic continuity and topical participants are usually not expressed by NPs. The translation of the example follows this analysis. The word order of the last clause is thus VOO. However, it is also possible that nijinepÿi is a subject NP, a delayed indication of topic switch in the previous clause. text: negation|( This section is about “the basic way(s) a language has for negating declarative verbal main clauses” . This has been called “standard negation”. Other types of negation are found in the individual sections about different non-verbal clauses (see ) and in the section about negative imperatives (see ). Standard negation builds on the negative particle kuina, which is placed directly before the verb.word order This particle seems to include the non-verbal irrealis marker -ina attached to a stem or affix ku. Note that a voiceless velar plosive is relatively common in standard negation of Arawakan languages , and the Mojeño languages have a prefix ku- for irrealis negation (cf. Rose 2020, p.c.), i.e. the “doubly irrealis construction”. In Paunaka’s standard negation, the verb necessarily has irrealis RS given that a non-realised event is always non-factual. Standard negation thus shows a paradigmatic asymmetry as regards RSreality status . There is no morphological “doubly irrealis construction” in declarative sentences. This is defined as a construction that explicitly marks that there are (at least) two parameters that trigger irrealis RS, one of them being negation . This may be worth mentioning explicitly, because closely related Trinitario,Mojeño Trinitario Terena and Kinikinau as well as the more distantly related Kampan languagesArawakan languages all have more or less elaborate doubly irrealis contructions . Consider ( ). The positive sentences in ( ) and ( ) differ from each other in RS,reality status with ( -2.1) encoding a factual event by default/realis and ( -2.2) a non-factual event by irrealis. When negated as in ( -2.3), this distinction is neutralised. Some more examples of negative declarative clauses follow, containing a stative intransitive verb in ( ), an active intransitive verb in ( ), a transitive verb in ( ), and a ditransitive verb in ( ). summary:
The passage describes standard negation in Paunaka declarative verbal main clauses, which uses the negative particle **kuina** placed directly before the verb. Negated verbs are marked with irrealis reality status, and unlike some related Arawakan languages, Paunaka does not have a morphological “doubly irrealis” construction in declaratives; negation also neutralizes the positive realis/irrealis contrast.

The passage further notes that word order is mostly unchanged, though conominal arguments are less common and usually follow the negated verb, unless they are fronted for contrastive focus. Negative clauses also show special behavior in TAME marking: the prospective and the ongoing meaning of the iamitive do not occur negatively, while the discontinuous marker **-bu** is used in negative clauses with the sense ‘not anymore.’

As for the latter we find juxtaposition of the predicate and the subject NP,noun phrase usage of the non-verbal copula kaku and other strategies. The semantic types of non-verbal predication comprise the ones typically found in the literature: equative, proper inclusion, attributive, location, existential and possessive, to use the terminology by . In addition, some other semantic types are found in Paunaka, which have been called “minor types”: genitive and benefactive,genitive/benefactive clause quantification, similative similative clause , and also locomotion , the latter being restricted to third person cislocative motion.motion predicate Strikingly, verbs are often borrowedborrowing from Spanish as non-verbal predicates, too. shows how semantic types and construction types correlate. All semantic types marked by an asterisk can also be expressed by a verbal strategy. Many semantic types in the table are assigned to the juxtaposition construction and a few to the one including a copula; however, this is a simplification of the issue. As for juxtaposition, a subject NPnoun phrase does not necessarily co-occur with the predicate just as in verbal predication. In non-verbal predication this can be related to the subject being topicaltopic and/or the predicate taking person indexes. As for the location,locative clause existential,existential clause and possessivepossessive clause non-verbal types, they include a copula in positive clauses, but do not need a copula in negative clausesnegation where its use is often related to emphasis. Before describing the different constructions in more detail, I want to provide a short illustration of the properties in which non-verbal predicates differ from verbal ones. Consider ( ), in which the nominal predicate is negated and thus has irrealis RS. summary:
The passage describes Paunaka non-verbal predication, noting that it includes several semantic types such as equative, proper inclusion, attributive, locative, existential, possessive, and a number of “minor” types like genitive, benefactive, similative, quantification, and locomotion. These predicates can be formed by juxtaposition, by using the non-verbal copula kaku, or by other strategies, and verbs are sometimes borrowed from Spanish and used as non-verbal predicates.  

It also states that non-verbal predication differs from verbal predication in two main ways: irrealis is marked, including by a special marker -ina on non-verbal words, and subject indexing follows a different alignment, with person markers appearing after the stem rather than before it. The copula kaku is restricted to third-person referents, while some non-verbal constructions use alternative forms or verbal strategies depending on person and clause type.

text: juxtaposition|( equative/proper inclusion clause|( The two semantic types of equation and proper inclusion usually include nounsnoun that serve as predicates,nominal predicate the difference among them being that equation expresses that the subject of the clause is an entity that is identical to the entity specified by the predicate, while proper inclusion encodes that the subject is member of a class which is specified by the predicate . There are some languages, in which both types are encoded differently, but the languages in South and Central America commonly use the same construction for both types . Since Paunaka does not obligatorily mark definiteness on NPs, some sentences are ambiguous as to the question whether they represent equation or proper inclusion, and one example of this ambiguity is presented in ( ) below. The attributive typeattributive clause|( is bound to adjectivesadjective|( having the role of predicates. However, in Paunaka most property concepts are expressed by stative verbs. Only a few words can felicitously be defined as adjectives. In addition, some properties, especially age, are predicated by nounsnoun (see ). This is where proper inclusion and attributive predication semantically overlap. In addition, attributive clauses are cross-linguistically often also identical to proper inclusion and equative clauses in structure , and this is also the case in Paunaka.adjective|) There are three possibilities how to encode all three types: first, the subject NPnoun phrase and the predicate are juxtaposed, second, the subject is indexed on the predicate, and third, subject NP and predicate are juxtaposed AND the subject is indexed on the predicate. ( ), which stems from elicitation with Miguel, shows all of these possibilities. If speakers choose the juxtaposition construction,word order|( the predicate usually precedes the subject NP unless the subject is expressed by a pronoun. In the latter case, the pronoun precedes the predicate. This is also the preferred word order in Trinitario’sMojeño Trinitario non-verbal clauses , and it mirrors the one found in verbal clauses, where non-emphasised subjects usually follow the verb, but not if they are pronominal (see ).word order|) A few examples with the order predicate -- subject NP follow. Genitive predication presupposes the existence of the item and states its relation to a possessor, while benefactive predication uses the oblique preposition *tÿpi* to express that something is for a beneficiary; both are analyzed as subtypes of equative or proper inclusion clauses.

summary:
Paunaka uses the verb/copula *-ubu* for stable locations and often prefers nonverbal strategies for temporary locations; the copula *kaku* ‘exist’ is also used in locative predication for third persons and in existential predication. The two constructions overlap semantically but can differ in word order: in locatives the locative phrase typically follows the copula, while in existentials the subject follows it, though discourse factors can alter this.

For first and second person location, *kaku* cannot be used. Instead, speakers either attach the locative suffix *-uku* to a personal pronoun or place the pronoun directly before the locative expression.

text: existential clause|( Existential and locative clauseslocative clause overlap in that both often express a spatial relation between a figure and a ground. Both prototypically encode “episodic spatial relationships between a concrete entity conceived as movable (the figure) and another concrete entity (the ground) conceived as occupying a fixed position in the space, or at least as being less easily movable than the figure” . Existential clauses, however, provide a different perspective on the spatial relation as locative clauses do,locative clause i.e. a perspective from the ground, not the figure . This is why they do not serve as “adequate answers to questions about the location of an entity, but can be used to identify an entity present at a certain location” . ( ) and ( ) are examples for prototypical existential clauses resembling the ones presented by : they have an indefinite referent,definiteness which is the moveable figure on a relatively fixed ground. Both examples were elicited, ( ) comes from María S., ( ) from Juana. kaku jike nikusepineyae\\ kaku jike ni-kusepi-ne-yae\\ exist fly 1sg-thread-possd-loc\\ ‘there is a fly on my thread’ kaku ÿne chÿupekÿyae keyu\\ kaku ÿne chÿ-upekÿ-yae keyu\\ exist water 3-place.under-loc snail\\ ‘there is water under the snail’ Thus an existential construction exists in Paunaka, and in many cases it can be distinguished from locative predicationlocative clause by placement of the subject directly following the copula.word order This, however, is not the only ambit of this construction type, and probably even not its main one. Consider ( ), which shows that the existential construction is not restricted to indefinite referentsdefiniteness|( in Paunaka. It was produced by María C. when it was about to rain. The hammock is mentioned here for the first time. This is probably the reason why María C. chose an existential construction rather than a locative one with the spatial expression following the copula directly. kaku niyumaji nekupai\\ kaku ni-yumaji nekupai\\ exist 1sg-hammock outside\\ ‘my hammock is outside (i.e. there is my hammock outside)’ A second example with a definite subject is ( ) from Juana. The cows she is speaking about were already well established in the story, which was about her grandparents buying cows in Moxos. However, they had not been mentioned for some time. The existential construction is thus used here to re-establish the cows as a topic. The location mentioned in this sentence is an enclosure by a hut where Juana’s grandparents slept on their way home, so it can be considered a temporary, episodic location rather than a permanent one. i kaku baka bakayayae\\ i kaku baka bakaya-yae\\ and exist cow enclosure-loc\\ ‘and the cows were in the enclosure (i.e. there were the cows in the enclosure)’ The Paunaka existential construction also relates to two types that explicitly distinguishes from existential predication, although he recognises that they are related and in some languages encoded by the same construction. First, the Paunaka construction serves a presentative function, i.e. the introduction of participants into the discourse . Actually, the presentative and the “prototypical” existential construction both introduce an indefinite referent into the discourse and thus only differ in presence or absence of a locative expression in the clause. It is because of this presentative type that existential predication partly overlaps with possessive predicationpossessive clause in Paunaka (see ). Second, the existential construction in Paunaka also encodes “habitual presence of an entity at some place” . The actual place does not have to be overtly expressed in this case if it is identifiable from the context or identical to the deictic centre. This is to say that if I speak of existential predication (or an existential clause or construction) in this work, this includes also presentatives as well as expressions of habitual presence. My usage of the term is thus more conform with the broader definition of existential predication given by or . A last word about the notion of “subject”subject is necessary. I agree with who state that “ he indefinite participant introduced in the existential construction often lacks some of the grammatical properties of a prototypical subject, but even so, there is usually no other argument available as a candidate to be the subject”. With this general background in mind, I turn to a few more examples of existential predication in Paunaka now. With ( ), Juana introduced the arroyo close to Santa Rita into the discourse as a place where the young people go swimming. This is another example of a definite subject being introduced by an existential clause. nauku Santa Ritayae kaku echÿu chÿkÿ\\ nauku Santa Rita -yae kaku echÿu chÿkÿ\\ there Santa Rita -loc exist demb arroyo\\ ‘there in Santa Rita, there is this arroyo’ definiteness|) ( ) is a typical beginning of a story by Miguel. A participant is introduced into the discourse here. There is no locative expression, but the whole story is posited in the remote past by the remote marker -bane being attached to the copula. kakubaneji chÿnachÿ jente i tipÿkubai\\ kaku-bane-ji chÿnachÿ jente i ti-pÿkubai\\ exist-rem-rprt one man and 3i-be.lazy\\ ‘once upon a time there was a man, it is said, and he was lazy’ The copula can also take the iamitive marker to contrast the state of existence of a referent with the time prior to this existence. The passage explains that Paunaka existential clauses overlap with locative clauses in expressing a spatial relation between a figure and a ground, but existential clauses present this relation from the ground’s perspective and are not primarily used to answer location questions. They can introduce indefinite referents, but in Paunaka they are also used with definite referents to reintroduce topics, present participants in discourse, and express habitual presence.

It further notes that existential predication in Paunaka includes presentative and habitual-presence uses, and that the “subject” in such clauses may lack typical subject properties even though no better candidate is available. The construction can also mark temporal meanings such as remote past or iamitive contrast, showing that it has a broader function than simple existence.
