summary: The passage explains that existential predications can refer to traditional or modern objects, as with a loanword for “pot” used for aluminium pots, and that such clauses may also express habitual or permanent presence rather than a specific event. It then describes negative existential clauses, which require the particle **kuina** and may appear with or without a copula; the copula is more likely when the subject is non-coindexed or in negative answers, but in most cases it is omitted.

text: possessive clause|( The non-verbal possessive clause is a type of existential clause (see above). Just like in the latter, in positive possessive clauses, there is a copula directly followed by the subject, while in negative clauses,negation the copula can be omitted.word order The difference to existential clauses is that the subject is marked as possessed in some way. A locative expression is not required in possessive clauses, but as we have just seen, a locative expression does not necessarily occur in existential clauses either. The main reason to describe possessive clauses in its own section here is that unlike existence, possession can also be expressed by a verbal strategy which builds on a verb composed of the attributive prefix ku- and a nominal stem (see for the verbal expression of possession). ( ) to ( ) show non-verbal possessive predication build on an inalienably possessed noun in positive clauses. ( ) comes from the creation story as told by Juana. It is Jesus who had a field. kaku chisane\\ kaku chi-sane\\ exist 3-field\\ ‘he had a field’ (lit.: ‘there was his field’) ( ) was produced by Clara who was trying to remember the name of the fish that bites. kaku chija echÿu\\ kaku chi-ija echÿu\\ exist 3-name demb\\ ‘it has a name’ With ( ), María C. made a judgement about the capacity of Clara’s daughters to learn Paunaka. kaku pijinejinube pero kuina puero chitanube\\ kaku pi-jine-ji-nube pero kuina puero chi-ita-nube\\ exist 2sg-daughter-col-pl but neg can 3-master.irr-pl\\ ‘you have daughters, but they can't figure it out (to speak Paunaka)’ The inalienably possessed noun may also be derived by the possessed marker as in ( ). This is often the case with Spanish loans. The example comes from María S. telling the story about how the tortoise got its carapace. She did not want to leave her house to welcome new-born Jesus, because she had a shop in that house. pimua, kaku chibentane\\ pi-imua kaku chi-benta-ne\\ 2sg-see.irr exist 3-shop-possd\\ ‘you see, she had a shop’ ( ) is an example of a negative possessive clause without copula. It is a statement by María C. about being all alone, without any siblings. kuina nÿatimÿnÿina nipijina \\ kuina nÿ-ati-mÿnÿ-ina ni-piji-ina\\ neg 1sg-brother-dim-irr.nv 1sg-sibling-irr.nv\\ ‘I don’t have a brother or sister’ The possessive clause can contain a locative expression as in ( ) and ( ). ( ) was elicited from Juana. ¿kaku pubiu nauku pisaneyae?\\ kaku pi-ubiu nauku pi-sane-yae\\ exist 2sg-house there 2sg-field-loc\\ ‘do you have a house at your field?’ ( ) also comes from Juana who was making a statement about her daughter here. kaku ruschÿ chilotene nauku\\ kaku ruschÿ chi-lote-ne nauku\\ exist two 3-plot-possd there\\ ‘she has two plots there’ Instead of marking the possession directly on the noun, the possessor can also be expressed by a person-markedperson marking preposition directly following the possessed entity. The causal and instrumentalinstrument/cause preposition -keuchi is used if the possessed is a concrete object, the general oblique preposition -tÿpi for possession of more abstract entities, usually some temporal units. In the latter case, it is arguable whether the clause can be analysed as a possessive clause at all or rather counts as existential, depending on the question whether temporal units can be considered as being possessed. This, however, is a philosophical rather than a linguistic question, because there is no difference in structure between existential and possessive clauses anyway. ( ) is particularly interesting, because it contains a kind of secondary possession of an inalienably possessed noun. This noun, chÿeche ‘meat’, has a third person markerperson marking by default if used to denote meat as an edible good (chÿ-eche 3-flesh). The third person marker can be replaced by an SAP person marker in reference to the flesh of the body (e.g. nÿ-eche ‘my flesh’). Since there is already a person marker on the noun denoting ‘meat’, attachment of a second possessor marker is blocked and another way of expressing the possessor is needed. In possessive predication, this is achieved by using the preposition -keuchi which carries the person marker of the possessor. The example comes from Juan Ch. who was recorded by Riester and speaks about consequences of a successful hunting expedition. tanÿmapaiku kaku chÿeche nikeuchi nubiuyae tÿpi chÿnachÿ semana\\ tanÿma-paiku kaku chÿeche ni-keuchi nÿ-ubiu-yae tÿpi chÿnachÿ semana\\ now-punct exist meat 1sg-ins 1sg-house-loc obl one week\\ ‘right now I have meat for one week in my house’ ( ) shows the same construction. In this case, I think it might also be possible to derive an inalienably possessed noun, but the possessive relation between a shell and a possessor is not a permanent one, unlike the relation to family members, fields or walking canes. Thus a construction with -keuchi is preferred. The sentence comes from Miguel who was asking Juana about a special kind of shell which they use to polish pottery before burning. ¿pero kaku nauku sipÿ pikeuchi?\\ pero kaku nauku sipÿ pi-keuchi\\ but exist there shell 2sg-ins\\ ‘but do you have shells (for polishing clay) there?’ ( ) is a negative possessive clause including -keuchi. It comes from María C. who said this to me regretfully, because I had told her that my little daughter wanted a plantain. kuinachu merÿna nikeuchi\\ kuina-chÿu? merÿ-ina ni-keuchi\\ neg-demb? plantain-irr.nv 1sg-ins\\ ‘I don’t have plantains’ Turning to the use of -tÿpi in possessive predication now, consider ( ). It was elicited from Isidro and is about the age of an invented person. metu kakutu nobenta anyo chitÿpi\\ metu kaku-tu nobenta anyo chi-tÿpi\\ already exist-iam ninety year 3-obl\\ ‘she was already 90 years old’ ( ) is from the recordings made by Riester with Juan Ch. tanÿma uchuini kaku tiempo nitÿpi\\ tanÿma uchuine? kaku tiempo ni-tÿpi\\ now just.now? exist time-irr.nv 1sg-obl\\ ‘now I have time’ ( ) is a negated version of ( ) and comes from María S. who provides the reason why she has not finished knotting a hammock. kuina tiempoina nÿtÿpi\\ kuina tiempo-ina nÿ-tÿpi\\ neg time-irr.nv 1sg-obl\\ ‘I didn’t have time’ Another negative
summary: The passage describes non-verbal possessive clauses as a subtype of existential clause: in positive clauses a copula precedes the subject, while in negative clauses the copula may be omitted. Unlike existential clauses, the subject is marked as possessed, either directly on the noun or through a person-marked preposition such as -keuchi for concrete possessions and -tÿpi for more abstract ones. It also notes that possession can alternatively be expressed by a verbal strategy based on ku- plus a nominal stem.

summary: The passage notes that some possessive clauses include the suffix **-tÿpi**, as in Juan C.’s statement about having had a very hard life. text: similative clause|( The similative construction is relatively simple in Paunaka. It includes a comparee, a standard marker and a standard , that is, there are clauses of the type ‘X is like Y’ in Paunaka, in which X is the comparee, like the standard marker and Y the standard. The standard marker is nena ‘like, resemble, be like’ in Paunaka. Specific parameters of comparison are not included in the cosntruction. Thus sentences equivalent to ‘She is as old as me’, which I will call “equality sentences”, do not exist. Such concepts are rather expressed by more than one clause, which do not convey exactly the same meaning. There are a few cases that resemble sentences like ‘She jumps like a frog’. This is the kind of sentence that has been described under the realm of “similative construction” by , I thus apply the term a bit differently here. I believe though that such concepts are also often expressed by two clauses. Spanish influence may play a role here in that originally biclausal structures are re-interpreted as monoclausal, because nena is used as a translational equivalent of como ‘like’, parece ‘it seems, resembles’ and igual que ‘equal to’.Because the question will probably arise at this point as to how comparative constructions look like in Paunaka, and since there is no other place in the grammar, where they would be described, I give a very short summary here: Comparative constructions include the adverb max ‘more, most’, a loanborrowing from Spanish más which has the same meaning. The adverb is placed before the word expressing a property or quality. This may be an adjective, a noun or a stative verb. Comparative constructions never include a standard, i.e. the item that is surpassed. This is rather deduced from the context. ( ) is an example with an adjective and thus also a case of non-verbal predication. It comes from Juana who was conversing with María S. \ea \begingl \glpreamble amukeyu max michaniki\\ \gla amukeyu max michaniki\\ \glb soft.corn more delicious\\ \glft ‘soft corn is more delicious’ \endgl \trailingcitation \xe Depending on topicality,topic it is possible that the comparee or the standard are not overtly expressed in the similative clause, but if there is a standard NP, it follows the standard marker nena ‘like, resemble, be like’ directly.word order I think it is generally not possible to index a subject directly, but there are a few counter-examples in the corpus. It is common though that the additive marker is added to nena, and in this case, a subject index can follow the additive marker (see below in this section). ( ) is an example in which both comparee and standard are expressed by NPs. It comes from María C. who uses a Bésiro word to refer to a specific tree with dark, blood-like resin. echÿu tokoxhirx nena iti\\ echÿu tokoxhirx nena iti\\ demb tree.sp like blood\\ ‘the (resin of the) tokoxhirxh tree is like blood’ The comparee can also follow the standard as in ( ), which is from the data collected by Riester in the 1960s. Juan Ch. compares the pututu soup with chicha here, i.e. the soup is not well garnished. nenayu aumue bijiemÿnÿjini\\ nena-yu aumue abijie-mÿnÿ-ji-ini\\ like-ints chicha pututu-dim-rprt-frust\\ ‘the so-called pututu soup is (thin) like chicha’ ( ) comes from Juana and is a description of the spirit of the water, with whom her grandparents had an unpleasant encounter on their way back home from Moxos, where they had bought cows. kananaji chikebÿke, nenayuji kuje chibÿke\\ kanana-ji chi-kebÿke nena-yu-ji kuje chi-bÿke\\ this.size-rprt 3-eye like-ints-rprt moon 3-face\\ ‘she had big eyes, her face was like the moon, it is said’ In ( ), there are two juxtaposed clauses. The comparee is expressed in the first clause, a possessive one. The similative clause follows, the comparee is not repeated. The fact that the parameter is the age has to be deduced from the context. The sentence comes from Juana who was talking about her relatives. i kaku echÿu chichechapÿi nena eka nisinepÿi\\ i kaku echÿu chi-chechapÿi nena eka ni-sinepÿi\\ and exist demb 3-son like dema 1sg-grandchild\\ ‘and she had a son, who was like my grandson (in age)’ In ( ), the comparee is incorporatedincorporation into the verb that precedes the similative clause. The sentence comes from Juana who reported what the old lady she met in Candelaria long ago said when some chicha dripped on her face. “nijirebÿketu nenayu chÿbÿke iyu”\\ ni-jire-bÿke-tu nena-yu chÿ-bÿke iyu\\ 1sg-wrinkle-face-iam like-ints 3-face monkey\\ ‘“my face wrinkled, it looks like the face of a monkey”’ On the other hand, in ( ), it is the standard which is not expressed. The sentence comes from a conversation between María S. and Juana. They were just talking about keeping ducks and Juana had mentioned that ducks are dirty, because they just squat and defecate everywhere and their excrements are liquid like diarrhea. María S. adds to this: kuina nenaina echÿu gansojane tirÿrÿ chisikuji\\ kuina nena-ina echÿu ganso-jane ti-rÿrÿ chi-sikuji\\ neg like-irr.nv demb goose-distr 3i-be.hard 3-excrement\\ ‘the geese are not like them, their poo is hard’ ( ) and ( ) come close to what was originally defined as the similative construction . I have found one example which comes even closer. It was produced by María S. when I was eliciting examples with the associated motion marker. Apparently, she found the idea of simultaneously moving and eating quite funny, saying: ninikukukÿu nena mura\\ ni-niku-kukÿu nena mura\\ 1sg-eat-am.conc.tr like horse\\ ‘I walk eating like a horse’ It is not clear to me whether ( ) is still a biclausal sentence or can be considered a monoclausal one. What becomes apparent in any case is that there is no subject marker on nena, although the comparee is a first person. Consider also ( ), which comes from Miguel who addressed Juana. The latter had just loaded a big bag full of loam onto her head. nenayu mutuÿ\\ nena-yu mutuÿ\\ like-ints termite\\ ‘you look like a termite’ There are, however, also a
summary: Paunaka has a relatively simple similative construction built with the standard marker nena ‘like, resemble, be like’ and a comparee plus standard, but it does not encode specific comparison parameters, so equality expressions like ‘as old as me’ are absent and usually require more than one clause. Comparative constructions are separate: they use max ‘more, most’ (also borrowed Spanish más) before the property expression, with the standard left implicit and inferred from context. The passage also notes variable word order and occasional biclausal or possibly reanalyzed monoclausal similative examples, with Spanish influence possibly contributing to the use of nena in these patterns.

The boy’s being on a trip is compared to our situation, because we were currently on a trip to Altavista. Note that the verb -chubiku ‘stroll’ is mostly used to denote hunting trips, which is probably why Miguel felt the need to specify what he wanted to say by use of a Spanish loan pasea ‘stroll’. tiyuna tichubikupa tiyuna paseana nenabi biti tanÿmapaiku\\ ti-yuna ti-chubiku-pa ti-yuna pasea-ina nena-bi biti tanÿma-paiku\\ 3i-go.irr 3i-stroll-dloc.irr 3i-go.irr stroll-irr.nv like-1pl 1pl.prn now-punct\\ ‘he will go on a hunting trip, he will go on a jaunt like we are doing right now’ It is common to add the additive marker -uku to the standard marker and then attach a person marker.person marking In ( ), Miguel uses the standard marker in this way to make a comparative statement to what Juan C. had said before. Both of them suffered lack of water in former times. nenaukubi nauku Santa Rita kuina ÿneina\\ nena-uku-bi nauku Santa Rita kuina ÿne-ina\\ like-add-1pl there Santa Rita neg water-irr.nv\\ ‘we didn’t have water either in Santa Rita’ (lit.: ‘like us, too, there in Santa Rita was no water’) In ( ), Juana compares her own state of being full to mine. I had just said before that I was ready with eating. nenaukunÿ metu\\ nena-uku-nÿ metu\\ like-add-1sg already\\ ‘me, too, I am finished’ One last example with nenauku follows, including the complete statement. Juana speaks about how much her foster child and her daughter love her. tesabichunÿ micha nimijÿna, (pause) nijinepÿi Gladys nenauku, tisumachune micha\\ ti-esabichu-nÿ micha ni-mijÿna ni-jinepÿi Gladys nena-uku ti-sumachu-ne micha\\ 3i-estimate-1sg good 1sg-foster.child 1sg-daughter Gladys like-add 3i-want-1sg good\\ ‘my foster child estimates me a lot, (pause) my daughter Gladys, too, she likes me a lot’ similative clause|)
summary: The passage shows that the standard marker can take a subject marker, and this construction is used in comparative or similative expressions. It also notes that the additive marker -uku is commonly added to the standard marker before a person marker, as in examples meaning “like us too” or “me too,” with the form nenauku functioning as the closest equivalent to equality sentences in other languages.

text: motion predicate|( non-verbal motion clause|( Cislocative locomotion of third person participants is usually expressed with a non-verbal strategy in Paunaka. It builds on the word kapunu ‘come’. There is also a verb -bÿsÿu ‘come’, but it is hardly ever used with a third person subject. Consider ( ), which clearly shows that kapunu is not a verb. There is no person index on the predicate and the irrealis marker is -ina.non-verbal irrealis marker The sentence was produced by Juana on my first visit to hers in 2015. tajaitu kapunuina Maria\\ tajaitu kapunu-ina Maria\\ tomorrow come-irr María\\ ‘María will come tomorrow’ Non-verbal predication includes stativity, so it may sound strange that the volitional action of motion is expressed non-verbally. There is, however, a connection between locomotion and stativity and this is expressed in some way in several languages of very different language families around the world . The similarity derives from locomotion predicates encoding a change of place, situation or scene which is analogous to the change of state encoded by other stative predicates . further states that locomotion may even be expressed non-verbally in some languages. This does still not explain why non-verbal expression of locomotion is restricted to cislocative motion of third person participants in Paunaka. A look at closely related TrinitarioMojeño Trinitario|( sheds some light on this issue. Mojeño Trinitario has a non-verbal predication type called “motion-presentationals” by . This construction is used to introduce new participants into the discourse, just like the existential construction does,existential clause but with an additional notion of movement onto the scene. That is, while the existential construction can be often translated by ‘there/here is ...’, the motion-presentational construction expresses meanings like ‘there/here comes ...’. Both constructions are based on a personal or demonstrative pronoun in Trinitario to which a suffix (existential or motion copula) is added. As I have argued in and above, the first syllable ka of kapunu is most probably a demonstrative root with third person reference. The rest is the associated motion marker -punu that encodes prior motion to and away from the deictic centre on non-motion verbs, but has exclusively cislocative semantics if combined with motion verbs (see ). Unlike in Trinitario, this marker never combines with personal pronounspersonal pronoun in Paunaka, thus there are no non-verbal expressions for motion of first or second persons. I would suggest that just like in the Trinitario case,Mojeño Trinitario|) a construction with kapunu was once used to introduce new participants into the discourse only, but at some point, use of the predicate became independent from the presentational function. It thus developed into the default cislocative motion predicate for third person referents. This means that nowadays kapunu can also occur in questions,interrogative clause it can be negated etc.negation Consider ( ). The subject is not conominated here and it is not the place of arrival but of precedence that is of importance here. This shows that this is not a presentational construction anymore. The sentence was elicited from Juana. kapununube tukiu tÿbane\\ kapunu-nube tukiu ti-ÿbane\\ come-pl from 3i-be.far\\ ‘they came from far away’ In ( ), kapunu is part of the antecedent clause of a conditional sentence. Thus no presentation is implied here. The sentence also comes from Juana, who was talking about a possible visit of her daughter to hers. kue kapunuina parauna kuatruchÿ kuje\\ kue kapunu-ina parau-ina kuatruchÿ kuje\\ if come-irr.nv stop-irr.nv four month\\ ‘if she comes, she stays four months’ Nonetheless, there are also cases in which a presentational function is notable as in ( ), a statement by Clara about the weather. mm, kapunu ÿku\\ mm kapunu ÿku\\ mh come rain\\ ‘mh, rain is coming’ Some more examples follow. ( ) comes from Miguel’s account about the history of Santa Rita. i depueskuku, kuina naejumibu chijakena anyokena, kapunu padre Xeinaldo\\ i depues-uku? kuina nÿ-a-ejumi-bu chija-kena anyo-kena kapunu padre Xeinaldo \\ and afterwards-add? neg 1sg-irr-remember-dsc what-uncert year-uncert come Father Reinaldo \\ ‘and also afterwards, I don’t remember anymore in which year, Father Reinaldo came’ ( ) also comes from Miguel, who was conversing with Juana. rumingo kapunu unekoyae echÿu don Mario\\ rumingo kapunu uneku-yae echÿu don Mario\\ Sunday come town-loc demb hon Mario\\ ‘on Sunday, don Mario came to town’ Unlike the copula kaku, kapunu is never omitted in negated sentences.negation|( One example is given in ( ). It comes from Juana who was disappointed that her daughter did not visit her over Christmas. kuina kapunuina nijinepÿi\\ kuina kapunu-ina ni-jinepÿi\\ neg come-irr.nv 1sg-daughter\\ ‘my daughter didn’t come’ negation|) Just like other motion predicates (see ), kapunu has a regressiveregressive/repetitive derivation, which is kapupunu ‘come back’. This is illustrated by ( ), which comes from María S. and is about me. tichÿunumi kuina kapupunuinabu naka\\ ti-chÿnumi kuina kapupunu-ina-bu naka\\ 3i-be.sad neg come.back-irr-dsc here\\ ‘she is sad, because she doesn’t come back here anymore’ non-verbal motion clause|) motion predicate|) The existence of a non-verbal predicate with active semantics may have played a role in non-verbal integration of verbs borrowed from Spanish into Paunaka. This is the topic of the following section.
summary:
In Paunaka, cislocative motion of third-person participants is usually expressed non-verbally with **kapunu** ‘come’, which behaves like a non-verbal predicate rather than a verb and takes the irrealis marker **-ina**. Although motion is an active meaning, the text argues that this pattern may reflect an older presentational construction, comparable to Trinitario, where a motion predicate introduced new participants into discourse.

Over time, **kapunu** seems to have lost its purely presentational use and become the default cislocative motion predicate for third person referents, appearing in questions, negation, and conditional clauses. It also has a regressive/repetitive form, **kapupunu** ‘come back’.

text: borrowing|( non-verbal clause with borrowed verbs|( Although verbs borrowed from Spanish can be verbalised and then be used just like normal active verbsactive verb in Paunaka (see ), this is not the preferred pattern. Speakers rather rely on integrating borrowed verbs as non-verbal predicates. No light verb is needed in order to accommodate these non-verbal predicates. They are rather treated as if they were nouns or adjectives (see above), i.e. they take person markers that follow the predicate to index the subjectperson marking|( and the non-verbal irrealis marker -ina in contexts that demand irrealis RS. This can be seen in ( ), where the borrowed form komorau, from Spanish acomodar ‘accomodate, arrange’, takes a second person singular marker following the predicate to index the subject and the non-verbal irrealis marker for future reference. It comes from Juana and refers to me packing my stuff shortly before I would fly back to Germany. metu komoraubinatu\\ metu komorau-bi-ina-tu\\ already accommodate-2sg-irr.nv-iam\\ ‘you are already going to arrange (your stuff)’ person marking|) In most cases the input form, i.e. the form of the original verb which is borrowed , is based on a Spanish past participle in -ado, which is pronounced in Eastern Bolivia. Some examples are listed in .In addition, borrowed participles are sometimes also used adverbially like in Spanish, consider ( ) which has purau from apurar(se) ‘hurry up’ : \ea \begingl \glpreamble purau tikubu\\ \gla purau ti-kubu\\ \glb hurry 3i-bath\\ \glft ‘she bathed quickly’ \endgl \trailingcitation \xe For verbs that do not provide participles in -ado, i.e. the ones with an infinitive ending in er and ir, there exist different strategies. summary:
The passage explains that, although Spanish borrowed verbs can be verbalized in Paunaka, speakers more often use them as non-verbal predicates, patterned like nouns or adjectives. These borrowed predicates take subject person markers after the predicate and, in irrealis contexts, the non-verbal irrealis marker -ina, without needing a light verb.

It also describes several borrowing patterns: most borrowed forms come from Spanish past participles in -ado, while verbs lacking -ado participles may be borrowed from -ido forms or reduced infinitives, with some minor irregular sources. Borrowed non-verbal predicates can also function adverbially, transitively, and in complex clauses, and one modal predicate puero is borrowed from Spanish poder ‘can, be able to’.

In negation of a permissive or abilitive constructions, however, two factors trigger irrealis marking, so that speakers may feel the need to be more explicit about the modal meaning. This is reminiscent of the doubly irrealis construction found in other Arawakan languages , the difference being that in Paunaka, the fact that two parameters trigger irrealis is expressed by a lexical rather than morphological means. The passage discusses borrowed modal verbs in Bésiro, especially *puero* ‘can, be able to,’ which is derived from the noun *puéru* ‘possibility.’ *Puero* usually lacks subject indexing and is mainly used in negative contexts, with irrealis marking appearing only in certain circumstances; the language also has the infrequent borrowed form *tiene ke* ‘must.’

It then notes that using borrowed Spanish verbs as non-verbal predicates is unusual because it extends non-verbal predication beyond stative meanings to active ones. In Bésiro, some borrowed verbs take subject enclitics like nominal and adjectival predicates, though some may instead be verbalized, and the overall frequency of this pattern remains unclear.

In Paunaka, imperatives usually build on active verbs.active verb They can be identical in structure to a declarative clause. I call this type of imperatives “unmarked”, although they require irrealis RS. Irrealis could occur in declarative clauses for other reasons. Unmarked imperatives inflect for person;person marking they either have second person singular or second person plural subjects.subject Objectsobject can be indexed on these imperatives and conominated objectsconomination can occur, but they are never placed in focus position preceding the verb.word order Some examples of unmarked imperatives can be found in . Alternatively, imperatives can be marked by adding the suffix -ji to the end of the verb. I cannot tell what is the exact difference to unmarked imperatives, but more emphasis seems to be involved. They are possibly only used to make requests and commands (i.e. no offers), but this remains to be verified. Emphatic imperatives are the topic of . There are two suppletive motion predicate nabi/nabue ‘go!’ and pana ‘come!’, they are dealt with in . Negative imperatives can look like negative declarative sentencesdeclarative clause if they include the standard negation particlenegative particle kuina and an irrealis predicate. However, they can also be formed with a realis predicate and the prohibitivedirective speech act!prohibitivenegation!prohibitive particle naka or the admonitive particle masaini. The latter is rather used in warnings. Different kinds of negative imperatives are described in . Hortatives are formed with the hortative particle jaje. This is the topic of .
summary: The passage explains that imperatives in Paunaka are directive speech acts and can be formed in several ways. Unmarked imperatives resemble declarative clauses but require irrealis marking and usually have second-person subjects, while marked imperatives add the suffix -ji and seem to be more emphatic; there are also suppletive forms for ‘go!’ and ‘come!’. Negative imperatives may use either the regular negation particle kuina with an irrealis predicate or the prohibitive/admonitive particles naka and masaini, and hortatives are formed with the particle jaje.

Thus, I can only share some observations here that remain to be checked. First of all, looking at the examples with this marker, it seems that they only include requests and commands. Offers or invitations and suggestions are absent. However, this may be a coincidence, as there are also more requests among the unmarked imperatives than there are offers or suggestions. Second, in an elicitation session, the gestures Juana made when using the word forms with -ji were bigger and more encompassing, which suggests to me that more emphasis is involved. This is why I speak of an emphatic imperative. Third, in the same elicitation session, the form ¡pupuna! was consistently translated by her with Spanish ¡trae! ‘bring!’, and ¡pupunaji! with ¡traélo! ‘bring it!’. summary:
The passage describes two suppletive imperatives in the language: **nabi** ‘go!’ and **pana** ‘come!’, with nabi being much more frequent. Both can combine with verbs or demonstrative adverbs, and nabi also occurs with locative-marked nouns; their internal composition is uncertain, though possible analyses are proposed for each form.

It further shows that when these imperatives combine with a following verb, the verb often carries the prior motion associated motion marker, and pana can also take the prospective marker in older data. The dislocative marker occurs only with verbs used with nabi, matching its translocative meaning.

text: directive speech act!prohibitive|(negation!prohibitive|( There are several ways to form a negative imperative. First of all, the negative particlenegative particle|( kuina can be used together with an irrealis verb. In this case, the negative imperative is identical to a negative declarative clause in structure. Second, it is also possible to use the specific negative particles naka or masaini. The first of them is used to form prohibitives, i.e. commands and requests not to do something. It is possibly related to the negative particle in Baure, which is noka . As for masaini, this is composed of the apprehensional connective masa (see ) and the frustrative marker -ini (see ). María S. seems to use it in the same fashion as naka, i.e. in prohibitives, but data from other speakers suggests that it is rather an admonitive particle, i.e. it appears in warnings.negative particle|) ( ) to ( ) are examples of negative imperatives with kuina. As can be seen in ( ), the negative particle precedes the irrealis verb and a declarative sentence would have exactly the same structure.word order This example was elicited from María S. ¡patÿkemiu nijinepÿi! ¡kuina piyuabu!\\ pi-a-tÿkemiu ni-jinepÿi kuina pi-iyua-bu\\ 2sg-irr-be.quiet 1sg-daughter neg 2sg-cry.irr-dsc\\ ‘be quiet, my daughter, don’t cry anymore! ( ) comes from María C. Actually, I am not entirely sure whether this is really meant to be a negative imperative or rather a sentence with future reference (‘you won’t die!’). In any case, María C. tells what she said to her mother, when the latter was poisoned by a sorcerer. ¡kuina pipaka!\\ kuina pi-paka\\ neg 2sg-die.irr\\ ‘don’t die!’ The case is clearer in ( ). This is what the vulture says to the jaguar, when he is supposed to be punished for having let the fox escape. The vulture starts his utterance in Spanish (no being the Spanish negative particle), but continues in Paunaka. entonses echÿu sÿmÿ tikechu: “no no no no, ¡kuina pinikanÿ!”\\ entonses echÿu sÿmÿ ti-kechu no no no no kuina pi-nika-nÿ\\ thus dema vulture 3i-say no no no no neg 2sg-eat.irr-1sg\\ ‘so the vulture said: “no, no, no, no, don’t eat me!”’ In prohibitives, speakers can make use of naka.reality status|( This negative particle is delimited to imperative contexts (commands, requests), so that no ambiguity arises. All examples of prohibitives with naka were elicited. They can contain a realis verb. Thus it seems that the fact that two parameters trigger irrealis here, negation and imperative, is encoded by using the RS markingreality status that matches none of them.doubly irrealis construction When studying negation among Arawakan languages, identified five types of possible prohibitive constructions. They are given in . The distinguishing factors include how the negative expression differs from the one found in standard negation (column “expression of negation”) and how the rest of the prohibitive sentence differs from a positive imperative (column “prohibitive construction”). According to this classification, the Paunaka prohibitive with naka belongs to type IV: the negative particle is different from the one used in standard negation and the rest of the construction is different from the imperative. In his sample of 23 Arawakan languages, only Kinikinau and Nanti share this specific behaviour with Paunaka . Consider ( ), which comes from Juana. The prohibitive particle naka is followed by a realis verb. ¡naka piyu!\\ naka pi-iyu\\ prohib 2sg-cry\\ ‘don’t cry!’ In elicitation, Juana also produced some prohibitives with an irrealis verb like the one in ( ); however, the seemingly more spontaneous uses (e.g. the first translation she gave in elicitation) all included realis predicates. ¡naka piyua!\\ naka pi-iyua\\ prohib 2sg-cry.irr\\ ‘don’t cry!’ Although María S. rather uses masaini as a negative particle in prohibitives (see below), she confirms the use of naka. ( ) is an example of a prohibitive with naka elicited from her. ¡naka pekubu!\\ naka pi-ekubu\\ prohib 2sg-laugh\\ ‘don’t laugh!’ ( ) comes from Juana again. ¡naka pikupaiku ÿne! tisÿeimuyu\\ naka pi-kupaiku ÿne ti-sÿei-umu-yu\\ prohib 2sg-step.on water 3i-be.cold- -ints\\ ‘don’t step in the water, it is very cold!’ It is less clear which RS is required in clauses with masaini.admonitive|( All examples that follow were elicited, except for the last one, ( ), and they vary with regard to RS. For this reason it is analysed as an admonitive particle here. To start with, consider ( ) from María S. The admonitive particle precedes the realis verb here. ¡masaini pijikupu!\\ masaini pi-jikupu\\ adm 2sg-swallow\\ ‘don’t swallow it!’\\%or:‘be careful not to swallow it’?? ( ) also has a realis verb. It is not ripe yet’ She also uses an irrealis verb in ( ). This warning was first uttered in Spanish and then translated. It was directed to a child (as ( ) above,

This particle usually implies some motionmotion predicate and can be translated as ‘let’s go!’. The case being like this, it can occur on its own ( ) or it can combine with adverbs ( ) or verbs ( ). Interestingly, Miguel also combines it with motion verbs ( ). ( ) comes from Miguel’s story about the cowherd and the spirit. The spirit has just told the man, who desperately searches for his cows, that he has taken them. He offers the man to go and have a look at them: “¡jaje!” chikechuchÿji \\ jaje chi-kechu-chÿ-ji\\ hort 3-say-3-rprt\\ ‘“let’s go!” he said to him, it is said ( ) is what Juana’s grandmother said to her husband when she realised that there was a water spirit in the arroyo they tried to cross with their cows on their way back from Moxos. “¡jaje nauku anÿke!”\\ jaje nauku anÿke\\ hort there up\\ ‘“let’s go up there!”’ ( ) also comes from Juana, this example is from the creation story and a citation of God talking to María Eva after she has eaten the apple. “¡pana naka! ¡jaje bana jiriensu tÿpi pimÿuna!”\\ pana naka jaje bi-ana jiriensu tÿpi pi-mÿu-ina\\ come.imp here hort 1pl-make.irr linen obl 2sg-clothes-irr.nv\\ ‘“come here! Let’s go and make linen for your future clothes!”’ In telling about his days in school, Miguel used ( ) to tell me what other children said to him, when they invited him to join school. “¡jaje biyuna xhikuerayae!”\\ jaje bi-yuna xhikuera-yae\\ hort 1pl-go.irr school-loc\\ ‘“let’s go to school!”’ The hortative particle can take some morphology. It has been found with the iamitive, the additiveadditive marker and the emphatic marker -ja. One example with the iamitive is given below. It is already noon!’ hortative|) directive speech act|) This was the last example in this section. The chapter on simple clauses is almost completed by now. summary: The hortative is a directive form used to make commands, requests, or invitations to first-person plural, including the speaker, and it is formed with the particle **jaje**, often with the sense of “let’s go!”. This particle can stand alone or combine with adverbs and verbs, including motion verbs, and it may also take morphology such as the iamitive, additive, and emphatic markers.

text: interrogative clause|( While declarative clauses typically assert information, the main function of interrogative clauses is to request information . Two main types of interrogative clauses can be distinguished. Polar questions seek an affirmation or negationnegation of information already given in the question . They can be distinguished from declarative sentences by intonation in Paunaka. Content questions seek information about a participant in an event or some circumstances in the event. They build on a question word. Question words always precede the verb, i.e. they are placed in focus positionword order (see ). In this section, I first describe polar questions in and then turn to content questions in .
summary: Interrogative clauses primarily request information rather than assert it, and they are divided into polar questions and content questions. Polar questions ask for affirmation or negation of the information given and differ from declaratives by intonation in Paunaka, while content questions ask about a participant or circumstance in an event and use a question word that always precedes the verb in focus position.

text: polar question|( The only feature that distinguishes polar questions from declarative sentences is intonation.intonation|( In polar questions, pitch rises towards the end of the utterance, sometimes considerably, sometimes only slightly. To start with, consider ( ). The question was produced by Juana and directed to me. It was uttered with a very high pitch towards the end. Another question-answer pair is given in ( ). The question was asked by Miguel, when he helped Juana digging for loam for her clay pot in the vicinity of Santa Rita. The shell he asks for is used to pull up and smoothen the clay rolls, nauku ‘there’ refers to Juana’s house in Santa Cruz, where she lived at that time. In ( ) the affirmative particle accompanies the repeated verb in the answer. This example stems from Miguel’s narration about his time in school. It is a citation of a question of his teacher and the answer of one pupil. In an answer to a negative question,negation|( the negative particle occurs together with the predicate to confirm the negative alternative, i.e. Paunaka exhibits a polarity-based system . An example is ( ) from Juana who reproduced what her brother asked her when their other brother had passed away. In this case, it also seems to be possible to omit the verb and only use the negative particle, as in ( ) from elicitation with Juana. However, all examples I have stem from elicitation or imagined or remembered dialogues reported by a single speaker, I have not found a single example of a question – answer pair including a negative question that comes from natural conversation between two Paunaka speakers. Thus it remains to be checked whether they employ the same patterns in real conversation. negation|) A negative question can be answered positively by repeating the predicate, which usually has realis RS in the answer (if irrealis is not demanded by another factor, e.g. future time reference). This is the case in ( ), which is a little imagined conversation by Juana and was triggered by me asking questions about lurking (in trying to make sense of the dislocative marker). This made Juana think about hunting and catching animals. answer to question|) polar question|)
summary: The passage says that the only formal feature distinguishing polar questions from declarative sentences is intonation: in polar questions, pitch rises toward the end of the utterance. It also describes Paunaka question-answer patterns, where affirmative responses may repeat the verb with an affirmative particle, and negative questions are answered with the negative particle plus the predicate to confirm the negative option. The author notes that examples of negative question-answer pairs come only from elicitation or remembered/imagined dialogue, so it remains unclear whether the same patterns occur in natural conversation.

text: content question|( Content questions “receive answers that provide the kind of information specified by the interrogative word” .answer to question Content questions build on question wordsquestion word|( in Paunaka, which are given in . The question words are always placed in the first position, i.e. they occupy the position of the sentence that is associated with emphasis. Question words often, but not always, combine with focus expressions. This may be a special form of the transitive verb including a third person markerperson marking following the verb stem, a relative clauserelative relation or a deranked verb, see , and for more information about these constructions. The different question words have different possibilities of combining with one or the other of them. In addition, “plain” finite verbsfinite verb can also be used in questions. Sometimes, question words take -chÿ, -chÿu or -chu. It is not entirely clear to me, what this form is, and whether it is always the same marker only pronounced differently. As for -chÿ, it is found on chija and (u)kajane. This might be the third person marker.person marking The form -chÿu, which may be a cliticisedclitic form of the demonstrativenominal demonstrative echÿu, occurs on chija, juchubu and (chi)kuyena, -chu is only found on juchubu. I gloss -chÿ as ‘3’, i.e. as third person marker on (u)kajane, every other occurrence of -chÿ, -chÿu or -chu is glossed as ‘demb?’, regardless of its actual pronunciation. question word|) The remainder of this section is structured as follows: is about questions for subject and object participants as well as actions, deals with questions about locations and points in time. In , questions for reason and manner are presented, and is about requesting quantities. Finally, describes some very general questions based on the uncertainty marker.
summary: In Paunaka content questions, the question word must appear first in the sentence, in the position associated with emphasis, and it often combines with focus expressions or with constructions such as special verb forms, relative clauses, or deranked verbs. Different question words have different combinatory possibilities, and they may also take forms like -chÿ, -chÿu, or -chu, whose exact function is not fully clear. The section then outlines questions about subjects, objects, actions, location, time, reason, manner, quantity, and general uncertainty-based questions.

text: The question word question word|( chija ‘what, who’ is used to form different kinds of questions for a referent: it can be used to request for human and non-human entities, animate and non-animate alike. It can be combined with a verbal or non-verbal predicatenon-verbal predication and the requested participant can be a subject or an object of a verbal clause, one of the constituents of an existentialexistential clause or equative clauseequative/proper inclusion clause or an action. The question word itself could possibly derive from the noun -ija ‘name’ with a third person possessor, but in any case it is totally grammaticalisedgrammaticalisation and may thus be called an interrogative pronoun. This becomes apparent in questions about the name of somebody, in which the word form chija doubles, as in ( ), which was produced by María C. to obtain some information about my family. ¿chija chija penu?\\ chija chi-ija pi-enu\\ what 3-name 2sg-mother\\ ‘what is your mother’s name?’ Sometimes, -chÿu or -chÿ is attached to chija, which could be a cliticised nominal demonstrative (echÿu). Like the question word itself, attachment of -chÿu seems to be relatively grammaticalised,grammaticalisation because a free demonstrative can co-occur, as in ( ), which represents Juana’s reaction as reported by herself, when she was offered frogs to eat. ¿chijachÿu echÿu?\\ chija-chÿu echÿu\\ what-demb? demb\\ ‘what is this?’ question word|) When asking for an action, speakers make use of the verb -chabu ‘do’, which almost exclusively occurs in questions. The question in ( ) belongs to the repertoire of exchange of pleasantries, when meeting each other, like ( ) and ( ) above. It was produced by Isidro when meeting Swintha. ¿chija pichabu?\\ chija pi-chabu\\ what 2sg-do\\ ‘what are you doing?’ The verb can also be used to request what others are doing as in ( ), in which María S. asks about her brother. ¿chija chichabu Miyel?\\ chija chi-chabu Miyel\\ what 3-do Miguel\\ ‘what is Miguel doing?’ Apart from -chabu ‘do’, chija is not often combined with a plain finite verb, but a few examples occurred nonetheless. Two are given here. ( ) is a question the jaguar asks the fox, when he finds him eating cheese in the story told by María S. “¿chija piniku?”\\ chija pi-niku\\ what 2sg-eat\\ ‘“what are you eating?“’ In ( ), the uncertainty marker on the question word tells us that we are dealing with a rhetorical question, that the one who asks does not expect the addressee to know the answer. Juana reports here what she asked her brother, when he told her that a family member had died, but could not say whom it was, because the message he received to tell him about the death was not clear. ¿chijakena tepaku?\\ chija-kena ti-paku\\ what-uncert 3i-die\\ ‘who may have died?’ If the verb is transitive, a third person markerperson marking can follow the verb stem, a construction reserved to express argument focus. This is the case in the following questions. ( ) was elicited from María S. ¿chija tikurabajikuchÿ nÿnikÿiki?\\ chija ti-kurabajiku-chÿ nÿ-nikÿiki\\ what 3i-break-3 1sg-pot\\ ‘who broke my pot?’ ( ) comes from Juana telling the story about how the silk floss tree obtained its big belly-like trunk: it swallowed all of Jesus’ corn, who asks for the fate of this supply of corn here. “¿chija tumuchÿ?”\\ chija ti-umu-chÿ\\ what 3i-take-3\\ ‘“who took it?”’ Questions for a possessor possessor|( are a subtype of this kind of questions, since they all build on a verb.attributive prefix|( The verb is composed of the attributive prefix ku- (see ) and either -peu ‘animal’, as in ( ), or -yae ‘grn’, as in ( ) and usually takes the third person markerperson marking -chÿ. The examples were elicited from María S. Both -peu and -yae also play a role in possession marking of non-possessable nouns (see ). ¿chija tikupeuchÿ ÿba?\\ chija ti-kupeu-chÿ ÿba\\ what 3i-have.animal-3 pig\\ ‘whose pig is this?’ ¿chijakena tikuyaechÿkenatu San Jorge?\\ chija-kena ti-kuyae-chÿ-kena-tu San Jorge \\ what-uncert 3i-own-3-uncert-iam San Jorge \\ ‘who may be the owner of (the estate) San Jorge now?’ The usage of an attributive verb based on either -peu or -yae can be considered the main strategy of asking for a possessor, but alternatively, any other noun can also be added to the attributive prefix to derivederivation a verb of possession, as in ( ), which was also elicited from María S. ¿chijakena tikumÿubanechÿ eka mÿuji?\\ chija-kena ti-kumÿu-bane-chÿ eka mÿu-ji\\ what-uncert 3i-have.garment-rem-3 dema clothes- .mass\\ ‘whose garment may this have been before?’ possessor|) attributive prefix|) Finally, chija often combines with a relative clause,relative relation especially when -kena is attached. In many relative clauses, the verb is totally unmarked, but they can be recognised by being introduced with a demonstrative (see ). Combination of chija with a relative clause can be considered a subtype of cleftcleft|( construction (see ) and reflects the structure of the corresponding question in Spanish: ¿qué/quién será que...? ‘what/who could it be that...?’. In ( ), Juana starts telling the story about the fox and the jaguarundi, but interrupts herself, because she does not remember which animal the fox met. i chitupukuku echÿu ¿chijachÿukena echÿu chitupuku?\\ i chi-tupuku-uku echÿu chija-chÿu-kena echÿu chi-tupuku\\ and 3-meet-add demb what-demb?-uncert demb 3-meet\\ ‘and he also met the, what was it that he met?’ ( ) was elicited from María S. The relative clause builds on a non-verbal predicate borrowed from Spanish. ¿chijakena eka pasau chitÿpi? kuina kapunuinabu \\ chija-kena eka pasau chi-tÿpi kuina kapunu-ina-bu\\ what-uncert dema pass 3-obl neg come-irr.nv-dsc\\ ‘what may have happened to him that he doesn’t come anymore?’ ( ) was elicited from Juana. Actually, she was asked to translate “why are the cows afraid?”, but she formed the question differently. tipikujane eka bakajane, ¿chijakena eka cheikukuikujane?\\ ti-piku-jane eka baka-jane chija-kena eka chÿ-eikukuiku-jane\\ 3i-be.afraid-distr dema cow-distr what-uncert dema 3-chase-distr\\ ‘the cows are afraid, what may it be that chases them?’ Occasionally, in questions with a relative clause,relative relation the Spanish relativiser ke (Span. que) shows up instead of a demonstrative, as in ( ). summary: The passage describes how the interrogative word *chija* ‘what, who’ is used broadly to ask about human and non-human referents, subjects, objects, existential or equative clause constituents, actions, and possessors. It is highly grammaticalized and can combine with markers such as *-chÿu* or *-kena*; questions about actions often use the verb *-chabu* ‘do’, while possession questions are formed with attributive verbs based on *-peu*, *-yae*, or other nouns. It also often appears with relative clauses, functioning like a cleft construction to ask “what/who is it that…?”.

text: Questions for location and points in time are formed with the question wordquestion word|( juchubu. The composition of the word is quite opaque, it may be decomposed into j-u-chu-bu, with an existential or locative root -u, also found in the defective verb -ubu ‘be, live’, the thematic suffix -chu and the middle marker -bu, so it possibly goes back to a verb denoting existence or location at a place. It may also be related to the uncertain future particle uchu (see ). As for the first part j-, this prefix is also found on the mirative particle jimu ‘you see, you know, right?’ (see Footnote in ), but it is not productive in any way. The middle markermiddle voice -bu in juchubu is dropped in a few examples and sometimes -chÿu or -chu is attached to the question word. Like chija juchubu can also be used as an indefinite pronoun, see . In questions for location, the question word juchubu is usually combined with the copula kaku or the defective verb -ubu ‘be, live’. The first two examples are formed with the non-verbal existential copula kaku.question word|) ( ) was produced by Miguel in an elicitation session, in which he and Alejo had two identical sets of wooden toys. The arrangement of toys Alejo saw was given and Miguel was supposed to arrange his set of wooden toys in an identical way by asking questions. Finally, ( ) also has -chÿu on the question word but is combined with a finite verb. The example comes from the recordings made by Riester and reflects the hopelessness of Juan Ch. who knows he is treated badly by his patrón, but sees no alternative to staying with him nonetheless. ¿juchubuchÿukena biyuna?\\ juchubu-chÿu-kena bi-yuna\\ where-demb?-uncert 1pl-go.irr\\ ‘where could we go?’ Requesting a location can be considered the primary function of juchubu, but it may also be used to ask for a point in time. In the latter case, juchubu is usually combined with a word with temporal meaning. In ( ), this is the word tijai ‘day’. In this case, the shorter form juchu is used, which lacks the middle marker. This form occurs infrequently in the corpus without any notable functional or semantic difference to juchubu. The question was asked by María C. in seeking information about which day the workshop on Paunaka would be held. ¿juchu tijai?\\ juchu tijai\\ where day\\ ‘what day?’ In ( ), juchubu combines with uchu, a particle denoting an uncertain and in most cases remote future (see ). Juana asked this question, when she was telling me about Cotoca and felt like going there together with me. ¿juchubukena uchukena biyuna nauku?\\ juchubu-kena uchu-kena bi-yuna nauku\\ where-uncert uncert.fut-uncert 1pl-go.irr there\\ ‘when may we go there?’ ( ) was produced by Juana in an elicitation session in an imagined beginning of a conversation. Note that the adverb uchuine ‘just now', which denotes a point in time some time ago on the same day, has a continuous marker attached here and a third person marker which follows the stem and thus resembles a verb. I do not know why this is the case. naka, ¿juchubu chuineneikuchÿ pibÿsÿu?\\ naka juchubu uchuine-neiku-chÿ pi-bÿsÿu\\ here where just.now-cont-3 2sg-come\\ ‘how much time has passed since you came here?’ -5.8ptFinally, sometimes there is no temporal expression in combination with juchubu; usually, this is the case when it is clear enough from the context or due to combination with the verb that a point in time is requested instead of a location. This is the case in the last example in this section, which comes from elicitation with Miguel and has the structure of a cleft construction. ¿juchubukena echÿu pibÿsÿupupunuka?\\ juchubu-kena echÿu pi-bÿsÿu-pupunuka\\ where-uncert demb 2sg-come-reg.irr\\ ‘when is it that you come back?’
summary: The question word **juchubu** is used primarily to ask about **locations** and **points in time**, though its internal composition is opaque and may reflect an old verb of existence or location. In location questions it is often combined with the copula **kaku** or the verb **-ubu** ‘be, live,’ while in temporal questions it usually co-occurs with a temporal word, but can also appear alone when context makes the time interpretation clear. It can also function as an indefinite pronoun, and its middle marker **-bu** is sometimes omitted or replaced by other suffixes.

text: Questions for manner and reason are formed with (chi)kuyena.question word|( Reason may be an extension of manner, as the overlap resembles the overlap between the instrumental and causalinstrument/cause function of the preposition -keuchi (see ). The question word derives from the manner verb -kuye ‘be like this’,demonstrative verb which always takes the third person marker chi- in my corpus, even though it is a stative verb by position of irrealis marking (i.e. its irrealis form is chakuye – see also –, but this one does not occur in questions). When used as a question word, -na is added to chikuye yielding chikuyena. It is not clear what kind of suffix this is; it could be the general classifier -na, which we also find with some adjectives (see ) or – less probably given the verbal origin – the non-verbal irrealis marker -ina. The third person marker is sometimes dropped, thus we also find kuyena in questions. The question word most often combines with a verb that is introduced by the demonstrative eka,nominal demonstrative a construction that we also sometimes find in complementationcomplement relation (see ). The verb may be finitefinite verb or deranked.deranked verb Sometimes, however, no demonstrative is included. question word|) I will start with some examples that show the use of the question word in requesting manner and then turn to some examples which illustrate its use in questions for reason. ( ) was elicited from María S. It has a deranked verb which is not introduced by a demonstrative. ¿kuyena panaiuchi yumaji?\\ kuyena pi-ana-i-u-chi yumaji\\ how 2sg-make-subord-real-3 hammock\\ ‘how do you make the hammock?’ A deranked verb combined with a demonstrative is found in ( ) from Juana telling the story about the fox and the jaguar. This is a question the hungry jaguar asks the fox when he finds him eating cheese. “¿chikuyena eka pitiuchi eka?” \\ chikuyena eka pi-it-i-u-chi eka\\ how dema 2sg-master-subord-real-3 dema\\ ‘“how did you get this?”’ ( ) has a finite verb introduced with eka. The sentence produced by Miguel, when he helped Juana dig for loam at a place close to Santa Rita. The remote marker -bane on the verb indicates that he knows that she has known this place long before. ¿chikuyena eka pitupubanechÿ eka muteji? \\ chikuyena eka pi-tupu-bane-chÿ eka muteji\\ how dema 2sg-find-rem-3 dema loam\\ ‘how did you once find the loam?’ ( ) could theoretically also be analysed as a request for manner, but it is a rhetorical question in this case, so no answer is expected. In this example, Juana uses finite verbs that are not introduced by eka. She told me about a place in the woods, where they wash in a big hollow rock. Apparently, the place is watched over by a spirit, because the clothes are often blown away and disappear in the woods, which are difficult to access with all the plants growing there. kimenu nauku ¿kuyena biyuna bisemaika bimÿu nauku?\\ kimenu nauku kuyena bi-yuna bi-semaika bi-mÿu nauku?\\ woods there how 1pl-go.irr 1pl-search.irr 1pl-clothes there\\ ‘there are the woods, how could we go and look for our clothes there?’ The next example clearly does not request manner, because it is about the non-realisation of an action. Here, -chÿ is attached to the question word; however, this is less frequent with (chi)kuyena than with chija or juchubu, see and above. Like in ( ) above, a finite verb is used, this time in combination with the demonstrative. Her other daughter was finally deported and had to fly back to Bolivia. ¿chikuyenachÿ eka kuina piyuna?\\ chikuyena-chÿu eka kuina pi-yuna\\ how-demb? dema neg 2sg-go.irr\\ ‘how could you NOT go?’\: ‘why didn’t you go?’ ( ) allows a manner and reason reading. It was produced by Clara and refers to Swintha’s dreadlocks. ¿kuyenakena eka chimukiji eka?\\ kuyena-kena eka chi-muki-ji eka\\ how-uncert dema 3-hair-col dema\\ ‘how can her hair be like this?’\: ‘why is her hair like this?’ The last two examples in this section rather request reason than manner and both make use of deranked verbs. This is what the jaguar asks the vulture, when he discovers that the vulture, who was supposed to watch over the fox, let him escape. “¿chikuyena eka pikujikiuchi eka kupisaÿrÿ?”\\ chikuyena eka pi-kujik-i-u-chi eka kupisaÿrÿ\\ how dema 2sg-let.go-subord-real-3 dema fox\\ ‘“why did you let the fox go?”’ Finally, ( ) was elicited from Miguel to be able to ask him questions about the process of baking rice bread that we had filmed. ¿chikuyena eka penukiuchÿ echÿu merÿpune naka latakÿye?\\ chikuyena eka pi-nuk-i-u-chÿ echÿu merÿ-pune naka lata-kÿ-yae\\ how dema 2sg-put-subord-real-3 demb plantain-leave here metal.sheet- -loc\\ ‘why do you put plantain leaves on the baking tray?’
summary:
Questions for manner and reason are formed with the question word **(chi)kuyena**, which comes from the manner verb **-kuye** ‘be like this’ plus **-na**; the third-person marker **chi-** is sometimes dropped, giving **kuyena**. The word most often appears with a verb introduced by the demonstrative **eka**, though the verb may be finite or deranked, and sometimes no demonstrative is present.

The examples show that **(chi)kuyena** can ask about manner, but it also frequently has a reason interpretation, especially in contexts where no answer is expected or where the question concerns why something did or did not happen. Some clauses allow both readings, while others clearly ask for reason rather than manner.

text: Questions for quantities build on the question wordquestion word|( kajane ‘how many’. It is composed of a root ka- and the distributive marker -jane. As for ka-, this is possibly the same root we find in the copula kaku and the non-verbal motion predicate kapunu ‘come’. This root might be related to the demonstrative eka (see ). In some cases, -chÿ is added to the question word. Unlike the similar sequence added to other question words, this is never pronounced -chÿu, so that there is no reason to believe that it could be a demonstrative. Consequently -chÿ is glossed as a third person marker here.person marking Sometimes u- is placed before the question word and in that case, the marker -chÿ always follows, yielding ukajanechÿ. question word|) There are not many examples in the corpus which stem from one of the speakers (there are some more examples that were produced by the researchers though). All but one refer to quantities of countable things. The only example in which the quantity of a solid object is requested is ( ), which was elicited from Miguel, when Swintha wanted to ask him how many baking trays of rice bread he had baked. ¿kajane latajane?\\ kajane lata-jane\\ how.many metal.sheet-distr\\ ‘how many baking trays?’ The question word is used to request age, as in ( ), which was elicited from Isidro. ¿kajane anyu pitÿpi?\\ kajane anyo pi-tÿpi\\ how.many year 2sg-obl\\ ‘how old are you?’ The same question was translated by María S. using ukajanechÿ, see ( ). It is not clear whether there is any difference to ( ). ¿ukajanechÿtu anyo pitÿpi?\\ ukajane-chÿ-tu anyo pi-tÿpi?\\ how.many-3-iam year 2sg-obl\\ ‘how old are you?’ ( ) comes from the story about the fox and the jaguarundi. The fox asks how many different jumps the jaguarundi knows and the latter answers him that he knows only one, while the fox brags about knowing twenty-five. Nonetheless, it is this one jump that saves the jaguarundi later; he escapes on a tree, while the fox is killed by dogs. “¿kajane eka piyae lanse?” tikechuchÿji\\ kajane eka pi-yae lanse ti-kechu-chÿ-ji\\ how.many dema 2sg-grn jump 3i-say-3-rprt\\ ‘“how many jumps do you know?” he said to him, it is said’ The one example in which kajane rather refers to a non-countable noun is given in ( ). Although the semantics of the distributive marker rather seems to impede requesting quantity of a mass noun, this example suggests that it is possible. summary:
Questions of quantity are formed with **kajane** ‘how many,’ which consists of the root **ka-** and the distributive suffix **-jane**. The particle **-chÿ** can also be added and is analyzed here as a third person marker; when **u-** is prefixed, the form becomes **ukajanechÿ**.

The corpus examples mostly ask about quantities of countable objects, but the word is also used for age and, in one case, for the quantity of money, showing a limited semantic extension to mass nouns.

summary: The marker **kena** is not a true question word, but it can form very general content questions when placed in focus position. It normally follows an NP or sometimes a relative clause, not a verb, and it indicates uncertainty about a referent, with meanings like “what about X?” depending on context. It can be used to ask about identity, condition, health, activity, or similar information.

text: complex sentence|( Complex sentences contain more than one predication. They typically consist of two (or more) clauses and are classically divided into two different main types: one type includes coordination and the other one subordination. Prototypically, coordinated clauses are semantically independent from each other, and this is reflected by the absence of dependency marking of any sort. Subordinate clauses, on the other hand, are semantically dependent and marked for this dependency. Unfortunately, however, there is not always a clear correlation between semantic dependency and overt marking of this dependency. The boundaries between coordination and subordination are far from clear-cut, and there is rather a continuum which reaches from clauses that are semantically and syntactically independent on one end to semantically and syntactically dependent clauses on the other end and possibly a large number of clauses that fall inbetween these two poles . It is thus wise to think about semantic and syntactic dependency independently. In addition to complex sentences consisting of two (or more) clauses that may be semantically and syntactically more or less dependent on each other, there is another kind of complex clause formation in which one predication is neatly integrated into another one so that the result is a single clause with multiple verbs. An indication of this monoclausality is that only one possibility to negatenegation the whole clause exists, with the negative particle having scope over both predicates ( in following ). -1.5ptThe case being complex like this, this chapter draws on the functional-semantic approach by with regard to subordination.subordination|( According to this approach a subordinate clause lacks assertiveness and subordination is defined as “a situation of functional asymmetry whereby the profile of one of two linked SoAs is overriden by that of the other” . Clause combinations in which one clause lacks assertiveness are thus considered cases of subordination. Clause combinations in which both events are asserted are taken as cases of coordination. This is illustrated by ( ) and ( ). The first one is a conditional clause, thus the realisation of the consequence clause is marked as dependent on the realisation of the antecedent – or rather non-realisation in this case because the predicate is negated. In any case, the consequent clause is non-asserted due to its dependence on the antecedent. The example comes from Juan Ch. speaking about the patrón, who was expected to arrive the next day in order to distribute some goods. In Paunaka’s subordinate clause formation, we can observe all of these strategies to a certain degree.subordination|( As for verbal strategies, the verb in the subordinate clause is totally finite,finite verb|( in the sense that all categories obligatorily expressed on a main clause predicate, i.e. personperson marking and RS,reality status|( are expressed in the same way on the subordinate predicate and there is no dependency marker. This does not preclude that the RS of the subordinate predicate is in some cases determined by the main clause predicatereality status|) or that certain TAME markers on the subordinate predicate provide clues for the interpretation about the specific semantic connection to the main clause. A subordinate clause with a finite verb not marked for dependency, i.e. a verb that is “balanced” to use the terminology of , can be juxtaposed to a main clause without any specific linking device. This is regarded as asyndetic juxtaposition.syndesis/asyndesis ( ) provides an example of an asyndetically juxtaposed relative clause. The verb of the main clause is tikijaneyu ‘they are many’ and its subject is chipeunube baka ‘their cows’. This subject is modified by tipabenteikunube ‘they sell (them)’. That the second verb is connected to the preceding clause is signalled by the intonation, but the exact relationship to it has to be deduced from the context. It is not shown on the verb nor anywhere else in the clause, i.e. an independent clause with the meaning ‘they sell (them)’ would have exactly the same structure. The sentence comes from Juana speaking about her grandparent’s journey to Moxos to buy cows. tikijaneyu chipeunube baka tipabenteikunube\\ ti-kijane-yu chi-peu-nube baka ti-pabenteiku-nube\\ 3i-be.many-ints 3-animal-pl cow 3i-sell-pl\\ ‘there are a whole lot of cows that they sell’ If there is a linker but no sign of dependency on the subordinate verb itself, I take it as a case of syndetic juxtaposition, as in ( ) above, where kue ‘if, when’ signals that we are dealing with a conditional sentence or one including temporal overlap. Linkers are usually independent words that introduce the subordinate clause. In adverbial clauses,adverbial relation we find connectives,connective in relative clauses,relative relation there are nominal demonstratives,nominal demonstrative and in complement clausescomplement relation we marginally find demonstratives,nominal demonstrativecomplementiser too. Regarding integrating strategies, these are found in complementation,complement relation such as in ( ), and also for verbal expressions of goals of motion predicates,motion predicate i.e. constructions expressing purpose of motion. The subordinate verbs in complementation are usually completely unmarked for dependency, in the expression of purpose of motion, we find two different construction types, one in which there is no sign of dependency either (serial verb construction) and one in which dependency is markeddependency marking on the purpose verb (motion-cum-purpose construction). ( ) comes from Clara asking María C. about her knowledge in Napeka. ¿pichuna pichujiku napeka?\\ pi-chuna pi-chujiku napeka\\ 2sg-be.capable 2sg-speak Napeka\\ ‘do you speak Napeka?’ (lit.: ‘are you capable to speak Napeka?’) finite verb|) Distinctly nominal strategies are rare in Paunaka, but see for some examples including nominalised verbs that have shown up in the corpus. More importantly, there is one form of the verb that I call “deranked”deranked verb|( throughout this grammar, using the terminology by , which has partly verbal and partly nominal characteristics. It seems that at least in some constructions such a deranked verb is chosen because a (more) nominal word is demanded. Regarding the partly nominal behaviour of deranked verbs, this is bound to these verbs not expressing the category of person in exactly the same way as main clause predicates do, but rather like (internal) possessorspossessor of inalienable nouns. summary: The passage explains that complex sentences may involve coordination or subordination, but the distinction is not always clear because semantic and syntactic dependency do not consistently match, so dependency should be treated independently of overt marking. It also notes a third type of complex clause formation in which one predication is integrated into another, yielding a single clause with multiple verbs, and it describes Paunaka subordinate clauses as often using finite, dependency-unmarked verbs, linkers, or other constructions to signal subordination.

summary: In Paunaka, the use of a deranked verb is the clearest sign of embedding: the clause with the deranked verb is dependent and usually cannot stand alone. The chapter then organizes complex clauses by functional-semantic type—coordination, adverbial, complement, and relative relations—and also discusses a focus construction with a deranked verb, after first presenting the construction types used throughout the chapter.

section: Construction types in clause combining and complex clause formation
text: When considering the combination of clauses and predicates, five general features turn out to be important in Paunaka: integration, syndesis,syndesis/asyndesis dependency marking, deranking,deranked verb and predetermination of the RS.reality status These features correspond to five general questions given in . Considering the overt encoding of relations only, i.e. the features syndesis, dependency marking and deranking, it turns out that there are three different general construction types and one minor one in clause combining and complex clause formation. I call them asyndetic juxtaposition, syndetic juxtaposition, dependency marking and deranking.deranked verbsyndesis/asyndesis These four types cross-cut the different functional categories of complex sentences in Paunaka, which are coordination, adverbial relations,adverbial relation complement relations,complement relation and relative relations.relative relation This means that there is usually no one-to-one correspondence between construction type and functional type of the complex sentence, but it also not the case that that each of the functional types is found with all construction types. In , the construction types are ordered from least overt marking of dependency to most overt marking of dependency (first column). Thus the construction type that includes no overt morphosyntactic marking of coordination or subordination, i.e. asyndetic juxtaposition, is positioned on top of the table. Syndetic juxtaposition occupies a middle position. In this construction type, a connective specifies the kind of relation between the two clauses.syndesis/asyndesis This is followed by dependency marking, which applies to only one specific construction. The dependent verb is non-controversially verbal. This is different in deranking. The deranked verb is partly verbal and partly nominal, which eases its embedding into the clause. Since deranking predominantly occurs in subordination contexts, we can consider it a sign of dependency marking. It is thus found at the bottom of the table. All three main construction types are found in clause combining as well as in complex monoclausal constructions, and the fourth one (dependency marking) is only found in one complex monoclausal construction. I provide more detailed descriptions for each construction type below. Having identified the different construction types, it is still necessary to check for degree of integration and predetermination of RS of each construction. summary:
The passage identifies five important features in Paunaka clause combining: integration, syndesis, dependency marking, deranking, and predetermination of reality status. Focusing on overt encoding, it distinguishes four construction types—asyndetic juxtaposition, syndetic juxtaposition, dependency marking, and deranking—which cross-cut the functional categories of coordination, adverbial, complement, and relative relations rather than mapping neatly onto them.

These construction types are ordered from least to most overt marking of dependency, with asyndetic juxtaposition at one end and deranking at the other. Deranking is characterized by a verb that is partly verbal and partly nominal, making embedding easier and functioning as a sign of dependency, while dependency marking is restricted to one specific complex monoclausal construction.

text: syndesis/asyndesis|( juxtaposition|( The linking of two clauses can be totally unmarked, i.e. there is neither a connective word of any kind nor does one of the predicates have a special form or carry a marker with a peculiar linking function. This is not to say that there is absolutely no means to express the relation between the clauses, on the contrary, TAME markerstenseaspectmodalityevidentiality on the predicates often provide the clue as to how to analyse the relation between the clauses. It is just that these markers are not specified for clause linking, they can also occur when no linking is involved. Asyndetic juxtaposition is frequently found in coordination of semantically independent clauses, called “parataxis” by , but also in subordination, where we recognise that one clause is pragmatically subordinate to the other one without this being marked overtly . This is the case with most complementcomplement relation and headedhead relative clausesrelative relation as well as some adverbial clauses.adverbial relation As for integration of the two predications into a single clause, this is different for each relation and construction as shown by inspired from the diagram given by . It can be claimed that all coordinatedcoordination clauses and all headedhead relative clausesrelative relation that are asyndetically juxtaposed to another clause have a relatively high degree of independence. Nonetheless, these clauses are not totally independent or separate, because they occur in a single intonation unit together with the clause they are combined with. On the other hand, in complementationcomplement relation as well as in expressions of purpose of motion the subordinate clause lacks independent negatability,negation a sign that it is neatly integrated into the main clause (and thus perhaps not a “clause” at all). Other types of asyndetically juxtaposed adverbial clausesadverbial relation are closer to the biclausal end of the continuum than to the monoclausal one, but they are not as independent as coordinatedcoordination and headed relative clauses.relative relation This is bound to the fact that the RSreality status of the subordinate predicatesubordination is sometimes determined in some way by the main clause predicate. Irrealis RSirrealis is necessarily found in adverbial clausesadverbial relation of the purpose (except for purpose of motion), apprehensional and counterfactualcounterfactuality conditional types. Irrealis RS is also found in complement clausescomplement relation of desiderative and manipulative predicates.manipulative verbdesiderative verb The RSreality status|( of the subordinate predicate must match the one of the matrix predicate in complement clauses of knowledge and perception predicates. In purpose-of-motion expressions, RS of the purpose predicate has to be either irrealis or identical to the motion verb.reality status|)motion predicate ( ) provides an example of two clauses that are coordinated by asyndetic juxtaposition. There is no sign of connection between the clauses, but the reportive markerevidentiality -ji that occurs twice gives a hint in this case that we are probably dealing with two clauses, since it usually occurs only once per clause (but may also occur twice in one clause, so that this is indeed only a hint and no reliable evidence). The example comes from Juana’s account about her criminal in-law. He hid away in the forest, but came home at night to eat and sleep until he was arrested one night. bueno, tibÿkuputuji tinikuji\\ bueno ti-bÿkupu-tu-ji ti-niku-ji\\ well 3i-enter-iam-rprt 3i-eat-rprt\\ ‘well, he came in and ate, it is said’ For contrast with the coordinated clauses in ( ) above, consider ( ) below, which encodes a subordinate relation, a complement clause whose predicate tinika is also completely unmarked for linkage to the matrix predicate, but has to occur with irrealis RS. The example was elicited from María S. and refers to her coati, which was chasing a butterfly. tisachu tinika churupepe\\ ti-sachu ti-nika churupepe\\ 3i-want 3i-eat.irr butterfly\\ ‘it wants to eat the butterfly’ There is little ambiguity about how to analyse the relations in the constructions that show a high degree of integration like complement clausescomplement relation and serial verb constructions.serial verb construction In coordination and in most expressions of adverbial relations,adverbial relation however, one clause is attached to another one at a higher level, the sentence. If the kind of relation between both clauses is not overtly marked by a connective, it is sometimes hard to determine whether a speaker wants to present both events as being asserted, i.e. coordinated, or one of the events as non-asserted and pre-supposed, i.e. in an adverbial relation to the other one. It may sometimes even be the case that a clause could alternatively be analysed as a coordinated, adverbial or relative clause. This is the case in ( ).
