summary:
In Paunaka, the suffix **-i** marks active verbs as subordinate, producing **deranked verbs** that occur in adverbial clauses, some complement clauses, relative clauses, and focus constructions. These forms are partly verbal and partly nominal: they keep the same reality-status marking as finite verbs, but they behave like nouns in person marking, using possessive-style markers and always taking **chÿ-** for third-person indexing rather than **ti-**.

The passage argues that deranked verbs occupy a middle position on a scale of clause integration: they are fully integrated in focus and complementation, but function more like modifiers in relative and adverbial clauses. The subordinate marker follows the verb stem and precedes the reality-status marker, even breaking up stem sequences, and deranked verbs are often translated with English gerunds or, in some cases, with nouns.

Coordinated clauses are asserted rather than subordinate, and they may be linked either by simple juxtaposition or by connectives, many of which are borrowed from Spanish; clause-internal coordination is distinguished from discourse connection when a connective links a clause that forms its own intonation unit.

It also notes that verbs in coordinated clauses are not deranked to mark dependency, and that the reality status of the two clauses is usually independent, except that an irrealis first clause expressing future reference cannot be followed by a realis clause expressing consequence or temporal succession. The section then announces a division into asyndetic coordination and several types of syndetic coordination: sequential, conjunctive, disjunctive, adversative, and consecutive.

By contrast, clauses separated by comma intonation typically represent conceptually distinct aspects of an action, event, or scene. The conjoined clauses most often describe sequential actions”. As for the notion of “single event”, this is hard to prove, because whether something is perceived as a single event or as multiple connected events is connected to cognitive processes, which I do not have access to. For the time being, I do not make any distinctions between single and multiple events. What we do find in coordination of clauses in Paunaka is that one clause sets the stage for another one by mentioning a participant. Both of these clauses typically have the same RS.reality status They usually share at least one participant and often but not always describe sequential actions. summary:
The passage argues that Paunaka allows asyndetic coordination, where clauses or NPs are simply juxtaposed within one intonation unit without an overt morphosyntactic linker. In coordinated clauses, one clause often sets the stage for the next by introducing a participant; the clauses usually share at least one participant, have the same reality status, and often describe sequential actions, though some examples show simultaneous or semantically linked actions.

The author notes that these constructions resemble serial verb constructions because the verbs are adjacent and share participants and status, but still prefers the label asyndetic coordination. This preference is maintained despite the difficulty of proving whether the clauses express a single event or multiple connected events.

summary: The passage argues that the examples are better analyzed as asyndetic coordination than as serial verb constructions, since serial verbs should be monoclausal and allow negation with scope over both predicates, which is not clearly shown here. It also notes that connectives are preferred when there is a larger time lapse between events, while minimal time lapse tends to favor asyndetic coordination, though neither pattern is obligatory. Finally, it shows that negation in Paunaka often applies only to one of two juxtaposed clauses, with repeated negators and special intonation sometimes functioning as bridging constructions rather than full tail-head linkage.

text: connective|( sequential|( The connective te is inserted between two clauses to express that the events happen in temporal succession, in a sequence. The events of both clauses are always semantically related. They belong to an overarching discourse topic. This means that te is usually not chosen when the topic changes. Juana makes extensive use of this connective, while Miguel uses it only rarely. In ( ) the general discourse topic is the rest of Juana’s grandparents on their journey back from Moxos, where they had bought cows. The sentence describes two things the grandparents did when they rested. The choice of the connective te not only signals that both actions belong together, but also that they happened in a certain sequence: first the cows were brought to the enclosure and locked in and only then the grandparents cooked. Irrealis RS in this sentence is due to this utterance reflecting a non-specific repeated (“habitual”) event, since the journey took several days, so several rests were necessary. All other clauses surrounding this example in the original text also have irrealis RS. chiratanÿkanube te tiyÿtikapunube\\ chi-ratanÿka-nube te ti-yÿtikapu-nube\\ 3-lock.in.irr-pl seq 3i-cook.irr-pl\\ ‘they would lock them (i.e. their cows) in and then they would cook’ ( ) was produced by María S. in an elicitation session. In this case te connects two actions by chicken: eating and going. The first verb has realis RS, which together with the iamitive marker marks this action as completed (perfective reading). The second verb has irrealis RS, which signals that the action is not completed yet, but the iamitive marker tells us that the chicken are about to go (imperfective reading).perfective/imperfective The connection of the two events in temporal succession is additionally expressed by the connective te. tinijaneutu takÿrajane te tiyunujaneatu\\ ti-ni-jane-u-tu takÿra-jane te ti-yunu-jane-a-tu\\ 3i-eat-distr-real-iam chicken-distr seq 3i-go-distr-irr-iam\\ ‘the chicken have eaten and now they go’ The next example, ( ) by Juana, stems from a description of how to make a clay pot. The first step after collecting the loam is grinding, then the pebbles turn up that have to be picked out in order to make a nice and smooth pot. bibikÿkeka maichubaji te banatu nÿkÿikina\\ bi-bikÿkeka maichuba-ji te bi-ana-tu nÿkÿiki-ina\\ 1pl-select.irr pebble-col seq 1pl-make.irr-iam pot-irr.nv\\ ‘we have to select the pebbles (from the ground loam) then we can make the pot’ In ( ) to ( ) the subjects of both coordinate clauses are the same. This is often the case given that both events belong to one discourse topic, but not necessarily so. The events may be connected in other ways than having the same subject, which can be seen in examples ( ) to ( ). In ( ) the patientpatient/theme is shared, which is the subject of the first, stative intransitive verb and the object of the second, transitive verb. It is not conominated. The second sentence has a first person plural subject. The example comes from one of the descriptions about making the clay pot by Juana. Here she speaks about cooking food in the pot. The sentence is best translated to English by using a subordinate clause including ‘when’, but it is not subordinate in Paunaka. taima te binikatu\\ ti-a-ima te bi-nika-tu\\ 3i-irr-be.cooked seq 1pl-eat.irr-iam\\ ‘when it was done, we would eat it’ In ( ), the two clauses do not share any participant. The first clause has an environment verb whose subject is the sun, while the subject of the second verb is the lazybones, who also acts as a subject of all other surrounding sentences and can thus be said to be topical (in terms of both information structure and larger discourse organisation). RS marking is the opposite of ( ), the combination of irrealis and iamitive on the first verb shows that it has an imperfective reading, while the second verb with realis RS and iamitive has a perfective reading.perfective/imperfective The sentence was produced by Miguel in telling the story about the lazybones, who did not do anything else than swinging in his liana hammock the whole day, before going home. tibÿkupatuji sache te tiyunupunukutuji timukupuji\\ ti-bÿkupa-tu-ji sache te ti-yunu-punuku-tu-ji ti-muku-pu-ji\\ 3i-enter.irr-iam-rprt sun seq 3i-go-reg-iam-rprt 3i-sleep-dloc-rprt\\ ‘at sunset (lit.: the sun was entering) he went home to sleep, it is said’ ( ) from María C. includes three clauses which are coordinated by te. The first and the second have the same subject, the corn, which is introduced by an NP in the first clause and conominated by a demonstrative in the second one. The third clause has a different subject, the speaker herself who is affected by the imminent shortage of corn, being already worried that soon she could not drink chicha anymore. The third clause does not share any participant with the other two, but is nonetheless semantically connected by the relation between corn and chicha, because chicha is made of corn. kakumÿnÿ amukemÿnÿ te tibukapu echÿu te kuinabu nea aumue\\ kaku-mÿnÿ amuke-mÿnÿ te ti-buka-pu echÿu te kuina-bu nÿ-ea aumue\\ exist-dim corn-dim seq 3i-finish.irr-mid demb seq neg-dsc 1sg-drink.irr chicha\\ ‘there is little corn and when it will be finished, then I cannot drink chicha anymore’ As for the question to which of the clauses the connective te belongs, there is no definite answer. There may be a short pause after te and a drop in pitch, which suggests it belongs to the first clause. However, it also occurs after a short pause and then rather seems to be attached to the second one or there may be no pause at all and no other hint in intonation that would point into one or the other direction. Te occasionally combines with i ‘and’, and we find both, te preceding i as in ( ) and te following i as in ( ). In ( ) there is a short pause after te, and the next clause starts with i. The example comes from Juana’s account about how her sister María S. was once attacked by a snake or water spirit. metu chikubiu te i chima
summary: The connective **te** links two clauses to indicate that their events occur in temporal sequence, and the clauses are usually semantically related and part of the same discourse topic, though they may share a subject, a participant, or only a broader thematic relation. The passage illustrates that **te** can connect actions with different perfective/imperfective readings and is common in Juana’s speech but rare in Miguel’s. It also notes that the exact clause boundary of **te** is sometimes unclear, and that **te** can occasionally co-occur with **i** ‘and’.

text: conjunctive|( The conjunctive connective i ‘and’ has been borrowedborrowing from Spanish y. It hardly ever conjoins NPs,noun phrase although a few examples of NP connection with i do occur in the corpus. The connective can conjoin clauses, and I got the impression that it is also often used to introduce a clause after change of discourse topic or turn-taking, but as I have mentioned before, information structure and the general organisation of discourse and conversation is beyond the scope of this work, so here I confine my analysis to connection of clauses. As for the latter, i does little more than connect. It can occur at the end of one intonation unit or at the beginning of the second one or without any hint in intonation as to which clause it belongs to. The connected clauses can have the same subject or different ones. The predicates of both clauses are fully inflected. A few examples follow. In ( ) and ( ), the subjects of both clauses are identical, and in ( ) the subjects of the two coordinated clauses are different. ( ) was produced by Clara to tell us how she prepared a fish. betuku jurunuyae i biyÿbapaku\\ bi-etuku jurunu-yae i bi-yÿbapaku\\ 1pl-put oven-loc and 1pl-grind\\ ‘we put it (the fish) into the oven and grind it’ ( ) is from the story about the lazybones and describes what the lazybones does in the woods instead of making his field, the work he is supposed to do. tebibikujiku kujipiyae i tikusabenunuiku chisabenu\\ ti-ebibiku-jiku kujipi-yae i ti-kusabenu-nuiku chi-sabenu\\ 3i-swing-lim1 liana.sp-loc and 3i-play.flute-cont 3-flute\\ ‘he only swung on the liana and was playing his flute’ In ( ), Miguel speaks about the past. The passage in his account from which the example is taken is about the time when debt bondage was forbidden and indigenous people were finally free. The sentence is about the unfair treatment of indigenous people prior to this. Note that the non-verbal predicate of the first clause irregularly takes a third person marker -chÿ here.person marking chamayÿchi trabakuyunubechÿ i kuina chisiupuchanube eka patron\\ chama-yÿchi trabaku-yu-nube-chÿ i kuina chi-siupucha-nube eka patrun\\ much-lim2 work-ints-pl-3 and neg 3-pay.irr-pl dema patrón\\ ‘they worked a lot and the patrón didn’t pay them’ There is hardly ever any ellipsis (or gapping) of predicates in the second of the conjoined clauses, which may be due to the fact that speakers seldom use the same predicate in two conjoined clauses. But even if this is the case, the predicate is rather repeated than omitted. Two sentences follow to exemplify this. While in ( ) both clauses have the same predicate but different subjects, in ( ) the predicates and the subjects of both clauses are identical. She raised him, because his parents had to work. tijÿku i netuku xhikuera i tichunatu te i tiyunu kuarterayae pretau chiserbisione premilitar\\ ti-jÿku i nÿ-etuku xhikuera i ti-ichuna-tu te i ti-yunu kuartera-yae pretau chi-serbisio-ne premilitar\\ 3i-grow and 1sg-put school and 3i-be.capable-iam seq and 3i-go military.base-loc lend 3-service-possd pre-military\\ ‘he grew and I put him into school and once he had acquired knowledge, then he went to the military base to do pre-military service’ conjunctive|) In the following section, the use of the much rarer connective o ‘or’ is described.
summary:
The conjunctive connective **i** ‘and’ is borrowed from Spanish **y** and is used mainly to conjoin clauses, not noun phrases. It generally contributes little beyond linking clauses: it can appear at either edge of an intonation unit, the clauses may have the same or different subjects, and both predicates are normally fully inflected with little or no omission.  

The passage also notes a few cases of gapping, but repetition of the predicate is more common than ellipsis. In one example, **i** co-occurs with the sequential connective **te**, and the section ends by introducing the rarer connective **o** ‘or’.

In contrast to clauses conjoined by i ‘and’ (see ), there is usually ellipsis of constituents in the second of the clauses connected by o ‘or’. Some examples follow. The context of ( ) was Juan C. communicating his wish for educational material for Paunaka, containing drawings of different animals of the region together with their names in Paunaka. entonses kakuina chija naka anÿke o naka chÿupekÿye\\ entonses kaku-ina chi-ija naka anÿke o naka chÿ-upekÿ-yae\\ thus exist-irr.nv 3-name here up or here 3-place.under-loc\\ ‘thus its name (of the animal) may be up here (on the page) or here under it (i.e. under the drawing)’ ( ) comes from an elicitation session on expression of spatial relations. summary: The disjunctive connective **o** ‘or’ in Paunaka is borrowed from Spanish, though it is sometimes pronounced **a**. In contrast to clauses joined by **i** ‘and’, the second clause in **o**-coordination usually has ellipsis, and **o** is also used in self-correction after a false start. Disjunction appears in both non-verbal and verbal predicates, but it is relatively infrequent in the corpus.

text: consecutive|( Consecutive clauses are similar to causal clauses (see ) in that both encode a cause and a consequence. Nonetheless, while causal clauses are considered to be a subclass of adverbial, i.e. subordinate clauses, consecutive clauses are asserted and should thus be considered a case of coordination . Consecutive clauses often include the connectives nechikue ‘therefore’ or entonses ‘thus’; however, these are mostly used to connect an utterance to the previous discourse rather than to connect two clauses. The connectives often present the consequence of what has been expressed by a text unit larger than one clause, as a kind of summary and signal that this discourse unit comes to an end. They usually introduce a new intonation unit, sometimes preceded by a pause, and this would then be a hint that the clause with the connective is independent from a previous one. Nonetheless, in the examples presented in this section, both clauses show a relatively high degree of connection by belonging to one intonation unit, so that we can assume that the connectives are used for clause combining here. ( ) is from a little tale told by Miguel about the ants. According to this tale, the ants are happy when a boy is born, because he goes on trips, and when he eats his travel supplies, little crumbs fall down and can be eaten by the ants. On the other hand, the trees are sad when a boy is born, because once he has grown up, he will fell trees to make his field. tipakajane echÿu yÿkÿkejane nechikueji tichÿnumi\\ ti-paka-jane echÿu yÿkÿke-jane nechikue-ji ti-chÿnumi\\ 3i-die.irr-distr demb tree-distr therefore-rprt 3i-be.sad\\ ‘the trees will die, therefore they are sad, it is said’ In ( ) Juana cites her grandmother explaining to her husband that he sees is a spirit and not a real woman and this is the reason for her behaviour. “es ke seunube echÿu ue nechikue tisachu tumapi”\\ es ke seunube echÿu ue nechikue ti-sachu ti-uma-pi\\ it is the case that woman demb water.spirit therefore 3i-want 3i-take.irr-2sg\\ ‘“it’s because the woman is the water spirit, that’s why she wants to take you”’ In ( ), Miguel deduces that a little wooden toy that I had brought to do some elicitation on locative expressions must be female, since it wears a dress. The main clause and the consequence clause are uttered in one intonation unit. chimÿu tÿnai entonses apimiyapÿimÿnÿ\\ chi-mÿu ti-ÿnai entonses apimiyapÿi-mÿnÿ\\ 3-clothes 3i-be.long thus girl-dim\\ ‘its garment is long, so it is a girl’ ( ) is from the same little tale as ( ) above and directly precedes it. Here, Miguel explains what happens when the boy has grown up. chejepuine echÿu aitubuchepÿi tijÿkatu, tiyunaji tebitaka chisaneina entonses chikeuchi echÿu yubuti chisatÿku yÿkÿkejane\\ chejepuine echÿu aitubuchepÿi ti-jÿka-tu ti-yuna-ji ti-ebitaka chi-sane-ina entonses chi-keuchi echÿu yubuti chi-satÿku yÿkÿke-jane\\ because demb boy 3i-grow.irr-iam 3i-go.irr-rprt 3i-clear.irr 3-field-irr.nv thus 3-ins demb axe 3-cut tree-distr\\ ‘because once the boy has grown up, he will go and clear his future field, it is said, thus with an axe he fells the trees’ consecutive|) connective|) juxtaposition|) With this example, I complete the discussion of coordination.coordination|) In the following sections, cases of subordination in clause combining and complex clause formation are presented.
summary: Consecutive clauses are like causal clauses in that they express a cause and a consequence, but they are treated as coordination rather than subordination because the consequence is asserted. The connectives *nechikue* ‘therefore’ and *entonses* ‘thus’ often link a clause to previous discourse and can introduce a new intonation unit, though in the examples here they connect clauses closely enough to count as clause combining.

text: subordination|( adverbial relation|( According to , one event is in an adverbial relation to another one if it describes the circumstances of the latter. Consider ( ) in which the second clause is introduced by porke ‘because’ and provides the reason or cause for the first one. It was elicited from Clara. kuina puero trabakuneina \\ kuina puero trabaku-ne-ina porke ni-kubÿu\\ neg can work-1sg-irr.nv because 1sg-be.drunk\\ ‘I cannot work because I am drunk’ The circumstances (such as cause in the example above) for an event are often expressed by a clause, which may be embeddedembedding into the main clause or show greater or lesser independency. They may, however, also be encoded by derivational affixes . Since this chapter is about complex clauses, adverbial relations encoded by verbal morphology are not within its scope. Three general patternssyndesis/asyndesis|( can be observed in Paunaka,verb|( each of them showing a different degree of integration of the predicate encoding the adverbial relation into the main clause. First, the adverbial predicate can be part of a separate clause which is asyndetically or syndetically juxtaposed to the main clause and takes a balanced predicate.finite verb There is no doubt that we are dealing with two clauses in this case, a main clause and an adverbial clause (AC). I call these constructions asyndetic and syndetic subordination, respectively. Asyndetic subordination is the most covert means of expressing a subordinate relation; structurally, there is no difference to asyndetic coordination (see ). Syndetic subordination offers the most elaborate means to encode which semantic type of adverbial relation is expressed by the AC by making use of different connective words, e.g. porke ‘because’ as in ( ) above.syndesis/asyndesis|) The second possibility to encode an adverbial relation is by a deranked predicatederanked verb that loses some of its verbal properties. It is more closely integrated into the main clause in this case, i.e. it is embedded. The highest degree of embedding is accomplished when a preposition is placed before the deranked verb thus showing its integration into the main clause as an oblique constituent. A different kind of integration is found with purpose-of-motion predicates,purpose|( both marked (motion-cum-purpose construction) and unmarked (serial verb construction). The purpose verb can be argued to be a verbal goal argument of the motion verb,motion predicate thus the whole construction is multi-verbal but monoclausal. Consequently, the question arises whether we can still speak of the purpose predicate and its arguments belonging to an adverbial clause.purpose|) I leave this issue to be solved by others. In any case, this is the highest degree of integration we find in Paunaka, although unlike in deranking, the predicates maintain their verbal properties.verb|) Of the semantic types of adverbial relations listed by , the following are expressed in complex adverbial clauses in Paunaka: temporal overlap, condition,temporal overlap/condition cause, purpose. Temporal anteriority and posteriority (i.e. before- and after-relations) are not commonly expressed by ACs. Instead of this, clauses marked for temporal sequence are used, which is analysed as a case of coordination (see ). The different semantic types have different encoding possibilities, which are given in . The remainder of this section is roughly organised by the degree of integration of the AC, evolving on a continuum from most independent to most dependent: all constructions in have balanced verbs, the ones with deranked verbs are presented in and monoclausal multi-verb constructions are described in . ACs are given in square brackets throughout this section.
summary: The passage explains that adverbial relations in Paunaka describe the circumstances of an event, such as cause, condition, time, or purpose, and are often expressed by clauses rather than by derivational morphology. It distinguishes three main patterns of subordination along a continuum of integration: separate balanced clauses linked asyndetically or syndetically, more tightly embedded clauses with deranked verbs, and the most integrated monoclausal multi-verb constructions, especially for purpose. It also notes that complex adverbial clauses commonly express temporal overlap, condition, cause, and purpose, while before/after relations are usually marked by temporal-sequence clauses treated as coordination.

text: finite verb|( juxtaposition|( The adverbial clauses (ACs) described in this section are connected to their main clauses at clause level. They are thus the ones that show least dependency on another clause. This is even truer for those clauses that are asyndetically juxtaposed: they could also appear completely independently. In clauses that are syndetically juxtaposed, there is a connective to overtly show the kind of relationship towards the other clause, but apart from the connective itself, there is no dependency marking.syndesis/asyndesis ACs with balanced verbs thus have exactly the same syntactic structure as coordinate clauses.coordination Both clauses can only be distinguished by functional or pragmatic factors. The structure of a complex sentence consisting of a main clause and a juxtaposed adverbial clause is illustrated in . The connectivesconnective|( that are used in syndetically juxtaposed ACs are summarised in . In addition to the ones listed there, speakers sometimes also use other connectives from Spanish; however, given their low frequency, they are neglected here. ACs with a connective usually follow the main clause, with an exception being those introduced with kue ‘if, when’, which can either precede or follow it. Purposepurpose clauses stick out, since the connective word used is a preposition. Since this preposition can be combined with balanced verbs, we can assume that it is developing a parallel function as a connective in clause combining. connective|) The remainder of this section is structured as follows: in some clauses encoding adverbial relations without the use of a connective are presented. is about temporal and conditional clauses with the connective kue, causal clauses with che(je)puine and porke are described in , purpose clauses with tÿpi in , and finally apprehensional clauses with masa are found in .
summary: The passage explains that adverbial clauses can be juxtaposed to their main clauses at the clause level, either asyndetically without an overt connective or syndetically with a connective marking the relationship. Asyndetic juxtaposed clauses are especially independent and can appear on their own, while syndetic ones have the same syntactic structure as coordinate clauses and are distinguished mainly by functional or pragmatic factors. Purpose clauses are noted as unusual because their connective is a preposition, which appears to be developing a clause-combining function.

text: In , I have shown that clauses can be coordinated by simply juxtaposing them. The same holds for adverbial, i.e. semantically subordinate, relations. A clause that represents a cause, purpose or temporal preconditiontemporal overlap/condition for another, main clause can be juxtaposed to it, without any specific linking device. In some cases, TAME markers on the predicates of both clauses suggest a certain interpretation, but this is not always the case. We often find asyndetic juxtaposition if the events overlap in time or are separated by a short time interval, i.e. in “when-relations” . The AC provides the temporal setting for the main clause in this case . A few examples of temporal-overlap clauses follow. ( ) is from a description by Juana of how to use a clay pot for cooking. Irrealis RS is due to the explaining/habitual character of the text. petupaika apuke\\ ti-a-ima pi-etupaika apuke\\ 3i-irr-be.cooked 2sg-put.down.irr ground\\ ‘when it (the food) is done, we can put it down (from the fire)’ Another sentence that expresses a when-relation without any overt marking is ( ), in which Juana talks about her brother José and the problems he has because of living remote from the village of Santa Rita. tiyununube chumeikunube chipeu eka takÿra\\ pasau-pu uneku ti-yunu-nube chÿ-umeiku-nube chi-peu eka takÿra\\ pass-dloc town 3i-go-pl 3-steal-pl 3-animal dema chicken\\ ‘when he goes to the town, they (people from Santa Rita) go and steal his chicken’ ( ) was offered by María S. as an answer to the question whether she smoked. Like in the examples above, no connective is involved and the relation between the clauses is only understood from the context. nijibÿku \\ ni-jibÿku ni-yunu asaneti\\ 1sg-smoke 1sg-go field\\ ‘I smoke when I go to the field’ The incompletive marker is often used if the events expressed by the clauses have past reference. In that case -kuÿ indicates that a certain state held at that time but does not hold anymore, and thus it sets the ground for the clause that follows. The clauses are otherwise completely unmarked for their relation to each other and -kuÿ can also occur in contexts that do not involve subordination. In ( ), María C. makes a statement about her consumption of alcohol in former times (she was known for enjoying life, when she was younger): the state of being a girl or young woman holds in relation to the predicate of the main clause. neu\\ bane pimiya-kuÿ-ne nÿ-eu\\ rem girl-incmp-1sg 1sg-drink\\ ‘long ago, when I was still a young woman, I drank’ A similar possibility is offered by continuous marking on one of the verbs. In this case, one event is marked as ongoing at the time another event, which has to be telictelicity and punctual, occurs. There are not many examples in the corpus of the use of the continuous marker in such a way, but one is given in ( ), where in Juana’s story the fugitive criminal has just arrived at his wife’s house to eat and is then arrested by the police (or soldiers). tinikukuikuji \\ ti-niku-kuiku-ji kapunu-uku-nube suntabu-nube\\ 3i-eat-cont-rprt come-add-pl soldier-pl\\ ‘he was eating, it is said, when the soldiers came, too’ (or: ‘while he was eating, the soldiers came, too’) Not only temporal relations can be expressed without overt linking. The following examples show causalcause ( ) and purposivepurpose ( ) clauses that are asyndetically juxtaposed to their main clauses. In ( ), the second clause provides the reason for the statement made in the main clause, the boy crying. This sentence was produced by Miguel, when looking at the pictures of the frog story and it refers to the picture on which the dog jumps against the tree and the boy holds his nose being bitten by a small rodent. entonses tiyuiyukubutu eka aitubuchepÿimÿnÿ \\ entonses ti-iyuyuiku-bu-tu eka aitubuchepÿi-mÿnÿ ti-piku\\ thus 3i-cry-mid-iam dema boy-dim 3i-be.afraid\\ ‘so the boy is crying, (because) he is afraid’ The following example, ( ), consists of several clauses. The part that I want to discuss here is underlined. These are the two clauses that express “look for wood” and “make a small board” (which are both in a complement relation to an utterance predicate, but this is of no concern at the moment). The second of these clauses encodes the purpose for the first one without being overtly marked for this relation. The example comes from Miguel’s description of how he learned to read, write and calculate and it cites his teacher who gave Miguel instructions how to obtain a board to write on. “pikechuchÿji echÿu pia tisemaika echÿu yÿkÿke \textup i nebu pisuikia”, tikechu\\ pi-kechu-chÿ-ji echÿu pi-a ti-semaika echÿu yÿkÿke ti-ana taurapachu-mÿnÿ i nebu pi-suik-i-a ti-kechu\\ 2sg-say-3-imp demb 2sg-father 3i-search.irr demb wood 3i-make.irr board-dim and 3obl.top.prn 2sg-write-subord-irr 3i-say\\ ‘“tell your father to look for wood to make a small board and on that one you can write”, he said’ I want to emphasise again that the adverbial nature of linking between the clauses in the examples of this section is based on purely pragmatic factors and thus the translations into English with a connective may be a bit misleading. It would certainly be possible to translate most of the examples into English by using coordinated clauses, too. In the following sections, I will present examples in which the subordinate relationship of one event towards another is expressed overtly by using a connective that tells us about the exact nature of the relationship. connective|(
summary: The passage argues that subordinate relations between clauses can be expressed simply by juxtaposition, without any overt connective, not only for coordination but also for adverbial meanings such as cause, purpose, and temporal relations. Temporal, causal, and purposive interpretations are often inferred from context, though TAME marking sometimes helps signal the relation, and the author notes that overt connectives are used in later sections to mark these relationships more explicitly.

text: temporal overlap/condition|( Like many other languages , Paunaka encodes conditional and temporal-overlap relations by using the same connective, kue ‘if, when’. A certain possibility to distinguish between temporal and conditional is offered by RSreality status marking of both clauses. According to , in conditional linking, both events are presented as non-factual. Thus we can deduce that conversely, if both clauses have realis predicates, we are dealing with a temporal relation. However, this is rare in Paunaka, and there are only a few examples of all-realis temporal sentences. All of them express non-singular events, i.e. repeated or repeatable. Three examples with realis predicates in both clauses shall be given here, ( )–( ). ( ) encodes a habitual event with present time reference. It is an answer to the question whether María S. smoked. Actually, it was a repetition of ( ) above, where the two predicates were asyndetically juxtaposed, and was produced to confirm what she had been saying before. nijibÿku \\ ni-jibÿku kue ni-yunu asaneti\\ 1sg-smoke if 1sg-go field\\ ‘I smoke when I go to the field’ The next example also encodes repeated events. It was produced by María S. when we were sitting in her yard and suddenly some piglets turned up grunting and wanted to suckle. tibiyujaneutu\\ kue ti-sabai-kÿupunu-jane ti-biyu-jane-u-tu\\ if 3i-shout-am.conc.cis-distr 3i-be.thirsty-distr-real-iam\\ ‘when they come grunting, they are thirsty’ Finally, ( ) comes from Juana telling me about the production of a pot in former times. Actually, it is rather exceptional that she uses realis predicates here, because past habitualhabitual|( events are often encoded by use of irrealis. However, there are some inconsistencies in the relation of past habitual events and irrealis encoding anyway (see ) and in this specific case, the surrounding sentences also have realis RS.habitual|) Note that in addition to having kue in the antecedent clause, the consequent clause takes the coordinating sequential connective te (see ). te beimachu\\ kue ti-mÿra-ki-mÿnÿ-tu te bi-eimachu\\ if 3i-dry- -dim-iam seq 1pl-cook.until.done\\ ‘when it had dried, then we fired it’ It is more common to find combinations of clauses, in which the main clause predicate has realis RS and the predicate of the clause introduced by kue has irrealis RS, thus only the conditional clause is presented as non-factual, see ( )–( ) below. summary: Paunaka uses the same connective, **kue** ‘if, when’, for both conditional and temporal-overlap relations, and reality-status marking helps distinguish them: when both clauses are realis, the relation is usually temporal, though such all-realis cases are rare and mostly involve repeated or habitual events. More commonly, conditional clauses have an irrealis predicate in the antecedent, while irrealis in both clauses can also result from future reference or negation rather than from the conditional relation itself. The passage also notes cases with irrealis antecedents and realis consequents, often still expressing repeated or repeatable events, and mentions that counterfactual conditionals likewise have irrealis marking because the clauses are non-factual.

text: cause|( Sometimes two events are in a relation of cause and consequence, thus one event is a prerequisite to the other. This can be expressed either by marking one event as a cause of another one (in a causal clause) or by marking one event as a consequence of the other (in a consecutive clause). Following , the latter is defined as a case of coordination and described in . This section is about causal clauses only. The causal clause can be introduced by the connective che(je)puine ‘because’. This connective is used by Miguel and María S. and it also appears in the recordings by Riester. The verb of a causal clause introduced by che(je)puine is always balanced and its RS is not restricted.reality status The causal clause always follows the main clause; however, it can also introduce a separate intonation unit, in which case the cause may be less tightly connected to the previous clause, but rather to the larger context. ( ) is an excerpt from the description of the frog story told by Miguel. He describes the picture on which the dog and the boy lean in the window, with the dog’s head being stuck in the glass of the frog. tipikutu eka aitubuchepÿimÿnÿ \\ ti-piku-tu eka aitubuchepÿi-mÿnÿ chejepuine-kena ti-ubÿu chi-chÿti eka chi-peu kabe naka\\ 3i-be.afraid-iam dema boy-dim because-uncert 3i-get.stuck 3-head dema 3-animal dog here\\ ‘the boy is afraid, maybe because the head of his dog is stuck here’ In ( ), María S. answers my question whether she had a friend when she was a child. summary: The passage explains that causal relations can be expressed either by marking an event as a cause or as a consequence, but this section focuses only on causal clauses. In the language described, causal clauses are introduced by the connective **che(je)puine** ‘because’ or, for some speakers, by Spanish **porke** ‘because’; the verb in such clauses is always balanced, and the clause normally follows the main clause, though it may also form a separate intonation unit.

text: purpose|( general oblique|( In purpose clause linking, one event “(the main one) is performed with the goal of obtaining the realization of another one (the dependent one)” . Purpose clauses always follow the main clause. They can be introduced by tÿpi, which is not strictly speaking a connective, but a preposition that is used with obliques (see ). However, the predicate following tÿpi in purpose clauses can be balanced, and thus should be described in this section. Purpose clauses with tÿpi and balanced predicates are typical for Juana, but occasionally also found with other speakers. We can thus state that the preposition is developing a parallel function as connective. This parallels what we find with Spanish para ‘for’, although in Spanish purpose clauses, the verb has to be an infinitive. In Paunaka, purpose clauses formed with a deranked verb can also additionally be marked by tÿpi. Those clauses are described in . The predicate of a purpose clause usually has irrealis RS. It is not necessary that both clauses have the same subject, but there needs to be some involvement “at least in that there is an element of will on part towards such realization” . The subjects of the main and the purpose verb may thus be the same or different. Actually, in most examples I found, they are different, see ( )–( ). ( ) comes from Juana’s account about how they made the reservoir in Santa Rita. The men prepared the ground by felling trees, and the women cooked for them. i biti metu biyÿtikatu nÿkÿiki \\ i biti metu bi-yÿtika-tu nÿkÿiki tÿpi chi-nika-nube\\ and 1pl.prn already 1pl-set.on.fire-iam pot obl 3-eat.irr-pl\\ ‘and we already set the pots onto fire for them to eat it’ From the same passage is ( ), in which Juana describes that the men were supplied with chicha. i eka kaku chijinepÿinube chiyenu te, tumunube aumue \\ i eka kaku chi-jinepÿi-nube chi-yenu te ti-umu-nube aumue tÿpi ti-ea-nube nauku\\ and dema exist 3-daughter-pl 3-wife seq 3i-take-pl chicha seq 3i-drink.irr-pl there\\ ‘and the ones who had daughters or a wife, they brought them chicha to drink there’ In ( ), Juana explains that she will give her daughter a post-pregnancy treatment: tie her belly to shrink it. nÿrÿtÿkabÿti chikÿ nijinepÿi \\ nÿ-rÿtÿka-bÿti chi-kÿ ni-jinepÿi tÿpi chi-rataka micha\\ 1sg-tie-prsp 3- 1sg-daughter obl 3-press.irr good\\ ‘I’m just going to tie my daughter’s belly so that it presses her well’ In ( ) the subjects are identical. The jar is the subject of the copula kaku as well as of the middle verb tetukapu ‘it is filled’. The example also comes from Juana, when she told me about the beautiful pottery they have in Cotoca, a city close to Santa Cruz and a popular destination for excursions. kaku yÿpijanemÿnÿ michananaji , tisÿeimumÿnÿ\\ kaku yÿpi-jane-mÿnÿ michana-na-ji tÿpi ti-etuka-pu ÿne ti-sÿei-umu-mÿnÿ\\ exist jar-distr-dim nice-rep-col obl 3i-put.irr-mid water 3i-be.cold- -dim\\ ‘there are beautiful jars for being filled with water, the water stays cold’ ( ) is a negative purpose clause with tÿpi produced by Juana describing the preparation of a medicine against cough to my colleague Lena. bea \\ bi-ea tÿpi kuina bi-jÿchikapu yuti-ina\\ 1sg-drink.irr obl neg 1pl-cough.irr night-irr.nv\\ ‘we drink it so that we won’t cough at night’ Combination of tÿpi with a negative clause like in the previous example is exceptional. Usually, apprehensional clauses take a different connective, masa ‘lest’. Apprehensional clauses are much rarer than purpose clauses. They are described in the following section. In addition, motion predicatesmotion predicate are never combined with purpose clauses introduced by tÿpi. Speakers either use a serial verb or a motion-cum-purpose construction to encode these notions (see ). general oblique|) purpose|)
summary: Purpose clauses in Paunaka express that the main event is done to achieve a dependent event, and they always follow the main clause. They may be introduced by tÿpi, which is originally a preposition but can function like a connective in these clauses; the purpose predicate usually has irrealis marking, and the main and purpose subjects may be either the same or different, though they are often different. Negative purpose clauses with tÿpi are exceptional, apprehensional clauses usually use masa instead, and motion predicates are not combined with tÿpi purpose clauses.

Apprehensional clauses are rare in the corpus, but three examples shall be given here nonetheless. The context of ( ) is as follows: together with Juana, we had just found María S., who was making adobe bricks at a place in the woods. This place is a bit remote from the village, and we had been walking through the shrubbery before we met her there (when walking back to the village, María S. showed us a better way). It was produced to exemplify the use of an expression that I had requested from her, ‘water a plant’. puchuneka ÿne \\ pi-uchu-ne-ka ÿne masa ti-paka\\ 2sg-pour.liquid-top-th1.irr water lest 3i-die\\ ‘water them (lit.: pour water on top) lest they die’ |) All ACs presented so far have balanced verbs.finite verb|) That a clause is in an adverbial relation to another one can also be signalled by deranking. summary: Apprehensional clauses express a negative kind of purpose: the main-clause event is carried out to prevent the event in the adverbial clause from happening. In the passage, they are introduced by **masa** ‘lest’ and their predicates always have **irrealis** status, and the author notes that these clauses are rare in the corpus. The examples show actions taken to avoid being found, being enchanted, or plants dying.

text: deranked verb|( ACs can be built on deranked verbs (see ). An AC with a deranked verb cannot occur on its own. It is thus more closely integrated into the main clause, i.e. embeddedembedding in it, without being an argument of the main clause. This is illustrated in . Integration into the main clause becomes most apparent if a preposition is placed in front of the deranked verb, thus marking it as an oblique constituent of the main clause. However, this is only occasionally found with verbs encoding purpose and even less frequent with those encoding causalcause relations. If no preposition is placed before the deranked verb, the semantic type of relation towards the main clause is as unmarked as in asyndetically juxtaposed ACs (see ) and can only be deduced from the context. ACs with deranked verbs usually follow the main clause with a few exceptions. Deranked verbs always index the subject, they can also index an object and this object can be conominated. Conominationconomination of subjects is exceptional though a few examples of this are found. I will proceed as in the previous section and first illustrate the use of embedded clauses unmarked for their semantic connection to the main clause in and then describe the ones that combine with a preposition in , thus explicitly encoding the type of relation.
summary: Adverbial clauses (ACs) can be formed with deranked verbs, but such clauses cannot stand alone and are therefore more tightly integrated into the main clause, though not as arguments of it. This integration is sometimes made explicit by a preposition before the deranked verb, marking it as an oblique constituent; when no preposition is present, the relation to the main clause is unmarked and must be inferred from context. Deranked verbs usually follow the main clause and always index the subject, though they may also index an object, while subject conomination is rare.

subsubsection: Adverbial clauses with bare deranked verbs
text: In ACs with “bare” deranked verbs, the deranked verb tells us that we are dealing with a subordinate relation. However, there is no information about the semantics of this relation, i.e. the exact nature of this relation has to be deduced from the context. We can then identify purpose, causalcause and temporal relations, but there is sometimes a certain ambiguity involved. The deranked verb can have realis or irrealis RSreality status for reasons that lie outside of the construction type and it can have the same or a different subject than the main clause predicate. I will first consider some examples in which both predicates have the same subject and then discuss the ones with different subjects. Towards the end of the section, a few cases in which the deranked verb precedes the main clause predicate are presented, and finally, some cases in which the information provided by the subordinate verb doubles what is expressed on the main clause verb. In ( ), the main clause tells us about the existence of an entity, the walking cane, and the subordinate clause provides information about the purpose of this walking cane. The sentence comes from Juana telling me about her encounter with two old ladies in Candelaria. It is a description of one of the ladies. kaku chibastunemÿnetu, mhm, \\ kaku chi-bastun-ne-mÿnÿ-tu mhm chi-yuik-i-u-mÿnÿ\\ exist 3-walking.cane-possd-dim-iam intj 3-walk-subord-real-dim\\ ‘she already had a cane, mhm, for walking’ ( ) has a similar structure as ( ) above. The main clause tells about an action of a participant, and the AC describes the reason of this action. It is from Miguel’s description of the frog story to José. More precisely, it provides a description of the picture in which the boy has climbed the rock. ja tipuna naka eka aitubuchepÿi \\ ja ti-puna naka eka aitubuchepÿi chi-pik-i-u-chi eka chumurkuku\\ intj 3i-go.up.irr here dema boy 3-be.afraid-subord-real-3 dema tropical.screech.owl\\ ‘ah, he is going to climb up here being afraid of the owl’ In ( ), Juana quite amusedly comments about her dog, which made a howling-barking sound when it scratched itself. In this example, the main clause verb is marked as continuous, but when Juana repeated the sentence for me just a moment later, she used a non-continuous verb form, the rest of the sentence being identical. The deranked verb either encodes the reason for barking or it simply expresses a temporal relation. timajaikukuiku \\ ti-majaiku-kuiku chi-bujak-i-u-bu\\ 3i-bark-cont 3-scratch-subord-real-mid\\ ‘it barks scratching itself’ In ( ) and ( ), the subjects differ; however, the singular agent of the main clause is also understood to be part of the plural subject of the deranked verb. ( ) is another example from Miguel telling the frog story, but on an occasion other than ( ) above. He describes the picture in which the beehive lies on the ground after the dog has jumped against the tree. The deranked verb describes the purpose of the main clause verb in this case. chibÿtupaiku echÿukena \\ chi-bÿtupaiku echÿu-kena chi-nik-i-a-nube ipiti-umu\\ 3-make.fall demb-uncert 3-eat-subord-irr-pl bee- \\ ‘it seems that it makes it fall so that they can eat honey’ ( ) was produced by Juana who was telling about the old times before there was the reservoir in Santa Rita and they had to walk far to get water. tÿbaneyu ÿne tikuti nimupeki \\ ti-ÿbane-yu ÿne ti-kuti ni-mupeki bi-ejik-i-u-mÿnÿ ÿne\\ 3i-be.far-ints water 3i-hurt 1sg-knee 1pl-take.away-subord-real-dim water\\ ‘the water was very far away, my knee hurt when we fetched water’ ( ) and ( ) have different subjects in main and subordinate clauses. However, the subject of the deranked verb is always affected by the event expressed by the main clause verb. Note that in ( ), the subordinate clause precedes the main clause. A few more examples of that will follow below. In ( ), there is a weather verb with a third person subject, and the deranked verb has a first person subject, i.e. Miguel, who gives the reason for him waiting for rain here. repentekena tikeba pario \\ repente-kena ti-keba pario ni-ebuk-i-a\\ maybe-uncert 3i-rain.irr some 1sg-sow-subord-irr \\ ‘maybe it rains a bit for me to sow’ ( ) has two third person subjects; however, one is singular and the other plural, and they refer to completely different participants. The subject of the deranked verb is the dog, and the subject of the main clause verb is the wasps. This is one of the few examples in which the clause with the deranked verb precedes the main clause. The sentence describes the same situation as ( ) above, but comes from the second occasion when Miguel told the frog story. tibÿbÿkujanetu\\ chi-bÿbÿtupaik-i-u-chÿ-tu eka chÿ-ubiu jane ti-bÿbÿku-jane-tu\\ 3-make.fall-subord-real-3-iam dema 3-house bee 3i-fly-distr-iam\\ ‘it (the dog) having made the wasps’ nest fall, they (the wasps) fly’ Like ( ), ( ) also has its subordinate clause preposed to the main clause. The subject of the deranked verb, piesta ‘feast day’ is conominated here, which is very rare. The sentence stems from María S. telling me about her childhood and the lack of knowledge they had in the old days. I am not sure why María S. uses a reportive marker on the main clause verb here, either it is quotative here – this is what I propose by the translation given – or it is used as a hearsay marker, the latter would suggest that María S. does not remember their sudden departure to town on a feast day herself and was only told by somebody else (maybe one of her older siblings). repenteyÿchi biyunupatuji uneku\\ kuyena chi-tupun-i-u-bu piesta repente-yÿchi bi-yunupa-tu-ji uneku\\ like.this 3-reach-subord-real-mid feast.day suddenly-lim2 1pl-go.to-iam-rprt town\\ ‘so when a feast day came, only that same day we said we would go to town’ ( ) is another example in which the deranked verb precedes the main clause. Both are used to set an event (i.e. the one encoding purpose) in relation to a motion event. The difference between the two constructions is that the non-motion verb in a MCPC is marked for this relation, while it is unmarked in a SVC. Consider ( ) and ( ). In ( ) we have a MCPC: the dislocative marker -pu on the second predicate shows that it is related to the motion predicate. In ( ) a similar event is expressed, but in this case, the second verb is completely unmarked. ( ) was produced by María S. when telling me what she did that day. They cannot be negated separately,negation and it can thus be claimed that the constructions consist of a single clause, not two separate ones. I will come back to this later in this section. The serial verb construction is marginally used to encode simultaneous events, but the main function of both constructions is to express motion and purpose of this motion. Purpose of motion shows a certain analogy to nominal or adverbial expression of a goal. This is because by metonymical extension an action can come to stand for the location where it is carried out . Compare ( ) and ( ). In the first example, the goal is expressed by a noun, which takes the locative marker -yae; in the second, the goal is a verb marked with the dislocative suffix -pa (with irrealis RS). In that case, the verb -yunu ‘go’ combines with -eiku ‘follow’ to indicate that the subject accompanies somebody else (‘go along with’). As is the case with those serial verbs encoding purpose of motion, this case of simultaneous event expression can be argued to encode a kind of goal, though not at a fixed location: the goal is the other person who is also moving. We can thus argue that just like complement clausescomplement relation|( are clausal expressions of an object of a verb, in the SVC and MCPC, a clause expresses the oblique (goal) argument of a motion verb. As for the term “serial verb construction”, it has been applied to a wide array of multi-verb clauses, which has led to a certain ambiguity about which constructions constitute SVCs and which ones should be classified differently. In the spirit of , the term is used to describe a technique to combine predicates that share at least one argument without morphosyntactically marking the relation between those predicates. According to this author, the construction encodes a single event and is monoclausal. As I have already stated in , I do not have the means to check whether something is conceived as a single event or as multiple events, so I will not further pursue this issue here. As for monoclausality, this also holds for complement clausescomplement relation in Paunaka, and indeed, we find complement clauses among the ones that are defined as SVCs in the aforementioned publications. A relatively narrow definition of SVC that deliberately excludes complement clauses and some other constructions has been proposed by : “A serial verb construction is a monoclausal construction consisting of multiple independent verbs with no element linking them and with no predicate–argument relation between the verbs”. Since I have just stated that the purpose clause can be defined as a clausal argument of the motion verb expressing the goal, the definition would possibly also exclude what I am just trying to define as a SVC here. However, if we replace “argument” by “core argument”, the definition works well for the purpose of this work. A crucial point of the definition of the SVC is its being monoclausal – and this also holds for the MCPC of Paunaka. A test for monoclausality that is cross-linguistically applicable is scope of negationnegation|( and place of the negator, i.e. “there is only one way to form the negation, usually with scope over all the verbs” . An example to illustrate the scope of negation over both predicates in a SVC is given in ( ). The negative particle kuina precedes the motion verb -yunu, and since this verb is negated, the verb encoding the purpose of the motion is negated, too. The sentence cannot be understood as ‘she did not go to the airport, (but) she took her’. summary: Paunaka has two multi-verb constructions for expressing motion with purpose: a serial verb construction (SVC), in which the non-motion verb is unmarked, and a motion-cum-purpose construction (MCPC), in which the non-motion verb is marked to show its relation to the motion predicate. Both constructions are monoclausal and the motion verb and purpose verb are tightly integrated, with negation typically scoping over both verbs; the SVC can also marginally express simultaneous events, especially with the verb sequence ‘go’ + ‘follow’ meaning ‘go along with.’

They require the same subject for both verbs, usually mark both verbs for person and reality status, and are mostly interchangeable, though only the SVC can marginally express simultaneous motion.

If the purpose event has a different subject or is non-motion, a different construction is needed, and the passage gives examples of coordination and mixed constructions illustrating these patterns.

summary: The passage describes serial verb constructions with motion verbs, especially those expressing purpose of motion: a motion verb like *-yunu* ‘go’ combines with another verb, and both verbs usually share the same subject, with the second verb unmarked for realis/irrealis status depending on context. It also notes a second type of SVC expressing simultaneous motion, mainly involving *-yunu* plus *-eiku* ‘follow’, which often has a comitative meaning ‘go with someone’ and may be developing into a preposition-like form.

summary:
The motion-cum-purpose construction consists of a motion verb, usually *-yunu* ‘go,’ followed by a purpose verb marked with the dislocative suffix as a dependency marker. The purpose predicate is typically irrealis, though it can be realis when the event has been realized, and the subject may appear between the two verbs or after the whole construction.  

The construction can also use other motion-like predicates such as the imperative particle *nabi* ‘go!’ and marginally *-bÿcheiku* ‘send/make someone do,’ but it never occurs with cislocative predicates.

subsubsection: Associated motion verbs combined with motion verbs
text: associated motion|( As has been described in , Paunaka has a number of associated motion (AM) markers that are attached to a verb to state that the event happens before, after or simultaneous with motion. This would be a prime example of an even more integrating strategy: encoding adverbial relations by verbal derivation, thus decreasing syntactic and increasing morphological complexity. A verb with an AM marker alone does already express an event including motion, but there are cases in which the verb with the AM marker is nonetheless combined with a motion verb. Two examples in which the speaker chose a deranked form for this motion verb have already been given as ( ) and ( ) in . The first was contrasted with ( ), which has a verb marked for concurrent motion juxtaposed to a motion verb. There are a few more examples in the corpus, where verbs marked for AM combine with motion predicates, resulting in (almost?) tautological statements. In ( ), the verb with the concurrent cislocative AM marker is surrounded by the non-verbal predicate kapunu. This sentence was elicited from María S. kapunu tibÿbÿkukukÿupunu kapunu\\ kapunu ti-bÿbÿku-kukÿupunu kapunu\\ come 3i-fly-am.conc.cis come\\ ‘it comes, flying it comes, it comes’ A similar example is ( ), which can be analysed as including a temporal clause juxtaposed to a main clause. This main clause has a verb with a translocative concurrent AM marker combined with the motion verb -yunu. The information conveyed doubles. The sentence was produced by Juana when telling me about the past. biyuna asaneti bichujikukukÿu biyunu asaneti\\ bi-yuna asaneti bi-chujiku-kukÿu bi-yunu asaneti\\ 1pl-go.irr field 1pl-speak-am.conc.tr 1pl-go field\\ ‘when we went to the field, going talking we went to the field’ I want to emphasise that not every verb with an AM marker is combined with a motion predicate. In many cases, the AM marker alone conveys the motion part of the meaning. However, it seems to be frequent cross-linguistically that motion verbs combine with verbs taking an AM marker . It is well possible that the two possibilities, i.e. motion verbs combined with verbs taking AM markers and verbs taking AM markers alone, have different functions in discourse. This remains a topic for further studies.associated motion|)motion predicate|)adverbial relation|) The following section is about complement relations.
summary: Paunaka has associated motion markers attached to verbs to express that an event occurs before, after, or simultaneously with motion, thereby encoding adverbial relations through verbal derivation. Although these markers often suffice on their own to express motion-related meaning, they are sometimes combined with separate motion verbs, producing partly redundant or “tautological” expressions; the author suggests that these two patterns may have different discourse functions, but this remains unresolved.

text: complement relation|( From a semantic-functional view, in a complement relation one event entails that there is reference to another one . If complementation is defined as a syntactic relation, it is the “syntactic situation that arises when a notional sentence or predication is an argument of a predicate” . The question arises whether the complement clause (CC) can be analysed as an argument argument|( of a predicate in Paunaka. The most typical instances of CCs are not marked for dependency. They cannot be indexed on the matrix verb nor be substituted by a pronoun. One example is given in ( ). Both the complement-taking verb and the complement verb are fully inflected for person and RS; they could occur independently in exactly this way. In this sentence from the story about the two men and the devil, Miguel quotes what the devil says. answer to question|) serial verb construction|) Besides serialisation, mentions another possible construction type for CCs that are not arguments, i.e. the paratactic construction, in which the CC is syntactically independent from the MC. However, this construction is ruled out, because, as has been shown above, the predicates are not independently negatable. Thus the question how to syntactically classify the CC in Paunaka remains open for the time being. Up to this point, only sentences with the most frequent complement-taking verb -sachu ‘want’ have been considered. Paunaka has a small number of verbs that take unmarked clausal complements like the ones shown in ( – ). Among those verbs are some secondary verbs, i.e. verbs that only take clausal complements, and some primary verbs, those that can also take objectsobject expressed by a person index on the verb and/or an NP . Some complement-taking verbs with different subject CCs index the shared argument as an object, while others do not. Although dependency is not overtly marked, the fact that the complement verb is dependent on the matrix verb can be deduced from its restrictions on RS status|( Some complement-taking verbs only take same-RS complements, others only irrealis complements. Only reported speech CCs stick out here, since their RS is not predetermined.reality status|) In some special cases, verbs that usually take unmarked CCs can also take CCs with a deranked verb. This is probably bound to some extraordinary circumstances that are not inherent in the relation between the complement-taking verb and its CC. For some verbs, there seems to be a certain variability though. They can take both balancedfinite verb and deranked verbs in their CCs. This may be bound to the generally sparse occurrence in discourse of these verbs. There are also some verbs that, if they occur with a clausal complement at all, only allow a CC with a deranked verb. Finally, I have also found a few cases in which a CC with a balanced verb is introduced by a demonstrative. The remainder of this section is organised as follows. I first show some more examples of unmarked CCs in . is dedicated to the discussion of cases in which CCs with deranked verbs show up. Finally, takes a look at CCs that include the demonstrative eka as a complementiser. Throughout this section, CCs are given in square brackets. If an argument that is shared by the complement-taking predicate and the complement predicate is conominated, it occurs outside the square brackets, i.e. as if belonging primarily to the main clause. This is motivated by a similar analysis of English CCs in which the subject of the CC is encoded as an object of the complement-taking verb (e.g. I hear him .) For Paunaka, however, this is an arbitrary decision, since there is nothing on the NP that would point towards it belonging to either of the two clauses.
summary: The passage argues that Paunaka complement clauses are often unmarked and not clearly dependent in the usual syntactic sense, since they are not indexed on the matrix verb, cannot be replaced by pronouns, and the complement and matrix verbs are both fully inflected and could stand alone. Although their dependence is suggested by restrictions on reality status and by patterns of argument indexing, their exact syntactic classification remains unresolved, especially because parataxis is ruled out and the evidence does not clearly distinguish other possibilities.

The passage summarizes which complement-taking predicates most often occur with unmarked complement clauses and notes that the list is likely incomplete. These predicates vary by semantic class and by how they combine with complement clauses: some require same-subject clauses, others different-subject clauses, and some index an argument of the complement clause as their object.  

It also states that most of these predicates restrict the reality status of the complement clause in different ways. For example, -sachu ‘want’, -sumachu ‘want, like’, -bÿche(i)ku ‘send, order’, and puero ‘can’ require irrealis complements, while -(i)chuna ‘know, be capable’ and -samu ‘hear’ require equal reality status; -kechu ‘say’ places no such restriction.

The passage describes two desiderative verbs that take clausal complements: **-sachu** ‘want’ and **-sumachu/-sumechu** ‘want, like’. **-sachu** is more frequent and only takes clausal complements, while **-sumachu** can also take nominal objects; with clausal complements they are largely interchangeable, though **-sumachu** more clearly expresses liking and **-sachu** can also mark imminence.  

In these constructions, the complement clause is always marked **irrealis**, and subjects may be shared with the main clause or differ from it. Objects and other non-subject constituents are indexed on the complement verb and follow it, including conominated objects, oblique NPs, and adverbs.

The passage discusses Paunaka uses of the desiderative/complement clause construction and the borrowed predicate *puero* ‘can’ from Spanish *poder*. It argues that *puero* functions as a complement-taking ability predicate rather than a modal verb, and that it is especially common in negative clauses because ability and negation both trigger irrealis marking in Paunaka.

The text also notes that *puero* is unusual among borrowed non-verbal predicates because it does not inflect for person and may or may not itself take irrealis when the complement is already irrealis. In a few positive sentences, *puero* appears with an irrealis complement, suggesting it may be expanding to mark ability independently of irrealis.

text: manipulative verb|( Manipulative predicates have been defined as such predicates that “express a relation between an agent or a situation which functions as a cause, an affectee, and a resulting situation. The affectee must be a participant in the resulting situation” . There is one manipulative predicate in Paunaka, -bÿche(i)ku ‘send, order’. The RS of the complement predicate is always irrealis, regardless of whether the situation described by the complement predicate has been realised by the time that the sentence is produced. One of the very few non-elicited examples with this verb is ( ). It shows that, unlike with desiderative verbs (see ), the conominated subject of the CC follows the complement-taking verb.word order This is due to the fact that it is expressed as its proper object, as will become apparent in the examples below, where we find indexes on the verb. The affectee is also expressed as the subject of the CC, and the complement verb thus takes the person marker ti-. Note that the second verb in this sentence, tipÿsisiku ‘be alone’, has realis RS, thus it probably belongs to the main clause, not to the CC, which has irrealis RS. I do not know why it does not take the middle voice marker in this case, as it usually does. The sentence was produced by Clara, who was sitting with us chatting. Clara earns her money by baking bread. Her daughter, apparently, when she went to school, had told Clara to ask her other daughter to help her make the bread. That was before we arrived and consequently her daughter was doing all the work alone now. Clara found it funny and at the same time felt a bit guilty about making her daughter do all the work alone. nibÿchekutu nijinepÿi tipÿsisiku \\ ni-bÿcheku-tu ni-jinepÿi ti-pÿsisiku ti-yÿbajika kÿjÿpi\\ 1sg-order-iam 1sg-daughter 3i-be.alone 3i-grind.irr manioc\\ ‘I ordered my daughter to grind the manioc all by herself’ A similar example is ( ). The shared conominated argument, which is the object of the manipulative verb and subject of the complement verb, is placed after the manipulative verb.word order This sentence was elicited from Juana. ¡pibÿchekaji kabe !\\ pi-bÿcheka-ji kabe chi-nijabaka echÿu ti-umei\\ 2sg-order-imp dog 3-bite.irr demb 3i-steal\\ ‘give the dog the command to bite the thief!’ In ( ), the shared argument is not conominated, but it is encoded as the object of the manipulative verb by use of the third person marker chÿ-, which is used for specific 3>3 relationships. This example was elicited from María S. Irrealis of the manipulative verb is probably due this sentence being elicited without any context. chibÿchekatu \\ chi-bÿcheka-tu ti-kutikapu\\ 3-order.irr-iam 3i-run.irr\\ ‘(s)he makes him run’ ( ) shows two things. First, the shared first person singular argument is indexed on the matrix verb as an object. And second, if movement is implied in the order, the dislocative marker (see ) can be attached to the complement verb. This shows how closely related this type of CC is to a motion-cum-purpose construction, which has been analysed to encode an adverbial relation (see ). The example was elicited from Miguel. nijinepÿi tibÿchekunÿ \\ ni-jinepÿi ti-bÿcheku-nÿ ni-yÿseiku-pa chÿeche\\ 1sg-daughter 3i-order-1sg 1sg-buy-dloc.irr meat\\ ‘my daughter sent me to buy meat’ A similar example was elicited from Juana, where she preferred a CC containing a complete motion-cum-purpose construction including the motion verb -yunu. Note that the motion verb has realis RS in this case. This issue cannot be resolved at the moment for lack of data. nÿbÿcheku \\ nÿ-bÿcheku ti-yunu ti-yÿseiku-pa eka kanela\\ 1sg-order 3i-go 3i-buy-dloc.irr dema cinnamon\\ ‘I made her go to buy cinnamon’ manipulative verb|)
summary:
Paunaka has one manipulative predicate, **-bÿche(i)ku** ‘send, order’, and its complement predicate is always marked **irrealis**, even when the situation may already have happened. In these constructions, the shared argument is typically expressed as the **object of the manipulative verb** and the **subject of the complement clause**, and the word order places the conominated subject after the manipulative verb. 

The passage also notes that these constructions can resemble **motion-cum-purpose** structures, especially when movement is implied and a dislocative marker appears on the complement verb.

According to , in perception complementation “semantically it is the entire event, not the argument coded as the matrix direct object, that is perceived”. It is difficult to determine whether a person perceives an entire event or primarily one participant in that event if there are no formal linguistic means to express the difference. If the shared argument of the main clause and the CC is conominated,conomination|( the CC has exactly the same structure as an unmarked relative clauserelative relation|( (see ). This can be seen in ( ): first comes the complement-taking verb, its object directly follows it, then comes a clause which could be either a CC or a relative clause modifying the object. The sentence is from Juana’s narration about the journey of her grandparents from Moxos. Her grandfather has had an unpleasant encounter with a water spirit at night and hardly slept, so that the singing of the partridge in the very early morning is a relief for him. chisamutu mukÿkÿi \\ chi-samu-tu mukÿkÿi ti-iyu-tu\\ 3-hear-iam partridge 3i-cry-iam\\ ‘he already heard the partridge singing’ (or: ‘he already heard the partridge that sang’) If the object is not conominated, a difference to relative clauses is notable. summary: Perception verbs rarely take complement clauses in this corpus, with only a few examples involving *-samu* ‘hear’. The text notes that when the shared argument is conominated, the clause may be ambiguous between a complement clause and a relative clause, but when it is not, headless relative clauses are usually marked by a demonstrative, whereas complement clauses are not. However, because the examples are few and some weather-related verbs can behave like nouns, the passage concludes that no firm generalization can be made about the distinction.

text: utterance verb|( The speech verb -kechu ‘say’ can take a CC to report what others have said, i.e. in indirect speech. This is not very common in Paunaka, as speakers clearly prefer to cite directly what others said, i.e. in direct speech. They may also express that something is reported by using the hearsay/reportive markerevidentiality -ji (see ). Nonetheless, indirect speech occurs from time to time. CCs of -kechu are different from all other CCs in that their RSreality status is not predetermined by the construction, but depends on its realisation in relation to the point in time of the original utterance, i.e. the one that is cited. Thus we have irrealis RS in ( ), because at the time Swintha made her statement, the event had not been realised. The example comes from Miguel. He just talked for the sake of the recording, narrating what he was thinking about, and this is why he uses third person markers to refer to Swintha, who was accompanying him. The sentence is about Swintha’s return to Germany. tiyunupunuka Alemania te pero tikechu \\ ti-yunu-punuka Alemania te pero ti-kechu ti-bÿsÿu-pupunuka punachÿ-ina-kena kuje o punachÿ-ina anyo\\ 3i-go-reg.irr Germany seq but 3i-say 3i-come-reg.irr other-irr.nv-uncert month or other-irr.nv year\\ ‘she will go back to Germany, but she said that she would come back, maybe the other month or the other year’ That use of RS depends on the point in time the original utterance was made becomes more clear in ( ). Juana speaks about the past here. The reported event has long been realised by the time she produced the sentence, but not by the time the reported utterance was made. In the meeting she talks about, people of Santa Rita should discuss a proposal of a lady who came to the region, a proposal that they make pasture for her in exchange for her taking charge of construction of the reservoir. i tikechunube \\ i ti-kechu-nube ti-ana-nube reunion\\ and 3i-say-pl 3i-make-pl meeting\\ ‘and she told them to make a meeting’ In the following example, realis RS is used in the CC, which contains another CC, because the statement held at the time the original utterance was made. The frustrative marker is placed on the verb due to Juana’s evaluation of her daughter’s wish to be unrealisable. Juana simply does not want what her daughter wants: accompany her to Europe. Irrealis RS of verb in the second CC is due to its own complement-taking verb, desiderative -sachu (see above). nijinepÿi tikechu ukuinebu ]\\ ni-jinepÿi ti-kechu ukuinebu ti-sachu-ini ti-uma-ne\\ 1sg-daughter 3i-say some.time.ago 3i-want-frust 3i-take.irr-1sg\\ ‘some time ago my daughter said that she wants to take me’ ( ) has indirect speech inside a direct quotation. The example comes from Miguel telling me about his experience in school. His teacher is the one who is cited by using direct speech and in this direct speech Miguel is requested to tell something to his father, namely, that he helps him obtain the things he needs in school. The utterance verb -kechu inside the quoted speech has a third person marker following the stem, which we also find on speech verbs introducing direct speech. This marker marks the verb as ditransitive, and we can thus deduce that the CC can theoretically be indexed on the verb as an argument, but this is by no means obligatory as can be seen in all other examples given in this section. “pikechuchÿji echÿu pia i nebu pisuikia”, tikechu\\ pi-kechu-chÿ-ji echÿu pi-a ti-semaika echÿu yÿkÿke ti-ana taurapachu-mÿnÿ i nebu pi-suik-i-a ti-kechu\\ 2sg-say-3-imp demb 2sg-father 3i-search.irr demb wood 3i-make.irr board-dim and 3obl.top.prn 2sg-write-subord-irr 3i-say\\ ‘“tell your father to look for wood to make a small board and on that one you can write”, he said’ utterance verb|) finite verb|)
summary: The passage explains that the speech verb *-kechu* ‘say’ can introduce indirect speech in Paunaka, though speakers generally prefer direct quotation or the reportive evidential *-ji*. Unlike other complement constructions, the reality status of complements of *-kechu* is not fixed by the construction itself, but depends on the time relation between the reported event and the original utterance, so the complement may be irrealis or realis depending on when the cited statement was made. It also notes that *-kechu* can occur inside direct speech, and that its indexing as an argument is possible but not obligatory.

text: complement verb|( deranked verb|( In addition to unmarked CCs, there are a number of sentences in the corpus that have clausal complements with a deranked verb. The reasons for this may be different. First of all, if a verb that usually takes an unmarked CC is combined with a deranked verb, there may be something unusual involved in the relation between both verbs. In the examples I found in the corpus, this was usually a greater amount of force or control on the subject of the complement verb by the subject of the complement-taking verb. However, many of the examples come from elicitation, so it is not clear how natural this overt marking of the subordinate relation is in general. Consider ( ), in which the complement verb is -niku. This verb can mean both ‘eat’ and ‘feed, give food’, and it might be this ambiguity that led Miguel use a subordinate verb to signal that the interpretation cannot be straightforward (‘I don’t want you to eat it’), but that there is some force implied. Note also that the subordinate verb irregularly takes realis RS. kuina nisacha \\ kuina ni-sacha pi-nik-i-u-chÿ\\ neg 1sg-want.irr 2sg-feed-subord-real-3\\ ‘I don’t want you to make him eat’ ( ), another example elicited from Miguel, has a perception verb, -mumuku ‘look, watch’, combined with a CC containing a deranked verb. In this case, the perception verb does not express mere perception, but rather has the overtone that the subject of the matrix predicate takes care that the subject of the complement verb fulfils the task of reading. nimumuka \\ ni-mumuka chi-chujimeik-i-a\\ 1sg-watch.irr 3-read-subord-irr\\ ‘I take care of her reading’ A similar example is ( ), elicited from María S. The sentence has two CCs: the first one is unmarked, the second one has a deranked verb. summary: The passage explains that, besides unmarked clausal complements, some sentences use complements with deranked verbs, often when the subordinate relation is unusually marked by greater force or control from the matrix subject. Examples show this with verbs of feeding, watching, telling, and ordering, where the deranked form can signal meanings such as coercion, supervision, or an order rather than mere report or perception. It also notes that some verbs appear to require deranked complements, and that there may be variation both by verb and by speaker, though the data are too limited to determine the overall pattern.
