subsection: The use of eka as a complementiser
text: nominal demonstrative|(complementiser|( There are a few cases in which the demonstrative eka seems to be used as a complementiser in CCs containing balanced predicates.finite verb Not every case in which we find eka between a complement-taking predicate and a CC is necessarily a complementiser though, as the demonstrative is also used as a filler in hesitation. All of the examples presented in this section were selected because they do not show signs of hesitation, like repeated starts, pauses, or use of the question word ¿chija? (which is also used as a filler in hesitation), so it is relatively certain that eka really functions as a complementiser there. It may be the case that use of a complementiser is due to influence of Spanish, but comparison with the most closely related languages reveals that in Trinitario,Mojeño Trinitario an article optionally introduces unmarked CCs , while in Baure an article or a demonstrative can introduce CCs with a participle, although this is not obligatory . This does not exclude the possibility that the use of an article or demonstrative in these languages is also due to influence of Spanish, but then again, it is striking that all three languages use a determiner rather than anything else. In Spanish, the complementiser que is identical to the relative pronoun and to the question word for ‘what’. In ( ), both the matrix and the complement verb have a first person subject and the complement verb is intransitive so that there is no argument in the sentence to which eka could refer. Therefore the demonstrative must be analysed as a complementiser belonging to the CC. The sentence is from the story about the fox and the jaguarundi as narrated by Miguel. It is an utterance of the drunken fox. “nÿsachutu ”\\ nÿ-sachu-tu eka nÿ-a-kusunine\\ 1sg-want-iam dema 1sg-irr-sing\\ ‘“I want to sing now”’ The case is less clear in all other examples, since they have third person arguments that the demonstrative could theoretically refer to. Consider ( ), which was elicited from Miguel. The complement verb has a third person subject, so the demonstrative could be analysed to conominate this subject. However, if we compare to the other CCs of desiderative verbs, we find that subject NPs never precede the verb in a CCword order (see ), so that this must be a case of eka being used as a complementiser, too. In addition, if this was a subject in preverbal position, i.e. in a position reserved for arguments with special discourse status, it would be emphasised by intonation, but the opposite is the case. This is also true for the rest of the examples. kuina nÿsumacha \\ kuina nÿ-sumacha eka ti-a-kutiu\\ neg 1sg-want.irr dema 3i-irr-be.ill\\ ‘I don’t want him to get ill’ ( ) was produced by Clara and directed to María C., who is a bit hard of hearing, in order to tell her that Swintha and I already knew that her husband had passed away. tisamuikunube \\ ti-samuiku-nube eka ti-paku eka pi-ima\\ 3i-listen-pl dema 3i-die dema 2sg-husband\\ ‘they heard that your husband is dead’ In ( ), Juana actually had some trouble with wording, but the last part, the CC including the demonstrative, was uttered without hesitation. The sentence expresses what she believed to be the reason for Federico going to Miguel’s daughter’s house, which I had just been telling her before. pensau \\ pensau eka chÿ-ayuraucha\\ think dema 3-help.irr\\ ‘he thought he could help him’ CCs introduced by a demonstrative resemble headless relative clauses a lot. It is then only through context and possibly due to the semantics of the main clause verb that both can be distinguished.complementiser|)nominal demonstrative|)complement relation|) Relative clauses are the topic of the next section.
summary:
The passage argues that in some complement clauses in Mojeño, the demonstrative **eka** functions as a genuine complementiser rather than a discourse filler or demonstrative pronoun. Although some instances are ambiguous, the examples selected lack hesitation markers, and in several cases context and word order show that **eka** cannot refer to an argument and must instead introduce the complement clause.

It also notes that similar determiner-like elements introduce complement clauses in related languages such as Trinitario and Baure, suggesting a broader pattern that may or may not reflect Spanish influence. Finally, complement clauses introduced by a demonstrative are said to resemble headless relative clauses closely, with context and matrix verb semantics helping to distinguish them.

text: relative relation|( A relative clause (RC) “provides some kind of specification about a participant” of the main clause with the aim of identifying this participant . Paunaka uses different means to express this kind of specification. This depends partly on whether the RC is headedhead|( or headless and partly on the role the relativised item has in the RC. A headed RC is one which relates to an NPnoun phrase in the main clause. Most of these headed RCs are completely unmarked in Paunaka, i.e. they are asyndeticallysyndesis/asyndesis juxtaposedjuxtaposition to the NP they modify. The modifiedmodification NP is usually the last constituent in the main clause. This being the case, an RC is formally not distinguishable from an asyndetically coordinated clausecoordination (see ). It is only a matter of semantic relation between the two clauses: if one clause modifies the NPnoun phrase to which it is juxtaposed,juxtaposition it can be analysed as an RC, and if no modification is involved, we rather deal with coordination (or possibly with unmarked subordination including an adverbial relation). ( ) is an unmarked RC whose head is pedasitokena ‘(possible) little bits and pieces’ (from Spanish pedacito and including the uncertainty marker -kena). The sentence comes from Miguel telling a tale about ants, which are happy when a man goes to his field and eats his provisions there. kakukena echÿu pedasitokena \\ kaku-kena echÿu pedasito-kena ti-bÿkupu apuke\\ exist-uncert demb piece.dim-uncert 3i-fall ground\\ ‘maybe there are crumbles that fall down’ head|) Headless RCs are those in which no NP conominatesconomination an argument of the main clause – remember that Paunaka uses person indexes to encode arguments of a verb and that co-occurrence of NPs is optional. In this case, the RC becomes the conominal itself. In contrast to headed RCs, headless RCs are usually introduced by a demonstrative,syndesis/asyndesisnominal demonstrative|( predominantly echÿu ‘demb’, but also eka ‘dema’. These demonstratives act as relative pronouns.pronoun The predicate of the RC is balanced,finite verb i.e. there is no sign of dependency on the predicate itself. ( ) illustrates this. There is no noun in the main clause which could be modified by the RCs here, and there is no sign of dependency on the verbs, but nonetheless the demonstrative eka is placed before them. The sentences was produced by Juana, who was speaking about different breeds of chicken. kuina tinijanea , tinijaneu entero amuke\\ kuina ti-ni-jane-a eka ti-kipÿpa-na-ji eka ti-si-na ti-pisÿ-na ti-ni-jane-u entero amuke\\ neg 3i-eat-distr-irr dema 3i-be.white- -col dema 3i-be.red- 3i-be.black- 3i-eat-distr-real whole corn\\ ‘the white ones don’t eat it, the red and black ones eat the whole corn kernels (i.e. without crushing them)’ demonstrative|) These two types of RCs just described can be considered the major ones. They have in common that they build on a balanced verbfinite verb and primarily apply to relativisation of Ssubject and Oobject arguments whose role in the main clause is also S or O. For the sake of simplicity, roles in stative non-verbal predication are subsumed under the label S here. The role A is much rarer in both main and relative clauses. The shared argument may also function as a possessor in the main clause, but not in the RC. I have not found any example in which it has the role of an oblique in the main clause, and in the RC, this is bound to relativisation of the indefinite pronoun juchubu ‘somewhere’. In addition to the RCs with balanced verbs, there is a third type of RC which is also relatively frequent and builds on a deranked verb. This type is majorly found with relativisation of obliques,oblique but also with objects.object Inside the main clause, the relativised item can have the same roles as the other kinds of RCs, and additionally oblique roles are found. The roles of the relativised item in the main clause and in the RC are summarised in , where the first two types are subsumed under one, because they are similar as to which roles are accessible to relativisation. The correspondence between type of predicate used and role of the relativised item in the RC is in line with the relative deranking hierarchyderanked verb in , which claims that deranked verbs rather occur on the right-hand side of the hierarchy. I proceed as in the previous sections from most unmarked to most marked clauses. Unmarked RCs are described in . They are usually headed, but a few examples of unmarked headless RCs have been found as well. In those RCs introduced by a demonstrative are presented. Most of them are headless, but some headed ones have also shown up in the corpus. RCs with deranked predicates are described in . Subsequently, a discussion on cleft constructions in completes this section. All RCs are given in square brackets in this section.
summary:
Paunaka relative clauses specify a participant in the main clause and can be headed or headless, with their form depending on whether they are linked to an NP and on the grammatical role of the relativised item. Most headed relative clauses are unmarked and simply juxtaposed to the modified NP, while headless relative clauses are usually introduced by a demonstrative such as *echÿu* or *eka*, which functions like a relative pronoun.

The main types of relative clauses are built with balanced verbs and mainly relativise S and O arguments, though a third, more frequent type uses a deranked verb and is especially common for oblique relativisation. The passage also notes that relative clauses may be hard to distinguish formally from coordination, so their analysis depends largely on the semantic relation between the clauses.

text: head|( juxtaposition|( RCs can be completely unmarked in Paunaka, a characteristic it shares with MojeñoMojeño languages ( ; ). By unmarked I refer to the fact that there is no syntactic or morphological hint at all that sets these clauses apart from independent clauses, although the RC and the main clause are uttered in one intonation unit. This has been argued to be “an early form of embedding” .embedding Unmarked RCs are usually headed. The head noun is the last constituent of the main clause and the RC follows. All RCs given in this section could alternatively also be analysed as asyndetically coordinated clauses,coordination but semantically they encode a relative relation, i.e. they help to identify a participant by providing some specification about this participant . However, there are cases in which it is not clear whether a juxtaposed clause is meant to provide specification or to develop the storyline. I will come back to these cases later in this section. I have not found any example in which an unmarked RC was independently negated,negation but cases of individual negation of marked RCs occur (see below). It might be the case that negation demands a more explicit strategy of RC marking. To start with, consider ( ). The head noun jimu ‘fish’ is the object of the main clause and its last constituent. The RC follows. It only consists of one verb tiyÿbapakubu ‘it is ground’. The relativised noun is the subject of this verb, and the verb ascribes a property to it, the property of being ground. Possible reference is thus restricted to ground fish. The sentence was produced by Clara, when asked what she did with fish after grinding them. Note that the middle marker on the verb for ‘cook’ is missing here for an unknown reason. This is indicated by the index “OMC/SRC” above the Paunaka sentence, where the letter with the MC subscript stands for its role in the main clause, the letter with RC subscript for its role in the RC. The relativised noun is not repeated in the RC nor is there any resumptive pronoun or other independent word relating to it. We can thus state that Paunaka uses a gapping strategy in RCs as far as one can speak of a “gap” at all in relation to a language that indexes its arguments on the verb. The verb in the RC is fully inflectedinflection for its arguments and for RS.reality status Backed by this description of the general characteristics of the unmarked RC, we can have a look at some more examples. An analysis favouring an RC over a coordinated clause is relatively clear whenever the clause ascribes some property to the head noun. Paunaka has few adjectives, and many properties are expressed by stative verbs that are juxtaposed to the noun they modify, thus in an RC. ( ) and ( ) are two examples of this. summary: Paunaka allows completely unmarked relative clauses, with no syntactic or morphological marker distinguishing them from independent clauses, though they are typically pronounced in one intonation unit and usually follow a head noun at the end of the main clause. These clauses often function to identify a participant by attributing a property to it, especially through stative or nominal predicates, and in such cases they are easy to analyze as relatives rather than coordinated clauses. However, when the second clause describes an event rather than a property, it becomes harder to tell whether it is a relative clause or asyndetic coordination; the text also notes that independent negation of unmarked relative clauses was not found.

summary:
The passage argues that many juxtaposed clauses in Paunaka are best analyzed as relative clauses when they serve to identify a noun in the other clause, especially if they specify how, where, or what something is. It also notes that such clauses can sometimes refer back to an earlier point in the discourse timeline, but when no such temporal switch occurs, a juxtaposed clause may instead be interpreted as either a relative clause or an independent coordinated clause.

The data show that relativization is common from S and O positions, though one example may involve A, and that relative clauses are consistently postnominal. Most RCs are completely unmarked and usually follow the whole main clause, though one example directly follows its head noun, and a few unmarked headless relative clauses are also mentioned.

summary: The passage explains that many nouns beginning with /t/ may actually have originated from stative verbs in headless relative clauses, and some are now so conventionalized that they function like noun phrases without an overt noun. These headless relative clauses are normally introduced by a demonstrative, though in some cases the demonstrative is dropped, especially when the construction has become fixed or when the relativized item is indefinite.

summary: Relative clauses in this language can be introduced by the demonstratives *eka* or *echÿu*, with *echÿu* more common; they may be headed, but are usually headless. The demonstrative belongs to the relative clause rather than the main clause, and the clause can relativize S, O, or occasionally A roles, with headless relative clauses often functioning as noun phrases on their own.

summary: The passage explains that Paunaka relative clauses can appear in several forms: as equative clauses where a head plus relative clause is identified with another entity, and as headless relative clauses introduced by a demonstrative. In the examples discussed, the relativized element is usually an S, O, or A role, though one hesitant example suggests an oblique relative clause; in such cases, speakers seem to prefer a deranked verb. The author concludes that unmarked headed relative clauses and demonstrative-introduced headless relative clauses are the most common types in Paunaka.

Most RCs with deranked verbs are actually part of cleft constructions, but in this section some examples which do not contain clefts are discussed. For clefts containing RCs with deranked verbs see . ( ) is the result of Miguel and Juana looking for an expression for ‘hostel’ that does not contain a Spanish loan. Swintha had asked for a sentence to tell them that she would go back to her hostel. A pause occurred between the adverb nauku and the subordinate verb, marked by a comma in the example. It is thus not entirely clear whether nauku can be analysed as the head of the RC or whether the RC should be analysed as headless and simply added to the main clause as an alternative, more explicit expression for the place. In any case, the relativised item has locative function in the RC. summary: The passage describes relative clauses built on deranked verbs, especially when the relativised element is an oblique, though they sometimes also occur with objects. Many of the examples are part of cleft constructions or are otherwise ambiguous, and the author notes that in several cases it is unclear whether the structure should be analysed as a headed relative clause, a headless relative clause, or even an adverbial clause.

text: cleft|( A cleft construction is usually defined as “a complex sentence structure consisting of a matrix clause headed by a copula and a relative or relative-like clause whose relativized argument is coindexed with the predicative argument of the copula. Taken together, the matrix and the relative express a logically simple proposition, which can also be expressed in the form of a single clause without a change in truth conditions” .copula|( This definition is problematic for Paunaka insofar as the clauses analysed here as clefts do not contain a copula. copula|) They could thus only be defined as clefts by a broad definition, such as the one proposed by that clefts are “biclausal focus constructions”.focus This is also in line with what identifies as the primary, defining property of clefts, that they express “a single proposition via bi-clausal syntax”. As for their biclausal status, let us consider one example: ( ) is from an account of María S. about her childhood. The family lived by subsistence farming, but food was sometimes scarce, so their mother also harvested leaves of wild plants that were mashed together with peanuts and then cooked in a stew. nÿenubane \\ nÿ-enu-bane echÿu chi-yejiku\\ 1sg-mother-rem demb 3-tear.out\\ ‘it was my late mother who tore them out (i.e. harvested the leaves of a plant)’ nominal demonstrative|(The verbal predicate of the RC is chiyejiku ‘she tears them out’. If this were a monoclausal sentence, the verb would have to be analysed as the predicate of the main clause, but in that case there would be two arguments preceding it: nÿenubane ‘my late mother’ and the demonstrative echÿu. Paunaka, however, has only one preverbal slot (see ). SVO orderword order is relatively frequent, OVS is (almost) absent and SOV is not allowed at all, and we must therefore assume that sentences like ( ) consist of two clauses, the matrix clause which only contains one noun in this case and a juxtaposed RC consisting of a demonstrative and a balanced verb,finite verb a pattern we usually find in headless RCs in which the relativised item has the role of S,O or A (see ).nominal demonstrative|) Clefts are often believed to be associated with focus,focus but reject this, since the positions of given and new information in the cleft are not fixed (depending on the type of cleft). Looking at clefts in context, they identify four distinctive features of clefts: “uniqueness, stativising, presupposition, and separate information structure” . All of these discourse features hold for the Paunaka cleft construction. The cleft construction can be analysed as a subcategory of equative or proper-inclusion clausesequative/proper inclusion clause in Paunaka (see ), the difference being that instead of a noun they take an RC as predicate and this predicate usually follows rather than precedes the subject.word order It is thus clearly a stative construction. Uniqueness is also given, since the clefted constituent is interpreted to be the only one to which the predication of the RC applies. Thus, in ( ) above, it is only the mother who harvested the leaves. In ( ), the uniqueness is even expressed lexically. The example is about fish. Swintha had found a dried piranha at the shore of the big water reservoir of Concepción, and she showed it to Clara and María C., wondering which kind of piranha that was, since there are different classes of piranhas. However, Clara first claimed with ( ) that there was only one class of piranhas. (María C. subsequently corrected her and explained to us that there are indeed different classes of piranha, which have different colours.) porke echÿu chinajiku \\ porke echÿu china-jiku echÿu ti-nijabai-jane micha\\ because demb one-lim1 demb 3i-bite-distr good\\ ‘because it is only these ones that bite hard’ The order of clefted constituent and RC can also be reversed, but this is very rare. One example is ( ), which was produced by Miguel when talking with Juan C. about the past. The clefted constituent is used to identify their teacher, Mother Trinidad. madre Trinidad, chibu\\ echÿu ti-mesumeiku-bane naka turno uneku-yae madre Trinidad chibu\\ demb 3i-teach-rem here shift town-loc Mother Trinidad 3top.prn\\ ‘the one who taught that school year here in town was Mother Trinidad, it was her’ Presupposition in cleft clauses is about the predication of the RC being factitive, i.e. in ( ) it is presupposed that there are some fish that bite well, in ( ) there is someone who harvests leaves, and in ( ) there is someone who taught in school. As for the “separate information structure”, propose that clefts always encode some new information, but never encode all new information. Their function then is “to make special and specific links with the preceding discourse”. Just like in English it-clefts, the clefted constituent in Paunaka can encode old or new information. ( ) and ( ) both are examples of “topic clause clefts”,topic in which the clefted constituent encodes the new information. In ( ), what is new is rather the relation between the given information in the clefted constituent and the juxtaposed NP, which also denotes a known participant. This is an example of a “comment cleft clause” . I will present some more examples of comment clause clefts below, in which the information in the clefted constituent is given. In this type of clefts, Paunaka speakers often make use of the topic pronountopic pronoun|( chibu. Just like in ( ), the new information is the relation of the given participant with a predication whose content may also be given or may be new. One example is ( ), which is about the scarcity of food. María C. had just listed names of different fruits and vegetables that they grow, which is what chibu refers to. chibu , kuina chÿecheina\\ chibu echÿu bi-nika kuina chÿeche-ina\\ 3top.prn demb 1pl-eat.irr neg meat-irr.nv\\ ‘this is what we can eat, there is no meat’ Like in ( ), the clefted constituent in these “chibu cleft constructions” is typically the object of the relative clause, but
summary: Paunaka cleft constructions are biclausal focus-like structures even though they lack an overt copula, so they can only be called clefts under a broad definition. The passage argues that they pattern with clefts because they express a single proposition through two clauses and show the discourse properties of uniqueness, stativizing meaning, presupposition, and separate information structure. It also notes that the clefted constituent may be old or new information, and that the order of the clefted constituent and relative clause can occasionally be reversed.

summary: The passage describes Paunaka constructions with balanced and deranked verbs that resemble clefts, especially when a demonstrative introduces the relative clause and two elements are equated, such as a person who will write the language or the place someone climbs. It notes that oblique relativized items can be introduced by topic pronouns like *nebu*, and that some examples lack a demonstrative, making their biclausal status less clear. The author concludes that while some cases can still be analyzed as clefts, others move away from canonical cleft structure and may be monoclausal.

text: focus|( oblique|( In the construction described in this section, an adverb, a quantifier or a noun that has oblique function in the clause precedes a deranked verb.word order There is no other verb in the clause. This construction is mainly used to shift focus from the predicate to the adverbial expression. Consider ( ), in which the locative adverb naka ‘here’ precedes the verb marked by the subordinate suffix -i. Why do we have a deranked verb in a sentence like ( ) above? This has to do with information structure and with the kind of predication intended by the speaker. This construction has the same identifying features as cleft constructions: “uniqueness, stativising, presupposition, and separate information structure” . The aspect of stativising is particularly interesting. Prototypically, predication in a sentence is achieved by a verb, and verbs prototypically denote processes . By predicating one process after another a piece of discourse develops in time and space. However, sometimes predication is not meant to be about a process, but rather about properties or characteristics of this process. In this case, just like in subordination, “verb forms are not used in their prototypical cognitive or discourse function” . This is where deranked verbs come into play. Deranked verbs have both verbal and nominal properties. They are considerably less finite than the verb forms we find in “normal” declarative sentences (see ). Nounsnoun are more time-stable than verbs , i.e. they are less dynamic, and they are cognitively processed as a whole rather than sequentially , just like the deranked verbs in the construction here. The process per se loses prominence in the predication. It is the relation between one entity and the process what predication is about. The process encoded by the deranked verb is thus not perceived dynamically but statively, and the development of discourse is stopped for a little while. The construction is then best analysed as a special form of equative clause,equative/proper inclusion clause in which a circumstance is related to a process as a whole. A locative adverb is often combined with a deranked verb to relate a place to a sequence in the life cycle, i.e. to a process that is mostly of a longer duration and in any case meaningful for the development of the individual being. The passage describes a construction in which a preposed adverb, quantifier, or oblique noun appears before a deranked verb and no other verb is present, mainly to shift focus from the predicate to the adverbial element. It argues that this construction resembles a cleft and should be analyzed as a special equative clause: the deranked verb presents the process statively, so the sentence relates a circumstance such as a place to a meaningful or prolonged process rather than to a dynamic event.

It further notes that locative adverbs are especially common in this pattern when the place is important to a person’s life history or development, whereas shorter or more incidental location relations normally do not take a deranked verb. The text also says that temporal/aspectual adverbs like metu ‘already, ready’ can function in a similar way.

summary:
The passage argues that Paunaka deranked verbs contribute a stative interpretation of the event, often presenting the process as finished rather than ongoing. It also shows that adverbs, nouns, and preposed oblique expressions can occur before a deranked verb to highlight that constituent, similar to fronting or left dislocation, while the deranked verb de-emphasizes the process itself.

In discourse, this construction is used to stress topics such as completion, duration, location, or manner, as in examples meaning ‘already speak,’ ‘had already buried him,’ or ‘by foot they went.’ Overall, the common effect of these constructions is to draw attention to what comes before the deranked verb and to construe the predication as stative.
